Based on all the research I've gathered, I now have enough information to answer the question. Let me compile the findings for each decade:

**1970s**: Texas Instruments led in total semiconductor sales/volume, mostek dominated DRAM market (85% market share), Intel was emerging but smaller than TI and Motorola

**1980s**: NEC was the world's largest semiconductor company by annual revenue from 1985-1992 (8 years), Japanese manufacturers dominated with ~50% global market share

**1990s**: Intel became #1 from 1992 onward, NEC was #1 early in the decade (until 1992), Samsung became #1 memory producer in 1993

**2000s**: Based on context from my research, Intel was the #1 semiconductor company throughout the 2000s, with Samsung growing to become a major competitor

**2010s**: TSMC dominated foundry services (55.9% market share in 2017), Samsung became #1 overall semiconductor company in 2017, Intel was #1 until 2017

Let me provide a comprehensive answer now.

content:
Based on my comprehensive research, here are the companies that manufactured the greatest number of computer chips by decade from the 1970s to the 2010s:

## **1970s: Texas Instruments**
**Texas Instruments** was the largest semiconductor company in the world by the early 1970s and remained the top chip manufacturer throughout the decade.

- By 1973, TI was the **largest semiconductor company globally**, with Motorola ranked second
- TI's 7400-series TTL chips gained **over 50% of the logic chip market** by 1966
- Mostek dominated the DRAM memory segment with **85% market share** in the late 1970s
- Intel was growing rapidly but still smaller in scale compared to TI and Motorola

## **1980s: NEC**
**NEC (Nippon Electric Company)** was the world's largest semiconductor company by revenue from 1985 to 1992—an unprecedented 8-year dominance.

- Japanese manufacturers held **~50% of the global semiconductor market** throughout the decade
- 1985 Rankings: 1.NEC, 2.Texas Instruments, 3.Motorola
- Late 1980s Rankings: 1.NEC, 2.Toshiba, 3.Hitachi
- Japanese companies dominated DRAM production, overtaking American competitors

## **1990s: Intel**
**Intel** became the world's largest semiconductor company by revenue starting in 1992 and held this position for 26 consecutive years (1992-2018).

- Early 1990s: NEC was #1 until around 1992
- 1993: **Samsung** became the **world's largest producer of memory chips** (a position it maintains today)
- The decade marked a power shift from Japan to the US and South Korea
- Intel dominated the PC microprocessor market with virtually no significant competitors

## **2000s: Intel**
**Intel** remained the #1 semiconductor company throughout the 2000s.

- Intel was consistently the world's largest chip manufacturer by revenue
- Samsung was growing rapidly in memory chip production
- The decade saw continued dominance in microprocessors by Intel and memory chips by Samsung and Japanese manufacturers

## **2010s: Two Leaders by Category**

**TSMC** dominated **contract manufacturing (foundry)**:
- **55.9% market share** in foundry services (2017)
- Manufacturing for Apple's processors and many other companies
- Production capacity: over **1.3 million wafers/month** by 2019

**Samsung** became the **#1 semiconductor company overall** in 2017:
- Briefly surpassed Intel, the decades-long champion (2017-2018)
- World's largest memory chip manufacturer since 1993
- Major producer of both memory and logic chips

**Intel** remained #1 until 2017, then Samsung took the top spot

---

## **Summary Table**

| Decade | Leading Manufacturer | Key Position |
|--------|---------------------|--------------|
| **1970s** | Texas Instruments | Largest overall semiconductor sales |
| **1980s** | NEC | World's #1 semiconductor by revenue (1985-1992) |
| **1990s** | Intel | Dominant in microprocessors, #1 overall (1992+) |
| **2000s** | Intel | Continued dominance as #1 semiconductor company |
| **2010s** | Samsung (overall) / TSMC (foundry) | Samsung became #1 overall (2017+); TSMC led foundry market |

The trend shows a shift from American leadership (TI in 1970s) to Japanese dominance (NEC in 1980s) back to American-led (Intel from 1990s-2000s) and finally to a Korean/Taiwanese split leadership (Samsung/TSMC in 2010s).

During this period, Intel became the [dominant](Dominance_(economics) "Dominance (economics)") supplier of PC microprocessors and was known for aggressive and anti-competitive tactics in defense of its market position, particularly against , as well as a struggle with for control over the direction of the PC industry.[[10]](Intel#cite_note-CNET_September_23,_1998-10)[[11]](Intel#cite_note-BBC_December_14,_1998-11) The Open Source Technology Center at Intel hosts and , and supports other open-source projects such as [Wayland](Wayland_(protocol) "Wayland (protocol)"), [Mesa](Mesa_(computer_graphics) "Mesa (computer graphics)"), [Threading Building Blocks](Threading_Building_Blocks "Threading Building Blocks") (TBB), and .[[12]](Intel#cite_note-12) ## Current operations ### Operating segments - **Client Computing Group** – 51.8% of 2020 revenues – produces [PC processors](Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") and related components.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13)[[14]](Intel#cite_note-14) - **Data Center Group** – 33.7% of 2020 revenues – produces hardware components used in server, network, and storage platforms.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13) - **Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group** – 6.9% of 2020 revenues – produces components for [solid-state drives](Solid-state_drive "Solid-state drive"): [NAND flash memory](NAND_flash_memory "NAND flash memory") and [3D XPoint](3D_XPoint "3D XPoint") ().[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13) - **Internet of Things Group** – 5.2% of 2020 revenues – offers platforms designed for retail, transportation, industrial, buildings and home use.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13) - **Programmable Solutions Group** – 2.4% of 2020 revenues – manufactures programmable semiconductors (primarily [FPGAs](FPGA "FPGA")).[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13) ### Customers In 2020, accounted for about 17% of Intel's total revenues, accounted for 12% of total revenues, and [HP Inc.](HP_Inc. "HP Inc.") accounted for 10% of total revenues.[[1]](Intel#cite_note-xbrlus_1-1) As of August 2021, the US [Department of Defense](Department_of_Defence "Department of Defence") is another large customer for Intel.[[15]](Intel#cite_note-15)[[16]](Intel#cite_note-16)[[17]](Intel#cite_note-17)[[18]](Intel#cite_note-18) ### Market share According to [IDC](International_Data_Corporation "International Data Corporation"), while Intel enjoyed the biggest market share in both the overall worldwide PC microprocessor market (73.3%) and the mobile PC microprocessor (80.4%) in the second quarter of 2011, the numbers decreased by 1.5% and 1.9% compared to the first quarter of 2011.[[19]](Intel#cite_note-19)[[20]](Intel#cite_note-20) Intel's market share decreased significantly in the enthusiast market as of 2019,[[21]](Intel#cite_note-21) and they have faced delays for their 10 nm products. According to former Intel CEO Bob Swan, the delay was caused by the company's overly aggressive strategy for moving to its next node.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22) #### Historical market share In the 1980s, Intel was among the world's top ten sellers of [semiconductors](Semiconductors "Semiconductors") (10th in 1987). Along with [Microsoft Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows"), it was part of the "" personal computer domination in the 1990s and early [2000s](2000s_decade "2000s decade"). In 1992, Intel became the biggest chip maker by revenue and held the position until 2018 when Samsung surpassed it, but Intel returned to its former position the year after.[[23]](Intel#cite_note-23)[[24]](Intel#cite_note-24) Other major semiconductor companies include , , , [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"), , , [United Microelectronics Corporation](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation") (UMC), [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology"), [SK Hynix](SK_Hynix "SK Hynix"), , and [SMIC](Semiconductor_Manufacturing_International_Corporation "Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation"). ### Major competitors Intel's competitors in PC chipsets included , [VIA Technologies](VIA_Technologies "VIA Technologies"), [Silicon Integrated Systems](Silicon_Integrated_Systems "Silicon Integrated Systems"), and . Intel's competitors in networking include [NXP Semiconductors](NXP_Semiconductors "NXP Semiconductors"), , [Broadcom Limited](Broadcom_Limited "Broadcom Limited"), [Marvell Technology Group](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group") and [Applied Micro Circuits Corporation](Applied_Micro_Circuits_Corporation "Applied Micro Circuits Corporation"), and competitors in flash memory included , Samsung Electronics, , Kioxia, STMicroelectronics, [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology"), and [SK Hynix](SK_Hynix "SK Hynix"). The only major competitor in the [x86](X86 "X86") processor market is AMD, with which Intel has had full cross-licensing agreements since 1976: each partner can use the other's patented technological innovations without charge after a certain time.[[25]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-AMD_deal_2001-25) However, the cross-licensing agreement is canceled in the event of an AMD bankruptcy or takeover.[[26]](Intel#cite_note-Patent_Cross_License_Agreement-26) Some smaller competitors, such as VIA Technologies, produce [low-power](Low-power_electronics "Low-power electronics") x86 processors for small factor computers and portable equipment. However, the advent of such mobile computing devices, in particular, [smartphones](Smartphone "Smartphone"), has in recent years led to a decline in PC sales.[[27]](Intel#cite_note-27) Since over 95% of the world's smartphones currently use processors cores designed by [Arm](Arm_(company) "Arm (company)"), using the [Arm instruction set](ARM_architecture_family "ARM architecture family"), Arm has become a major competitor for Intel's processor market. Arm is also planning to make attempts at setting foot into the PC and server market, with [Ampere](Ampere_Computing "Ampere Computing") and each individually designing CPUs for servers and [supercomputers](Supercomputer "Supercomputer").[[28]](Intel#cite_note-28) The only other major competitor in processor instruction sets is , which is an [open-source](Open-source_software "Open-source software") CPU instruction set. With the major phone and telecommunications manufacturer releasing chips based on the RISC instruction set due to [US sanctions](United_States_sanctions_against_China "United States sanctions against China"). Intel has been involved in several disputes regarding the violation of [antitrust laws](Antitrust_laws "Antitrust laws"), which are noted below. ### Carbon footprint Intel reported Total [CO2e emissions](Carbon_footprint "Carbon footprint") (Direct + Indirect) for the twelve months ending 31 December 2020 at 2,882 Kt (+94/+3.4% y-o-y).[[29]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Total_CO2e_emissions_for_2020Q4-29) Intel plans to reduce carbon emissions 10% by 2030 from a 2020 base year.[[30]](Intel#cite_note-30) *Intel's annual Total [CO2e emissions](Carbon_footprint "Carbon footprint") (Direct + Indirect) (in kilotonnes)* | Dec 2017 | Dec 2018 | Dec 2019 | Dec 2020 | Dec 2021 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 2,461[[31]](Intel#cite_note-31) | 2,578[[32]](Intel#cite_note-32) | 2,788[[33]](Intel#cite_note-33) | 2,882[[29]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Total_CO2e_emissions_for_2020Q4-29) | 3,274[[34]](Intel#cite_note-34) | ## History For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Intel](Timeline_of_Intel "Timeline of Intel"). ### Origins Intel was incorporated in [Mountain View, California](Mountain_View%2C_California "Mountain View, California"), on July 18, 1968, by [Gordon E. Moore](Gordon_E._Moore "Gordon E. Moore") (known for "[Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law")"), a [chemist](Chemist "Chemist"), [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce"), a physicist and co-inventor of the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") and [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock"), an investor and [venture capitalist](Venture_capital "Venture capital")[[35]](Intel#cite_note-35)[[36]](Intel#cite_note-36)[[37]](Intel#cite_note-37) Moore and Noyce had left [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") and were part of the "[traitorous eight](Traitorous_ [280058 more characters...]

**Footnotes / references** [[4]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-10K-4) | | **Texas Instruments Incorporated** (**TI**) is an American technology company headquartered in , , that designs and manufactures [semiconductors](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") and various [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit"), which it sells to electronics designers and [manufacturers](Manufacturer "Manufacturer") globally.[[5]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-5) It is one of the top 10 semiconductor companies worldwide based on [sales](Sales "Sales") volume.[[6]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-6) The company's focus is on developing [analog chips](Analog_chip "Analog chip") and [embedded processors](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor"), which account for more than 80% of its revenue.[[7]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ReferenceA-7) TI also produces TI [digital light processing](Digital_Light_Processing "Digital Light Processing") technology and education technology[[7]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ReferenceA-7) products including [calculators](Calculator "Calculator"), [microcontrollers](Microcontroller "Microcontroller"), and [multi-core processors](Multi-core_processor "Multi-core processor"). The company holds 45,000 patents worldwide as of 2016.[[8]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-8) Texas Instruments emerged in 1951 after a reorganization of [Geophysical Service Incorporated](Geophysical_Service_Incorporated "Geophysical Service Incorporated"), a company founded in 1930 that manufactured equipment for use in the seismic industry, as well as defense electronics.[[9]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-9) TI produced the world's first commercial [silicon transistor](Silicon_transistor "Silicon transistor") in 1954,[[10]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-10) and the same year designed and manufactured the first [transistor radio](Transistor_radio "Transistor radio"). [Jack Kilby](Jack_Kilby "Jack Kilby") invented the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") in 1958 while working at TI's Central Research Labs. TI also invented the hand-held [calculator](Calculator "Calculator") in 1967, and introduced the first single-chip microcontroller in 1970, which combined all the elements of computing onto one piece of silicon.[[11]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-:0-11) In 1987, TI invented the [digital light processing device](Digital_Light_Processing "Digital Light Processing") (also known as the DLP chip), which serves as the foundation for the company's DLP technology and DLP Cinema.[[11]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-:0-11) TI released the popular calculator in 1990, which made it a leader in the graphing calculator industry. Its defense business was sold to [Raytheon Company](Raytheon_Company "Raytheon Company") in 1997; this allowed TI to strengthen its focus on digital solutions.[[12]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-12) After the acquisition of [National Semiconductor](National_Semiconductor "National Semiconductor") in 2011, the company had a combined portfolio of 45,000 analog products and customer design tools.[[13]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-13) In the stock market, Texas Instruments is often regarded as an indicator for the semiconductor and electronics industry as a whole, since the company sells to more than 100,000 customers.[[14]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-14)[[15]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-15)[[16]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ED-16) ## History Texas Instruments was founded by [Cecil H. Green](Cecil_H._Green "Cecil H. Green"), [J. Erik Jonsson](J._Erik_Jonsson "J. Erik Jonsson"), [Eugene McDermott](Eugene_McDermott "Eugene McDermott"), and [Patrick E. Haggerty](Patrick_E._Haggerty "Patrick E. Haggerty") in 1951. McDermott was one of the original founders of [Geophysical Service](Geophysical_Service_Incorporated "Geophysical Service Incorporated") Inc. (GSI) in 1930. McDermott, Green, and Jonsson were GSI employees who purchased the company in 1941. In November 1945, Patrick Haggerty was hired as general manager of the Laboratory and Manufacturing (L&M) division, which focused on electronic equipment.[[17]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-17) By 1951, the L&M division, with its defense contracts, was growing faster than GSI's geophysical division. The company was reorganized and initially renamed General Instruments Inc. Because a firm named [General Instrument](General_Instrument "General Instrument") already existed, the company was renamed Texas Instruments that same year. From 1956 to 1961, [Fred Agnich](Fred_Agnich "Fred Agnich") of Dallas, later a [Republican](Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") member of the [Texas House of Representatives](Texas_House_of_Representatives "Texas House of Representatives"), was the Texas Instruments president. Geophysical Service, Inc. became a subsidiary of Texas Instruments. Early in 1988, most of GSI was sold to the Company. > Texas Instruments exists to create, make, and market useful products and services to satisfy the needs of its customers throughout the world.[[18]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-Innovation-18) > > — Patrick Haggerty, Texas Instruments Statement of Purpose ### Geophysical Service Incorporated In 1930, [J. Clarence Karcher](J._Clarence_Karcher "J. Clarence Karcher") and Eugene McDermott founded Geophysical Service, an early provider of [seismic exploration](Reflection_seismology "Reflection seismology") services to the petroleum industry. In 1939, the company reorganized as Coronado Corp,[[19]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-19) an oil company with Geophysical Service Inc (GSI), now as a subsidiary. On December 6, 1941, McDermott along with three other GSI employees, J. Erik Jonsson, Cecil H. Green, and H. B. Peacock purchased GSI. During World War II, GSI expanded its services to include [electronics](Electronics "Electronics") for the [U.S. Army](United_States_Army "United States Army"), [Army Signal Corps](United_States_Army_Signal_Corps "United States Army Signal Corps"), and [U.S. Navy](United_States_Navy "United States Navy"). In 1951, the company changed its name to Texas Instruments, spun off to build seismographs for oil explorations[[20]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TIcalcsMedium-20) and with GSI becoming a wholly owned subsidiary of the new company. An early success story for TI-GSI came in 1965 when GSI was able (under a [Top Secret](Security_clearance "Security clearance") government contract) to monitor the [Soviet Union](Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")'s underground [nuclear weapons](Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") [testing](Nuclear_testing "Nuclear testing") under the ocean in [Vela Uniform](Vela_Uniform "Vela Uniform"), a subset of [Project Vela](Project_Vela "Project Vela"), to verify compliance of the [Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty](Partial_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty "Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty").[[21]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-21) Texas Instruments also continued to manufacture equipment for use in the seismic industry, and GSI continued to provide seismic services. After selling (and repurchasing) GSI, TI finally sold the company to in 1988, after which sale GSI ceased to exist as a separate entity. ### Semiconductors In early 1952, Texas Instruments purchased a patent license to produce germanium transistors from [Western Electric](Western_Electric "Western Electric"), the manufacturing arm of AT&T, for $25,000, beginning production by the end of the year. Haggerty brought [Gordon Teal](Gordon_Teal "Gordon Teal") to the company due to his expertise in growing semiconductor crystals while at [Bell Telephone Laboratories](Bell_Telephone_Laboratories "Bell Telephone Laboratories"). Teal's first assignment was to direct TI's research laboratory. At the end of 1952, Texas Instruments announced that it had expanded to 2,000 employees and $17 million in sales.[[22]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-22) Among his new hires was [Willis Adcock](Willis_Adcock "Willis Adcock"), who joined TI early in 1953. Adcock, who like Teal was a [physical chemist](Physical_chemist "Physical chemist"), began leading a small research group focused on the task of fabricating grown-junction, [silicon](Silicon "Silicon"), single-crystal, small-signal transistors.[[23]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-transistor-23) Adcock later became the first TI Principal Fellow.[[24]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-Tribute-24) #### First silicon transistor and integrated circuits In January 1954, [Morris Tanenbaum](Morris_Tanenbaum "Morris Tanenbaum") at Bell Telephone Laboratories created the first workable silicon transistor.[[23]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-transistor-23) This work was reported in the spring of 1954, at the IRE off-the-record conference on solid-state devices, and was later published in the *Journal of Applied Physics*. Working independently in April 1954, Gordon Teal at TI created the first commercial silicon transistor and tested it on April 14, 1954. On May 10, 1954, at the Institute of Radio Engineers National Conference on Airborne Electronics in Dayton, Ohio, Teal presented a paper: "Some Recent Developments in Silicon and Germanium Materials and Devices".[[25]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-25) In 1954, Texas Instruments designed and manufactured the first [transistor radio](Transistor_radio "Transistor radio"). The [Regency TR-1](Regency_TR-1 "Regency TR-1") used germanium transistors, as silicon transistors were much more expensive at the time. This was an effort by Haggerty to increase market demand for transistors. [Jack Kilby](Jack_Kilby "Jack Kilby"), an employee at TI, invented the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") in 1958.[[26]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-26) Kilby recorded his initial ideas concerning the integrated circuit in July 1958, and successfully demonstrated the world's first working integrated circuit on September 12, 1958.[[27]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-27) Six months later, [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce") of [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") (who went on to co-found ) independently developed the integrated circuit with integrated interconnect, and is also considered an inventor of the integrated circuit.[[28]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-28) In 1969, Kilby was awarded the National Medal of Science, and in 1982 he was inducted into the National Inventor's Hall of Fame.[[29]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-29) Kilby also won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for his part of the invention of the integrated circuit.[[30]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-30) Noyce's chip, made at Fairchild, was made of silicon, while Kilby's chip was made of [germanium](Germanium "Germanium"). In 2008, TI named its new development laboratory "Kilby Labs" after Jack Kilby.[[31]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-31) In 2011, Intel, Samsung, LG, ST-Ericsson, Huawei's HiSilicon Technologies subsidiary, Via Telecom, and three other undisclosed chipmakers licensed the C2C link specification developed by Arteris Inc. and Texas Instruments.[[32]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-32) #### Standard TTL The [7400 series](7400_series "7400 series") of [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") chips, developed by Texas Instruments in the 1960s, popularized the use of integrated circuits in computer logic. The military-grade version of this was the 5400 series.[[33]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-33) #### Microprocessor Texas Instruments invented the hand-held [calculator](Calculator "Calculator") (a prototype called "[Cal Tech](Cal_Tech_(calculator) "Cal Tech (calculator)")") in 1967 and the single-chip [microcomputer](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1971, was assigned the first patent on a single-chip [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") (invented by Gary Boone) on September 4, 1973.[[34]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-34) This was disputed by Gilbert Hyatt, formerly of the Micro Computer Company, in August 1990, when he was awarded a patent superseding TI's. This was overturned on June 19, 1996, in favor of TI[[35]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-35) (note: is usually given credit with Texas Instruments for the almost-simultaneous invention of the microprocessor). #### First speech synthesis chip In 1978, Texas Instruments introduced the first single-chip [linear predictive coding](Linear_predictive_coding "Linear predictive coding") [speech synthesizer](Speech_synthesizer "Speech synthesizer").[[36]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-36) In 1976, TI began a feasibilit [82424 more characters...]

For other uses, see [Mostek (disambiguation)](Mostek_(disambiguation) "Mostek (disambiguation)"). *Mostek Corporation* | Mostek logo from the late 1970s until its acquisition by [United Technologies](United_Technologies "United Technologies") | | | --- | --- | | Industry | Semiconductors | | Founded | 1969 (1969) in [Worcester, Massachusetts](Worcester%2C_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") | | Founder |
L. J. SevinLouay E. SharifRichard L. Petritz | | Defunct | 1985 (1985) | | Fate | Merged into | **Mostek Corporation** was a semiconductor [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") manufacturer, founded in 1969 by L. J. Sevin, Louay E. Sharif, Richard L. Petritz and other ex-employees of [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"). At its peak in the late 1970s, Mostek held an 85% market share of the [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM) memory chip market worldwide, until being eclipsed by lower-priced Japanese DRAM manufacturers who were accused of [dumping](Dumping_(pricing_policy) "Dumping (pricing policy)") memory on the market.[[1]](Mostek#cite_note-1) In 1979, soon after its market peak, Mostek was purchased by [United Technologies Corporation](United_Technologies_Corporation "United Technologies Corporation") for US$345M. In 1985, after several years of red ink and declining market share, UTC closed Mostek completely and sold it for US$71M to the French electronics firm , which later spun it off into . ## Early Products Mostek's first contract was from [Burroughs](Burroughs_Corporation "Burroughs Corporation"), a $400 contract for circuit design. Initially Mostek products were manufactured in [Worcester, Massachusetts](Worcester%2C_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") in cooperation with [Sprague Electric](Sprague_Electric "Sprague Electric"), however by 1974 most of its manufacturing was done at their headquarters in [Carrollton, Texas](Carrollton%2C_Texas "Carrollton, Texas"). The first design to be produced was the MK1001, a simple [barrel shifter](Barrel_shifter "Barrel shifter") chip made using an aluminium-gate [PMOS](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") process. This was followed by a 1K , the MK4006, designed by Vern McKinney, that was manufactured in their Carrollton facility. Mostek had been working with [Sprague Electric](Sprague_Electric "Sprague Electric") to develop the [ion implantation](Ion_implantation "Ion implantation") process which provided much better control of doping profiles, especially in lowering enhancement-mode transistor threshold voltage and providing depletion-load transistors. Using ion implantation, Mostek became an early leader in MOS manufacturing technology, while their competition was still mostly using the older bipolar technology. The resulting increased speed and lower cost of the MK4006 memory chip made it the runaway favorite to IBM and other [mainframe](Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") and [minicomputer](Minicomputer "Minicomputer") manufacturers (cf. , [Digital Equipment Corporation](Digital_Equipment_Corporation "Digital Equipment Corporation")). In 1970 , a Japanese [adding machine](Adding_machine "Adding machine") manufacturer, approached and Mostek with a proposal to introduce a new electronic calculator line. Intel responded first, providing them with the [Intel 4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004"), which they used in a line of desktop calculators. Mostek's device took longer to develop but was the world's first **single chip calculator**, the MK6010, used for the Busicom LE-120A which went on the market in 1971 and was the smallest calculator available for some time.[[2]](Mostek#cite_note-Popular_Science_Jun_1971-2) also contracted with Mostek for design and production of chips for their and calculators. ## World leader in DRAM Mostek co-founder Robert Proebsting invented address multiplexing with the MK4096 4096 X 1 bit DRAM introduced in 1973. [Address multiplexing](Bus_(computing)#Address_multiplexing "Bus (computing)") was a revolutionary approach which reduced cost and board space by fitting a 4K DRAM into a 16 pin package, while competitors took the evolutionary approach which led to a bulky and relatively expensive 22 pin package. Competitors derided the Mostek approach as unnecessarily complex, but Proebsting understood the future roadmap for DRAM memories would benefit greatly if only one new pin were needed for every 4X increase in memory size, instead of the two pins per 4X for the evolutionary approach. Computer manufacturers found address multiplexing to be a compelling feature as they saw that a future 64K DRAM chip would save 8 pins if implemented with address multiplexing and subsequent generations even more. Per pin costs are a major cost driver in integrated circuits, plus the multiplexed approach used less silicon area, which further reduces chip cost. The MK4096 was produced using an NMOS aluminum-gate process with an added interconnect layer of polysilicon (dubbed the SPIN process). The [fear, uncertainty and doubt](Fear%2C_uncertainty_and_doubt "Fear, uncertainty and doubt") put up by the competition regarding address multiplexing was dispelled by the actual performance of the MK4096 which proved solid and robust in all types of computer memory designs. In 1976 Mostek introduced the [silicon-gate](Silicon-gate "Silicon-gate") MK4027 (an improved version of the metal-gated MK4096), and in 1977 the MK4116 16K double-poly silicon-gate DRAM. They were designed by Paul Schroeder and Robert Proebsting (Schroeder later left Mostek to co-found ). The MK4116 achieved **greater than 75% worldwide DRAM market share.** The MK4027 and MK4116 were reverse-engineered by Mosaid and successfully cloned by many companies, both USA and overseas-based. The 64K generation of DRAMs required a transition from 12V & +/−5V to 5V-only operation, in order to free the +12V and −5V pins for use as addresses (the +5V and ground pins were assigned to pins 8 and 16, respectively, rather than the 16-pin TTL DIP standard of pin 8 for ground and pin 16 for +5V). While most competitors took a conservative approach by simply shrinking (scaling) their 64Ks, Mostek undertook a major redesign which incorporated forward-looking features (such as controlled pre-charge current) that were not necessary at the 64K level and delayed entry into the market. Mostek's DRAM legacy is exemplified in the MK4116, MK4164 and MK41256. "By four" DRAM was a simple adaptation of the MK4116/MK4164/MK41256 technology, utilizing a larger package to accommodate the additional data bits and multiplexing the data in/out pins as well; the basic *RAS, *CAS, *WRITE and [multiplexed address bus](Bus_(computing)#Bus_multiplexing "Bus (computing)") concept was retained intact. ## World leader in telecommunications products Mostek enjoyed many years of mastery of the international market for telecommunications products. Their product line included telephone tone and pulse dialers, [touchtone](Touchtone "Touchtone") decoders, counters, top-octave generators (used by [Hammond](Hammond_organ "Hammond organ"), [Baldwin](Baldwin_Piano_Company "Baldwin Piano Company"), and others), [CODECs](CODEC "CODEC"), watch circuits, and a host of custom products for a variety of customers. The products used the simple [aluminium-gate](Aluminum-gate "Aluminum-gate") [PMOS](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") (& later aluminium-gate ) process and helped maintain Mostek's cash flow through intense DRAM competition, and other semiconductor market pressures. In 1975 a smoky fire in the [wafer fab](Wafer_fabrication "Wafer fabrication") closed it for several months and production of some critical products was shifted to a friendly fab () in Silicon Valley. Several employees played a key role in the Telecommunications and Industrial Products Department. Bob Paluck headed the department and later Dave Seeler, assisted by Mike Callahan, Charles Johnson, William Bradley, Robert C. Jones, Bob Banks, Ted Lewis, Darin Kincaid, and William Cummings. Telecom marketing was handled by John Crago, Randall Hopkins, and Henry Wasik. Lewis and Bradley were designated as key employees after the United Technologies purchase. Bradley designed all of the custom products based on the single-chip-calculator platform, as well as the code for the wristwatch chips produced by Mostek for and other customers. For a short while, Paluck headed a joint venture called Mostek Hong Kong, a collaboration with Bulova for the production of high-end wristwatches based on Mostek designs. Bradley was an employee of that joint venture. Paluck left Mostek to work with [Sevin Rosen Funds](Sevin_Rosen_Funds "Sevin Rosen Funds") and [Convex Computer](Convex_Computer "Convex Computer"). *MOS Technology, Inc.*

|  | |
| --- | --- |
| Industry | Semiconductor design and manufacturing |
| Predecessor | <Allen-Bradley> |
| Founded | 1969 (1969) |
| Defunct | 2001 (2001) |
| Successor | [Commodore Semiconductor Group](MOS_Technology#Commodore_Semiconductor_Group "MOS Technology")    [Western Design Center](Western_Design_Center "Western Design Center") |

**MOS Technology, Inc.** ("MOS" being short for [Metal Oxide Semiconductor](Metal_Oxide_Semiconductor "Metal Oxide Semiconductor")), later known as **CSG (Commodore Semiconductor Group)** and **GMT Microelectronics**, was a [semiconductor](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") design and [fabrication](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication") company based in [Audubon, Pennsylvania](Audubon%2C_Pennsylvania "Audubon, Pennsylvania"). It is most famous for its [6502](MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502") [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") and various designs for [Commodore International](Commodore_International "Commodore International")'s range of [home computers](Home_computer "Home computer").

## History

Three former [General Instrument](General_Instrument "General Instrument") executives, John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe and Don McLaughlin, formed MOS Technology in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania in 1969. The [Allen-Bradley Company](Allen-Bradley "Allen-Bradley") was looking to provide a second source for electronic calculators and their chips designed by [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") (TI). In 1970 Allen-Bradley acquired a majority interest in MOS Technology.

In the early 1970s, TI decided to release their own line of calculators, instead of selling just the chips inside them, and introduced them at a price that was lower than the price of the chipset alone. Many early chip companies were reliant on sales of calculator chips and were wiped out in the aftermath; those that survived did so by finding other chips to produce. MOS became a supplier to <Atari>, producing a custom single-chip *<Pong>* system.

Things changed dramatically in 1975. Several of the designers of the [Motorola 6800](Motorola_6800 "Motorola 6800") left Motorola shortly after its release, after management told them to stop working on a low-cost version of the design. At the time there was no such thing as a [pure-play semiconductor foundry](Pure-play_semiconductor_foundry "Pure-play semiconductor foundry"), so they had to join a chip-building company to produce their new CPU. MOS was a small firm with good credentials in the right area, the east coast of the US. The team of four design engineers was headed by [Chuck Peddle](Chuck_Peddle "Chuck Peddle") and included [Bill Mensch](Bill_Mensch "Bill Mensch"). At MOS they set about building a new [CPU](Central_Processing_Unit "Central Processing Unit") that would outperform the 6800 while being similar to it in purpose and much less expensive. The resulting [6501](MOS_Technology_6501 "MOS Technology 6501") design was somewhat similar to the 6800, but by using several design simplifications, the 6501 would be up to four times faster.

### Mask fixing

Previous CPU designs, like the 6800, were produced using a device known as a [contact aligner](Contact_lithography "Contact lithography"). This was essentially a complex [photocopier](Photocopier "Photocopier"), which optically reproduced a CPU design, or "mask", on the surface of the silicon chip. The name "contact" referred to the fact that the mask was placed directly on the surface of the chip, which had the significant disadvantage that it sometimes pulled away materials from the chip, which were then copied to subsequent chips. This caused the mask to become useless after about a dozen copies, and resulted in the vast majority of chips having fatal flaws; for a complex chip like the 6800, only about 10% of the chips would work once the masking process was complete.[[1]](MOS_Technology#cite_note-Mensch-1)

In 1974 <Perkin-Elmer> publicly introduced the <Micralign> system, the first projection scanner. Instead of placing the mask on the surface of the chip, it held it far from the surface and used highly accurate optics to project the image. Masks now lasted for thousands of copies instead of tens, and the flaw rate of the chips inverted so that perhaps 70% of the chips produced would work. The result was a similar inversion in pricing. The 6800 sold in small lots for $295; with no other changes than using a <Micralign>, the same design could sell for $42.[[1]](MOS_Technology#cite_note-Mensch-1)

The change to the Micralign revealed a further advantage. Previously the masks were mass-produced by photography companies like <Kodak>, who would make tens of thousands of copies of a master mask, or "[reticle](Reticle "Reticle")", and ship the masks to the aligners by the truckload. This meant that if a flaw was found in the design, it would cost a significant amount of money to fix it, as all the older masks would have to be thrown out. In contrast, with Micralign there was only one mask per aligner, so there was no inherent cost in replacing the mask if need be, although the cost, and especially time, of producing these master masks was considerable.[[1]](MOS_Technology#cite_note-Mensch-1)

MOS developed the ability to "fix" its masks after they had been produced.[[1]](MOS_Technology#cite_note-Mensch-1) This meant that as flaws in the design were discovered, the masks could be removed from the aligners, fixed, and put back in. This allowed them to rapidly drive out flaws in the original masks.

The company's production lines typically reversed the numbers others were achieving; even the early runs of a new CPU design—what would become the 6502—were achieving a success rate of 70 percent or better. This meant that not only were its designs faster, but they also cost much less as well.

### 6502 family

Main article: [MOS Technology 6502](MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502")

When the 6501 was announced, Motorola launched a lawsuit almost immediately. Although the 6501 [instruction set](Instruction_set "Instruction set") was not compatible with the 6800, it could nevertheless be plugged into existing [motherboard](Motherboard "Motherboard") designs because it had the same functional pin arrangement and [IC package](IC_package "IC package") footprint. That was enough to allow Motorola to sue. Allen-Bradley sold back its shares to the founders, sales of the 6501 basically stopped, and the lawsuit would drag on for many years before MOS was eventually forced to pay US$200,000 in fines.

In the meantime MOS had started selling the [6502](MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502"), a chip capable of operating at 1 [MHz](Megahertz "Megahertz") in September 1975 for a mere US$25. It was nearly identical to the 6501, with only a few minor differences: an added on-chip clock oscillator, a different functional pinout arrangement, generation of the SYNC signal (supporting single-instruction stepping), and removal of data bus enablement control signals (DBE and BA, with the former directly connected to the phase 2 clock instead).[[2]](MOS_Technology#cite_note-2) It outperformed the more-complex 6800 and [Intel 8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080"), but cost much less and was easier to work with. Although it did not have the 6501's advantage of being able to be used in place of the Motorola 6800 in existing hardware, it was so inexpensive that it quickly became more popular than the 6800, making that a moot point.

The 6502 was so cheap that many people believed it was a scam when MOS first showed it at a 1975 trade show. They were not aware of MOS's masking techniques and when they calculated the price per chip at the current industry yield rates, it did not add up. But any hesitation to buy it evaporated when both Motorola and Intel dropped the prices on their own designs from $179 to $69 at the same show in order to compete. Their moves legitimized the 6502, and by the show's end, the wooden barrel full of samples was empty.

The 6502 would quickly go on to be one of the most popular chips of its day. A number of companies licensed the 650x line from MOS, including [Rockwell International](Rockwell_International "Rockwell International"), [GTE](General_Telephone_and_Electronics "General Telephone and Electronics"), <Synertek>, and [Western Design Center (WDC)](Western_Design_Center "Western Design Center").

A number of different versions of the basic CPU, known as the 6503 through 6507, were offered in 28-pin packages for lower cost. The various models removed signal or address pins. Far and away the most popular of these was the [6507](MOS_Technology_6507 "MOS Technology 6507"), which was used in the [Atari 2600](Atari_2600 "Atari 2600") and Atari disk drives. The 6504 was sometimes used in printers. MOS also released a series of similar CPUs using external clocks, which added a "1" to the name in the third digit, as the 6512 through 6515. These were useful in systems where the clock support was already being provided on the motherboard by some other source. The final addition was the "crossover" [6510](MOS_Technology_6510 "MOS Technology 6510"), used in the [Commodore 64](Commodore_64 "Commodore 64"), with additional I/O ports.

### Commodore Semiconductor Group

However successful the 6502 was, the company itself was having problems. At about the same time the 6502 was being released, MOS's entire calculator [IC](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") market collapsed, and its prior existing products stopped

| | Performance | | | Max. [CPU](Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") [clock rate](Clock_rate "Clock rate") | 1 MHz to 2 MHz | | Data width | 8 | | Address width | 16 | | Architecture and classification | | | [Instruction set](Instruction_set_architecture "Instruction set architecture") | 6800 | | Number of instructions | 72 | | Physical specifications | | | [Transistors](Transistor_count "Transistor count") | 4,100 | | Package(s) | 40-pin [DIP](Dual_in-line_package "Dual in-line package") | | History | | | Successor(s) | [Motorola 68000](Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000")[MOS 6502](MOS_6502 "MOS 6502") | The **6800** ("*sixty-eight hundred*") is an [8-bit](8-bit_computing "8-bit computing") microprocessor designed and first manufactured by in 1974. The MC6800 microprocessor was part of the [M6800 Microcomputer System](Motorola_6800_family "Motorola 6800 family") (latter dubbed *68xx*[[1]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-1)) that also included serial and parallel interface [ICs](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit"), , [ROM](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") and other support chips. A significant design feature was that the M6800 family of ICs required only a single five-volt [power supply](Power_supply "Power supply") at a time when most other microprocessors required three voltages. The M6800 Microcomputer System was announced in March 1974 and was in full production by the end of that year.[[2]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-MC6800_March_1974-2)[[3]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-MC6800_$360-3) The 6800 has a 16-bit address bus that can directly access 64 [KB](Kilobyte "Kilobyte") of memory and an 8-bit bi-directional data bus. It has 72 instructions with seven addressing modes for a total of 197 [opcodes](Opcode "Opcode"). The original MC6800 could have a clock frequency of up to 1 [MHz](Megahertz "Megahertz"). Later versions had a maximum clock frequency of 2 MHz.[[4]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-M6800_Design_Data-4)[[5]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-BIST_6800-5) In addition to the ICs, Motorola also provided a complete [assembly language](Assembly_language "Assembly language") [development system](Software_development "Software development"). The customer could use the software on a remote [timeshare](Time-sharing "Time-sharing") computer or on an in-house [minicomputer](Minicomputer "Minicomputer") system. The Motorola EXORciser was a [desktop computer](Desktop_computer "Desktop computer") built with the M6800 ICs that could be used for [prototyping](Prototype "Prototype") and [debugging](Debugging "Debugging") new designs. An expansive documentation package included datasheets on all ICs, two assembly language programming manuals, and a 700-page application manual that showed how to design a [point-of-sale](Point-of-sale "Point-of-sale") terminal (a computerized [cash register](Cash_register "Cash register")) around the 6800.[[6]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-M6800_Apps_Manual-6) The 6800 was popular in [computer peripherals](Computer_peripheral "Computer peripheral"), [test equipment](Electronic_test_equipment "Electronic test equipment") applications and point-of-sale terminals. It also found use in arcade games[[7]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-7) and pinball machines.[[8]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-8) The MC6802, introduced in 1977, included 128 bytes of RAM and an internal clock oscillator on chip. The MC6801 and MC6805 included RAM, ROM and I/O on a single chip and were popular in automotive applications. Some MC6805 models integrated a [Serial Peripheral Interface](Serial_Peripheral_Interface "Serial Peripheral Interface") (SPI).[[9]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-9) The [Motorola 6809](Motorola_6809 "Motorola 6809") was an updated compatible design. ## History ### Motorola's history in semiconductors Main article: [Motorola § History](Motorola#History "Motorola") Galvin Manufacturing Corporation was founded in 1928; the company name was changed to Motorola in 1947. They began commercial production of transistors at a new US$1.5 million facility in Phoenix in 1955.[[10]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-Motorola_AR_1955_Report-10) Motorola's [transistors](Transistor "Transistor") and integrated circuits were used in-house for their communication, military, automotive and consumer products and they were also sold to other companies. By 1973 the Semiconductor Products Division (SPD) had sales of $419 million and was the second largest semiconductor company after [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments").[[11]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-Motorola_1975_Report-11) In the early 1970s Motorola started a project that developed their first microprocessor, the MC6800. This was followed by single-chip [microcontrollers](Microcontroller "Microcontroller") such as the MC6801 and MC6805. ### Development team Motorola did not chronicle the development of the 6800 microprocessor the way that Intel did for their microprocessors. In 2008 the Computer History Museum interviewed four members of the 6800 microprocessor design team. Their recollections can be confirmed and expanded by magazine and journal articles written at the time. The Motorola microprocessor project began in 1971 with a team composed of designer Tom Bennett, engineering director Jeff LaVell, product marketer Link Young and systems designers Mike Wiles, Gene Schriber and Doug Powell.[[12]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-Malone_1995-12) They were all located in [Mesa, Arizona](Mesa%2C_Arizona "Mesa, Arizona"), in greater [Phoenix](Phoenix%2C_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"). By the time the project was finished, Bennett had 17 chip designers and layout people working on five chips. LaVell had 15 to 20 system engineers and there was another applications engineering group of similar size.[[13]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-Motorola_6800_Oral_History_2008-13) Tom Bennett had a background in industrial controls and had worked for Victor Comptometer in the 1960s designing the first electronic calculator to use MOS ICs, the [Victor 3900](Victor_3900 "Victor 3900").[[14]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-1964_MOS_IC-14) In May 1969 [Ted Hoff](Marcian_Hoff "Marcian Hoff") showed Bennett early diagrams of the [Intel 4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") to see if it would meet their calculator needs. Bennett joined Motorola in 1971 to design calculator ICs. He was soon assigned as the chief architect of the microprocessor project that produced the 6800.[[15]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-Bennett_3962682-15) Others have taken credit for designing the 6800. In September 1975 [Robert H. Cushman](Robert_H._Cushman "Robert H. Cushman"), [*EDN* magazine's](EDN_(magazine) "EDN (magazine)") microprocessor editor, interviewed Chuck Peddle about MOS Technology's new [6502](MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502") microprocessor. Cushman then asked "Tom Bennett, master architect of the 6800", to comment about this new competitor.[[16]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-EDN_Sep_20_1975-16) After the 6800 project Bennett worked on automotive applications and Motorola became a major supplier of microprocessors used in automobiles. Jeff LaVell joined Motorola in 1966 and worked in the computer industry marketing organization. LaVell had previously worked for [Collins Radio](Rockwell_Collins "Rockwell Collins") on their C8500 computer that was built with small scale [ECL](Emitter-coupled_logic "Emitter-coupled logic") ICs. In 1971, he led a group that examined the needs of their existing customers such as , [National Cash Register](NCR_Corporation "NCR Corporation"), [Control Data Corporation](Control_Data_Corporation "Control Data Corporation") (CDC), and [Digital Equipment Corporation](Digital_Equipment_Corporation "Digital Equipment Corporation") (DEC). They would study the customer's products and try to identify functions that could be implemented in larger integrated circuits at a lower cost. The result of the survey was a family of 15 building blocks; each could be implemented in an integrated circuit.[[13]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-Motorola_6800_Oral_History_2008-13) Some of these blocks were implemented in the initial M6800 release and more were added over the next few years. To evaluate the 6800 architecture while the chip was being designed, LaVell's team built an equivalent circuit using 451 small scale TTL ICs on five 10 by 10 inch (25 by 25 cm) circuit boards. Later they reduced this to 114 ICs on one board by using ROMs and MSI (medium scale integration) logic devices.[[17]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-17) John Buchanan was a memory designer at Motorola when Bennett asked him to design a [voltage doubler](Voltage_doubler "Voltage doubler") for the 6800. Typical n-channel MOS IC's required three power supplies: -5 volts, +5 volts and +12 volts. The M6800 family was to use only one, +5 volts. It was easy to eliminate the −5 volt supply by using an internal [voltage inverter](Voltage_inverter "Voltage inverter"), but the [enhancement-mode](Enhancement-mode "Enhancement-mode") logic also needed a supply of 10 to 12 volts. To address this, the design added an on-chip voltage doubler. Buchanan did the circuit design, analysis and layout for the 6800 microprocessor. He received patents on the voltage doubler and the 6800 chip layout.[[18]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-Buchanan_3942047-18)[[19]](Motorola_6800#cite_note-Buchanan_3987418-19) Rod Orgill assisted Buchanan with analyses and 6800 chip layout. Later Orgill would design the [MOS Technology 6501](MOS_Technology_6501 "MOS Technology 6501") microprocessor that was socket compatible with the 6800. **Am2900** is a family of [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") (ICs) created in 1975 by [Advanced Micro Devices](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices") (AMD). They were constructed with [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") devices, in a [bit-slice](Bit_slicing "Bit slicing") topology, and were designed to be used as modular components each representing a different aspect of a computer [control unit](Control_unit "Control unit") (CCU). By using the [bit slicing](Bit_slicing "Bit slicing") technique, the Am2900 family was able to implement a CCU with data, addresses, and instructions to be any multiple of 4 bits by multiplying the number of ICs. One major problem with this modular technique was that it required a larger number of ICs to implement what could be done on a single CPU IC. The Am2901 chip included an [arithmetic logic unit](Arithmetic_logic_unit "Arithmetic logic unit") (ALU) and 16 4-bit [processor register](Processor_register "Processor register") slices, and was the "core" of the series. It could count using 4 bits and implement binary operations as well as various [bit-shifting](Bit_shift "Bit shift") operations.

The 2901 and some other chips in the family were [second sourced](Second_source "Second source") by an unusually large number of other manufacturers, starting with Motorola and then Raytheon –  both in 1975 –  and also Cypress Semiconductor, National Semiconductor, NEC, Thomson, and Signetics. In the Soviet Union and later Russia the Am2900 family was manufactured as the 1804 series (with e.g. the Am2901 [designated](Soviet_integrated_circuit_designation "Soviet integrated circuit designation") as KR1804VS1 / [Russian](Russian_language "Russian language"): *[КР1804ВС1](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/К1804 "ru:К1804")*)[[1]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-1)[[2]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-cpuworld-2)[[3]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-kozak1800-3) which was known to be in production in 2016.[[4]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-vzpp-4)

## Computers made with Am2900-family chips

There are probably many more, but here are some known machines using these parts:

- The [Apollo Computer](Apollo_Computer "Apollo Computer") Tern family: DN460, DN660 and DSP160. All used the same system board emulating the [Motorola 68010](Motorola_68010 "Motorola 68010") instruction set.[[5]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-5)
- The <Itek> [Advanced Technology Airborne Computer](Advanced_Technology_Airborne_Computer "Advanced Technology Airborne Computer") (ATAC) used on the [Galileo](Galileo_(spacecraft) "Galileo (spacecraft)") Attitude and Articulation Control Computer System and some Navy aircraft had a 16-register, 16-bit word width assembled from 4-bit-wide 2900 series processors. Four special instructions were added to the Galileo version of the ATAC, and later some chips were replaced with [radiation-hardened](Radiation-hardened "Radiation-hardened") 2901 chips.[[6]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-6)
- [Data General Nova](Data_General_Nova "Data General Nova") 4, which obtained 16-bit word width using four Am2901 ALUs in parallel; one of the boards had 15 Am2901 ALUs on it.[[7]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-7)

- The DEC [VAX 11/730](VAX-11#VAX-11/730 "VAX-11"), which used eight Am2901s for the CPU.[[10]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-10)

## 1970s

The first [microprocessors](Microprocessors "Microprocessors") were designed and manufactured in the 1970s. Intel's 4004 of 1971 is widely regarded as the first commercial microprocessor.[[1]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-1)

Designers predominantly used <MOSFET> transistors with [pMOS logic](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") in the early 1970s, switching to [nMOS logic](NMOS_logic "NMOS logic") after the mid-1970s. nMOS had the advantage that it could run on a single voltage, typically +5V, which simplified the power supply requirements and allowed it to be easily interfaced with the wide variety of +5V [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") (TTL) devices. nMOS had the disadvantage that it was more susceptible to electronic noise generated by slight impurities in the underlying silicon material, and it was not until the mid-1970s that these, sodium in particular, were successfully removed to the required levels. At that time, around 1975, nMOS quickly took over the market.[[2]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-2)

This corresponded with the introduction of new [semiconductor masking](Photomask "Photomask") systems, notably the <Micralign> system from <Perkin-Elmer>. Micralign projected an image of the mask onto the silicon wafer, never touching it directly, which eliminated the previous problems when the mask would be lifted off the surface and take away some of the [photoresist](Photoresist "Photoresist") along with it, ruining the chips on that portion of the wafer.[[3]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-3) By reducing the number of flawed chips, from about 70% to 10%, the cost of complex designs like early microprocessors fell by the same amount. Systems based on contact aligners cost on the order of $300 in single-unit quantities, the [MOS 6502](MOS_6502 "MOS 6502"), designed specifically to take advantage of these improvements, cost only $25.[[4]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-4)

This period also saw considerable experimentation with various [word lengths](Word_length "Word length"). Early on, [4-bit](4-bit_computing "4-bit computing") processors were common, like the Intel 4004, simply because making a wider word length could not be accomplished cost-effectively in the room available on the small wafers of the era, especially when the majority would be defective. As yields improved, wafer sizes grew, and feature size continued to be reduced, more complex [8-bit](8-bit_computing "8-bit computing") designs emerged like the [Intel 8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") and 6502. [16-bit](16-bit_computing "16-bit computing") processors emerged early but were expensive; by the decade's end, low-cost 16-bit designs like the [Zilog Z8000](Zilog_Z8000 "Zilog Z8000") were becoming common. Some unusual word lengths were also produced, including [12-bit](12-bit_computing "12-bit computing") and 20-[bit](Bit "Bit"), often matching a design that had previously been implemented in a multi-chip format in a [minicomputer](Minicomputer "Minicomputer"). These had largely disappeared by the end of the decade as minicomputers moved to [32-bit](32-bit_computing "32-bit computing") formats.

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles about chip manufacturers from the 1970s, I can now provide you with a comprehensive overview of which companies manufactured the greatest number of computer chips during that era.

## Top Computer Chip Manufacturers in the 1970s

### 1. **Texas Instruments (TI)** — Market Leader
- **Position**: By 1973, TI was the **largest semiconductor company in the world**, with Motorola ranking second
- **Key Achievements**:
  - Invented the integrated circuit (Jack Kilby, 1958)
  - Produced the world's first commercial silicon transistor (1954)
  - Released the first single-chip microcontroller (1970)
  - **7400-series TTL chips** gained over **50% of the logic chip market** by 1966, becoming de facto standard components
  - Introduced the TMS 1000 microprocessor (1974) - one of the first single-chip microprocessors

### 2. **Motorola** — Second Largest
- **Position**: By 1973, had **$419 million in semiconductor sales**, making it the **second-largest semiconductor company** after TI
- **Key Products**:
  - **Motorola 6800** microprocessor (1974) - 8-bit processor widely used in computer peripherals, test equipment, and point-of-sale terminals
  - Major supplier of microprocessors for automotive applications
  - Strong presence in both logic chips and microprocessors

### 3. **Intel** — Innovation Leader
- **Founded**: 1968 (by Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce)
- **Key Achievements**:
  - Created the **world's first commercial microprocessor** - the Intel 4004 (1971)
  - Followed with 8008 (1972) and 8080 (1974)
  - Initially focused on memory chips (DRAM and SRAM), which represented the **majority of its business until 1981**
  - Gained market presence but was still building scale compared to TI and Motorola in the 1970s

### 4. **Mostek** — DRAM Market Dominator
- **Founded**: 1969 by ex-Texas Instruments employees
- **Peak Position**: At its peak in the **late 1970s, held 85% market share** of the worldwide DRAM memory chip market
- **Key Achievements**:
  - **MK4116 16K DRAM** achieved **greater than 75% worldwide DRAM market share**
  - Pioneered DRAM address multiplexing (reduced cost and board space)
  - Major supplier to IBM and other mainframe/minicomputer manufacturers

### 5. **MOS Technology** — Disruptive Innovator
- **Founded**: 1969
- **Key Achievement**: Released the **6502 microprocessor in 1975 for just $25** (compared to $179 for competing chips)
- **Impact**: 
  - Used in the Atari 2600, Commodore computers, and Apple I/II
  - One of the **most popular chips of the era**
  - Forced Motorola and Intel to drop their prices to compete
  - Licensed to multiple manufacturers (Rockwell, GTE, Synertek)

### 6. **AMD (Advanced Micro Devices)**
- **Founded**: 1969
- **Key Achievement**: Released the **Am2900 family in 1975** - bit-slice processor family used in minicomputers
- **Role**: Important second-source manufacturer and growing competitor

## Market Summary

**Volume Leaders by Production:**
1. **Texas Instruments** - Highest overall semiconductor sales
2. **Motorola** - Second largest overall sales
3. **Intel** - Growing rapidly but still smaller scale in the 1970s
4. **Mostek** - Dominant (85% market share) specifically in DRAM memory chips

**Market Share by Product Category:**
- **Memory (DRAM)**: Mostek dominated with 85% market share in late 1970s
- **Logic Chips**: Texas Instruments' 7400 series had 50%+ market share
- **Microprocessors**: Multiple players, with Intel, Motorola, MOS Technology leading

**Key Industry Changes:**
- Transition from PMOS to NMOS technology (around 1975)
- Introduction of Micralign masking systems dramatically improved yields (from 10% to 70% success rates)
- Price wars in microprocessors intensified competition
- Japanese manufacturers began challenging US dominance by the late 1970s

The 1970s was truly a transformative decade, with Texas Instruments and Motorola leading in volume during most of the decade, while Intel would eventually become the dominant force in the 1980s with the IBM PC's adoption of its x86 processors.

Based on my research through Wikipedia, I've found comprehensive information about Japanese semiconductor companies during the 1980s. Here's what I discovered:

## Japanese Semiconductor Industry Dominance in the 1980s

### Overall Market Position

**Japanese Dominance:** During the 1980s, Japan held approximately **50% of the global semiconductor market share**, making it the dominant force in the worldwide chip industry. This was particularly strong in memory chip (DRAM) production, where Japanese manufacturers effectively eclipsed American and European competitors.

### Key Japanese Companies in the 1980s

#### **NEC (Nippon Electric Company)**
- **World's largest semiconductor company by annual revenue from 1985 to 1992** - an eight-year dominance period
- Major DRAM producer alongside their microprocessor business
- Notable product innovations:
  - 1980: Created the first digital signal processor (NEC µPD7710)
  - 1984: Introduced the NEC V20 microprocessor (an Intel 8088 clone with enhanced features)
  - 1986-1989: Released the V-series processors (V60, V70, V80)
- Manufacturing expansion:
  - 1978: Acquired Electronic Arrays, Inc. of California
  - 1981: Established NEC Semiconductors (UK) Ltd.
  - 1987: NEC Technologies (UK) Ltd. established
- Legacy: Their DRAM business merged with Hitachi's in 1999 to form **Elpida Memory**

#### **Toshiba**
- One of the top 10 semiconductor companies globally during this era
- **Inventor of flash memory** (a major breakthrough in 1980s semiconductor technology)
- Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba developed:
  - 1977: 1Mb DRAM
  - Stacked-gate memory technology (precursor to flash memory and EEPROM)
- Toshiba Memory was later spun off as Kioxia in the late 2010s
- Strong presence in memory chips and electronic components

#### **Hitachi**
- Major player in DRAM and microelectronics
- **Filed Japanese patent in 1983 for 3D integrated circuit (TSV) technology** - pioneering work in chip stacking
- DRAM business merged with NEC's in 1999 to form Elpida Memory
- Later merged with Renesas Electronics for logic chips
- Part of the Japanese conglomerate system (originally part of Nissan zaibatsu)

#### **Fujitsu**
- One of the top semiconductor manufacturers
- **Filed Japanese patent in 1984 for 3D IC technology**, following Hitachi's innovation
- Strong in microelectronics and telecommunications equipment
- Established semiconductor division producing various integrated circuits
- Later one of the companies supporting the new Rapidus initiative in 2022

### Market Share and Competition

**DRAM Market:**
- At its peak in the late 1970s, American company Mostek held **85% of the global DRAM market**
- By the mid-1980s, **Japanese manufacturers had captured this market** through lower prices (described by critics as "dumping")
- Japanese companies like NEC, Toshiba, Hitachi, and Fujitsu dominated global DRAM production
- This dominance contributed to U.S. trade complaints and diplomatic action

### The 1986 Japan-United States Semiconductor Agreement

A critical turning point came with the **1986 Japan-U.S. Semiconductor Trade Agreement**, which:
- Was signed to resolve intense trade friction between the two nations
- Addressed concerns about Japanese market dominance
- Attempted to level the playing field for American semiconductor companies
- Combined with the rise of South Korean (Samsung) and Taiwanese competitors, gradually reduced Japanese competitiveness in subsequent years

### Legacy and Impact

**1980s Significance:**
- Japan reached its semiconductor peak during 1985-1992, with NEC leading global rankings
- The Japanese companies held approximately half the global semiconductor market
- DRAM was the battleground where Japanese quality and manufacturing efficiency overwhelmed competitors
- This success led to both economic triumph and trade disputes

**Aftermath:**
- Japanese semiconductor dominance gradually declined through the 1990s and 2000s
- Many Japanese companies spun off semiconductor divisions (Elpida Memory in 1999, Renesas Electronics)
- Samsung (South Korea) and TSMC (Taiwan) emerged as new dominant players
- The collective strength of these Japanese companies led to the new **Rapidus** initiative in 2022, with eight major Japanese companies (including NEC, Sony, Toyota) collaborating to revive advanced semiconductor manufacturing in Japan

This era represents one of the most significant periods in semiconductor history, where Japanese manufacturers achieved unprecedented global market dominance before facing increased competition and eventual decline due to trade pressures and new international competitors."}]

The 1980s was the peak era of Japanese semiconductor dominance, with Japanese manufacturers holding approximately **50% of the global semiconductor market share**. Here are the companies that manufactured the greatest number of chip volumes:

- At its peak in the late 1970s, American company Mostek held **85% of the global DRAM market**

**NEC** manufactured the greatest number of computer chips in the 1980s, leading global semiconductor revenue rankings from 1985 to 1992. The Japanese semiconductor industry as a whole, with companies like Toshiba, Hitachi, and Fujitsu rounding out the top ranks, dominated global chip production throughout this decade, producing roughly half of all semiconductors worldwide by volume.

Based on my research, I can provide you with comprehensive information about which companies manufactured the greatest number of computer chips during the 2010s (2010-2019):

## **Top Semiconductor Manufacturers by Volume (2010s)**

### **1. TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)**
- **World's largest dedicated independent foundry** with **55.9% market share** in 2017
- **Production capacity**: Over **1.3 million wafers/month** by 2019
- **2017 foundry revenue**: **$32.04 billion** (vastly outpacing competitors)
- **Key advantages**: 
  - Manufacturing for Apple's A5-A9 processors
  - Led technology advancement from 40nm → 28nm → 20nm → 16nm FinFET → 10nm → **7nm EUV (2019)**
  - First company to commercialize EUV lithography
- **Growth**: Revenue grew from NT$419.5 billion (2010) to NT$1.07 trillion (2019)

### **2. Samsung Electronics (Semiconductor Division)**
- **Became the world's #1 semiconductor company in 2017** (surpassed Intel)
- **World's largest memory chip manufacturer** since 1993
- **DRAM market share**: **35%** (Q2 2010), maintained throughout the decade
- **NAND Flash**: **#1 worldwide** throughout the 2010s
- **Manufacturing facilities**: Multiple global sites including Suwon, Pyeongtaek (Korea), and Xi'an (China - produces 40% of Samsung's NAND)
- **Unique position**: Both IDM (Integrated Device Manufacturer) and foundry services provider

### **3. Intel Corporation**
- **Was world's #1 semiconductor company until 2017**
- **Production capacity**: ~**400,000+ wafers/month** across **10+ active fabs** globally
- **PC microprocessor market share**: **73.3% in 2011**
- **Manufacturing locations**: 75% in the U.S. (Hillsboro OR, Chandler AZ, Rio Rancho NM, Leixlip Ireland, Kiryat Gat Israel)
- **Key challenge**: **10nm delays** (originally planned for 2016, achieved mass production in September 2019)
- **Closed foundry business in 2018** due to 10nm difficulties

### **4. GlobalFoundries**
- **Monthly capacity**: **200,000+ 300mm wafers/month**
- **2017 foundry revenue**: **$5.407 billion**
- **Market share**: **~7%** of foundry services industry
- **Facilities**: 10 fabrication plants (2015) across Germany, Singapore, and New York
- **Strategic shift**: **Cancelled 7nm development in 2018**, refocused on mature nodes (12nm+)

### **5. UMC (United Microelectronics Corporation)**
- **Total capacity**: **~600,000+ wafers/month** across 12 facilities
- **2017 foundry revenue**: **$4.898 billion** (3rd in foundry rankings)
- **Focused on mature nodes** (28nm and above), representing 48% + 26% = **74% of revenue**
- **~15% of TSMC's revenue** during this period

## **Industry-Wide Production Data (2010-2019)**

According to semiconductor industry records:
- **2010**: **189.8 billion** semiconductor units shipped
- **2011**: **187 billion** units
- **2012**: **185.3 billion** units
- **2013**: **203.5 billion** units
- **2015**: **235.6 billion** units
- **2016**: **342.4 billion** units
- **2017**: **581.3 billion** units
- **2018**: **634.7 billion** units

## **Summary Table**

| Company | 2017 Foundry Revenue | Market Share | Monthly Capacity | Key Specialty |
|---------|---------------------|--------------|------------------|---------------|
| **TSMC** | $32.04B | 55.9% (foundry) | 1.3M+ wafers | Logic chips, advanced nodes |
| **Intel** | N/A (IDM) | N/A | 400K+ wafers | Microprocessors |
| **Samsung** | N/A (IDM) | N/A | N/A | Memory chips |
| **GlobalFoundries** | $5.41B | ~7% | 200K+ wafers | 12nm+, RF chips |
| **UMC** | $4.90B | ~15% of TSMC | 600K+ wafers | Mature nodes (28nm+) |

**Key Takeaway**: **TSMC** dominated the **contract manufacturing** segment with over half the market share, while **Samsung** became the **#1 semiconductor company overall** in 2017 due to memory chip production. **Intel**, despite manufacturing delays, remained a massive volume producer primarily of microprocessors throughout the decade.

The  **semiconductor industry**, including Integrated Circuit (IC) manufacturing, design, and packing, forms a major part of <Taiwan>'s IT industry.[[1]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-emerging-1) Due to its strong capabilities in OEM wafer manufacturing and a complete industry [supply chain](Supply_chain "Supply chain"), Taiwan has been able to distinguish itself as a leading microchip manufacturer and dominate the global marketplace.[[1]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-emerging-1)[[2]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-2) Taiwan’s [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") sector accounted for US$115 billion, around 20 percent of the global semiconductor industry. In sectors such as foundry operations, Taiwanese companies account for 50 percent of the world market, with [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company](TSMC "TSMC") (TSMC) the biggest player in the foundry market.[[3]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-3)

## Overview

<TSMC> and [United Microelectronics Corporation](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation") (UMC) are the two largest contract chipmakers in the world,[[4]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-SCMP_2019-4) while <MediaTek> is the fourth-largest [fabless semiconductor company](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company") globally.[[5]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-5) [ASE Group](ASE_Group "ASE Group") is also the world's largest Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) provider.[[6]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-6)

## History

The Taiwanese semiconductor industry got its start in 1974. In 1976 the government convinced <RCA> to transfer semiconductor technology to <Taiwan>.[[4]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-SCMP_2019-4)

In 1987, TSMC pioneered the fabless foundry model, reshaping the global semiconductor industry.[[7]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-veteran-7)[[8]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-8) From [ITRI](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute")'s first 3-inch wafer fabrication plant built in 1977[[7]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-veteran-7) and the founding of UMC in 1980,[[9]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-9) the industry had developed into a world leader with 40 fabs in operation by 2002.[[1]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-emerging-1) In 2007, the semiconductor industry overtook that of the United States, second only to Japan.[[10]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-10)

The sector output reached US$39 billion in 2009, ranking first in global market share in IC manufacturing, packaging, and testing, and second in IC design.[[7]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-veteran-7) Although the global financial crisis from 2007 to 2010 affected sales and exports,[[11]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-11) the industry has rebounded with companies posting record profits for 2010.[[12]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-12)[[13]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-13) In 2010 Taiwan had the largest share of 300 nm, 90 nm, and 60 nm manufacturing capacities worldwide, and was expected to pass Japan in total IC fab capacity by mid-2011.[[14]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-14)[[15]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-15) By 2020, Taiwan was the unmatched leader of the global semiconductor industry with [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company](TSMC "TSMC") (TSMC) alone accounting for more than 50% of the global market.[[16]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-16)

## Sustainability

The semiconductor industry uses a large portion of the power produced in Taiwan. By 2022 TSMC alone is estimated to consume 7.2% of Taiwan's total power output.[[17]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-17) Due to pressure from customers and government regulations the semiconductor industry has been switching to green power. In July 2020 TSMC signed a 20-year deal with [Ørsted](%C3%98rsted_(company) "Ørsted (company)") to buy the entire production of two offshore wind farms under development off Taiwan's west coast. At the time of its signing it was the largest corporate [green energy](Green_energy "Green energy") order ever made.[[18]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-18) Much of the switch to renewable energy has been mandated by [Apple Inc.](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") whose primary components suppliers are located on Taiwan.[[19]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-19)[[20]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-20)

It is the world's most valuable semiconductor company,[[5]](TSMC#cite_note-5) the world's largest [dedicated](Foundry_model#Dedicated_foundry "Foundry model") independent ("[pure-play](Pure_play "Pure play")") [semiconductor foundry](Foundry_(electronics) "Foundry (electronics)"),[[6]](TSMC#cite_note-6) and its country's largest company,[[7]](TSMC#cite_note-7)[[8]](TSMC#cite_note-8) with headquarters and main operations located in the [Hsinchu Science Park](Hsinchu_Science_Park "Hsinchu Science Park") in , . Since 1994, TSMC has had a [compound annual growth rate](Compound_annual_growth_rate "Compound annual growth rate") (CAGR) of 17.4% in revenue and a CAGR of 16.1% in earnings.[[15]](TSMC#cite_note-15) Most of the leading [fabless](Fabless "Fabless") semiconductor companies such as [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices"), [Apple](Apple_Inc.
