"Broadcom Inc."), [Marvell](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group"), , and , are customers of TSMC, as are emerging companies such as [Allwinner Technology](Allwinner_Technology "Allwinner Technology"), , Spectra7, and .[[16]](TSMC#cite_note-16) Leading [programmable logic device](Programmable_logic_device "Programmable logic device") companies and previously also make or made use of TSMC's foundry services.[[17]](TSMC#cite_note-17) Some [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") that have their own [fabrication facilities](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant"), such as [Intel](Intel_Corporation "Intel Corporation"), , and [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"), outsource some of their production to TSMC.[[18]](TSMC#cite_note-18)[[19]](TSMC#cite_note-19) At least one semiconductor company, [LSI](LSI_Corporation "LSI Corporation"), re-sells TSMC wafers through its [ASIC](Application-specific_integrated_circuit "Application-specific integrated circuit") design services and design [IP](Intellectual_property "Intellectual property") portfolio. TSMC has a global capacity of about thirteen million 300 mm-equivalent wafers per year as of 2020 and makes chips for customers with process nodes from 2 microns to [5 nanometres](5_nm_process "5 nm process"). TSMC was the first foundry to market [7-nanometre](7_nm_process "7 nm process") and [5-nanometre](5_nm_process "5 nm process") (used by the 2020 [Apple A14](Apple_A14 "Apple A14") and [M1](Apple_M1 "Apple M1") [SoCs](System_on_a_chip "System on a chip"), the MediaTek [Dimensity 8100](List_of_MediaTek_processors "List of MediaTek processors"), and [AMD Ryzen 7000](List_of_AMD_Ryzen_processors#Raphael_desktop "List of AMD Ryzen processors") series processors) production capabilities, and the first to commercialize [extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography](Extreme_ultraviolet_lithography "Extreme ultraviolet lithography") technology in high volume. ## History In 1986, [Li Kwoh-ting](Li_Kwoh-ting "Li Kwoh-ting"), representing the [Executive Yuan](Executive_Yuan "Executive Yuan"), invited Morris Chang to serve as the president of the [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute") (ITRI). At that time, the Taiwanese government wanted to develop its semiconductor industry, but its high investment and high risk nature made it difficult to find investors. Only was willing to sign a joint venture contract with Taiwan to put up $58 million, transfer its production technology, and license intellectual property in exchange for a 27.5 percent stake in TSMC. The Taiwanese government provided another 48 percent of the startup capital for TSMC and the rest of the capital was raised from wealthy Taiwanese who were “asked” by the government to invest. “What generally happened was that one of the ministers in the government would call a businessman in Taiwan,” Chang explained, “to get him to invest.” The government asked several of the island’s wealthiest families, who owned firms that specialized in plastics, textiles, and chemicals, to put up the money. Now I have comprehensive data from all five semiconductor companies. Let me compile this into a unified summary:

## Major Semiconductor Companies - Manufacturing Capacity, Production Volumes & Market Position (2010-2019)

---

### **1. TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)**

**Manufacturing Facilities:**
- **6+ major 300mm wafer fabs** (Fab 12A, 14, 15, 16, 18, WaferTech in Washington)
- Multiple 200mm fabs (Fab 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, plus SSMC in Singapore)
- **Fab 15 investment**: US$9.4 billion (announced 2010) - added >100,000 wafers/month

**Monthly Capacity & Growth:**
- **2011**: Planned 30% capacity expansion
- **2014**: Q4 production capacity "almost fully booked" - unprecedented demand
- **2019**: Over 1.3M wafers/month across all facilities

**Revenue (NT$ millions):**
| Year | Revenue |
|------|---------|
| 2010 | 419,538 |
| 2014 | 762,806 |
| 2019 | 1,069,985 |

**Market Position:**
- **55.9% market share** in 2017 (pure-play foundry)
- World's largest dedicated independent semiconductor foundry
- **Apple** was the most important customer (A5-A9 chips)

**Technology Leadership:**
- Successfully led at every node: 40nm → 28nm → 20nm → 16nm FinFET → 10nm → **7nm EUV (2019)**
- First company to commercialize EUV lithography

---

### **2. Intel Corporation**

**Manufacturing Facilities:**
- **~10+ active fabs globally** (75% in the United States)
- **Key U.S. locations**: Hillsboro (OR), Chandler (AZ - including Fab 42), Rio Rancho (NM)
- **International**: Leixlip (Ireland), Kiryat Gat (Israel)

**Major Capacity Expansion:**
- **Fab 42 (Chandler, AZ)**: $5 billion investment (construction 2011-2013)
- **Process nodes**: 32nm → 22nm Tri-Gate → 14nm → 10nm

**Foundry Business:**
- **2013**: Intel Custom Foundry launched (5 initial customers)
- **2018**: Foundry business closed due to 10nm manufacturing difficulties

**Revenue & Market Share:**
- **2011**: 73.3% worldwide PC microprocessor market share
- **2019**: Significant decline due to 10nm delays and AMD competition
- Became the world's #1 semiconductor company until **2017 when Samsung surpassed Intel**

**Key Challenges:**
- **10nm delays**: Originally planned for 2016, mass production achieved September 2019
- Security vulnerabilities (Meltdown/Spectre) in 2018 required CPU redesigns
- Shifted from "tick-tock" to "process-architecture-optimization" model in 2016

---

### **3. Samsung Electronics (Semiconductor Division)**

**Manufacturing Facilities:**
- **Multi-site global operations**: Suwon, Pyeongtaek (Korea), Xi'an (China)
- **Xi'an facility (2014)**: Flagship NAND flash plant, produces **40% of Samsung's NAND**

**Memory Chip Capacity:**
- **World's largest memory chip manufacturer** since 1993
- **DRAM Market Share (Q2 2010)**: 35% (Gartner data)
- **NAND Flash**: World's #1 throughout the 2010s

**Process Technology Progression:**
- **2010**: 30nm-class DRAM, 20nm-class NAND
- **2013**: 10nm-class FinFET, V-NAND (3D NAND) introduced
- **2018**: 7nm FinFET, 5nm node production began
- **2020**: EUV mass production plans

**Financial Performance:**
- **2017**: Samsung became **world's #1 semiconductor company**, surpassing Intel
- **Q4 2016**: Memory chips + flexible displays = **68% of operating profit**
- Revenue from memory chip booms 2016-2019 significantly boosted financial performance

**Foundry Services:**
- Established as strategic growth pillar in **2006**
- Competed with TSMC in advanced process nodes
- Dual role as IDM and foundry (unique position)

---

### **4. GlobalFoundries**

**Manufacturing Facilities:**
- **2010-2011**: Formed from AMD's manufacturing + Chartered Semiconductor acquisition
- **2015**: Owned **10 fabrication plants**
  - Fab 1: Dresden (Germany) - 80,000 300mm wafers/month
  - Fab 7: Singapore - 50,000-80,000 300mm wafers/month
  - Fab 8: Malta, NY - 60,000 300mm wafers/month
  - Additional fabs in Vermont, New York, Singapore

**Wafer Capacity:**
- **Combined**: 200,000+ 300mm wafers/month at full capacity
- Equivalent to ~500,000 200mm wafers/month

**Revenue Trends:**
- **2022**: $8.1 billion (post-2019 reporting)
- **IPO October 2021**: Raised ~$2.6 billion (valued at ~$2.4B)

**Market Position:**
- **2021**: Fourth largest semiconductor manufacturer
- **~7% market share** of the $86 billion semiconductor manufacturing services industry
- **Major customer**: AMD (wafer agreement through 2024, 12nm and above)

**Strategic Shifts During 2010s:**
- **2014**: Acquired IBM Microelectronics ($1.5B, including Fab 9 & 10)
- **2018**: **Cancelled 7nm development** citing unaffordable costs
- **2018**: Shifted strategy to specialized processes (FD-SOI, automotive, IoT)
- **2019**: Divested Fab 3E (MEMS to VIS) and Fab 10 (to ON Semiconductor)

---

### **5. UMC (United Microelectronics Corporation)**

**Manufacturing Facilities:**
- **12 manufacturing facilities worldwide** (2010-2019)
- **300mm fabs**: 4 major facilities (192,000 wafers/month combined)
  - Fab 12A (Taiwan): 87,000 wafers/month
  - Fab 12i (Singapore): 53,000 wafers/month
  - Fab 12X (Xiamen, China): 19,000-25,000 wafers/month
  - Fab 12M (Japan): 33,000 wafers/month
- **200mm and smaller fabs**: ~450,000+ wafers/month

**Total Capacity**: ~600,000+ wafers/month

**Revenue (USD millions):**
| Year | Revenue |
|------|---------|
| 2016 | $4,587 |
| 2017 | $4,898 |

**Market Position (2017 Foundry Revenue Rankings):**
| Rank | Company | 2017 Revenue |
|------|---------|--------------|
| 1 | TSMC | $32,040 million |
| 2 | GlobalFoundries | $5,407 million |
| **3** | **UMC** | **$4,898 million** |

**Technology Position:**
- **Process node revenue (2019)**: Focus on mature nodes
  - 14nm-28nm: 12%
  - 28nm-40nm: 26%
  - 40nm-65nm: 14%
  - 65nm-280nm+: 48%

**Comparison to TSMC:**
- **~15% of TSMC's revenue** during this period
- Focused on **mature nodes (28nm and above)** rather than cutting-edge technology
- ~7x smaller capacity than TSMC

---

## **Summary Comparison Table**

| Metric | TSMC | Intel | Samsung | GlobalFoundries | UMC |
|--------|------|-------|---------|-----------------|-----|
| **2017 Foundry Revenue** | $32.0B | N/A (IDM) | N/A (IDM) | $5.4B | $4.9B |
| **Market Share (Foundry)** | 55.9% | N/A | N/A | ~7% | ~15% of TSMC |
| **Fab Count (2015)** | 6+ (300mm) | 10+ | 5+ (semiconductor) | 10 | 12 |
| **Monthly Capacity** | 1.3M+ wafers | 400K+ wafers | N/A | 200K+ wafers | 600K+ wafers |
| **Advanced Node (2019)** | 5nm (EUV) | 10nm | 5nm (EUV) | 12nm | 14nm |
| **Key Customers** | Apple, AMD, Qualcomm | Own products | Own + foundry customers | AMD | Various fabless |
| **Key Challenge** | Capacity scaling | 10nm delays | Memory cyclicality | 7nm cancellation | Competition with TSMC |

This decade saw **TSMC solidify its dominance** in the foundry space, **Samsung overtake Intel** as the world's largest semiconductor company (driven by memory), and **GlobalFoundries strategically retreat** from cutting-edge competition while **UMC maintained a stable position** as a focused mature-node specialist.

In the [microelectronics](Microelectronics "Microelectronics") industry, a **semiconductor fabrication plant** (commonly called a **fab**; sometimes **foundry**) is a factory for [semiconductor device fabrication](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication").[[1]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-1)

Fabs require many expensive devices to function. Estimates put the cost of building a new fab over one billion [U.S. dollars](United_States_dollars "United States dollars") with values as high as $3–4 billion not being uncommon. <TSMC> invested $9.3 billion in its *Fab15* 300 mm [wafer](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") manufacturing facility in Taiwan.[[2]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-2) The same company estimations suggest that their future fab might cost $20 billion.[[3]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-3) A [foundry model](Foundry_model "Foundry model") emerged in the 1990s: Foundries that produced their own designs were known as [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDMs). Companies that farmed out manufacturing of their designs to foundries were termed [fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company"). Those foundries, which did not create their own designs, were called [pure-play semiconductor foundries](Pure-play_semiconductor_foundry "Pure-play semiconductor foundry").[[4]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-4)

The central part of a fab is the [clean room](Clean_room "Clean room"), an area where the environment is controlled to eliminate all dust, since even a single speck can ruin a microcircuit, which has nanoscale features much smaller than dust particles. The clean room must also be damped against vibration to enable nanometer-scale alignment of machines and must be kept within narrow bands of temperature and humidity. Vibration control may be achieved by using deep piles in the cleanroom's foundation that anchor the cleanroom to the bedrock, careful selection of the construction site, and/or using vibration dampers. Controlling temperature and humidity is critical for minimizing [static electricity](Static_electricity "Static electricity"). Corona discharge sources can also be used to reduce static electricity. Often, a fab will be constructed in the following manner: (from top to bottom): the roof, which may contain air handling equipment that draws, purifies and cools outside air, an air plenum for distributing the air to several floor-mounted [fan filter units](Fan_filter_unit "Fan filter unit"), which are also part of the cleanroom's ceiling, the cleanroom itself, which may or may not have more than one story, [[5]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-5) a return air plenum, the clean subfab that may contain support equipment for the machines in the cleanroom such as chemical delivery, purification, recycling and destruction systems, and the ground floor, that may contain electrical equipment. Fabs also often have some office space.

The clean room is where all fabrication takes place and contains the machinery for integrated circuit production such as [steppers](Stepper "Stepper") and/or scanners for [photolithography](Photolithography "Photolithography"), in addition to [etching](Etching_(microfabrication) "Etching (microfabrication)"), cleaning, [doping](Doping_(semiconductors) "Doping (semiconductors)") and [dicing](Wafer_dicing "Wafer dicing") machines. All these devices are extremely precise and thus extremely expensive. Prices for most common pieces of equipment for the processing of 300 mm wafers range from $700,000 to upwards of $4,000,000 each with a few pieces of equipment reaching as high as $340,000,000 each (e.g. [EUV](Extreme_ultraviolet_lithography "Extreme ultraviolet lithography") scanners). A typical fab will have several hundred equipment items.

## History

Typically an advance in chip-making technology requires a completely new fab to be built. In the past, the equipment to outfit a fab was not very expensive and there were a huge number of smaller fabs producing chips in small quantities. However, the cost of the most up-to-date equipment has since grown to the point where a new fab can cost several billion dollars.

Another side effect of the cost has been the challenge to make use of older fabs. For many companies these older fabs are useful for producing designs for unique markets, such as [embedded processors](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor"), [flash memory](Flash_memory "Flash memory"), and [microcontrollers](Microcontroller "Mic

## History

In 1986, [Li Kwoh-ting](Li_Kwoh-ting "Li Kwoh-ting"), representing the [Executive Yuan](Executive_Yuan "Executive Yuan"), invited Morris Chang to serve as the president of the [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute") (ITRI). At that time, the Taiwanese government wanted to develop its semiconductor industry, but its high investment and high risk nature made it difficult to find investors. Only <Philips> was willing to sign a joint venture contract with Taiwan to put up $58 million, transfer its production technology, and license intellectual property in exchange for a 27.5 percent stake in TSMC. The Taiwanese government provided another 48 percent of the startup capital for TSMC and the rest of the capital was raised from wealthy Taiwanese who were “asked” by the government to invest. “What generally happened was that one of the ministers in the government would call a businessman in Taiwan,” Chang explained, “to get him to invest.” The government asked several of the island’s wealthiest families, who owned firms that specialized in plastics, textiles, and chemicals, to put up the money. From day one, TSMC wasn’t really a private business: it was a project of the Taiwanese state.[[20]](TSMC#cite_note-20)[[21]](TSMC#cite_note-21)[[22]](TSMC#cite_note-22)

Since then, the company has continued to grow, albeit subject to the cycles of demand. In 2011, the company planned to increase research and development expenditures by almost 39% to [NT$](New_Taiwan_dollar "New Taiwan dollar")50 billion to fend off growing competition.[[23]](TSMC#cite_note-23) The company also planned to expand capacity by 30% in 2011 to meet strong market demand.[[24]](TSMC#cite_note-24) In May 2014, TSMC's board of directors approved capital appropriations of [US$](United_States_dollar "United States dollar")568 million to increase and improve manufacturing capabilities after the company forecast higher than expected demand.[[25]](TSMC#cite_note-Q2_2014_forecast-25) In August 2014, TSMC's board of directors approved additional capital appropriations of US$3.05 billion.[[26]](TSMC#cite_note-26)

In 2011, it was reported that TSMC had begun trial production of the [A5](Apple_A5 "Apple A5") SoC and [A6](Apple_A6 "Apple A6") SoCs for Apple's [iPad](IPad "IPad") and [iPhone](IPhone "IPhone") devices.[[27]](TSMC#cite_note-27)[[28]](TSMC#cite_note-28) According to reports,[[29]](TSMC#cite_note-29) in May 2014 Apple sourced its [A8](Apple_A8 "Apple A8") and [A8X](Apple_A8X "Apple A8X") SoCs from TSMC.[[30]](TSMC#cite_note-TechNews_Apple_A8_article-30)[[31]](TSMC#cite_note-CNET_64-bit_processor_article-31) Apple then sourced the [A9](Apple_A9 "Apple A9") SoC with both TSMC and Samsung (to increase volume for [iPhone 6S](IPhone_6S "IPhone 6S") launch) and the [A9X](Apple_A9X "Apple A9X") exclusively with TSMC, thus resolving the issue of sourcing a chip in two different [microarchitecture](Microarchitecture "Microarchitecture") sizes. As of 2014, Apple was TSMC's most important customer.[[31]](TSMC#cite_note-CNET_64-bit_processor_article-31)[[32]](TSMC#cite_note-Taipei_Times_Apple_article-32)

In October 2014, [ARM](ARM_Holdings "ARM Holdings") and TSMC announced a new multi-year agreement for the development of ARM based 10 nm [FinFET](Multigate_device#FinFET "Multigate device") processors.[[33]](TSMC#cite_note-33)

In 2020, TSMC became the first semiconductor company in the world to sign up for the [RE100](The_Climate_Group "The Climate Group") initiative, pledging to use 100% [renewable energy](Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") by 2050.[[34]](TSMC#cite_note-34) TSMC accounts for roughly 5% of the energy consumption in Taiwan, even exceeding that of the capital city Taipei. This initiative was thus expected to accelerate the transformation to renewable energy in the country.[[35]](TSMC#cite_note-35)

For 2020, TSMC had a net income of US$17.60 billion on a consolidated revenue of US$45.51 billion, an increase of 57.5% and 31.4% respectively from the 2019 level of US$11.18 billion net income and US$34.63 billion consolidated revenue.[[36]](TSMC#cite_note-36) Its [market capitalization](Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") was over $550 billion in April 2021. # Multi-Agent Delegation

When the user asks a complex question, do not attempt to answer it yourself. Break it up into smaller pieces, then use the `fork` tool to delegate each piece to a subagent. If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

The instructions you give to each subagent SHOULD be a smaller piece of the instructions you were given. Do not delegate your full task to a subagent. Subagents do not have access to the information you have retrieved in prior turns or your thoughts. You must provide each subagent with the necessary context it needs in its instructions.

Your instructions to a subagent can be long, up to about 5000 characters. Each subagent is as capable as you are, but starts with a blank slate, so you must provide it specific and detailed information in its instructions.

For other uses, see [Mostek (disambiguation)](Mostek_(disambiguation) "Mostek (disambiguation)"). *Mostek Corporation* | Mostek logo from the late 1970s until its acquisition by [United Technologies](United_Technologies "United Technologies") | | | --- | --- | | Industry | Semiconductors | | Founded | 1969 (1969) in [Worcester, Massachusetts](Worcester%2C_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") | | Founder |
L. J. SevinLouay E. SharifRichard L. Petritz | | Defunct | 1985 (1985) | | Fate | Merged into | **Mostek Corporation** was a semiconductor [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") manufacturer, founded in 1969 by L. J. Sevin, Louay E. Sharif, Richard L. Petritz and other ex-employees of [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"). At its peak in the late 1970s, Mostek held an 85% market share of the [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM) memory chip market worldwide, until being eclipsed by lower-priced Japanese DRAM manufacturers who were accused of [dumping](Dumping_(pricing_policy) "Dumping (pricing policy)") memory on the market.[[1]](Mostek#cite_note-1) In 1979, soon after its market peak, Mostek was purchased by [United Technologies Corporation](United_Technologies_Corporation "United Technologies Corporation") for US$345M. In 1985, after several years of red ink and declining market share, UTC closed Mostek completely and sold it for US$71M to the French electronics firm , which later spun it off into . ## Early Products Mostek's first contract was from [Burroughs](Burroughs_Corporation "Burroughs Corporation"), a $400 contract for circuit design. Initially Mostek products were manufactured in [Worcester, Massachusetts](Worcester%2C_Massachusetts "Worcester, Massachusetts") in cooperation with [Sprague Electric](Sprague_Electric "Sprague Electric"), however by 1974 most of its manufacturing was done at their headquarters in [Carrollton, Texas](Carrollton%2C_Texas "Carrollton, Texas"). The first design to be produced was the MK1001, a simple [barrel shifter](Barrel_shifter "Barrel shifter") chip made using an aluminium-gate [PMOS](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") process. This was followed by a 1K , the MK4006, designed by Vern McKinney, that was manufactured in their Carrollton facility. Mostek had been working with [Sprague Electric](Sprague_Electric "Sprague Electric") to develop the [ion implantation](Ion_implantation "Ion implantation") process which provided much better control of doping profiles, especially in lowering enhancement-mode transistor threshold voltage and providing depletion-load transistors. Using ion implantation, Mostek became an early leader in MOS manufacturing technology, while their competition was still mostly using the older bipolar technology. The resulting increased speed and lower cost of the MK4006 memory chip made it the runaway favorite to IBM and other [mainframe](Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") and [minicomputer](Minicomputer "Minicomputer") manufacturers (cf. , [Digital Equipment Corporation](Digital_Equipment_Corporation "Digital Equipment Corporation")). In 1970 , a Japanese [adding machine](Adding_machine "Adding machine") manufacturer, approached and Mostek with a proposal to introduce a new electronic calculator line. Intel responded first, providing them with the [Intel 4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004"), which they used in a line of desktop calculators. Mostek's device took longer to develop but was the world's first **single chip calculator**, the MK6010, used for the Busicom LE-120A which went on the market in 1971 and was the smallest calculator available for some time.[[2]](Mostek#cite_note-Popular_Science_Jun_1971-2) also contracted with Mostek for design and production of chips for their and calculators. ## World leader in DRAM Mostek co-founder Robert Proebsting invented address multiplexing with the MK4096 4096 X 1 bit DRAM introduced in 1973. [Address multiplexing](Bus_(computing)#Address_multiplexing "Bus (computing)") was a revolutionary approach which reduced cost and board space by fitting a 4K DRAM into a 16 pin package, while competitors took the evolutionary approach which led to a bulky and relatively expensive 22 pin package. Competitors derided the Mostek approach as unnecessarily complex, but Proebsting understood the future roadmap for DRAM memories would benefit greatly if only one new pin were needed for every 4X increase in memory size, instead of the two pins per 4X for the evolutionary approach. Computer manufacturers found address multiplexing to be a compelling feature as they saw that a future 64K DRAM chip would save 8 pins if implemented with address multiplexing and subsequent generations even more. Per pin costs are a major cost driver in integrated circuits, plus the multiplexed approach used less silicon area, which further reduces chip cost. The MK4096 was produced using an NMOS aluminum-gate process with an added interconnect layer of polysilicon (dubbed the SPIN process). The [fear, uncertainty and doubt](Fear%2C_uncertainty_and_doubt "Fear, uncertainty and doubt") put up by the competition regarding address multiplexing was dispelled by the actual performance of the MK4096 which proved solid and robust in all types of computer memory designs. In 1976 Mostek introduced the [silicon-gate](Silicon-gate "Silicon-gate") MK4027 (an improved version of the metal-gated MK4096), and in 1977 the MK4116 16K double-poly silicon-gate DRAM. They were designed by Paul Schroeder and Robert Proebsting (Schroeder later left Mostek to co-found ). The MK4116 achieved **greater than 75% worldwide DRAM market share.** The MK4027 and MK4116 were reverse-engineered by Mosaid and successfully cloned by many companies, both USA and overseas-based. The 64K generation of DRAMs required a transition from 12V & +/−5V to 5V-only operation, in order to free the +12V and −5V pins for use as addresses (the +5V and ground pins were assigned to pins 8 and 16, respectively, rather than the 16-pin TTL DIP standard of pin 8 for ground and pin 16 for +5V). While most competitors took a conservative approach by simply shrinking (scaling) their 64Ks, Mostek undertook a major redesign which incorporated forward-looking features (such as controlled pre-charge current) that were not necessary at the 64K level and delayed entry into the market. Mostek's DRAM legacy is exemplified in the MK4116, MK4164 and MK41256. "By four" DRAM was a simple adaptation of the MK4116/MK4164/MK41256 technology, utilizing a larger package to accommodate the additional data bits and multiplexing the data in/out pins as well; the basic *RAS, *CAS, *WRITE and [multiplexed address bus](Bus_(computing)#Bus_multiplexing "Bus (computing)") concept was retained intact. ## World leader in telecommunications products Mostek enjoyed many years of mastery of the international market for telecommunications products. Their product line included telephone tone and pulse dialers, [touchtone](Touchtone "Touchtone") decoders, counters, top-octave generators (used by [Hammond](Hammond_organ "Hammond organ"), [Baldwin](Baldwin_Piano_Company "Baldwin Piano Company"), and others), [CODECs](CODEC "CODEC"), watch circuits, and a host of custom products for a variety of customers. The products used the simple [aluminium-gate](Aluminum-gate "Aluminum-gate") [PMOS](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") (& later aluminium-gate ) process and helped maintain Mostek's cash flow through intense DRAM competition, and other semiconductor market pressures. In 1975 a smoky fire in the [wafer fab](Wafer_fabrication "Wafer fabrication") closed it for several months and production of some critical products was shifted to a friendly fab () in Silicon Valley. Several employees played a key role in the Telecommunications and Industrial Products Department. Bob Paluck headed the department and later Dave Seeler, assisted by Mike Callahan, Charles Johnson, William Bradley, Robert C. Jones, Bob Banks, Ted Lewis, Darin Kincaid, and William Cummings. Telecom marketing was handled by John Crago, Randall Hopkins, and Henry Wasik. Lewis and Bradley were designated as key employees after the United Technologies purchase. Bradley designed all of the custom products based on the single-chip-calculator platform, as well as the code for the wristwatch chips produced by Mostek for and other customers. For a short while, Paluck headed a joint venture called Mostek Hong Kong, a collaboration with Bulova for the production of high-end wristwatches based on Mostek designs. *Rapidus Corporation*

|  | |
| --- | --- |
| [Trade name](Trade_name "Trade name") | Rapidus |
| Native name | Rapidus株式会社 |
| Type | Private [KK](Kabushiki_Gaisha "Kabushiki Gaisha") |
| Industry | [Semiconductor industry](Semiconductor_industry "Semiconductor industry") |
| Founded | August 10, 2022 (2022-08-10) in <Tokyo>, <Japan> |
| Headquarters | [Chiyoda, Tokyo](Chiyoda%2C_Tokyo "Chiyoda, Tokyo"), Japan |
| Key people | Tetsuro Higashi (Chairman)[[1]](Rapidus#cite_note-1)    Atsuyoshi Koike (President and CEO) |
| Website | [www.rapidus.inc](https://www.rapidus.inc/) |


**Rapidus Corporation** ([Japanese](Japanese_language "Japanese language"): Rapidus株式会社, [Hepburn](Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *Rapidus <Kabushiki-gaisha>*) is a [semiconductor manufacturer](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication") headquartered in [Chiyoda, Tokyo](Chiyoda%2C_Tokyo "Chiyoda, Tokyo"), <Japan>. Rapidus was established in August 2022 with the support of eight major Japanese companies: <Denso>, <Kioxia>, [MUFG Bank](MUFG_Bank "MUFG Bank"), <NEC>, [NTT](Nippon_Telegraph_and_Telephone "Nippon Telegraph and Telephone"), <SoftBank>, <Sony>, and <Toyota>. The goal of Rapidus is to increase advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity with a [2 nm process](2_nm_process "2 nm process") by 2027.[[2]](Rapidus#cite_note-2)

## Background history

The semiconductor industry in Japan was highly competitive in the 1980s, with a global share reaching 50%.[[3]](Rapidus#cite_note-3) However, the 1986 Japan-United States semiconductor agreement concluded to resolve [trade friction](Japan-United_States_relations "Japan-United States relations") and the rise of [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea") and <Taiwan> gradually reduced competitiveness.[[4]](Rapidus#cite_note-4) In 1999, [Elpida Memory](Micron_Memory_Japan "Micron Memory Japan") was established by integrating the businesses of <Hitachi> and <NEC> for [DRAM](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory"), one of the semiconductors for memory, and later took over the business of [Mitsubishi Electric](Mitsubishi_Electric "Mitsubishi Electric"), and at one point acquired the world's third largest market share in this field. However, management deteriorated due to the [Lehman shock](Bankruptcy_of_Lehman_Brothers "Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers") in 2009 and the subsequent [yen appreciation recession](Endaka "Endaka"), and although support was provided with government funds, it went bankrupt in 2012.[[5]](Rapidus#cite_note-5) Elpida was acquired by [Micron Technology](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology") in 2013,[[6]](Rapidus#cite_note-6) and changed its name to [Micron Memory Japan](Micron_Memory_Japan "Micron Memory Japan") in 2014.[[7]](Rapidus#cite_note-:0-7) Due to international competition from companies including <TSMC>, [Samsung Electronics](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"), and <Intel>, the share of Japanese companies in the semiconductor industry as a whole has fallen to 10% as of 2019.[[8]](Rapidus#cite_note-8)[[9]](Rapidus#cite_note-9)

In May 2022, United States President [Joe Biden](Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") and Japanese Prime Minister [Fumio Kishida](Fumio_Kishida "Fumio Kishida") met in Tokyo and discussed increased collaboration on important technologies, including semiconductors, [nuclear power](Nuclear_power "Nuclear power"), [space exploration](Space_exploration "Space exploration"), [electric batteries](Electric_batteries "Electric batteries"), [critical minerals](List_of_elements_facing_shortage "List of elements facing shortage"), and [supply chains](Supply_chains "Supply chains").[[10]](Rapidus#cite_note-10) The [Second Kishida Cabinet](Second_Kishida_Cabinet "Second Kishida Cabinet")'s basic policy (*[Honebuto no hōshin](Honebuto_no_h%C5%8Dshin "Honebuto no hōshin")*) announced on 7 June 2022 included consideration of support for private companies developing next-generation advanced technologies and the establishment of a design and manufacturing infrastructure for next-generation semiconductors in the latter half of the 2020s. On 29 July 2022, high-level talks were held between the United States and Japan by U.S. Secretary of State [Antony Blinken](Antony_Blinken "Antony Blinken"), U.S. Commerce Secretary [Gina Raimondo](Gina_Raimondo "Gina Raimondo"), Japanese Foreign Minister [Yoshimasa Hayashi](Yoshimasa_Hayashi "Yoshimasa Hayashi") and Japanese Trade Minister [Koichi Hagiuda](Koichi_Hagiuda "Koichi Hagiuda") to discuss collaboration for semiconductors development.[[11]](Rapidus#cite_note-11) In addition, Prime Minister Fumio Kishida's policy speech at the 210th session of the Diet on 3 October 2022 included [digital transformation](Digital_transformation "Digital transformation") (DX) by encouraging public and private investment, and announced that it would promote the technological development and mass production of next-generation semiconductors through Japan-U.S. collaboration. The [Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry](Ministry_of_Economy%2C_Trade_and_Industry "Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry") (METI) has decided to establish the Leading-edge Semiconductor Technology Center (LSTC) as an organization to conduct next-generation semiconductor research in anticipation of joint research between the two countries based on the basic principles of semiconductor cooperation between Japan and the United States agreed on in May. LSTC and Rapidus collaborate to establish a design and manufacturing platform for next-generation semiconductors in Japan.[[12]](Rapidus#cite_note-:1-12)

## Company history

### 2022

On 10 August 2022, Rapidus was established by eight Japanese companies with total investment of 7.3 billion yen[[13]](Rapidus#cite_note-13) for domestic production of advanced semiconductors; with further investments totaling $36 billion expected over a decade.[[14]](Rapidus#cite_note-14)[[15]](Rapidus#cite_note-15) Rapidus is led by Tetsuro Higashi (who formerly led [Tokyo Electron](Tokyo_Electron "Tokyo Electron"))[[16]](Rapidus#cite_note-16) and Atsuyoshi Koike (who formerly led [Western Digital](Western_Digital "Western Digital")'s Japanese subsidiary).[[17]](Rapidus#cite_note-17) In the same year, METI and the [New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization](New_Energy_and_Industrial_Technology_Development_Organization "New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization") (NEDO) publicly solicited applications for advanced semiconductor development consignment projects related to strengthening the foundation of [post-5G](6G_(network) "6G (network)") communication systems, which resulted in 70 billion yen of government subsidies for Rapidus.[[18]](Rapidus#cite_note-18)[[19]](Rapidus#cite_note-19)

On 6 December 2022, <IMEC> announced it had signed a Memorandum of Cooperation with Rapidus, where both companies will set up a long-term and sustainable collaboration on advanced semiconductor technologies, while Rapidus would plan to mass-produce chips in 2-nanometer technology in Japan in the latter half of 2020s.[[20]](Rapidus#cite_note-20)[[21]](Rapidus#cite_note-21)[[22]](Rapidus#cite_note-22)[[23]](Rapidus#cite_note-23)

On 13 December 2022, <IBM> and Rapidus announced the development of 2 nanometer node technology, with production of the [nanosheet](Nanosheet "Nanosheet") [gate-all-around FET](Multigate_device#Gate-all-around_FET_(GAAFET) "Multigate device") (GAA FET) devices previously announced by IBM in 2021[[12]](Rapidus#cite_note-:1-12)[[24]](Rapidus#cite_note-24) to be done by Rapidus at its fab in Japan.[[25]](Rapidus#cite_note-25)[[26]](Rapidus#cite_note-26)[[27]](Rapidus#cite_note-27)[[28]](Rapidus#cite_note-28) The 2 nm semiconductor chips which Rapidus is aiming to produce are expected to have up to 45% better performance and use 75% less energy compared to 7 nm chips on the market in 2022.[[29]](Rapidus#cite_note-29)

### 2023

In January 2023, representatives of Rapidus and IBM participated in a meeting between Japanese Trade Minister Hagiuda's successor, [Yasutoshi Nishimura](Yasutoshi_Nishimura "Yasutoshi Nishimura"), and Secretary Raimondo.[[30]](Rapidus#cite_note-30)

In February 2023, Rapidus announced the selection of a site close to the [New Chitose Airport](New_Chitose_Airport "New Chitose Airport") in [Chitose](Chitose%2C_Hokkaido "Chitose, Hokkaido"), <Hokkaido> for the location of its planned factory.[[31]](Rapidus#cite_note-31)[[32]](Rapidus#cite_note-32) Rapidus also increased its partnership with imec by joining the latter's "Core Partner Program" in April 2023,[[33]](Rapidus#cite_note-33)[[34]](Rapidus#cite_note-34) and in the same month received additional funding of 260 billion yen from the Japanese government.[[35]](Rapidus#cite_note-35) An estimated $37 billion in total funding is needed before Rapidus can begin production.[[36]](Rapidus#cite_note-36)

In July 2023, Rapidus and [Tokyo Electron](Tokyo_Electron "Tokyo Electron") were discussed as companies that would "play a major role" in a new [memorandum of understanding](Memorandum_of_understanding "Memorandum of understanding") between Japan and <India> that is expected to involve $35.9 billion of investment by Japan in India by 2027[[37]](Rapidus#cite_note-37) and was officially signed in [New Delhi](New_Delhi "New Delhi") by ministers Yasutoshi Nishimura and [Ashwini Vaishnaw](Ashwini_Vaishnaw "Ashwini Vaishnaw") for their countries respectively.[[38]](Rapidus#cite_note-38)[[39]](Rapidus#cite_note-39) This agreement closely followed a similar deal between the United States and India which had been reached by President Joe Biden and Prime Minister [Narendra Modi](Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi") in June.[[40]](Rapidus#cite_note-40)[[41]](Rapidus#cite_note-41)

Intel (*Int*egrated *el*ectronics) was founded on July 18, 1968, by semiconductor pioneers [Gordon Moore](Gordon_Moore "Gordon Moore") (of [Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law")), [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce") (1927–1990), [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock") (venture capitalist) and is associated with the executive leadership and vision of [Andrew Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove").[[7]](Intel#cite_note-7) Intel was a key component of the rise of [Silicon Valley](Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley") as a high-tech center. Noyce was a key inventor of the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit#Invention "Integrated circuit") (microchip).[[8]](Intel#cite_note-8)[[9]](Intel#cite_note-9) Intel was an early developer of [SRAM](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") and [DRAM](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") memory chips, which represented the majority of its business until 1981. Although Intel created the world's first commercial microprocessor chip in 1971, it was not until the success of the [personal computer](Personal_computer "Personal computer") (PC) that this became its primary business. During the 1990s, Intel invested heavily in new microprocessor designs fostering the rapid growth of the [computer industry](Information_technology "Information technology"). During this period, Intel became the [dominant](Dominance_(economics) "Dominance (economics)") supplier of PC microprocessors and was known for aggressive and anti-competitive tactics in defense of its market position, particularly against , as well as a struggle with for control over the direction of the PC industry.[[10]](Intel#cite_note-CNET_September_23,_1998-10)[[11]](Intel#cite_note-BBC_December_14,_1998-11) The Open Source Technology Center at Intel hosts and , and supports other open-source projects such as [Wayland](Wayland_(protocol) "Wayland (protocol)"), [Mesa](Mesa_(computer_graphics) "Mesa (computer graphics)"), [Threading Building Blocks](Threading_Building_Blocks "Threading Building Blocks") (TBB), and .[[12]](Intel#cite_note-12) ## Current operations ### Operating segments - **Client Computing Group** – 51.8% of 2020 revenues – produces [PC processors](Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") and related components.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13)[[14]](Intel#cite_note-14) - **Data Center Group** – 33.7% of 2020 revenues – produces hardware components used in server, network, and storage platforms.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13) - **Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group** – 6.9% of 2020 revenues – produces components for [solid-state drives](Solid-state_drive "Solid-state drive"): [NAND flash memory](NAND_flash_memory "NAND flash memory") and [3D XPoint](3D_XPoint "3D XPoint") ().[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13) - **Internet of Things Group** – 5.2% of 2020 revenues – offers platforms designed for retail, transportation, industrial, buildings and home use.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13) - **Programmable Solutions Group** – 2.4% of 2020 revenues – manufactures programmable semiconductors (primarily [FPGAs](FPGA "FPGA")).[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13) ### Customers In 2020, accounted for about 17% of Intel's total revenues, accounted for 12% of total revenues, and [HP Inc.](HP_Inc. "HP Inc.") accounted for 10% of total revenues.[[1]](Intel#cite_note-xbrlus_1-1) As of August 2021, the US [Department of Defense](Department_of_Defence "Department of Defence") is another large customer for Intel.[[15]](Intel#cite_note-15)[[16]](Intel#cite_note-16)[[17]](Intel#cite_note-17)[[18]](Intel#cite_note-18) ### Market share According to [IDC](International_Data_Corporation "International Data Corporation"), while Intel enjoyed the biggest market share in both the overall worldwide PC microprocessor market (73.3%) and the mobile PC microprocessor (80.4%) in the second quarter of 2011, the numbers decreased by 1.5% and 1.9% compared to the first quarter of 2011.[[19]](Intel#cite_note-19)[[20]](Intel#cite_note-20) Intel's market share decreased significantly in the enthusiast market as of 2019,[[21]](Intel#cite_note-21) and they have faced delays for their 10 nm products. According to former Intel CEO Bob Swan, the delay was caused by the company's overly aggressive strategy for moving to its next node.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22) #### Historical market share In the 1980s, Intel was among the world's top ten sellers of [semiconductors](Semiconductors "Semiconductors") (10th in 1987). Along with [Microsoft Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows"), it was part of the "" personal computer domination in the 1990s and early [2000s](2000s_decade "2000s decade"). In 1992, Intel became the biggest chip maker by revenue and held the position until 2018 when Samsung surpassed it, but Intel returned to its former position the year after.[[23]](Intel#cite_note-23)[[24]](Intel#cite_note-24) Other major semiconductor companies include , , , [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"), , , [United Microelectronics Corporation](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation") (UMC), [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology"), [SK Hynix](SK_Hynix "SK Hynix"), , and [SMIC](Semiconductor_Manufacturing_International_Corporation "Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation"). ### Major competitors Intel's competitors in PC chipsets included , [VIA Technologies](VIA_Technologies "VIA Technologies"), [Silicon Integrated Systems](Silicon_Integrated_Systems "Silicon Integrated Systems"), and . The only major competitor in the [x86](X86 "X86") processor market is AMD, with which Intel has had full cross-licensing agreements since 1976: each partner can use the other's patented technological innovations without charge after a certain time.[[25]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-AMD_deal_2001-25) However, the cross-licensing agreement is canceled in the event of an AMD bankruptcy or takeover.[[26]](Intel#cite_note-Patent_Cross_License_Agreement-26) Some smaller competitors, such as VIA Technologies, produce [low-power](Low-power_electronics "Low-power electronics") x86 processors for small factor computers and portable equipment. However, the advent of such mobile computing devices, in particular, [smartphones](Smartphone "Smartphone"), has in recent years led to a decline in PC sales.[[27]](Intel#cite_note-27) Since over 95% of the world's smartphones currently use processors cores designed by [Arm](Arm_(company) "Arm (company)"), using the [Arm instruction set](ARM_architecture_family "ARM architecture family"), Arm has become a major competitor for Intel's processor market.
