Intel has been involved in several disputes regarding the violation of [antitrust laws](Antitrust_laws "Antitrust laws"), which are noted below. ### Carbon footprint Intel reported Total [CO2e emissions](Carbon_footprint "Carbon footprint") (Direct + Indirect) for the twelve months ending 31 December 2020 at 2,882 Kt (+94/+3.4% y-o-y).[[29]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Total_CO2e_emissions_for_2020Q4-29) Intel plans to reduce carbon emissions 10% by 2030 from a 2020 base year.[[30]](Intel#cite_note-30) *Intel's annual Total [CO2e emissions](Carbon_footprint "Carbon footprint") (Direct + Indirect) (in kilotonnes)* | Dec 2017 | Dec 2018 | Dec 2019 | Dec 2020 | Dec 2021 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 2,461[[31]](Intel#cite_note-31) | 2,578[[32]](Intel#cite_note-32) | 2,788[[33]](Intel#cite_note-33) | 2,882[[29]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Total_CO2e_emissions_for_2020Q4-29) | 3,274[[34]](Intel#cite_note-34) | ## History For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Intel](Timeline_of_Intel "Timeline of Intel"). ### Origins Intel was incorporated in [Mountain View, California](Mountain_View%2C_California "Mountain View, California"), on July 18, 1968, by [Gordon E. Moore](Gordon_E._Moore "Gordon E. Moore") (known for "[Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law")"), a [chemist](Chemist "Chemist"), [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce"), a physicist and co-inventor of the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") and [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock"), an investor and [venture capitalist](Venture_capital "Venture capital")[[35]](Intel#cite_note-35)[[36]](Intel#cite_note-36)[[37]](Intel#cite_note-37) Moore and Noyce had left [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") and were part of the "[traitorous eight](Traitorous_eight "Traitorous eight")". There were originally 500,000 shares outstanding of which Dr. Noyce bought 245,000 shares, Dr. Moore 245,000 shares, and Mr. Rock 10,000 shares; all at $1 per share. Rock offered $2,500,000 of convertible debentures to a limited group of private investors (equivalent to $21 million in 2022), convertible at $5 per share.[[38]](Intel#cite_note-38)[[39]](Intel#cite_note-39) Just 2 years later, Intel became a [public company](Public_company "Public company") via an [initial public offering](Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO), raising $6.8 million ($23.50 per share).[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) Intel's third employee was [Andy Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove"),[[note 1]](Intel#cite_note-41) a [chemical engineer](Chemical_engineer "Chemical engineer"), who later ran the company through much of the 1980s and the high-growth 1990s. In deciding on a name, Moore and Noyce quickly rejected "Moore Noyce",[[41]](Intel#cite_note-42) near [homophone](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/homophone "wikt:homophone") for "more noise" – an ill-suited name for an [electronics](Electronics "Electronics") company, since [noise in electronics](Electronic_noise "Electronic noise") is usually undesirable and typically associated with bad [interference](Electromagnetic_interference "Electromagnetic interference"). Instead, they founded the company as **NM Electronics** (or **MN Electronics**) on July 18, 1968, but by the end of the month had changed the name to **Intel** which stood for **Int**egrated **El**ectronics.[[note 2]](Intel#cite_note-48) Since "Intel" was already trademarked by the hotel chain Intelco, they had to buy the rights for the name.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[47]](Intel#cite_note-49) ### Early history At its founding, Intel was distinguished by its ability to make [logic circuits](Logic_circuit "Logic circuit") using [semiconductor devices](Semiconductor_device "Semiconductor device"). The founders' goal was the [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") market, widely predicted to replace [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory"). Its first product, a quick entry into the small, high-speed memory market in 1969, was the 3101 [Schottky TTL](Schottky_transistor "Schottky transistor") [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") 64-bit [static random-access memory](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") (SRAM), which was nearly twice as fast as earlier Schottky diode implementations by Fairchild and the Electrotechnical Laboratory in [Tsukuba, Japan](Tsukuba%2C_Ibaraki "Tsukuba, Ibaraki").[[48]](Intel#cite_note-50)[[49]](Intel#cite_note-51) In the same year, Intel also produced the 3301 Schottky bipolar 1024-bit [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM)[[50]](Intel#cite_note-52) and the first commercial [metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor](MOSFET "MOSFET") (MOSFET) [silicon gate](Silicon_gate "Silicon gate") SRAM chip, the 256-bit 1101.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[52]](Intel#cite_note-54) While the 1101 was a significant advance, its complex static [cell structure](Memory_cell_(computing) "Memory cell (computing)") made it too slow and costly for [mainframe](Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") memories. The three-[transistor](Transistor "Transistor") cell implemented in the first commercially available [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM), the [1103](Intel_1103 "Intel 1103") released in 1970, solved these issues. The 1103 was the bestselling semiconductor memory chip in the world by 1972, as it replaced core memory in many applications.[[53]](Intel#cite_note-55)[[54]](Intel#cite_note-Bellis-56) Intel's business grew during the 1970s as it expanded and improved its manufacturing processes and produced a wider range of [products](Product_(business) "Product (business)"), still dominated by various memory devices. Intel created the [first commercially available microprocessor (Intel 4004)](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") in 1971.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) The microprocessor represented a notable advance in the technology of integrated circuitry, as it miniaturized the central processing unit of a computer, which then made it possible for small machines to perform calculations that in the past only very large machines could do. Considerable technological innovation was needed before the microprocessor could actually become the basis of what was first known as a "mini computer" and then known as a "personal computer".[[55]](Intel#cite_note-57) Intel also created one of the first [microcomputers](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1973.[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[56]](Intel#cite_note-Intellec-1973-58) Intel opened its first international manufacturing facility in 1972, in , which would host multiple Intel operations, before opening assembly facilities and semiconductor plants in and in the early 1980s, and manufacturing and development centers in China, India, and Costa Rica in the 1990s.[[57]](Intel#cite_note-59) By the early 1980s, its business was dominated by [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM) chips. However, increased competition from Japanese semiconductor manufacturers had, by 1983, dramatically reduced the profitability of this market. The growing success of the personal computer, based on an Intel microprocessor, was among factors that convinced Gordon Moore (CEO since 1975) to shift the company's focus to microprocessors and to change fundamental aspects of that business model. Moore's decision to sole-source Intel's 386 chip played into the company's continuing success. By the end of the 1980s, buoyed by its fortuitous position as microprocessor supplier to IBM and IBM's competitors within the rapidly growing [personal computer market](IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible"), Intel embarked on a 10-year period of unprecedented growth as the primary (and most profitable) hardware supplier to the PC industry, part of the winning 'Wintel' combination. Moore handed over his position as CEO to Andy Grove in 1987. By launching its Intel Inside [marketing campaign](Marketing_campaign "Marketing campaign") in 1991, Intel was able to associate [brand loyalty](Brand_loyalty "Brand loyalty") with consumer selection, so that by the end of the 1990s, its line of processors had become a household name. ### Challenges to dominance (2000s) After 2000, growth in demand for high-end microprocessors slowed. Competitors, most notably (Intel's largest competitor in its primary [x86](X86 "X86") architecture market), garnered significant market share, initially in low-end and mid-range processors but ultimately across the product range, and Intel's dominant position in its core market was greatly reduced,[[58]](Intel#cite_note-Wong-60) mostly due to controversial microarchitecture. In the early 2000s then-CEO, [Craig Barrett](Craig_Barrett_(businessman) "Craig Barrett (businessman)") attempted to diversify the company's business beyond semiconductors, but few of these activities were ultimately successful. #### Litigation Intel had also for a number of years been embroiled in litigation. US law did not initially recognize [intellectual property rights](Intellectual_property_rights "Intellectual property rights") related to microprocessor [topology](Topology_(electrical_circuits) "Topology (electrical circuits)") (circuit layouts), until the [Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984](Semiconductor_Chip_Protection_Act_of_1984 "Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984"), a law sought by Intel and the [Semiconductor Industry Association](Semiconductor_Industry_Association "Semiconductor Industry Association") (SIA).[[59]](Intel#cite_note-61) During the late 1980s and 1990s (after this law was passed), Intel also sued companies that tried to develop competitor chips to the [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386") .[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) The lawsuits were noted to significantly burden the competition with legal bills, even if Intel lost the suits.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) allegations had been simmering since the early 1990s and had been the cause of one [lawsuit](Lawsuit "Lawsuit") against Intel in 1991. In 2004 and 2005, AMD brought [further claims](Intel_Corp._v._Advanced_Micro_Devices%2C_Inc. "Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.") against Intel related to [unfair competition](Unfair_competition "Unfair competition"). ### Reorganization and success with Intel Core (2005–2015) In 2005, CEO [Paul Otellini](Paul_Otellini "Paul Otellini") reorganized the company to refocus its core processor and chipset business on platforms (enterprise, digital home, digital health, and mobility). On June 6, 2005, [Steve Jobs](Steve_Jobs "Steve Jobs"), then CEO of [Apple](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), announced that Apple would be using Intel's x86 processors for its computers, switching from the architecture developed by the [AIM alliance](AIM_alliance "AIM alliance").[[61]](Intel#cite_note-auto2-63) This was seen as win for Intel;[[62]](Intel#cite_note-auto1-64) An analyst called the move "risky" and "foolish", as Intel's current offerings at the time were considered to be behind those of AMD and IBM.[[63]](Intel#cite_note-Computerworld1-65) In 2006, Intel unveiled its [Core microarchitecture](Core_(microarchitecture) "Core (microarchitecture)") to widespread critical acclaim; the product range was perceived as an exceptional leap in processor performance that at a stroke regained much of its leadership of the field.[[64]](Intel#cite_note-66)[[65]](Intel#cite_note-67) In 2008, Intel had another "tick" when it introduced the Penryn microarchitecture, fabricated using the 45 nm process node. Later that year, Intel released a processor with the [Nehalem](Nehalem_(microarchitecture) "Nehalem (microarchitecture)") architecture to positive reception.[[66]](Intel#cite_note-68) On June 27, 2006, the sale of Intel's assets was announced. Intel agreed to sell the XScale processor business to [Marvell Technology Group](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group") for an estimated $600 million and the assumption of unspecified liabilities. The move was intended to permit Intel to focus its resources on its core x86 and server businesses, and the [acquisition](Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions") completed on November 9, 2006.[[67]](Intel#cite_note-XScale-69) In 2008, Intel spun off key assets of a solar startup business effort to form an independent company, SpectraWatt Inc. In 2011, SpectraWatt filed for bankruptcy.[[68]](Intel#cite_note-eetimes1-70) In February 2011, Intel began to build a new microprocessor manufacturing facility in [Chandler, Arizona](Chandler%2C_Arizona "Chandler, Arizona"), completed in 2013 at a cost of $5 billion.[[69]](Intel#cite_note-71) The building is now the 10 nm-certified Fab 42 and is connected to the other Fabs (12, 22, 32) on Ocotillo Campus via an enclosed bridge known as the Link.[[70]](Intel#cite_note-72)[[71]](Intel#cite_note-73)[[72]](Intel#cite_note-74)[[73]](Intel#cite_note-75) The company produces three-quarters of its products in the United States, although three-quarters of its revenue come from overseas.[[74]](Intel#cite_note-76) The [Alliance for Affordable Internet](Alliance_for_Affordable_Internet "Alliance for Affordable Internet") (A4AI) was launched in October 2013 and Intel is part of the coalition of public and private organizations that also includes , , and . Led by [Sir Tim Berners-Lee](Tim_Berners-Lee "Tim Berners-Lee"), the A4AI seeks to make Internet access more affordable so that access is broadened in the developing world, where only 31% of people are online. Google will help to decrease Internet access prices so that they fall below the UN Broadband Commission's worldwide target of 5% of monthly income.[[75]](Intel#cite_note-77) #### Attempts at entering the smartphone market In April 2011, Intel began a pilot project with [ZTE Corporation](ZTE_Corporation "ZTE Corporation") to produce smartphones using the [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processor for China's domestic market. In December 2011, Intel announced that it reorganized several of its business units into a new mobile and communications group[[76]](Intel#cite_note-78) that would be responsible for the company's smartphone, tablet, and wireless efforts. Intel planned to introduce Medfield – a processor for tablets and smartphones – to the market in 2012, as an effort to compete with Arm.[[77]](Intel#cite_note-79) As a 32-nanometer processor, Medfield is designed to be energy-efficient, which is one of the core features in Arm's chips.[[78]](Intel#cite_note-autogenerated12-80) At the Intel Developers Forum (IDF) 2011 in San Francisco, Intel's partnership with Google was announced. In January 2012, Google announced Android 2.3, supporting Intel's Atom microprocessor.[[79]](Intel#cite_note-81)[[80]](Intel#cite_note-82)[[81]](Intel#cite_note-83) In 2013, Intel's Kirk Skaugen said that Intel's exclusive focus on Microsoft platforms was a thing of the past and that they would now support all "tier-one operating systems" such as Linux, Android, iOS, and Chrome.[[82]](Intel#cite_note-84) In 2014, Intel cut thousands of employees in response to "evolving market trends",[[83]](Intel#cite_note-85) and offered to subsidize manufacturers for the extra costs involved in using Intel chips in their tablets. In April 2016, Intel cancelled the platform and the Broxton Atom SoC for smartphones,[[84]](Intel#cite_note-86)[[85]](Intel#cite_note-87)[[86]](Intel#cite_note-88)[[87]](Intel#cite_note-89) effectively leaving the smartphone market.[[88]](Intel#cite_note-MyUser_Theverge.com_June_1_2016c-90)[[89]](Intel#cite_note-verge2-91) #### Intel custom foundry Finding itself with excess fab capacity after the failure of the to gain market traction and with PC sales declining, in 2013 Intel reached a [foundry](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") agreement to produce chips for using a 14nm process. General Manager of Intel's custom foundry division Sunit Rikhi indicated that Intel would pursue further such deals in the future.[[90]](Intel#cite_note-92) This was after poor sales of [Windows 8](Windows_8 "Windows 8") hardware caused a major retrenchment for most of the major semiconductor manufacturers, except for Qualcomm, which continued to see healthy purchases from its largest customer, Apple.[[91]](Intel#cite_note-93) As of July 2013, five companies were using Intel's fabs via the *Intel Custom Foundry* division: , [Tabula](Tabula_(company) "Tabula (company)"), , , and  – most are [field-programmable gate array](Field-programmable_gate_array "Field-programmable gate array") (FPGA) makers, but Netronome designs network processors. Only Achronix began shipping chips made by Intel using the 22nm Tri-Gate process.[[92]](Intel#cite_note-94)[[93]](Intel#cite_note-95) Several other customers also exist but were not announced at the time.[[94]](Intel#cite_note-96) The foundry business was closed in 2018 due to Intel's issues with its manufacturing.[[95]](Intel#cite_note-97)[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98) ### Security and manufacturing challenges (2016–2021) Intel continued its [tick-tock](Tick%E2%80%93tock_model "Tick–tock model") model of a microarchitecture change followed by a die shrink until the 6th generation Core family based on the [Skylake](Skylake_(microarchitecture) "Skylake (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture. This model was deprecated in 2016, with the release of the seventh generation Core family (codenamed [Kaby Lake](Kaby_Lake "Kaby Lake")), ushering in the [process–architecture–optimization model](Process%E2%80%93architecture%E2%80%93optimization_model "Process–architecture–optimization model"). As Intel struggled to shrink their process node from [14 nm](14_nm_process "14 nm process") to [10 nm](10_nm_process "10 nm process"), processor development slowed down and the company continued to use the Skylake microarchitecture until 2020, albeit with optimizations.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22) #### 10 nm process node issues While Intel originally planned to introduce 10 nm products in 2016, it later became apparent that there were manufacturing issues with the node.[[97]](Intel#cite_note-99) The first microprocessor under that node, [Cannon Lake](Cannon_Lake_(microarchitecture) "Cannon Lake (microarchitecture)") (marketed as 8th generation Core), was released in small quantities in 2018.[[98]](Intel#cite_note-Cutress-100)[[99]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_discontinues_Cannon_Lake_NUC-101) The company first delayed the mass production of their 10 nm products to 2017.[[100]](Intel#cite_note-102)[[101]](Intel#cite_note-103) They later delayed mass production to 2018,[[102]](Intel#cite_note-104) and then to 2019. Despite rumors of the process being cancelled,[[103]](Intel#cite_note-105) Intel finally introduced mass-produced 10 nm 10th generation Intel Core mobile processors (codenamed "[Ice Lake](Ice_Lake_(microprocessor) "Ice Lake (microprocessor)")") in September 2019.[[104]](Intel#cite_note-106) Intel later acknowledged that their strategy to shrink to 10 nm was too aggressive.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)[[105]](Intel#cite_note-107) While other foundries used up to four steps in 10 nm or 7 nm processes, the company's 10 nm process required up to five or six multi-pattern steps.[[106]](Intel#cite_note-108) In addition, Intel's 10 nm process is denser than its counterpart processes from other foundries.[[107]](Intel#cite_note-109)[[108]](Intel#cite_note-110) Since Intel's microarchitecture and process node development were coupled, processor development stagnated.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22) #### Security flaws In early January 2018, it was reported that all [Intel processors](Intel_CPUs "Intel CPUs") made since 1995,[[109]](Intel#cite_note-111) excluding [Intel Itanium](Intel_Itanium "Intel Itanium") and pre-2013 [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processors, have been subject to two security flaws dubbed [Meltdown](Meltdown_(security_vulnerability) "Meltdown (security vulnerability)") and [Spectre](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)").[[110]](Intel#cite_note-112)[[111]](Intel#cite_note-wiredflaw-113) It is believed that "hundreds of millions" of systems could be affected by these flaws.[[112]](Intel#cite_note-telegraph2018flaw-114)[[113]](Intel#cite_note-115) More security flaws were disclosed on May 3, 2018,[[114]](Intel#cite_note-116) on August 14, 2018, on January 18, 2019, and on March 5, 2020.[[115]](Intel#cite_note-ZDNET-20200305-117)[[116]](Intel#cite_note-AT-20200305-118)[[117]](Intel#cite_note-EG-20200306-119)[[118]](Intel#cite_note-INTEL-20200211-120) On March 15, 2018, Intel reported that it will redesign its [CPUs](Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") to protect against the [Spectre security vulnerability](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)"), the redesigned processors were sold later in 2018.[[119]](Intel#cite_note-TVRG-20180315-121)[[120]](Intel#cite_note-CNET-20180315-122) Existing chips vulnerable to Meltdown and Spectre can be fixed with a [software patch](Patch_(computing) "Patch (computing)") at a cost to performance.[[121]](Intel#cite_note-PCW-20180109-123)[[122]](Intel#cite_note-NYT-20180103-124)[[123]](Intel#cite_note-bbcflaw-125)[[124]](Intel#cite_note-TV-20180104-126) ### Renewed competition and other developments (2018–present) Due to Intel's issues with its 10 nm process node and the company's slow processor development,[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22) the company now found itself in a market with intense competition.[[125]](Intel#cite_note-127) The company's main competitor, AMD, introduced the [Zen](Zen_(microarchitecture) "Zen (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture and a new [chiplet](Chiplet "Chiplet") based design to critical acclaim. Since its introduction, AMD, once unable to compete with Intel in the high-end CPU market, has undergone a resurgence,[[126]](Intel#cite_note-128) and Intel's dominance and market share have considerably decreased.[[127]](Intel#cite_note-129) In addition, Apple began to transition away from the x86 architecture and Intel processors to their own [Apple silicon](Apple_silicon "Apple silicon") for their Macintosh computers in 2020. The transition is expected to affect Intel minimally; however, it might prompt other PC manufacturers to reevaluate their reliance on Intel and the x86 architecture.[[128]](Intel#cite_note-Bloomberg1-130)[[129]](Intel#cite_note-Jean-Louis_Gassée,_2020.06.21-131) #### 'IDM 2.0' strategy On March 23, 2021, CEO Pat Gelsinger laid out new plans for the company.[[130]](Intel#cite_note-132) These include a new strategy, called IDM 2.0, that includes investments in manufacturing facilities, use of both internal and external foundries, and a new foundry business called Intel Foundry Services (IFS), a standalone business unit.[[131]](Intel#cite_note-133)[[132]](Intel#cite_note-134) Unlike Intel Custom Foundry, IFS will offer a combination of packaging and process technology, and Intel's IP portfolio including x86 cores. Other plans for the company include a partnership with and a new event for developers and engineers, called "Intel ON".[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98) Gelsinger also confirmed that Intel's 7 nm process is on track, and that the first products using their 7 nm process (also known as Intel 4) are Ponte Vecchio and Meteor Lake.[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98) In January 2022, Intel reportedly selected [New Albany, Ohio](New_Albany%2C_Ohio "New Albany, Ohio"), near [Columbus, Ohio](Columbus%2C_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), as the site for a major new manufacturing facility.[[133]](Intel#cite_note-135) The facility will cost at least $20 billion.[[134]](Intel#cite_note-136) The company expects the facility to begin producing chips by 2025.[[135]](Intel#cite_note-137) The same year Intel also choose , , as a site for two new chip mega factories for €17 billion (topping [Tesla's](Tesla%2C_Inc. "Tesla, Inc.") [investment](Gigafactory_Berlin-Brandenburg "Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg") in ). Groundbreaking is planned for 2023, while production start is planned for 2027. Including subcontractors this would create 10.000 new jobs.[[136]](Intel#cite_note-138) In August 2022, Intel signed a $30 billion partnership with [Brookfield Asset Management](Brookfield_Asset_Management "Brookfield Asset Management") to fund its recent factory expansions. As part of the deal, Intel would have a controlling stake by funding 51% of the cost of building new chip-making facilities in Chandler, with Brookfield owning the remaining 49% stake, allowing the companies to split the revenue from those facilities.[[137]](Intel#cite_note-139)[[138]](Intel#cite_note-140) On January 31, 2023, as part of $3 billion in cost reductions, Intel announced pay cuts affecting employees above midlevel, ranging from 5% upwards. It also suspended bonuses and merit pay increases, while reducing retirement plan matching. These cost reductions followed layoffs announced in the fall of 2022.[[139]](Intel#cite_note-141) ## Product and market history ### SRAMs, DRAMs, and the microprocessor Intel's first products were [shift register](Shift_register "Shift register") memory and random-access [memory](Primary_storage "Primary storage") integrated circuits, and Intel grew to be a leader in the fiercely competitive [DRAM](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory"), [SRAM](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory"), and [ROM](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") markets throughout the 1970s. Concurrently, Intel engineers [Marcian Hoff](Marcian_Hoff "Marcian Hoff"), [Federico Faggin](Federico_Faggin "Federico Faggin"), [Stanley Mazor](Stanley_Mazor "Stanley Mazor"), and [Masatoshi Shima](Masatoshi_Shima "Masatoshi Shima") invented Intel's first [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor"). Originally developed for the Japanese company to replace a number of [ASICs](Application-specific_integrated_circuit "Application-specific integrated circuit") in a calculator already produced by Busicom, the [Intel 4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") was introduced to the mass market on November 15, 1971, though the microprocessor did not become the core of Intel's business until the mid-1980s. (Note: Intel is usually given credit with [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") for the almost-simultaneous invention of the microprocessor) In 1983, at the dawn of the personal computer era, Intel's profits came under increased pressure from Japanese memory-chip manufacturers, and then-president Andy Grove focused the company on microprocessors. Grove described this transition in the book *[Only the Paranoid Survive](Only_the_Paranoid_Survive "Only the Paranoid Survive")*. A key element of his plan was the notion, then considered radical, of becoming the single source for successors to the popular [8086](Intel_8086 "Intel 8086") microprocessor. Until then, the manufacture of complex integrated circuits was not reliable enough for customers to depend on a single supplier, but Grove began producing processors in three geographically distinct factories, and ceased licensing the chip designs to competitors such as [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices").[[140]](Intel#cite_note-142) When the PC industry boomed in the late 1980s and 1990s, Intel was one of the primary beneficiaries. ### Early x86 processors and the IBM PC Despite the ultimate importance of the microprocessor, the [4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") and its successors the [8008](Intel_8008 "Intel 8008") and the [8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") were never major revenue contributors at Intel. As the next processor, the [8086](Intel_8086 "Intel 8086") (and its variant the 8088) was completed in 1978, Intel embarked on a major marketing and sales campaign for that chip nicknamed "Operation Crush", and intended to win as many customers for the processor as possible. One design win was the newly created [IBM PC](IBM_PC "IBM PC") division, though the importance of this was not fully realized at the time. introduced its personal computer in 1981, and it was rapidly successful. In 1982, Intel created the [80286](Intel_80286 "Intel 80286") microprocessor, which, two years later, was used in the [IBM PC/AT](IBM_Personal_Computer/AT "IBM Personal Computer/AT"). , the first IBM PC "clone" manufacturer, produced a desktop system based on the faster 80286 processor in 1985 and in 1986 quickly followed with the first [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386")-based system, beating IBM and establishing a competitive market for PC-compatible systems and setting up Intel as a key component supplier. In 1975, the company had started a project to develop a highly advanced 32-bit microprocessor, finally released in 1981 as the [Intel iAPX 432](Intel_iAPX_432 "Intel iAPX 432"). The project was too ambitious and the processor was never able to meet its performance objectives, and it failed in the marketplace. Intel extended the [x86 architecture](X86 "X86") to 32 bits instead.[[141]](Intel#cite_note-143)[[142]](Intel#cite_note-144) #### 386 microprocessor During this period [Andrew Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove") dramatically redirected the company, closing much of its business and directing resources to the [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") business. Of perhaps greater importance was his decision to "single-source" the 386 microprocessor. Prior to this, microprocessor manufacturing was in its infancy, and manufacturing problems frequently reduced or stopped production, interrupting supplies to customers. To mitigate this risk, these customers typically insisted that multiple manufacturers produce chips they could use to ensure a consistent supply. The 8080 and 8086-series microprocessors were produced by several companies, notably AMD, with which Intel had a technology-sharing contract. Grove made the decision not to license the 386 design to other manufacturers, instead, producing it in three geographically distinct factories: [Santa Clara](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California"), California; [Hillsboro](Hillsboro%2C_Oregon "Hillsboro, Oregon"), Oregon; and [Chandler](Chandler%2C_Arizona "Chandler, Arizona"), a suburb of [Phoenix](Phoenix%2C_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"), Arizona. He convinced customers that this would ensure consistent delivery. In doing this, Intel breached its contract with AMD, which sued and was paid millions of dollars in damages but could not manufacture new Intel CPU designs any longer. (Instead, AMD started to develop and manufacture its own competing x86 designs.) As the success of 's [Deskpro 386](Compaq_Deskpro_386 "Compaq Deskpro 386") established the 386 as the dominant CPU choice, Intel achieved a position of near-exclusive dominance as its supplier. Profits from this funded rapid development of both higher-performance chip designs and higher-performance manufacturing capabilities, propelling Intel to a position of unquestioned leadership by the early 1990s. #### 486, Pentium, and Itanium Intel introduced the [486](Intel_80486 "Intel 80486") microprocessor in 1989, and in 1990 established a second design team, designing the processors code-named "[P5](P5_(microarchitecture) "P5 (microarchitecture)")" and "[P6](P6_(microarchitecture) "P6 (microarchitecture)")" in parallel and committing to a major new processor every two years, versus the four or more years such designs had previously taken. Engineers [Vinod Dham](Vinod_Dham "Vinod Dham") and [Rajeev Chandrasekhar](Rajeev_Chandrasekhar "Rajeev Chandrasekhar") (Member of Parliament, India) were key figures on the core team that invented the 486 chip and later, Intel's signature Pentium chip. The P5 project was earlier known as "Operation Bicycle", referring to the cycles of the processor through two parallel execution pipelines. The P5 was introduced in 1993 as the Intel , substituting a registered trademark name for the former part number (numbers, such as 486, cannot be legally registered as trademarks in the United States). The P6 followed in 1995 as the [Pentium Pro](Pentium_Pro "Pentium Pro") and improved into the [Pentium II](Pentium_II "Pentium II") in 1997. New architectures were developed alternately in [Santa Clara, California](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California") and [Hillsboro, Oregon](Hillsboro%2C_Oregon "Hillsboro, Oregon"). The Santa Clara design team embarked in 1993 on a successor to the [x86 architecture](X86 "X86"), codenamed "P7". The first attempt was dropped a year later but quickly revived in a cooperative program with engineers, though Intel soon took over primary design responsibility. The resulting implementation of the [IA-64](Itanium "Itanium") 64-bit architecture was the , finally introduced in June 2001. The Itanium's performance running legacy x86 code did not meet expectations, and it failed to compete effectively with [x86-64](X86-64 "X86-64"), which was AMD's 64-bit extension of the 32-bit x86 architecture (Intel uses the name **Intel 64**, previously **EM64T**). In 2017, Intel announced that the [Itanium 9700 series (Kittson)](Kittson_(processor) "Kittson (processor)") would be the last Itanium chips produced.[[143]](Intel#cite_note-Davis_2017-145)[[144]](Intel#cite_note-IA-PCWorld-146) The Hillsboro team designed the [Willamette](Pentium_4#Willamette "Pentium 4") processors (initially code-named P68), which were marketed as the Pentium 4. During this period, Intel undertook two major supporting advertising campaigns. The first campaign, the 1991 "Intel Inside" marketing and branding campaign, is widely known and has become synonymous with Intel itself. The idea of "[ingredient branding](Ingredient_branding "Ingredient branding")" was new at the time, with only and a few others making attempts to do so.[[145]](Intel#cite_note-147) One of the key architects of the marketing team was the head of the microprocessor division, [David House](David_House_(computer_designer) "David House (computer designer)").[[146]](Intel#cite_note-148) He coined the slogan "Intel Inside".[[147]](Intel#cite_note-149) This campaign established Intel, which had been a component supplier little-known outside the PC industry, as a household name. The second campaign, Intel's Systems Group, which began in the early 1990s, showcased manufacturing of PC [motherboards](Motherboard "Motherboard"), the main board component of a personal computer, and the one into which the processor (CPU) and memory (RAM) chips are plugged.[[148]](Intel#cite_note-150) The Systems Group campaign was lesser known than the Intel Inside campaign. Shortly after, Intel began manufacturing fully configured "[white box](White_box_(computer_hardware) "White box (computer hardware)")" systems for the dozens of PC clone companies that rapidly sprang up. At its peak in the mid-1990s, Intel manufactured over 15% of all PCs, making it the third-largest supplier at the time. During the 1990s, [Intel Architecture Labs](Intel_Architecture_Labs "Intel Architecture Labs") (IAL) was responsible for many of the hardware innovations for the PC, including the [PCI](Conventional_PCI "Conventional PCI") Bus, the [PCI Express](PCI_Express "PCI Express") (PCIe) bus, and [Universal Serial Bus](Universal_Serial_Bus "Universal Serial Bus") (USB). IAL's software efforts met with a more mixed fate; its video and graphics software was important in the development of software digital video, but later its efforts were largely overshadowed by competition from . The competition between Intel and Microsoft was revealed in testimony by then IAL Vice-president [Steven McGeady](Steven_McGeady "Steven McGeady") at the [Microsoft antitrust trial](United_States_v._Microsoft_Corp._(2001) "United States v. Microsoft Corp. (2001)") (*United States v. Microsoft Corp.*). #### Pentium flaw Main article: [Pentium FDIV bug](Pentium_FDIV_bug "Pentium FDIV bug") In June 1994, Intel engineers discovered a flaw in the [floating-point](Floating-point "Floating-point") math subsection of the [P5](P5_(microarchitecture) "P5 (microarchitecture)") [Pentium microprocessor](Pentium "Pentium"). (circa) 25,000 (2022) | | Website | [www.amd.com](https://www.amd.com/) | | **Footnotes / references** [[1]](AMD#cite_note-10K-1) | | **Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.**, commonly abbreviated as **AMD**, is an American multinational [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") company based in [Santa Clara, California](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California"), that develops [computer processors](Processor_(computing) "Processor (computing)") and related technologies for business and consumer markets. The company was founded in 1969 by [Jerry Sanders](Jerry_Sanders_(businessman) "Jerry Sanders (businessman)") and a group of other technology professionals. AMD's early products were primarily memory chips and other components for computers. The company later expanded into the microprocessor market, competing with , its main rival in the industry. In the early 2000s, AMD experienced significant growth and success, thanks in part to its strong position in the PC market and the success of its and processors. However, the company faced challenges in the late 2000s and early 2010s, as it struggled to keep up with Intel in the race to produce faster and more powerful processors. In the late 2010s, AMD regained some of its market share thanks to the success of its processors which are now widely regarded as superior to Intel products in business applications including cloud applications. AMD's processors are used in a wide range of computing devices, including personal computers, servers, laptops, and gaming consoles. While it initially manufactured its own processors, the company later outsourced its manufacturing, a practice known as going [fabless](Fabless_manufacturing "Fabless manufacturing"), after was spun off in 2009. AMD's main products include [microprocessors](Microprocessor "Microprocessor"), [motherboard](Motherboard "Motherboard") [chipsets](Chipset "Chipset"), [embedded processors](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor"), [graphics processors](Graphics_processing_unit "Graphics processing unit"), and [FPGAs](FPGA "FPGA") for [servers](Server_(computing) "Server (computing)"), [workstations](Workstation "Workstation"), personal computers, and [embedded system](Embedded_system "Embedded system") applications. The company has also expanded into new markets, such as the data center and gaming markets, and has announced plans to enter the high-performance computing market. ## History ### First twelve years Advanced Micro Devices was formally incorporated by [Jerry Sanders](Jerry_Sanders_(businessman) "Jerry Sanders (businessman)"), along with seven of his colleagues from [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor"), on May 1, 1969.[[2]](AMD#cite_note-2)[[3]](AMD#cite_note-3) Sanders, an [electrical engineer](Electrical_engineer "Electrical engineer") who was the director of marketing at Fairchild, had, like many Fairchild executives, grown frustrated with the increasing lack of support, opportunity, and flexibility within the company. He later decided to leave to start his own [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") company,[[4]](AMD#cite_note-4) following the footsteps of [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce") (developer of the first silicon [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") at Fairchild in 1959)[[5]](AMD#cite_note-5) and [Gordon Moore](Gordon_Moore "Gordon Moore"), who together founded the semiconductor company in July 1968.[[6]](AMD#cite_note-abc-6) In September 1969, AMD moved from its temporary location in [Santa Clara](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California") to [Sunnyvale](Sunnyvale%2C_California "Sunnyvale, California"), California.[[7]](AMD#cite_note-7) To immediately secure a customer base, AMD initially became a [second source](Second_source "Second source") supplier of microchips designed by Fairchild and [National Semiconductor](National_Semiconductor "National Semiconductor").[[8]](AMD#cite_note-directory-8)[[9]](AMD#cite_note-9) AMD first focused on producing logic chips.[[10]](AMD#cite_note-10) The company guaranteed quality control to [United States Military Standard](MIL-STD-883 "MIL-STD-883"), an advantage in the early computer industry since unreliability in microchips was a distinct problem that customers – including [computer manufacturers](Computer_manufacturer "Computer manufacturer"), the [telecommunications industry](Telecommunications_industry "Telecommunications industry"), and instrument manufacturers – wanted to avoid.[[8]](AMD#cite_note-directory-8)[[11]](AMD#cite_note-singer-11)[[12]](AMD#cite_note-12)[[13]](AMD#cite_note-svh-13) In November 1969, the company manufactured its first product: the Am9300, a [4-bit](4-bit_computing "4-bit computing") [MSI](Integrated_circuit#SSI,_MSI_and_LSI "Integrated circuit") [shift register](Shift_register "Shift register"), which began selling in 1970.[[13]](AMD#cite_note-svh-13)[[14]](AMD#cite_note-14) Also in 1970, AMD produced its first proprietary product, the Am2501 logic counter, which was highly successful.[[15]](AMD#cite_note-lojek220-15)[[16]](AMD#cite_note-history-16) Its bestselling product in 1971 was the Am2505, the fastest [multiplier](Binary_multiplier "Binary multiplier") available.[[15]](AMD#cite_note-lojek220-15)[[17]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen41-17) In 1971, AMD entered the [RAM](Random-access_memory "Random-access memory") chip market, beginning with the Am3101, a [64-bit](64-bit_computing "64-bit computing") bipolar RAM.[[17]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen41-17)[[18]](AMD#cite_note-18) That year AMD also greatly increased the sales volume of its linear integrated circuits, and by year-end the company's total annual sales reached US$4.6 million.[[15]](AMD#cite_note-lojek220-15)[[19]](AMD#cite_note-19) AMD went public in September 1972.[[8]](AMD#cite_note-directory-8)[[20]](AMD#cite_note-20)[[21]](AMD#cite_note-21) The company was a second source for Intel [MOS](MOSFET "MOSFET")/[LSI](Large_Scale_Integration "Large Scale Integration") circuits by 1973, with products such as Am14/1506 and Am14/1507, dual 100-bit dynamic shift registers.[[22]](AMD#cite_note-22)[[23]](AMD#cite_note-23) By 1975, AMD was producing 212 products – of which 49 were proprietary, including the Am9102 (a [static](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") [N-channel](N-type_semiconductor "N-type semiconductor") 1024-bit RAM)[[24]](AMD#cite_note-24) and three low-power [Schottky](Schottky_barrier "Schottky barrier") [MSI](Mid-scale_integration "Mid-scale integration") circuits: Am25LS07, Am25LS08, and Am25LS09.[[25]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen55-25) Intel had created the first [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor"), its 4-bit [4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004"), in 1971.[[26]](AMD#cite_note-26)[[27]](AMD#cite_note-27) By 1975, AMD entered the microprocessor market with the [Am9080](AMD_Am9080 "AMD Am9080"), a [reverse-engineered](Reverse_engineering "Reverse engineering") clone of the [Intel 8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080"),[[28]](AMD#cite_note-28)[[29]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen50-29)[[30]](AMD#cite_note-30) and the [Am2900](AMD_Am2900 "AMD Am2900") [bit-slice](Bit-slice "Bit-slice") microprocessor family.[[29]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen50-29) When Intel began installing [microcode](Microcode "Microcode") in its microprocessors in 1976, it entered into a [cross-licensing](Cross-licensing "Cross-licensing") agreement with AMD, which was granted a copyright license to the microcode in its microprocessors and peripherals, effective October On February 10, 2003, the Athlon XP with 512KB L2 Cache was released.[[111]](AMD#cite_note-The_AMD_Athlon_XP_Processor_with_512KB_L2_Cache-111) #### Athlon 64, Opteron and Phenom Main articles: [Athlon 64](Athlon_64 "Athlon 64"), , and [Phenom](AMD_Phenom "AMD Phenom") The K8 was a major revision of the K7 architecture, with the most notable features being the addition of a [64-bit](64-bit_computing "64-bit computing") extension to the x86 instruction set (called [x86-64](X86-64 "X86-64"), AMD64, or x64), the incorporation of an on-chip memory controller, and the implementation of an extremely high-performance point-to-point interconnect called , as part of the [Direct Connect Architecture](Direct_Connect_Architecture "Direct Connect Architecture"). The technology was initially launched as the server-oriented processor on April 22, 2003.[[112]](AMD#cite_note-112) Shortly thereafter, it was incorporated into a product for desktop PCs, branded [Athlon 64](Athlon_64 "Athlon 64").[[113]](AMD#cite_note-113) On April 21, 2005, AMD released the first [dual-core](Multi-core_processor "Multi-core processor") , an x86-based server CPU.[[114]](AMD#cite_note-114) A month later, it released the [Athlon 64 X2](Athlon_64_X2 "Athlon 64 X2"), the first desktop-based [dual-core processor](Multi-core_(computing) "Multi-core (computing)") family.[[115]](AMD#cite_note-115) In May 2007, AMD abandoned the string "64" in its dual-core desktop product branding, becoming Athlon X2, downplaying the significance of [64-bit computing](X86-64 "X86-64") in its processors. Both will be built on a [45 nm](45_nm "45 nm") [SOI](Silicon_on_insulator "Silicon on insulator") process. #### Fusion becomes the AMD APU Main articles: [AMD APU](AMD_APU "AMD APU") and [AMD mobile platform](AMD_mobile_platform "AMD mobile platform") Following AMD's 2006 acquisition of Canadian graphics company [ATI Technologies](ATI_Technologies "ATI Technologies"), an initiative codenamed *Fusion* was announced to integrate a and together on some of AMD's microprocessors, including a built in [PCI Express](PCI_Express "PCI Express") link to accommodate separate PCI Express peripherals, eliminating the [northbridge](Northbridge_(computing) "Northbridge (computing)") chip from the motherboard. content:
Based on my research through Wikipedia, I've found comprehensive information about Japanese semiconductor companies during the 1980s. Here's what I discovered:

## Japanese Semiconductor Industry Dominance in the 1980s

### Overall Market Position

**Japanese Dominance:** During the 1980s, Japan held approximately **50% of the global semiconductor market share**, making it the dominant force in the worldwide chip industry. This was particularly strong in memory chip (DRAM) production, where Japanese manufacturers effectively eclipsed American and European competitors.

### Key Japanese Companies in the 1980s

#### **NEC (Nippon Electric Company)**
- **World's largest semiconductor company by annual revenue from 1985 to 1992** - an eight-year dominance period
- Major DRAM producer alongside their microprocessor business
- Notable product innovations:
  - 1980: Created the first digital signal processor (NEC µPD7710)
  - 1984: Introduced the NEC V20 microprocessor (an Intel 8088 clone with enhanced features)
  - 1986-1989: Released the V-series processors (V60, V70, V80)
- Manufacturing expansion:
  - 1978: Acquired Electronic Arrays, Inc. of California
  - 1981: Established NEC Semiconductors (UK) Ltd.
  - 1987: NEC Technologies (UK) Ltd. established
- Legacy: Their DRAM business merged with Hitachi's in 1999 to form **Elpida Memory**

#### **Toshiba**
- One of the top 10 semiconductor companies globally during this era
- **Inventor of flash memory** (a major breakthrough in 1980s semiconductor technology)
- Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba developed:
  - 1977: 1Mb DRAM
  - Stacked-gate memory technology (precursor to flash memory and EEPROM)
- Toshiba Memory was later spun off as Kioxia in the late 2010s
- Strong presence in memory chips and electronic components

#### **Hitachi**
- Major player in DRAM and microelectronics
- **Filed Japanese patent in 1983 for 3D integrated circuit (TSV) technology** - pioneering work in chip stacking
- DRAM business merged with NEC's in 1999 to form Elpida Memory
- Later merged with Renesas Electronics for logic chips
- Part of the Japanese conglomerate system (originally part of Nissan zaibatsu)

#### **Fujitsu**
- One of the top semiconductor manufacturers
- **Filed Japanese patent in 1984 for 3D IC technology**, following Hitachi's innovation
- Strong in microelectronics and telecommunications equipment
- Established semiconductor division producing various integrated circuits
- Later one of the companies supporting the new Rapidus initiative in 2022

### Market Share and Competition

**DRAM Market:**
- At its peak in the late 1970s, American company Mostek held **85% of the global DRAM market**
- By the mid-1980s, **Japanese manufacturers had captured this market** through lower prices (described by critics as "dumping")
- Japanese companies like NEC, Toshiba, Hitachi, and Fujitsu dominated global DRAM production
- This dominance contributed to U.S. trade complaints and diplomatic action

### The 1986 Japan-United States Semiconductor Agreement

A critical turning point came with the **1986 Japan-U.S. Semiconductor Trade Agreement**, which:
- Was signed to resolve intense trade friction between the two nations
- Addressed concerns about Japanese market dominance
- Attempted to level the playing field for American semiconductor companies
- Combined with the rise of South Korean (Samsung) and Taiwanese competitors, gradually reduced Japanese competitiveness in subsequent years

### Legacy and Impact

**1980s Significance:**
- Japan reached its semiconductor peak during 1985-1992, with NEC leading global rankings
- The Japanese companies held approximately half the global semiconductor market
- DRAM was the battleground where Japanese quality and manufacturing efficiency overwhelmed competitors
- This success led to both economic triumph and trade disputes

**Aftermath:**
- Japanese semiconductor dominance gradually declined through the 1990s and 2000s
- Many Japanese companies spun off semiconductor divisions (Elpida Memory in 1999, Renesas Electronics)
- Samsung (South Korea) and TSMC (Taiwan) emerged as new dominant players
- The collective strength of these Japanese companies led to the new **Rapidus** initiative in 2022, with eight major Japanese companies (including NEC, Sony, Toyota) collaborating to revive advanced semiconductor manufacturing in Japan

This era represents one of the most significant periods in semiconductor history, where Japanese manufacturers achieved unprecedented global market dominance before facing increased competition and eventual decline due to trade pressures and new international competitors.

However, increased competition from Japanese semiconductor manufacturers had, by 1983, dramatically reduced the profitability of this market. The growing success of the <IBM> personal computer, based on an Intel microprocessor, was among factors that convinced Gordon Moore (CEO since 1975) to shift the company's focus to microprocessors and to change fundamental aspects of that business model. Moore's decision to sole-source Intel's 386 chip played into the company's continuing success.

By the end of the 1980s, buoyed by its fortuitous position as microprocessor supplier to IBM and IBM's competitors within the rapidly growing [personal computer market](IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible"), Intel embarked on a 10-year period of unprecedented growth as the primary (and most profitable) hardware supplier to the PC industry, part of the winning 'Wintel' combination. Moore handed over his position as CEO to Andy Grove in 1987. By launching its Intel Inside [marketing campaign](Marketing_campaign "Marketing campaign") in 1991, Intel was able to associate [brand loyalty](Brand_loyalty "Brand loyalty") with consumer selection, so that by the end of the 1990s, its line of <Pentium> processors had become a household name.

### Challenges to dominance (2000s)

After 2000, growth in demand for high-end microprocessors slowed. Competitors, most notably <AMD> (Intel's largest competitor in its primary [x86](X86 "X86") architecture market), garnered significant market share, initially in low-end and mid-range processors but ultimately across the product range, and Intel's dominant position in its core market was greatly reduced,[[58]](Intel#cite_note-Wong-60) mostly due to controversial <NetBurst> microarchitecture. In the early 2000s then-CEO, [Craig Barrett](Craig_Barrett_(businessman) "Craig Barrett (businessman)") attempted to diversify the company's business beyond semiconductors, but few of these activities were ultimately successful.

#### Litigation

Intel had also for a number of years been embroiled in litigation. US law did not initially recognize [intellectual property rights](Intellectual_property_rights "Intellectual property rights") related to microprocessor [topology](Topology_(electrical_circuits) "Topology (electrical circuits)") (circuit layouts), until the [Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984](Semiconductor_Chip_Protection_Act_of_1984 "Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984"), a law sought by Intel and the [Semiconductor Industry Association](Semiconductor_Industry_Association "Semiconductor Industry Association") (SIA).[[59]](Intel#cite_note-61) During the late 1980s and 1990s (after this law was passed), Intel also sued companies that tried to develop competitor chips to the [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386") <CPU>.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) The lawsuits were noted to significantly burden the competition with legal bills, even if Intel lost the suits.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) <Antitrust> allegations had been simmering since the early 1990s and had been the cause of one [lawsuit](Lawsuit "Lawsuit") against Intel in 1991. In 2004 and 2005, AMD brought [further claims](Intel_Corp._v._Advanced_Micro_Devices%2C_Inc. "Intel Corp. v. **[Intel Corporation](../../../A/Intel_Corporation "Intel Corporation")** is the world's largest [semiconductor](../../../A/Semiconductor "Semiconductor") company and the inventor of the [x86](../../../A/X86_architecture "X86 architecture") series of microprocessors, the processors found in most [personal computers](../../../A/Personal_computers "Personal computers"). Founded in 1968 as **Int**egrated **El**ectronics Corporation and based in [Santa Clara, California](../../../A/Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California"), [USA](../../../A/United_States "United States"), Intel also makes [motherboard](../../../A/Motherboard "Motherboard") chipsets, [network cards](../../../A/Network_card "Network card") and ICs, [flash memory](../../../A/Flash_memory "Flash memory"), graphic chips, embedded processors, and other devices related to communications and computing. Founded by semiconductor pioneers [Robert Noyce](../../../A/Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce") and [Gordon Moore](../../../A/Gordon_Moore "Gordon Moore"), Intel combines advanced chip design capability with a leading-edge manufacturing capability. Originally known primarily to engineers and technologists, Intel's successful "Intel Inside" advertising campaign of the 1990s made it and its [Pentium](../../../A/Pentium_(brand) "Pentium (brand)") processor household names. While Intel created the first commercial microprocessor chip in 1971, it was not until the creation of the [personal computer](../../../A/Personal_computer "Personal computer") (PC) that this became their primary business. During the 1990s, Intel invested heavily in new microprocessor designs and in fostering the rapid growth of the PC industry. During this period Intel became the dominant supplier of microprocessors for PCs, and was known for aggressive and sometimes controversial tactics in defense of its market position, as well as a struggle with [Microsoft](../../../A/Microsoft "Microsoft") for control over the direction of the PC industry. The 2007 rankings of the world's 100 most powerful brands published by Millward Brown Optimor showed the company's brand value falling 10 places – from number 15 to number 25. Intel is the largest employer in [Oregon](../../../A/Oregon "Oregon"), with facilities mainly in [Hillsboro](../../../A/Hillsboro%2C_Oregon "Hillsboro, Oregon") where it employs over 16,000 at three main locations.

This article is issued from [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/?title=Portal%3AOregon%2FSelected_article%2F29&oldid=1020929183 "Last edited on 2021-05-01"). ## History

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Intel](Timeline_of_Intel "Timeline of Intel").

### Origins

Intel was incorporated in [Mountain View, California](Mountain_View%2C_California "Mountain View, California"), on July 18, 1968, by [Gordon E. Moore](Gordon_E._Moore "Gordon E. Moore") (known for "[Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law")"), a [chemist](Chemist "Chemist"), [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce"), a physicist and co-inventor of the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") and [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock"), an investor and [venture capitalist](Venture_capital "Venture capital")[[35]](Intel#cite_note-35)[[36]](Intel#cite_note-36)[[37]](Intel#cite_note-37) Moore and Noyce had left [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") and were part of the "[traitorous eight](Traitorous_eight "Traitorous eight")". There were originally 500,000 shares outstanding of which Dr. Noyce bought 245,000 shares, Dr. Moore 245,000 shares, and Mr. Rock 10,000 shares; all at $1 per share. Rock offered $2,500,000 of convertible debentures to a limited group of private investors (equivalent to $21 million in 2022), convertible at $5 per share.[[38]](Intel#cite_note-38)[[39]](Intel#cite_note-39) Just 2 years later, Intel became a [public company](Public_company "Public company") via an [initial public offering](Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO), raising $6.8 million ($23.50 per share).[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) Intel's third employee was [Andy Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove"),[[note 1]](Intel#cite_note-41) a [chemical engineer](Chemical_engineer "Chemical engineer"), who later ran the company through much of the 1980s and the high-growth 1990s.

In deciding on a name, Moore and Noyce quickly rejected "Moore Noyce",[[41]](Intel#cite_note-42) near [homophone](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/homophone "wikt:homophone") for "more noise" – an ill-suited name for an [electronics](Electronics "Electronics") company, since [noise in electronics](Electronic_noise "Electronic noise") is usually undesirable and typically associated with bad [interference](Electromagnetic_interference "Electromagnetic interference"). Instead, they founded the company as **NM Electronics** (or **MN Electronics**) on July 18, 1968, but by the end of the month had changed the name to **Intel** which stood for **Int**egrated **El**ectronics.[[note 2]](Intel#cite_note-48) Since "Intel" was already trademarked by the hotel chain Intelco, they had to buy the rights for the name.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[47]](Intel#cite_note-49)

### Early history

At its founding, Intel was distinguished by its ability to make [logic circuits](Logic_circuit "Logic circuit") using [semiconductor devices](Semiconductor_device "Semiconductor device"). The founders' goal was the [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") market, widely predicted to replace [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory"). Its first product, a quick entry into the small, high-speed memory market in 1969, was the 3101 [Schottky TTL](Schottky_transistor "Schottky transistor") [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") 64-bit [static random-access memory](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") (SRAM), which was nearly twice as fast as earlier Schottky diode implementations by Fairchild and the Electrotechnical Laboratory in [Tsukuba, Japan](Tsukuba%2C_Ibaraki "Tsukuba, Ibaraki").[[48]](Intel#cite_note-50)[[49]](Intel#cite_note-51) In the same year, Intel also produced the 3301 Schottky bipolar 1024-bit [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM)[[50]](Intel#cite_note-52) and the first commercial [metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor](MOSFET "MOSFET") (MOSFET) [silicon gate](Silicon_gate "Silicon gate") SRAM chip, the 256-bit 1101.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[52]](Intel#cite_note-54)

While the 1101 was a significant advance, its complex static [cell structure](Memory_cell_(computing) "Memory cell (computing)") made it too slow and costly for [mainframe](Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") memories. The three-[transistor](Transistor "Transistor") cell implemented in the first commercially available [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM), the [1103](Intel_1103 "Intel 1103") released in 1970, solved these issues. The 1103 was the bestselling semiconductor memory chip in the world by 1972, as it replaced core memory in many applications.[[53]](Intel#cite_note-55)[[54]](Intel#cite_note-Bellis-56) Intel's business grew during the 1970s as it expanded and improved its manufacturing processes and produced a wider range of [products](Product_(business) "Product (business)"), still dominated by various memory devices.

Intel created the [first commercially available microprocessor (Intel 4004)](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") in 1971.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) The microprocessor represented a notable advance in the technology of integrated circuitry, as it miniaturized the central processing unit of a computer, which then made it possible for small machines to perform calculations that in the past only very large machines could do. Considerable technological innovation was needed before the microprocessor could actually become the basis of what was first known as a "mini computer" and then known as a "personal computer".[[55]](Intel#cite_note-57) Intel also created one of the first [microcomputers](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1973.[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[56]](Intel#cite_note-Intellec-1973-58)

72, in <Malaysia>, which would host multiple Intel operations, before opening assembly facilities and semiconductor plants in <Singapore> and <Jerusalem> in the early 1980s, and manufacturing and development centers in China, India, and Costa Rica in the 1990s.[[57]](Intel#cite_note-59) By the early 1980s, its business was dominated by [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM) chips. However, increased competition from Japanese semiconductor manufacturers had, by 1983, dramatically reduced the profitability of this market. The growing success of the <IBM> personal computer, based on an Intel microprocessor, was among factors that convinced Gordon Moore (CEO since 1975) to shift the company's focus to microprocessors and to change fundamental aspects of that business model. Moore's decision to sole-source Intel's 386 chip played into the company's continuing success.

By the end of the 1980s, buoyed by its fortuitous position as microprocessor supplier to IBM and IBM's competitors within the rapidly growing [personal computer market](IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible"), Intel embarked on a 10-year period of unprecedented growth as the primary (and most profitable) hardware supplier to the PC industry, part of the winning 'Wintel' combination. Moore handed over his position as CEO to Andy Grove in 1987. By launching its Intel Inside [marketing campaign](Marketing_campaign "Marketing campaign") in 1991, Intel was able to associate [brand loyalty](Brand_loyalty "Brand loyalty") with consumer selection, so that by the end of the 1990s, its line of <Pentium> processors had become a household name.

### Challenges to dominance (2000s)

After 2000, growth in demand for high-end microprocessors slowed. Competitors, most notably <AMD> (Intel's largest competitor in its primary [x86](X86 "X86") architecture market), garnered significant market share, initially in low-end and mid-range processors but ultimately across the product range, and Intel's dominant position in its core market was greatly reduced,[[58]](Intel#cite_note-Wong-60) mostly due to controversial <NetBurst> microarchitecture. In the early 2000s then-CEO, [Craig Barrett](Craig_Barrett_(businessman) "Craig Barrett (businessman)") attempted to diversify the company's business beyond semiconductors, but few of these activities were ultimately successful.

#### Litigation

Intel had also for a number of years been embroiled in litigation. US law did not initially recognize [intellectual property rights](Intellectual_property_rights "Intellectual property rights") related to microprocessor [topology](Topology_(electrical_circuits) "Topology (electrical circuits)") (circuit layouts), until the [Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984](Semiconductor_Chip_Protection_Act_of_1984 "Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984"), a law sought by Intel and the [Semiconductor Industry Association](Semiconductor_Industry_Association "Semiconductor Industry Association") (SIA).[[59]](Intel#cite_note-61) During the late 1980s and 1990s (after this law was passed), Intel also sued companies that tried to develop competitor chips to the [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386") <CPU>.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) The lawsuits were noted to significantly burden the competition with legal bills, even if Intel lost the suits.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) <Antitrust> allegations had been simmering since the early 1990s and had been the cause of one [lawsuit](Lawsuit "Lawsuit") against Intel in 1991. In 2004 and 2005, AMD brought [further claims](Intel_Corp._v._Advanced_Micro_Devices%2C_Inc. "Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.") against Intel related to [unfair competition](Unfair_competition "Unfair competition").

### Reorganization and success with Intel Core (2005–2015)

In 2005, CEO [Paul Otellini](Paul_Otellini "Paul Otellini") reorganized the company to refocus its core processor and chipset business on platforms (enterprise, digital home, digital health, and mobility).

On June 6, 2005, [Steve Jobs](Steve_Jobs "Steve Jobs"), then CEO of [Apple](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), announced that Apple would be using Intel's x86 processors for its <Macintosh> computers, switching from the <PowerPC> architecture developed by the [AIM alliance](AIM_alliance "AIM alliance").[[61]](Intel#cite_note-auto2-63) This was seen as win for Intel;[[62]](Intel#cite_note-auto1-64) An analyst called the move "risky" and "foolish", as Intel's current offerings at the time were considered to be behind those of AMD and IBM.[[63]](Intel#cite_note-Computerworld1-65)

In 2006, Intel unveiled its [Core microarchitecture](Core_(microarchitecture) "Core (microarchitecture)") to widespread critical acclaim; the product range was perceived as an exceptional leap in processor performance that at a stroke regained much of its leadership of the field.[[64]](Intel#cite_note-66)[[65]](Intel#cite_note-67) In 2008, Intel had another "tick" when it introduced the Penryn microarchitecture, fabricated using the 45 nm process node. Later that year, Intel released a processor with the [Nehalem](Nehalem_(microarchitecture) "Nehalem (microarchitecture)") architecture to positive reception.[[66]](Intel#cite_note-68)

On June 27, 2006, the sale of Intel's <XScale> assets was announced. Intel agreed to sell the XScale processor business to [Marvell Technology Group](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group") for an estimated $600 million and the assumption of unspecified liabilities. The move was intended to permit Intel to focus its resources on its core x86 and server businesses, and the [acquisition](Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions") completed on November 9, 2006.[[67]](Intel#cite_note-XScale-69)

In 2008, Intel spun off key assets of a solar startup business effort to form an independent company, SpectraWatt Inc. In 2011, SpectraWatt filed for bankruptcy.[[68]](Intel#cite_note-eetimes1-70)

In February 2011, Intel began to build a new microprocessor manufacturing facility in [Chandler, Arizona](Chandler%2C_Arizona "Chandler, Arizona"), completed in 2013 at a cost of $5 billion.[[69]](Intel#cite_note-71) The building is now the 10 nm-certified Fab 42 and is connected to the other Fabs (12, 22, 32) on Ocotillo Campus via an enclosed bridge known as the Link.[[70]](Intel#cite_note-72)[[71]](Intel#cite_note-73)[[72]](Intel#cite_note-74)[[73]](Intel#cite_note-75) The company produces three-quarters of its products in the United States, although three-quarters of its revenue come from overseas.[[74]](Intel#cite_note-76)

The [Alliance for Affordable Internet](Alliance_for_Affordable_Internet "Alliance for Affordable Internet") (A4AI) was launched in October 2013 and Intel is part of the coalition of public and private organizations that also includes <Facebook>, <Google>, and <Microsoft>. Led by [Sir Tim Berners-Lee](Tim_Berners-Lee "Tim Berners-Lee"), the A4AI seeks to make Internet access more affordable so that access is broadened in the developing world, where only 31% of people are online. Google will help to decrease Internet access prices so that they fall below the UN Broadband Commission's worldwide target of 5% of monthly income.[[75]](Intel#cite_note-77)

#### Attempts at entering the smartphone market

In April 2011, Intel began a pilot project with [ZTE Corporation](ZTE_Corporation "ZTE Corporation") to produce smartphones using the [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processor for China's domestic market. In December 2011, Intel announced that it reorganized several of its business units into a new mobile and communications group[[76]](Intel#cite_note-78) that would be responsible for the company's smartphone, tablet, and wireless efforts. Intel planned to introduce Medfield – a processor for tablets and smartphones – to the market in 2012, as an effort to compete with Arm.[[77]](Intel#cite_note-79) As a 32-nanometer processor, Medfield is designed to be energy-efficient, which is one of the core features in Arm's chips.[[78]](Intel#cite_note-autogenerated12-80)

At the Intel Developers Forum (IDF) 2011 in San Francisco, Intel's partnership with Google was announced. In January 2012, Google announced Android 2.3, supporting Intel's Atom microprocessor.[[79]](Intel#cite_note-81)[[80]](Intel#cite_note-82)[[81]](Intel#cite_note-83) In 2013, Intel's Kirk Skaugen said that Intel's exclusive focus on Microsoft platforms was a thing of the past and that they would now support all "tier-one operating systems" such as Linux, Android, iOS, and Chrome.[[82]](Intel#cite_note-84)

In 2014, Intel cut thousands of employees in response to "evolving market trends",[[83]](Intel#cite_note-85) and offered to subsidize manufacturers for the extra costs involved in using Intel chips in their tablets. In April 2016, Intel cancelled the <SoFIA> platform and the Broxton Atom SoC for smartphones,[[84]](Intel#cite_note-86)[[85]](Intel#cite_note-87)[[86]](Intel#cite_note-88)[[87]](Intel#cite_note-89) effectively leaving the smartphone market.[[88]](Intel#cite_note-MyUser_Theverge.com_June_1_2016c-90)[[89]](Intel#cite_note-verge2-91)

#### Intel custom foundry

Finding itself with excess fab capacity after the failure of the <Ultrabook> to gain market traction and with PC sales declining, in 2013 Intel reached a [foundry](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") agreement to produce chips for <Altera> using a 14nm process. General Manager of Intel's custom foundry division Sunit Rikhi indicated that Intel would pursue further such deals in the future.[[90]](Intel#cite_note-92) This was after poor sales of [Windows 8](Windows_8 "Windows 8") hardware caused a major retrenchment for most of the major semiconductor manufacturers, except for Qualcomm, which continued to see healthy purchases from its largest customer, Apple.[[91]](Intel#cite_note-93)

**Wintel** ([portmanteau](Portmanteau "Portmanteau") of [Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and <Intel>) is the partnership of [Microsoft Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and <Intel> producing [personal computers](Personal_computer "Personal computer") using Intel [x86](X86 "X86")-compatible processors running Microsoft Windows.

## Background

By the early 1980s, the chaos and incompatibility that was rife in the early [microcomputer](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") market had given way to a smaller number of de facto industry standards, including the [S-100 bus](S-100_bus "S-100 bus"), <CP/M>, the [Apple II](Apple_II_series "Apple II series"), [Microsoft BASIC](Microsoft_BASIC "Microsoft BASIC") in [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM), and the 5+1⁄4 inch [floppy drive](Floppy_disk "Floppy disk"). No single firm controlled the industry, and fierce competition ensured that innovation in both hardware and software was the rule rather than the exception. [Microsoft Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and <Intel> processors gained ascendance and their ongoing alliance gave them market dominance.[[1]](Wintel#cite_note-1)

Intel claimed that this partnership has enabled the two companies to give customers the benefit of "a seemingly unending spiral of falling prices and rising performance".[[2]](Wintel#cite_note-2) In addition, they claim a "history of innovation" and "a shared vision of flexible computing for the agile business".

## IBM

Main article: [Influence of the IBM PC on the personal computer market](Influence_of_the_IBM_PC_on_the_personal_computer_market "Influence of the IBM PC on the personal computer market")

In 1981, IBM entered the microcomputer market. The IBM PC was created by a small subdivision of the firm. It was unusual for an IBM product because it was largely sourced from outside component suppliers and was intended to run third-party operating systems and software. IBM published the technical specifications and schematics of the PC, which allowed third-party companies to produce compatible hardware, the so-called [open architecture](Open_architecture "Open architecture"). The IBM PC became one of the most successful computers of all time.

The key feature of the IBM PC was that it had IBM's enormous public respect behind it. It was an accident of history that the IBM PC happened to have an Intel CPU (instead of the technically superior[[3]](Wintel#cite_note-3) [Motorola 68000](Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") that had been tipped for it, or an IBM in-house design), and that it shipped with [IBM PC DOS](IBM_PC_DOS "IBM PC DOS") (a licensed version of Microsoft's <MS-DOS>) rather than the <CP/M-86> operating system, but these accidents were to have enormous significance in later years.

Because the IBM PC was an IBM product with the IBM badge, personal computers became respectable. It became easier for a business to justify buying a microcomputer than it had been even a year or two before, and easiest of all to justify buying the [IBM Personal Computer](IBM_Personal_Computer "IBM Personal Computer"). Since the PC architecture was well documented in IBM's manuals, and PC DOS was designed to be similar to earlier CP/M operating system, the PC soon had thousands of different third-party add-in cards and software packages available. This made the PC the preferred option for many, since the PC supported the hardware and software they needed.

## Competitors

Industry competitors took one of several approaches to the changing market. Some (such as [Apple](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), <Amiga>, <Atari>, and [Acorn](Acorn_Computers "Acorn Computers")) persevered with their independent and quite different systems. Of those systems, Apple's [Mac](Mac_(computer) "Mac (computer)") is the only one remaining on the market. Others (such as [Digital](Digital_Equipment_Corporation "Digital Equipment Corporation"), then the world's second-largest computer company, Hewlett-Packard, and [Apricot](Apricot_PC "Apricot PC")) concentrated on making similar but technically superior models. Other early market leaders (such as Tandy-Radio Shack or Texas Instruments) stayed with outdated architectures and proprietary operating systems for some time before belatedly realizing which way market trends were going and switching to the most successful long-term business strategy, which was to build a machine that duplicated the IBM PC as closely as possible and sell it for a slightly lower price, or with higher performance. Given the very conservative engineering of the early IBM personal computers and their higher than average prices, this was not a terribly difficult task at first, bar only the great technical challenge of crafting a <BIOS> that duplicated the function of the IBM BIOS exac

At the Intel Developers Forum (IDF) 2011 in San Francisco, Intel's partnership with Google was announced. In January 2012, Google announced Android 2.3, supporting Intel's Atom microprocessor.[[79]](Intel#cite_note-81)[[80]](Intel#cite_note-82)[[81]](Intel#cite_note-83) In 2013, Intel's Kirk Skaugen said that Intel's exclusive focus on Microsoft platforms was a thing of the past and that they would now support all "tier-one operating systems" such as Linux, Android, iOS, and Chrome.[[82]](Intel#cite_note-84)
