#### Intel custom foundry

Finding itself with excess fab capacity after the failure of the <Ultrabook> to gain market traction and with PC sales declining, in 2013 Intel reached a [foundry](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") agreement to produce chips for <Altera> using a 14nm process. General Manager of Intel's custom foundry division Sunit Rikhi indicated that Intel would pursue further such deals in the future.[[90]](Intel#cite_note-92) This was after poor sales of [Windows 8](Windows_8 "Windows 8") hardware caused a major retrenchment for most of the major semiconductor manufacturers, except for Qualcomm, which continued to see healthy purchases from its largest customer, Apple.[[91]](Intel#cite_note-93)

As of July 2013, five companies were using Intel's fabs via the *Intel Custom Foundry* division: <Achronix>, [Tabula](Tabula_(company) "Tabula (company)"), <Netronome>, <Microsemi>, and <Panasonic> –  most are [field-programmable gate array](Field-programmable_gate_array "Field-programmable gate array") (FPGA) makers, but Netronome designs network processors. Only Achronix began shipping chips made by Intel using the 22nm Tri-Gate process.[[92]](Intel#cite_note-94)[[93]](Intel#cite_note-95) Several other customers also exist but were not announced at the time.[[94]](Intel#cite_note-96)

The foundry business was closed in 2018 due to Intel's issues with its manufacturing.[[95]](Intel#cite_note-97)[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98)

### Security and manufacturing challenges (2016–2021)

Intel continued its [tick-tock](Tick%E2%80%93tock_model "Tick–tock model") model of a microarchitecture change followed by a die shrink until the 6th generation Core family based on the [Skylake](Skylake_(microarchitecture) "Skylake (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture. This model was deprecated in 2016, with the release of the seventh generation Core family (codenamed [Kaby Lake](Kaby_Lake "Kaby Lake")), ushering in the [process–architecture–optimization model](Process%E2%80%93architecture%E2%80%93optimization_model "Process–architecture–optimization model"). As Intel struggled to shrink their process node from [14 nm](14_nm_process "14 nm process") to [10 nm](10_nm_process "10 nm process"), processor development slowed down and the company continued to use the Skylake microarchitecture until 2020, albeit with optimizations.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)

#### 10 nm process node issues

While Intel originally planned to introduce 10 nm products in 2016, it later became apparent that there were manufacturing issues with the node.[[97]](Intel#cite_note-99) The first microprocessor under that node, [Cannon Lake](Cannon_Lake_(microarchitecture) "Cannon Lake (microarchitecture)") (marketed as 8th generation Core), was released in small quantities in 2018.[[98]](Intel#cite_note-Cutress-100)[[99]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_discontinues_Cannon_Lake_NUC-101) The company first delayed the mass production of their 10 nm products to 2017.[[100]](Intel#cite_note-102)[[101]](Intel#cite_note-103) They later delayed mass production to 2018,[[102]](Intel#cite_note-104) and then to 2019. Despite rumors of the process being cancelled,[[103]](Intel#cite_note-105) Intel finally introduced mass-produced 10 nm 10th generation Intel Core mobile processors (codenamed "[Ice Lake](Ice_Lake_(microprocessor) "Ice Lake (microprocessor)")") in September 2019.[[104]](Intel#cite_note-106)

Intel later acknowledged that their strategy to shrink to 10 nm was too aggressive.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)[[105]](Intel#cite_note-107) While other foundries used up to four steps in 10 nm or 7 nm processes, the company's 10 nm process required up to five or six multi-pattern steps.[[106]](Intel#cite_note-108) In addition, Intel's 10 nm process is denser than its counterpart processes from other foundries.[[107]](Intel#cite_note-109)[[108]](Intel#cite_note-110) Since Intel's microarchitecture and process node development were coupled, processor development stagnated.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)

#### Security flaws

In early January 2018, it was reported that all [Intel processors](Intel_CPUs "Intel CPUs") made since 1995,[[109]](Intel#cite_note-111) excluding [Intel Itanium](Intel_Itanium "Intel Itanium") and pre-2013 [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processors, have been subject to two security flaws dubbed [Meltdown](Meltdown_(security_vulnerability) "Meltdown (security vulnerability)") and [Spectre](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)").[[110]](Intel#cite_note-112)[[111]](Intel#cite_note-wiredflaw-113) It is believed that "hundreds of millions" of systems could be affected by these flaws.[[112]](Intel#cite_note-telegraph2018flaw-114)[[113]](Intel#cite_note-115) More security flaws were disclosed on May 3, 2018,[[114]](Intel#cite_note-116) on August 14, 2018, on January 18, 2019, and on March 5, 2020.[[115]](Intel#cite_note-ZDNET-20200305-117)[[116]](Intel#cite_note-AT-20200305-118)[[117]](Intel#cite_note-EG-20200306-119)[[118]](Intel#cite_note-INTEL-20200211-120)

On March 15, 2018, Intel reported that it will redesign its [CPUs](Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") to protect against the [Spectre security vulnerability](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)"), the redesigned processors were sold later in 2018.[[119]](Intel#cite_note-TVRG-20180315-121)[[120]](Intel#cite_note-CNET-20180315-122) Existing chips vulnerable to Meltdown and Spectre can be fixed with a [software patch](Patch_(computing) "Patch (computing)") at a cost to performance.[[121]](Intel#cite_note-PCW-20180109-123)[[122]](Intel#cite_note-NYT-20180103-124)[[123]](Intel#cite_note-bbcflaw-125)[[124]](Intel#cite_note-TV-20180104-126)

### Renewed competition and other developments (2018–present)

Due to Intel's issues with its 10 nm process node and the company's slow processor development,[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22) the company now found itself in a market with intense competition.[[125]](Intel#cite_note-127) The company's main competitor, AMD, introduced the [Zen](Zen_(microarchitecture) "Zen (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture and a new [chiplet](Chiplet "Chiplet") based design to critical acclaim. Since its introduction, AMD, once unable to compete with Intel in the high-end CPU market, has undergone a resurgence,[[126]](Intel#cite_note-128) and Intel's dominance and market share have considerably decreased.[[127]](Intel#cite_note-129) In addition, Apple began to transition away from the x86 architecture and Intel processors to their own [Apple silicon](Apple_silicon "Apple silicon") for their Macintosh computers in 2020. The transition is expected to affect Intel minimally; however, it might prompt other PC manufacturers to reevaluate their reliance on Intel and the x86 architecture.[[128]](Intel#cite_note-Bloomberg1-130)[[129]](Intel#cite_note-Jean-Louis_Gassée,_2020.06.21-131)

Other plans for the company include a partnership with <IBM> and a new event for developers and engineers, called "Intel ON".[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98) Gelsinger also confirmed that Intel's 7 nm process is on track, and that the first products using their 7 nm process (also known as Intel 4) are Ponte Vecchio and Meteor Lake.[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98)

In 1983, at the dawn of the personal computer era, Intel's profits came under increased pressure from Japanese memory-chip manufacturers, and then-president Andy Grove focused the company on microprocessors. Grove described this transition in the book *[Only the Paranoid Survive](Only_the_Paranoid_Survive "Only the Paranoid Survive")*. A key element of his plan was the notion, then considered radical, of becoming the single source for successors to the popular [8086](Intel_8086 "Intel 8086") microprocessor.

Until then, the manufacture of complex integrated circuits was not reliable enough for customers to depend on a single supplier, but Grove began producing processors in three geographically distinct factories, and ceased licensing the chip designs to competitors such as [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices").[[140]](Intel#cite_note-142) When the PC industry boomed in the late 1980s and 1990s, Intel was one of the primary beneficiaries.

### Early x86 processors and the IBM PC

Despite the ultimate importance of the microprocessor, the [4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") and its successors the [8008](Intel_8008 "Intel 8008") and the [8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") were never major revenue contributors at Intel. As the next processor, the [8086](Intel_8086 "Intel 8086") (and its variant the 8088) was completed in 1978, Intel embarked on a major marketing and sales campaign for that chip nicknamed "Operation Crush", and intended to win as many customers for the processor as possible. One design win was the newly created [IBM PC](IBM_PC "IBM PC") division, though the importance of this was not fully realized at the time.

<IBM> introduced its personal computer in 1981, and it was rapidly successful. In 1982, Intel created the [80286](Intel_80286 "Intel 80286") microprocessor, which, two years later, was used in the [IBM PC/AT](IBM_Personal_Computer/AT "IBM Personal Computer/AT"). <Compaq>, the first IBM PC "clone" manufacturer, produced a desktop system based on the faster 80286 processor in 1985 and in 1986 quickly followed with the first [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386")-based system, beating IBM and establishing a competitive market for PC-compatible systems and setting up Intel as a key component supplier.

In 1975, the company had started a project to develop a highly advanced 32-bit microprocessor, finally released in 1981 as the [Intel iAPX 432](Intel_iAPX_432 "Intel iAPX 432"). The project was too ambitious and the processor was never able to meet its performance objectives, and it failed in the marketplace. Intel extended the [x86 architecture](X86 "X86") to 32 bits instead.[[141]](Intel#cite_note-143)[[142]](Intel#cite_note-144)

#### 386 microprocessor

During this period [Andrew Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove") dramatically redirected the company, closing much of its <DRAM> business and directing resources to the [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") business. Of perhaps greater importance was his decision to "single-source" the 386 microprocessor. Prior to this, microprocessor manufacturing was in its infancy, and manufacturing problems frequently reduced or stopped production, interrupting supplies to customers. To mitigate this risk, these customers typically insisted that multiple manufacturers produce chips they could use to ensure a consistent supply. The 8080 and 8086-series microprocessors were produced by several companies, notably AMD, with which Intel had a technology-sharing contract.

Grove made the decision not to license the 386 design to other manufacturers, instead, producing it in three geographically distinct factories: [Santa Clara](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California"), California; [Hillsboro](Hillsboro%2C_Oregon "Hillsboro, Oregon"), Oregon; and [Chandler](Chandler%2C_Arizona "Chandler, Arizona"), a suburb of [Phoenix](Phoenix%2C_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"), Arizona. He convinced customers that this would ensure consistent delivery. In doing this, Intel breached its contract with AMD, which sued and was paid millions of dollars in damages but could not manufacture new Intel CPU designs any longer. (Instead, AMD started to develop and manufacture its own competing x86 designs.)

As the success of <Compaq>'s [Deskpro 386](Compaq_Deskpro_386 "Compaq Deskpro 386") established the 386 as the dominant CPU choice, Intel achieved a position of near-exclusive dominance as its supplier. Profits from this funded rapid development of both higher-performance chip designs and higher-performance manufacturing capabilities, propelling Intel to a position of unquestioned leadership by the early 1990s.

#### 486, Pentium, and Itanium

Intel introduced the [486](Intel_80486 "Intel 80486") microprocessor in 1989, and in 1990 established a second design team, designing the processors code-named "[P5](P5_(microarchitecture) "P5 (microarchitecture)")" and "[P6](P6_(microarchitecture) "P6 (microarchitecture)")" in parallel and committing to a major new processor every two years, versus the four or more years such designs had previously taken. Engineers [Vinod Dham](Vinod_Dham "Vinod Dham") and [Rajeev Chandrasekhar](Rajeev_Chandrasekhar "Rajeev Chandrasekhar") (Member of Parliament, India) were key figures on the core team that invented the 486 chip and later, Intel's signature Pentium chip. The P5 project was earlier known as "Operation Bicycle", referring to the cycles of the processor through two parallel execution pipelines. The P5 was introduced in 1993 as the Intel <Pentium>, substituting a registered trademark name for the former part number (numbers, such as 486, cannot be legally registered as trademarks in the United States). The P6 followed in 1995 as the [Pentium Pro](Pentium_Pro "Pentium Pro") and improved into the [Pentium II](Pentium_II "Pentium II") in 1997. The **Information Age** (also known as the **Computer Age**, **Digital Age**, **Silicon Age**, **New Media Age**, or **Media Age**[[1]](Information_Age#cite_note-1)) is a [historical period](History_by_period "History by period") that began in the mid-20th century. It is characterized by a rapid shift from traditional industries, as established during the [Industrial Revolution](Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), to an economy centered on [information technology](Information_technology "Information technology").[[2]](Information_Age#cite_note-Manuel-2) The onset of the Information Age has been linked to the development of the [transistor](Transistor "Transistor") in 1947,[[2]](Information_Age#cite_note-Manuel-2) the [optical amplifier](Optical_amplifier "Optical amplifier") in 1957,[[3]](Information_Age#cite_note-grobe-3) and [Unix time](Unix_time "Unix time"),[[4]](Information_Age#cite_note-4) which began on January 1, 1970. These technological advances have had a significant impact on the way information is processed and transmitted.

According to the [United Nations Public Administration Network](United_Nations_Public_Administration_Network "United Nations Public Administration Network"), the Information Age was formed by capitalizing on [computer microminiaturization](Miniaturization "Miniaturization") advances,[[5]](Information_Age#cite_note-5) which led to [modernized](Modernization_theory "Modernization theory") [information](Information "Information") systems and internet communications as the driving force of [social evolution](Sociocultural_evolution "Sociocultural evolution").[[6]](Information_Age#cite_note-Idea-6)

Library expansion was calculated in 1945 by [Fremont Rider](Fremont_Rider "Fremont Rider") to double in capacity every 16 years where sufficient space made available.[[7]](Information_Age#cite_note-The_Scholar-7) He advocated replacing bulky, decaying printed works with [miniaturized](Miniaturization "Miniaturization") [microform](Microform "Microform") [analog photographs](Analog_photography "Analog photography"), which could be duplicated on-demand for library patrons and other institutions.

## 1970s

The first [microprocessors](Microprocessors "Microprocessors") were designed and manufactured in the 1970s. Intel's 4004 of 1971 is widely regarded as the first commercial microprocessor.[[1]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-1)

Designers predominantly used <MOSFET> transistors with [pMOS logic](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") in the early 1970s, switching to [nMOS logic](NMOS_logic "NMOS logic") after the mid-1970s. nMOS had the advantage that it could run on a single voltage, typically +5V, which simplified the power supply requirements and allowed it to be easily interfaced with the wide variety of +5V [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") (TTL) devices. nMOS had the disadvantage that it was more susceptible to electronic noise generated by slight impurities in the underlying silicon material, and it was not until the mid-1970s that these, sodium in particular, were successfully removed to the required levels. At that time, around 1975, nMOS quickly took over the market.[[2]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-2)

This corresponded with the introduction of new [semiconductor masking](Photomask "Photomask") systems, notably the <Micralign> system from <Perkin-Elmer>. Micralign projected an image of the mask onto the silicon wafer, never touching it directly, which eliminated the previous problems when the mask would be lifted off the surface and take away some of the [photoresist](Photoresist "Photoresist") along with it, ruining the chips on that portion of the wafer.[[3]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-3) By reducing the number of flawed chips, from about 70% to 10%, the cost of complex designs like early microprocessors fell by the same amount. Systems based on contact aligners cost on the order of $300 in single-unit quantities, the [MOS 6502](MOS_6502 "MOS 6502"), designed specifically to take advantage of these improvements, cost only $25.[[4]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-4)

This period also saw considerable experimentation with various [word lengths](Word_length "Word length"). Early on, [4-bit](4-bit_computing "4-bit computing") processors were common, like the Intel 4004, simply because making a wider word length could not be accomplished cost-effectively in the room available on the small wafers of the era, especially when the majority would be defective. As yields improved, wafer sizes grew, and feature size continued to be reduced, more complex [8-bit](8-bit_computing "8-bit computing") designs emerged like the [Intel 8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") and 6502. [16-bit](16-bit_computing "16-bit computing") processors emerged early but were expensive; by the decade's end, low-cost 16-bit designs like the [Zilog Z8000](Zilog_Z8000 "Zilog Z8000") were becoming common. The **history of general-purpose [CPUs](CPU "CPU")** is a continuation of the earlier [history of computing hardware](History_of_computing_hardware "History of computing hardware").

## 1950s: Early designs

In the early 1950s, each computer design was unique. There were no upward-compatible machines or computer architectures with multiple, differing implementations. Programs written for one machine would run on no other kind, even other kinds from the same company. This was not a major drawback then because no large body of software had been developed to run on computers, so starting programming from scratch was not seen as a large barrier.

The design freedom of the time was very important because designers were very constrained by the cost of electronics, and only starting to explore how a computer could best be organized. Some of the basic features introduced during this period included [index registers](Index_register "Index register") (on the [Ferranti Mark 1](Ferranti_Mark_1 "Ferranti Mark 1")), a [return address](Return_statement "Return statement") saving instruction ([UNIVAC I](UNIVAC_I "UNIVAC I")), immediate operands ([IBM 704](IBM_704 "IBM 704")), and detecting invalid operations ([IBM 650](IBM_650 "IBM 650")).

By the end of the 1950s, commercial builders had developed factory-constructed, truck-deliverable computers. The most widely installed computer was the [IBM 650](IBM_650 "IBM 650"), which used [drum memory](Drum_memory "Drum memory") onto which programs were loaded using either paper [punched tape](Punched_tape "Punched tape") or [punched cards](Punched_card "Punched card"). Some very high-end machines also included [core memory](Core_memory "Core memory") which provided higher speeds. [Hard disks](Hard_disk "Hard disk") were also starting to grow popular.

A computer is an automatic [abacus](Abacus "Abacus"). The type of number system affects the way it works. In the early 1950s, most computers were built for specific numerical processing tasks, and many machines used decimal numbers as their basic number system; that is, the mathematical functions of the machines worked in base-10 instead of base-2 as is common today. These were not merely [binary-coded decimal](Binary-coded_decimal "Binary-coded decimal") (BCD). Most machines had ten vacuum tubes per digit in each [processor register](Processor_register "Processor register"). Some early [Soviet](Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") computer designers implemented systems based on [ternary logic](Ternary_logic "Ternary logic"); that is, a bit could have three states: +1, 0, or -1, corresponding to positive, zero, or negative voltage.

An early project for the [U.S. Air Force](U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force"), <BINAC> attempted to make a lightweight, simple computer by using binary arithmetic. It deeply impressed the industry.

As late as 1970, major computer languages were unable to standardize their numeric behavior because decimal computers had groups of users too large to alienate.

Even when designers used a binary system, they still had many odd ideas. Some used sign-magnitude arithmetic (-1 = 10001), or [ones' complement](Ones'_complement "Ones' complement") (-1 = 11110), rather than modern [two's complement](Two's_complement "Two's complement") arithmetic (-1 = 11111). Most computers used six-bit character sets because they adequately encoded Hollerith [punched cards](Punched_card "Punched card"). It was a major revelation to designers of this period to realize that the data word should be a multiple of the character size. They began to design computers with 12-, 24- and 36-bit data words (e.g., see the <TX-2>).

In this era, [Grosch's law](Grosch's_law "Grosch's law") dominated computer design: computer cost increased as the square of its speed.

## 1960s: Computer revolution and CISC

One major problem with early computers was that a program for one would work on no others. Computer companies found that their customers had little reason to remain loyal to a given brand, as the next computer they bought would be incompatible anyway. At that point, the only concerns were usually price and performance.

Intel (*Int*egrated *el*ectronics) was founded on July 18, 1968, by semiconductor pioneers [Gordon Moore](Gordon_Moore "Gordon Moore") (of [Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law")), [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce") (1927–1990), [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock") (venture capitalist) and is associated with the executive leadership and vision of [Andrew Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove").[[7]](Intel#cite_note-7) Intel was a key component of the rise of [Silicon Valley](Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley") as a high-tech center. Noyce was a key inventor of the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit#Invention "Integrated circuit") (microchip).[[8]](Intel#cite_note-8)[[9]](Intel#cite_note-9) Intel was an early developer of [SRAM](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") and [DRAM](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") memory chips, which represented the majority of its business until 1981. Although Intel created the world's first commercial microprocessor chip in 1971, it was not until the success of the [personal computer](Personal_computer "Personal computer") (PC) that this became its primary business.

During the 1990s, Intel invested heavily in new microprocessor designs fostering the rapid growth of the [computer industry](Information_technology "Information technology"). During this period, Intel became the [dominant](Dominance_(economics) "Dominance (economics)") supplier of PC microprocessors and was known for aggressive and anti-competitive tactics in defense of its market position, particularly against <AMD>, as well as a struggle with <Microsoft> for control over the direction of the PC industry.[[10]](Intel#cite_note-CNET_September_23,_1998-10)[[11]](Intel#cite_note-BBC_December_14,_1998-11)

The Open Source Technology Center at Intel hosts <PowerTOP> and <LatencyTOP>, and supports other open-source projects such as [Wayland](Wayland_(protocol) "Wayland (protocol)"), [Mesa](Mesa_(computer_graphics) "Mesa (computer graphics)"), [Threading Building Blocks](Threading_Building_Blocks "Threading Building Blocks") (TBB), and <Xen>.[[12]](Intel#cite_note-12)

## Current operations

### Operating segments

- **Client Computing Group** –  51.8% of 2020 revenues –  produces [PC processors](Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") and related components.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13)[[14]](Intel#cite_note-14)
- **Data Center Group** –  33.7% of 2020 revenues –  produces hardware components used in server, network, and storage platforms.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13)
- **Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group** –  6.9% of 2020 revenues –  produces components for [solid-state drives](Solid-state_drive "Solid-state drive"): [NAND flash memory](NAND_flash_memory "NAND flash memory") and [3D XPoint](3D_XPoint "3D XPoint") (<Optane>).[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13)
- **Internet of Things Group** –  5.2% of 2020 revenues –  offers platforms designed for retail, transportation, industrial, buildings and home use.[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13)
- **Programmable Solutions Group** –  2.4% of 2020 revenues –  manufactures programmable semiconductors (primarily [FPGAs](FPGA "FPGA")).[[13]](Intel#cite_note-:2-13)


### Customers

In 2020, <Dell> accounted for about 17% of Intel's total revenues, <Lenovo> accounted for 12% of total revenues, and [HP Inc.](HP_Inc. "HP Inc.") accounted for 10% of total revenues.[[1]](Intel#cite_note-xbrlus_1-1) As of August 2021, the US [Department of Defense](Department_of_Defence "Department of Defence") is another large customer for Intel.[[15]](Intel#cite_note-15)[[16]](Intel#cite_note-16)[[17]](Intel#cite_note-17)[[18]](Intel#cite_note-18)

### Market share

According to [IDC](International_Data_Corporation "International Data Corporation"), while Intel enjoyed the biggest market share in both the overall worldwide PC microprocessor market (73.3%) and the mobile PC microprocessor (80.4%) in the second quarter of 2011, the numbers decreased by 1.5% and 1.9% compared to the first quarter of 2011.[[19]](Intel#cite_note-19)[[20]](Intel#cite_note-20)

Intel's market share decreased significantly in the enthusiast market as of 2019,[[21]](Intel#cite_note-21) and they have faced delays for their 10 nm products. According to former Intel CEO Bob Swan, the delay was caused by the company's overly aggressive strategy for moving to its next node.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)

#### Historical market share

In the 1980s, Intel was among the world's top ten sellers of [semiconductors](Semiconductors "Semiconductors") (10th in 1987). Along with [Microsoft Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows"), it was part of the "<Wintel>" personal computer domination in the 1990s and early [2000s](2000s_decade "2000s decade"). In 1992, Intel became the biggest chip maker by revenue and held the position until 2018 when Samsung surpassed it, but Intel returned to its former position the year after.[[23]](Intel#cite_note-23)[[24]](Intel#cite_note-24) Other major semiconductor companies include <TSMC>, <GlobalFoundries>, <Samsung>, [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"), <Toshiba>, <STMicroelectronics>, [United Microelectronics Corporation](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation") (UMC), [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology"), [SK Hynix](SK_Hynix "SK Hynix"), <Kioxia>, and [SMIC](Semiconductor_Manufacturing_International_Corporation "Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation").

### Major competitors

Intel's competitors in PC chipsets included <AMD>, [VIA Technologies](VIA_Technologies "VIA Technologies"), [Silicon Integrated Systems](Silicon_Integrated_Systems "Silicon Integrated Systems"), and <Nvidia>. Intel's competitors in networking include [NXP Semiconductors](NXP_Semiconductors "NXP Semiconductors"), <Infineon>, [Broadcom Limited](Broadcom_Limited "Broadcom Limited"), [Marvell Technology Group](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group") and [Applied Micro Circuits Corporation](Applied_Micro_Circuits_Corporation "Applied Micro Circuits Corporation"), and competitors in flash memory included <Spansion>, Samsung Electronics, <Qimonda>, Kioxia, STMicroelectronics, [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology"), and [SK Hynix](SK_Hynix "SK Hynix").

Some smaller competitors, such as VIA Technologies, produce [low-power](Low-power_electronics "Low-power electronics") x86 processors for small factor computers and portable equipment. Compared to the incumbent technology, the SGT integrated on the same chip area twice the number of transistors with five times the operating speed. This step-function increase in performance made possible a single-chip CPU, replacing the existing multi-chip CPUs. The innovative 4004 chip design served as a model on how to use the SGT for complex logic and memory circuits, thus accelerating the adoption of the SGT by the world’s semiconductor industry. **Freescale Semiconductor, Inc.** was an American [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") manufacturer. It was created by the divestiture of the Semiconductor Products Sector of <Motorola> in 2004. Freescale focused their [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") products on the automotive, [embedded](Embedded_system "Embedded system") and communications markets. It was bought by a private investor group in 2006, and subsequently merged into [NXP Semiconductors](NXP_Semiconductors "NXP Semiconductors") in 2015.[[2]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-2)

## History

### Divesture from Motorola and first IPO

As of 2003, Motorola Semiconductor Products Sector earned US$5.0 [billion](Billion "Billion") in semiconductor sales in 2002 (out of US$27 billion sales for all of Motorola).[[3]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-3)

Motorola announced that their semiconductor division would be divested on October 6, 2003, to create Freescale.

Freescale completed its [Initial public offering](Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO) on July 16, 2004, at a price of US$13. In its announcement, it estimated the stock price to be US$17.50- 19.50 but following a cooling of the market towards tech stocks, it lowered its price to US$13. Existing shareholders of Motorola stock received 0.110415 shares of Freescale stock for every share of Motorola stock as a dividend which was distributed on December 2, 2004.[[4]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-4)

### Buyout

On September 15, 2006, Freescale agreed to accept a [buyout](Buyout "Buyout") for the sum of $17.6 billion ($40 per share) by a consortium led by the [Blackstone Group](Blackstone_Group "Blackstone Group"). Share prices of $13 at the July 2004 IPO had risen to $39.35 in afterhours trading that Friday when the news, rumored that week, broke. A special shareholders meeting on November 13, 2006, voted to accept the buyout offer. The purchase, which closed on December 1, 2006, is reportedly the largest private buyout of a technology company and one of the ten largest buyouts of all time.[[5]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-5)[[6]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-6)[[7]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-7)[[8]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-8)

### Second IPO

Freescale filed to go public again on February 11, 2011, and completed its IPO on May 26, 2011. Freescale was traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the [ticker symbol](Ticker_symbol "Ticker symbol") FSL. At the time of the IPO, the company had $7.6 billion in outstanding debt on its books,[[9]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-Freescale_Debt-9) and the company was investigated for misconduct related to this IPO.[[10]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-10)

### MH370

On March 8, 2014, Freescale announced that 20 of its employees were lost aboard [Malaysia Airlines Flight 370](Malaysia_Airlines_Flight_370 "Malaysia Airlines Flight 370").[[11]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-11)

## Products

### Automotive

MSG (Micro-controller Solutions Group) is the largest business unit within Freescale and is currently the largest semiconductor supplier to the [automotive industry](Automotive_industry "Automotive industry"). Modern cars use electronics to manage the engine for peak performance and to reduce [emissions](Automobile_emissions_control "Automobile emissions control"), and Freescale is the largest supplier of engine system microcontrollers in the world. **MOS Technology, Inc.** ("MOS" being short for [Metal Oxide Semiconductor](Metal_Oxide_Semiconductor "Metal Oxide Semiconductor")), later known as **CSG (Commodore Semiconductor Group)** and **GMT Microelectronics**, was a [semiconductor](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") design and [fabrication](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication") company based in [Audubon, Pennsylvania](Audubon%2C_Pennsylvania "Audubon, Pennsylvania"). It is most famous for its [6502](MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502") [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") and various designs for [Commodore International](Commodore_International "Commodore International")'s range of [home computers](Home_computer "Home computer").

## History

Three former [General Instrument](General_Instrument "General Instrument") executives, John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe and Don McLaughlin, formed MOS Technology in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania in 1969. The [Allen-Bradley Company](Allen-Bradley "Allen-Bradley") was looking to provide a second source for electronic calculators and their chips designed by [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") (TI). In 1970 Allen-Bradley acquired a majority interest in MOS Technology.

In the early 1970s, TI decided to release their own line of calculators, instead of selling just the chips inside them, and introduced them at a price that was lower than the price of the chipset alone. Many early chip companies were reliant on sales of calculator chips and were wiped out in the aftermath; those that survived did so by finding other chips to produce. MOS became a supplier to <Atari>, producing a custom single-chip *<Pong>* system.

Things changed dramatically in 1975. Previous CPU designs, like the 6800, were produced using a device known as a [contact aligner](Contact_lithography "Contact lithography"). This was essentially a complex [photocopier](Photocopier "Photocopier"), which optically reproduced a CPU design, or "mask", on the surface of the silicon chip. The name "contact" referred to the fact that the mask was placed directly on the surface of the chip, which had the significant disadvantage that it sometimes pulled away materials from the chip, which were then copied to subsequent chips. This caused the mask to become useless after about a dozen copies, and resulted in the vast majority of chips having fatal flaws; for a complex chip like the 6800, only about 10% of the chips would work once the masking process was complete.[[1]](MOS_Technology#cite_note-Mensch-1)

In 1974 <Perkin-Elmer> publicly introduced the <Micralign> system, the first projection scanner. Instead of placing the mask on the surface of the chip, it held it far from the surface and used highly accurate optics to project the image. Masks now lasted for thousands of copies instead of tens, and the flaw rate of the chips inverted so that perhaps 70% of the chips produced would work. The result was a similar inversion in pricing. The 6800 sold in small lots for $295; with no other changes than using a <Micralign>, the same design could sell for $42.[[1]](MOS_Technology#cite_note-Mensch-1)

The **MC14500B** Industrial Control Unit (ICU) is a <CMOS> [one-bit](1-bit_architecture "1-bit architecture") [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") designed by <Motorola> for simple control applications in 1977.[[1]](Motorola_MC14500B#cite_note-Motorola_1977_MC14500B-1)

## Overview

MC14500B (ICU) is well-suited to the implementation of [ladder logic](Ladder_logic "Ladder logic"), and thus could be used to replace [relay](Relay "Relay") systems and [programmable logic controllers](Programmable_logic_controller "Programmable logic controller"), also intended for serial data manipulation.[[2]](Motorola_MC14500B#cite_note-Motorola_1995_MC14500B-2) The processor supports 16 commands, operating at a frequency of 1 MHz.[[2]](Motorola_MC14500B#cite_note-Motorola_1995_MC14500B-2) The MC14500B unit does not include a [program counter](Program_counter "Program counter") (PC); instead, a clock signal drives a separate PC chip; therefore the size of supported memory is dependent on the implementation of that chip. It was still in production in 1995.[[2]](Motorola_MC14500B#cite_note-Motorola_1995_MC14500B-2)

The ICU architecture is similar to that of the [DEC](Digital_Equipment_Corporation "Digital Equipment Corporation") <PDP-14> computer.

## Developers

The ICU was conceived by Vern Gregory in the mid-1970s while working as an engineer in a marketing / applications group of Motorola Semiconductor Products Sector in Phoenix, Arizona, USA; Brian Dellande originated circuit and sub-routine designs, and co-wrote the manual; Ray DiSilvestro was the bench technician; Terry Malarkey provided management support.

In the CMOS Logic Division in Austin, Texas, USA (where it was made) Phil Smith was the chip designer; Mike Hadley provided product applications support.

## Derivatives

A form of the design served as an embedded controller in a custom automotive chip made for [Nippon Denso](Nippon_Denso "Nippon Denso") by Motorola—Japan.

[I.P.R.S. Băneasa](I.P.R.S._B%C4%83neasa "I.P.R.S. Băneasa") manufactured a clone of the MC14500B with the designation βP14500 in [IIL](Integrated_injection_logic "Integrated injection logic") technology (rather than the original CMOS).[[3]](Motorola_MC14500B#cite_note-Cracea-Raiu_1990-3)

## Notable uses

One of the computers known to be based on this processor is the educational [WDR 1](http://wdr-1-bit-computer.talentraspel.de/)-bit computer (512 bits of RAM, LED, I/O, keyboard).[[4]](Motorola_MC14500B#cite_note-Ludwig_1986_WDR-1-4)

A modern take, in retro style, of a computer based on this processor is the [PLC14500-Nano](https://github.com/nicolacimmino/PLC-14500). It is certified as Open Source Hardware [PL000011](https://certification.oshwa.org/pl000011.html) so anyone can learn from its design and can freely build it.

## See also

- [WDR paper computer](WDR_paper_computer "WDR paper computer")
- [WDR Computerclub](WDR_Computerclub "WDR Computerclub")
- [NDR computer](NDR_computer "NDR computer")

**Am2900** is a family of [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") (ICs) created in 1975 by [Advanced Micro Devices](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices") (AMD). They were constructed with [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") devices, in a [bit-slice](Bit_slicing "Bit slicing") topology, and were designed to be used as modular components each representing a different aspect of a computer [control unit](Control_unit "Control unit") (CCU). By using the [bit slicing](Bit_slicing "Bit slicing") technique, the Am2900 family was able to implement a CCU with data, addresses, and instructions to be any multiple of 4 bits by multiplying the number of ICs. One major problem with this modular technique was that it required a larger number of ICs to implement what could be done on a single CPU IC. The Am2901 chip included an [arithmetic logic unit](Arithmetic_logic_unit "Arithmetic logic unit") (ALU) and 16 4-bit [processor register](Processor_register "Processor register") slices, and was the "core" of the series. It could count using 4 bits and implement binary operations as well as various [bit-shifting](Bit_shift "Bit shift") operations.

The 2901 and some other chips in the family were [second sourced](Second_source "Second source") by an unusually large number of other manufacturers, starting with Motorola and then Raytheon –  both in 1975 –  and also Cypress Semiconductor, National Semiconductor, NEC, Thomson, and Signetics. In the Soviet Union and later Russia the Am2900 family was manufactured as the 1804 series (with e.g. the Am2901 [designated](Soviet_integrated_circuit_designation "Soviet integrated circuit designation") as KR1804VS1 / [Russian](Russian_language "Russian language"): *[КР1804ВС1](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/К1804 "ru:К1804")*)[[1]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-1)[[2]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-cpuworld-2)[[3]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-kozak1800-3) which was known to be in production in 2016.[[4]](AMD_Am2900#cite_note-vzpp-4)

The [Regency TR-1](Regency_TR-1 "Regency TR-1") used germanium transistors, as silicon transistors were much more expensive at the time. This was an effort by Haggerty to increase market demand for transistors.

[Jack Kilby](Jack_Kilby "Jack Kilby"), an employee at TI, invented the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") in 1958.[[26]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-26) Kilby recorded his initial ideas concerning the integrated circuit in July 1958, and successfully demonstrated the world's first working integrated circuit on September 12, 1958.[[27]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-27) Six months later, [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce") of [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") (who went on to co-found <Intel>) independently developed the integrated circuit with integrated interconnect, and is also considered an inventor of the integrated circuit.[[28]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-28) In 1969, Kilby was awarded the National Medal of Science, and in 1982 he was inducted into the National Inventor's Hall of Fame.[[29]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-29) Kilby also won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for his part of the invention of the integrated circuit.[[30]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-30) Noyce's chip, made at Fairchild, was made of silicon, while Kilby's chip was made of [germanium](Germanium "Germanium"). In 2008, TI named its new development laboratory "Kilby Labs" after Jack Kilby.[[31]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-31)

In 2011, Intel, Samsung, LG, ST-Ericsson, Huawei's HiSilicon Technologies subsidiary, Via Telecom, and three other undisclosed chipmakers licensed the C2C link specification developed by Arteris Inc. and Texas Instruments.[[32]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-32)

#### Standard TTL

The [7400 series](7400_series "7400 series") of [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") chips, developed by Texas Instruments in the 1960s, popularized the use of integrated circuits in computer logic. The military-grade version of this was the 5400 series.[[33]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-33)

#### Microprocessor

Texas Instruments invented the hand-held [calculator](Calculator "Calculator") (a prototype called "[Cal Tech](Cal_Tech_(calculator) "Cal Tech (calculator)")") in 1967 and the single-chip [microcomputer](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1971, was assigned the first patent on a single-chip [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") (invented by Gary Boone) on September 4, 1973.[[34]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-34) This was disputed by Gilbert Hyatt, formerly of the Micro Computer Company, in August 1990, when he was awarded a patent superseding TI's. This was overturned on June 19, 1996, in favor of TI[[35]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-35) (note: <Intel> is usually given credit with Texas Instruments for the almost-simultaneous invention of the microprocessor).

#### First speech synthesis chip

In 1978, Texas Instruments introduced the first single-chip [linear predictive coding](Linear_predictive_coding "Linear predictive coding") [speech synthesizer](Speech_synthesizer "Speech synthesizer").[[36]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-36) In 1976, TI began a feasibility study of memory-intensive applications for bubble memory then being developed. They soon focused on speech applications. This resulted in the development the TMC0280 one-chip linear predictive coding speech synthesizer, which was the first time a single silicon chip had electronically replicated the human voice.[[37]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TITimeLine-37)[[38]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-38) This was used in several TI commercial products beginning with [Speak & Spell](Speak_%26_Spell_(toy) "Speak & Spell (toy)"), which was introduced at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in June 1978. In 2001, TI left the speech synthesis business, selling it to Sensory Inc. of Santa Clara, California.[[39]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TI_will_exit_dedicated_speech-synthesis_chips,_transfer_products_to_Sensory-39)

### Consumer electronics and computers

In May 1954, Texas Instruments designed and built a prototype of the world's first [transistor radio](Transistor_radio "Transistor radio"), and, through a partnership with Industrial Development Engineering Associates of Indianapolis, Indiana, the 100% solid-state radio was sold to the public beginning in October of that year.[[40]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-40)

"8400 series", "7400 series", "6400 series", "5400 series", and "74 series" redirect here. For other uses, see [8400](8400_(disambiguation) "8400 (disambiguation)"), [7400](7400_(disambiguation) "7400 (disambiguation)"), [6400](6400_(disambiguation) "6400 (disambiguation)"), [5400](5400_(disambiguation) "5400 (disambiguation)"), and [74 (disambiguation)](74_(disambiguation) "74 (disambiguation)").

"7402", "7404", and "7486" redirect here. For the highway, see [Hawaii Route 7402](Hawaii_Route_7402 "Hawaii Route 7402"). For the asteroids, see [(7402) 1987 YH]((7402)_1987_YH "(7402) 1987 YH"), [(7404) 1988 AA5]((7404)_1988_AA5 "(7404) 1988 AA5"), and [7486 Hamabe](7486_Hamabe "7486 Hamabe"). For the military unit, see [7486th Air Defense Group](7486th_Air_Defense_Group "7486th Air Defense Group").

The **7400 series** is a popular [logic family](Logic_family "Logic family") of [transistor–transistor logic](Transistor%E2%80%93transistor_logic "Transistor–transistor logic") (TTL) [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") (ICs).[[3]](7400-series_integrated_circuits#cite_note-3)

In 1964, [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") introduced the SN5400 series of logic chips, in a ceramic [semiconductor package](Semiconductor_package "Semiconductor package"). A low-cost plastic package SN7400 series was introduced in 1966 which quickly gained over 50% of the logic chip market, and eventually becoming *de facto* standardized electronic components.[[4]](7400-series_integrated_circuits#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](7400-series_integrated_circuits#cite_note-TI_1967_Databook-5) Over the decades, many generations of [pin-compatible](Pin-compatibility "Pin-compatibility") descendant families evolved to include support for low power <CMOS> technology, [lower supply voltages](LVCMOS "LVCMOS"), and [surface mount packages](Surface-mount_technology "Surface-mount technology").[[6]](7400-series_integrated_circuits#cite_note-TI_2004_LRG-6)

## Overview

See also: [Transistor–transistor logic § History](Transistor%E2%80%93transistor_logic#History "Transistor–transistor logic")

The 7400 series contains hundreds of devices that provide everything from basic [logic gates](Logic_gate "Logic gate"), [flip-flops](Flip-flop_(electronics) "Flip-flop (electronics)"), and counters, to special purpose bus transceivers and [arithmetic logic units](Arithmetic_logic_unit "Arithmetic logic unit") (ALU). Specific functions are described in a [list of 7400 series integrated circuits](List_of_7400_series_integrated_circuits "List of 7400 series integrated circuits"). Some TTL logic parts were made with an extended military-specification temperature range. These parts are prefixed with **54** instead of **74** in the part number. The less-common **64** prefix on [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") parts indicated an industrial temperature range. Since the 1970s, new product families have been released to replace the original 7400 series. More recent TTL logic families were manufactured using <CMOS> or <BiCMOS> technology rather than TTL.

Today, [surface-mounted](Surface-mount "Surface-mount") CMOS versions of the 7400 series are used in various applications in electronics and for [glue logic](Glue_logic "Glue logic") in computers and industrial electronics. The original [through-hole](Through-hole "Through-hole") devices in [dual in-line packages](Dual_in-line_package "Dual in-line package") (DIP/DIL) were the mainstay of the industry for many decades. They are useful for rapid [breadboard](Breadboard "Breadboard")-prototyping and for education and remain available from most manufacturers. The fastest types and very low voltage versions are typically [surface-mount](Surface-mount "Surface-mount") only, however.

The first part number in the series, the 7400, is a 14-pin IC containing four two-input [NAND gates](NAND_gate "NAND gate"). Each gate uses two input pins and one output pin, with the remaining two pins being power (+5 V) and ground. This part was made in various through-hole and surface-mount packages, including flat pack and plastic/ceramic dual in-line. Additional characters in a part number identify the package and other variations.

Unlike the older [resistor-transistor logic](Resistor-transistor_logic "Resistor-transistor logic") integrated circuits, bipolar TTL gates were unsuitable to be used as analog devices, providing low gain, poor stability, and low input impedance.[[7]](7400-series_integrated_circuits#cite_note-7) Special-purpose TTL devices were used to provide interface functions such as [Schmitt triggers](Schmitt_trigger "Schmitt trigger") or [monostable multivibrator](Monostable_multivibrator "Monostable multivibrator") timing circuits. Inverting gates could be cascaded as a [ring oscillator](Ring_oscillator "Ring oscillator"), useful for purposes where high stability was not required.

### History

Although the 7400 series was the first *de facto* industry standard TTL logic family (i.e. second-sourced by several semiconductor companies), there were earlier TTL logic families such as:

- [Sylvania](Sylvania_Electric_Products "Sylvania Electric Products") Universal High-level Logic in 1963[[8]](7400-series_integrated_circuits#cite_note-8)[[9]](7400-series_integrated_circuits#cite_note-9)[[10]](7400-series_integrated_circuits#cite_note-10)

 1979, TI entered the [home computer](Home_computer "Home computer") market with the [TI-99/4](TI-99/4A "TI-99/4A"), a competitor to such entries as the [Apple II](Apple_II_series "Apple II series"), <TRS-80>, and the later [Atari 400/800](Atari_8-bit_family "Atari 8-bit family") series and <VIC-20>. By late 1982, TI was dominating the U.S. home computer market, shipping 5,000 computers a day from their factory in Lubbock.[[42]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-death_1984_04_texasmonthly-42) It discontinued the <TI-99/4A> (1981), the sequel to the 99/4, in late 1983 amid an intense [price war](North_American_video_game_crash_of_1983 "North American video game crash of 1983") waged primarily against Commodore. At the 1983 Winter CES, TI showed models 99/2 and the [Compact Computer 40 (CC-40)](Compact_Computer_40 "Compact Computer 40"), the latter aimed at professional users. The company for years successfully made and sold PC-compatible laptops before withdrawing from the market and selling its product line to [Acer](Acer_Inc. "Acer Inc.") in 1998.[[44]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-44)

### Defense electronics

TI entered the [defense](Defense_(military) "Defense (military)") electronics market in 1942 with submarine detection equipment,[[45]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-45) based on the seismic exploration technology previously developed for the oil industry. The division responsible for these products was known at different times as the Laboratory & Manufacturing Division, the Apparatus Division, the Equipment Group, and the Defense Systems & Electronics Group (DSEG).

During the early 1980s, TI instituted a quality program which included [Juran](Joseph_M._Juran "Joseph M. Juran") training, as well as promoting [statistical process control](Statistical_process_control "Statistical process control"), [Taguchi methods](Taguchi_methods "Taguchi methods"), and [Design for Six Sigma](Design_for_Six_Sigma "Design for Six Sigma"). In the late '80s, the company, along with [Eastman Kodak](Eastman_Kodak "Eastman Kodak") and [Allied Signal](Allied_Signal "Allied Signal"), began involvement with <Motorola>, institutionalizing Motorola's [Six Sigma](Six_Sigma "Six Sigma") methodology.[[46]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-46) Motorola, which originally developed the Six Sigma methodology, began this work in 1982. In 1992, the DSEG division[[47]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-47) of Texas Instruments' quality-improvement efforts were rewarded by winning the [Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award](Malcolm_Baldrige_National_Quality_Award "Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award") for manufacturing.

#### Infrared and radar systems

TI developed the AAA-4 [infrared search and track](Infrared_search_and_track "Infrared search and track") device in the late '50s and early '60s for the [F-4B Phantom](F-4B_Phantom "F-4B Phantom")[[48]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweetmanBonds1987526-48) for passive scanning of jet-engine emissions, but it possessed limited capabilities and was eliminated on F-4Ds and later models.[[49]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweetmanBonds1987552-49)

In 1956, TI began research on [infrared](Infrared "Infrared") technology that led to several line scanner contracts and with the addition of a second scan mirror the invention of the first [forward looking infrared](Forward_looking_infrared "Forward looking infrared") (FLIR) in 1963 with production beginning in 1966. In 1972, TI invented the common module FLIR[[50]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-50) concept, greatly reducing cost and allowing reuse of common components.

TI went on to produce side-looking radar systems, the first [terrain-following radar](Terrain_following_radar "Terrain following radar") and surveillance radar systems for both the military and FAA. TI demonstrated the first solid-state radar called Molecular Electronics for Radar Applications.[[51]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-51) In 1976, TI developed a [microwave landing system](Microwave_landing_system "Microwave landing system") prototype. In 1984, TI developed the first [inverse synthetic aperture radar](Inverse_synthetic_aperture_radar "Inverse synthetic aperture radar"). The first single-chip [gallium arsenide](Gallium_arsenide "Gallium arsenide") radar module was developed. In 1991, the military microwave integrated circuit[[52]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-52) program was initiated –  a joint effort with Raytheon.

#### Missiles and laser-guided bombs

In 1961, TI won the guidance and control system contract for the defense suppression [AGM-45 Shrike](AGM-45_Shrike "AGM-45 Shrike") [antiradiation missile](Antiradiation_missile "Antiradiation missile"). This led later to the prime on the [high-speed antiradiation missile](AGM-88_HARM "AGM-88 HARM") (AGM-88 HARM) development contract in 1974 and production in 1981.

In 1964, TI began development of the first laser guidance system for [precision-guided munitions](Precision-guided_munition "Precision-guided munition"), leading to the <Paveway> series of [laser-guided bombs](Laser-guided_bomb "Laser-guided bomb") (LGBs). The first LGB was the <BOLT-117>.

In 1969, TI won the Harpoon (missile) Seeker contract. In 1986, TI won the Army [FGM-148 Javelin](FGM-148_Javelin "FGM-148 Javelin") [fire-and-forget](Fire-and-forget "Fire-and-forget") man portable antitank guided missile in a joint venture with [Martin Marietta](Martin_Marietta "Martin Marietta"). In 1991, TI was awarded the contract for the [AGM-154 Joint Standoff Weapon](AGM-154_Joint_Standoff_Weapon "AGM-154 Joint Standoff Weapon").[[53]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-53)

In 1988, TI paid the U.S. government $5.2 million "to settle allegations one of its divisions overcharged the government on contracts for guided missiles sold to the [Navy](United_States_Navy "United States Navy")".[[54]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-54)

#### Military computers

See also: [Military computers](Military_computers "Military computers")

Because of TI's research and development of military temperature-range silicon transistors and integrated circuits (ICs), TI won contracts for the first IC-based computer for the U.S. Air Force in 1961 (molecular electronic computer)[[55]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-55) and for ICs for the Minuteman Missile the following year. The **history of computing hardware** starting at 1960 is marked by the conversion from [vacuum tube](Vacuum_tube "Vacuum tube") to [solid-state](Solid-state_electronics "Solid-state electronics") devices such as [transistors](Transistor "Transistor") and then [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") (IC) chips. Around 1953 to 1959, discrete transistors started being considered sufficiently reliable and economical that they made further vacuum tube computers [uncompetitive](Competition_(economics) "Competition (economics)"). [Metal–oxide–semiconductor](Metal%E2%80%93oxide%E2%80%93semiconductor "Metal–oxide–semiconductor") (MOS) [large-scale integration](Large-scale_integration "Large-scale integration") (LSI) technology subsequently led to the development of [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") in the mid-to-late 1960s and then the [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") in the early 1970s. This led to primary [computer memory](Computer_memory "Computer memory") moving away from [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory") devices to solid-state static and dynamic semiconductor memory, which greatly reduced the cost, size, and power consumption of computers. These advances led to the miniaturized [personal computer](Personal_computer "Personal computer") (PC) in the 1970s, starting with [home computers](Home_computer "Home computer") and [desktop computers](Desktop_computer "Desktop computer"), followed by [laptops](Laptop "Laptop") and then [mobile computers](Mobile_computer "Mobile computer") over the next several decades.

See also: [List of transistorized computers](List_of_transistorized_computers "List of transistorized computers") and [Transistor computer](Transistor_computer "Transistor computer")

For the purposes of this article, the term "second generation" refers to computers using discrete transistors, even when the vendors referred to them as "third-generation". The **TMS9900** was one of the first commercially available, single-chip <16-bit> [microprocessors](Microprocessor "Microprocessor").[[lower-alpha 1]](TMS9900#cite_note-1) Introduced in June 1976, it implemented [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments")' <TI-990> [minicomputer](Minicomputer "Minicomputer") architecture in a single-chip format, and was initially used for low-end models of that lineup.

Its 64-pin [DIP](Dual_in-line_package "Dual in-line package") format made it more expensive to implement in smaller machines than the more common 40-pin format, and it saw relatively few design wins outside TI's own use. Among those uses was their [TI-99/4 and TI-99/4A](TI-99/4A "TI-99/4A") home computers, which ultimately sold about 2.8 million units.

Microcomputer-on-chip implementations of the 9900 in 40-pin packages included the TMS9940, TMS9980/81, TMS9995. The TMS99105/10 was the last iteration of the 9900 in 1981 and incorporated features of TI's 990/10 minicomputer.[[1]](TMS9900#cite_note-:0-2)

By the mid-1980s the microcomputer field was moving to 16-bit systems like the [Intel 8088](Intel_8088 "Intel 8088") and newer 16/32-bit designs like the [Motorola 68000](Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000"). ## 1970s

The first [microprocessors](Microprocessors "Microprocessors") were designed and manufactured in the 1970s. Intel's 4004 of 1971 is widely regarded as the first commercial microprocessor.[[1]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-1)

Designers predominantly used <MOSFET> transistors with [pMOS logic](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") in the early 1970s, switching to [nMOS logic](NMOS_logic "NMOS logic") after the mid-1970s. nMOS had the advantage that it could run on a single voltage, typically +5V, which simplified the power supply requirements and allowed it to be easily interfaced with the wide variety of +5V [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") (TTL) devices. nMOS had the disadvantage that it was more susceptible to electronic noise generated by slight impurities in the underlying silicon material, and it was not until the mid-1970s that these, sodium in particular, were successfully removed to the required levels. At that time, around 1975, nMOS quickly took over the market.[[2]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-2)

This corresponded with the introduction of new [semiconductor masking](Photomask "Photomask") systems, notably the <Micralign> system from <Perkin-Elmer>. Micralign projected an image of the mask onto the silicon wafer, never touching it directly, which eliminated the previous problems when the mask would be lifted off the surface and take away some of the [photoresist](Photoresist "Photoresist") along with it, ruining the chips on that portion of the wafer.[[3]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-3) By reducing the number of flawed chips, from about 70% to 10%, the cost of complex designs like early microprocessors fell by the same amount. Systems based on contact aligners cost on the order of $300 in single-unit quantities, the [MOS 6502](MOS_6502 "MOS 6502"), designed specifically to take advantage of these improvements, cost only $25.[[4]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-4)

This period also saw considerable experimentation with various [word lengths](Word_length "Word length"). Early on, [4-bit](4-bit_computing "4-bit computing") processors were common, like the Intel 4004, simply because making a wider word length could not be accomplished cost-effectively in the room available on the small wafers of the era, especially when the majority would be defective. As yields improved, wafer sizes grew, and feature size continued to be reduced, more complex [8-bit](8-bit_computing "8-bit computing") designs emerged like the [Intel 8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") and 6502. [16-bit](16-bit_computing "16-bit computing") processors emerged early but were expensive; by the decade's end, low-cost 16-bit designs like the [Zilog Z8000](Zilog_Z8000 "Zilog Z8000") were becoming common. Some unusual word lengths were also produced, including [12-bit](12-bit_computing "12-bit computing") and 20-[bit](Bit "Bit"), often matching a design that had previously been implemented in a multi-chip format in a [minicomputer](Minicomputer "Minicomputer"). These had largely disappeared by the end of the decade as minicomputers moved to [32-bit](32-bit_computing "32-bit computing") formats.

## 1980s

As [Moore's Law](Moore's_Law "Moore's Law") continued to drive the industry towards more complex chip designs, the expected widespread move from 8-bit designs of the 1970s to 16-bit designs almost didn't occur; instead, new [32-bit](32-bit_computing "32-bit computing") designs like the [Motorola 68000](Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") and [National Semiconductor NS32000](National_Semiconductor_NS32000 "National Semiconductor NS32000") emerged that offered far more performance. Whereas earlier systems used a single [transistor](Transistor "Transistor") as the basis for each "gate", CMOS used a two-sided design, essentially making it twice as expensive to build. Its advantage was that its logic was not based on the voltage of a transistor compared to the silicon substrate, but the *difference* in voltages between the two sides, which was detectable at much lower power levels. ## 1970s

The first [microprocessors](Microprocessors "Microprocessors") were designed and manufactured in the 1970s. Intel's 4004 of 1971 is widely regarded as the first commercial microprocessor.[[1]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-1)

Designers predominantly used <MOSFET> transistors with [pMOS logic](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") in the early 1970s, switching to [nMOS logic](NMOS_logic "NMOS logic") after the mid-1970s. nMOS had the advantage that it could run on a single voltage, typically +5V, which simplified the power supply requirements and allowed it to be easily interfaced with the wide variety of +5V [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") (TTL) devices. nMOS had the disadvantage that it was more susceptible to electronic noise generated by slight impurities in the underlying silicon material, and it was not until the mid-1970s that these, sodium in particular, were successfully removed to the required levels. At that time, around 1975, nMOS quickly took over the market.[[2]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-2)

This corresponded with the introduction of new [semiconductor masking](Photomask "Photomask") systems, notably the <Micralign> system from <Perkin-Elmer>. Micralign projected an image of the mask onto the silicon wafer, never touching it directly, which eliminated the previous problems when the mask would be lifted off the surface and take away some of the [photoresist](Photoresist "Photoresist") along with it, ruining the chips on that portion of the wafer.[[3]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-3) By reducing the number of flawed chips, from about 70% to 10%, the cost of complex designs like early microprocessors fell by the same amount. Systems based on contact aligners cost on the order of $300 in single-unit quantities, the [MOS 6502](MOS_6502 "MOS 6502"), designed specifically to take advantage of these improvements, cost only $25.[[4]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-4)

This period also saw considerable experimentation with various [word lengths](Word_length "Word length"). Early on, [4-bit](4-bit_computing "4-bit computing") processors were common, like the Intel 4004, simply because making a wider word length could not be accomplished cost-effectively in the room available on the small wafers of the era, especially when the majority would be defective. As yields improved, wafer sizes grew, and feature size continued to be reduced, more complex [8-bit](8-bit_computing "8-bit computing") designs emerged like the [Intel 8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") and 6502. [16-bit](16-bit_computing "16-bit computing") processors emerged early but were expensive; by the decade's end, low-cost 16-bit designs like the [Zilog Z8000](Zilog_Z8000 "Zilog Z8000") were becoming common. An **integrated circuit** or **monolithic integrated circuit** (also referred to as an **IC**, a **chip**, or a **microchip**) is a set of [electronic circuits](Electronic_circuit "Electronic circuit") on one small flat piece (or "chip") of [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") material, usually [silicon](Silicon "Silicon"). Large numbers of miniaturized [transistors](Transistors "Transistors") and other [electronic components](Electronic_components "Electronic components") are integrated together on the chip. This results in circuits that are orders of magnitude smaller, faster, and less expensive than those constructed of discrete components, allowing a large [transistor count](Transistor_count "Transistor count"). The IC's [mass production](Mass_production "Mass production") capability, reliability, and building-block approach to [integrated circuit design](Integrated_circuit_design "Integrated circuit design") have ensured the rapid adoption of standardized ICs in place of designs using discrete transistors. ICs are now used in virtually all electronic equipment and have revolutionized the world of [electronics](Electronics "Electronics"). [Computers](Computer "Computer"), [mobile phones](Mobile_phone "Mobile phone") and other [home appliances](Home_appliance "Home appliance") are now essential parts of the structure of modern societies, made possible by the small size and low cost of ICs such as modern [computer processors](Computer_processor "Computer processor") and [microcontrollers](Microcontroller "Microcontroller").

[Very-large-scale integration](Very-large-scale_integration "Very-large-scale integration") was made practical by technological advancements in [semiconductor device fabrication](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication"). Since their origins in the 1960s, the size, speed, and capacity of chips have progressed enormously, driven by technical advances that fit more and more transistors on chips of the same size – a modern chip may have many billions of transistors in an area the size of a human fingernail. These advances, roughly following [Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law"), make the computer chips of today possess millions of times the capacity and thousands of times the speed of the computer chips of the early 1970s.

## Industry structure

The global semiconductor industry is dominated by companies from the [United States](United_States "United States"), <Taiwan>, [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea"), <Japan> and the <Netherlands>.

Unique features of the industry include continuous growth but in a cyclical pattern with high volatility. While the current 20 year annual average growth of the semiconductor industry is on the order of 13%, this has been accompanied by equally above-average market volatility, which can lead to significant if not dramatic cyclical swings. This has required the need for high degrees of flexibility and innovation in order to constantly adjust to the rapid pace of change in the market as many products embedding semiconductor devices often have a very short life cycle.

At the same time, the rate of constant price-performance improvement in the semiconductor industry is staggering. As a consequence, changes in the semiconductor market not only occur extremely rapidly but also anticipate changes in industries evolving at a slower pace. The semiconductor industry is widely recognized as a key driver and technology enabler for the whole electronics value chain.[[10]](Semiconductor_industry#cite_note-10)

Some companies, known as [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer"), both design and manufacture semiconductors. **MOS Technology, Inc.** ("MOS" being short for [Metal Oxide Semiconductor](Metal_Oxide_Semiconductor "Metal Oxide Semiconductor")), later known as **CSG (Commodore Semiconductor Group)** and **GMT Microelectronics**, was a [semiconductor](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") design and [fabrication](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication") company based in [Audubon, Pennsylvania](Audubon%2C_Pennsylvania "Audubon, Pennsylvania"). It is most famous for its [6502](MOS_Technology_6502 "MOS Technology 6502") [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") and various designs for [Commodore International](Commodore_International "Commodore International")'s range of [home computers](Home_computer "Home computer").

## History

Three former [General Instrument](General_Instrument "General Instrument") executives, John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe and Don McLaughlin, formed MOS Technology in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania in 1969. The [Allen-Bradley Company](Allen-Bradley "Allen-Bradley") was looking to provide a second source for electronic calculators and their chips designed by [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") (TI). In 1970 Allen-Bradley acquired a majority interest in MOS Technology.

In the early 1970s, TI decided to release their own line of calculators, instead of selling just the chips inside them, and introduced them at a price that was lower than the price of the chipset alone. Many early chip companies were reliant on sales of calculator chips and were wiped out in the aftermath; those that survived did so by finding other chips to produce. MOS became a supplier to <Atari>, producing a custom single-chip *<Pong>* system.

Things changed dramatically in 1975. At the time there was no such thing as a [pure-play semiconductor foundry](Pure-play_semiconductor_foundry "Pure-play semiconductor foundry"), so they had to join a chip-building company to produce their new CPU. ## 1970s

The first [microprocessors](Microprocessors "Microprocessors") were designed and manufactured in the 1970s. Intel's 4004 of 1971 is widely regarded as the first commercial microprocessor.[[1]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-1)

Designers predominantly used <MOSFET> transistors with [pMOS logic](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") in the early 1970s, switching to [nMOS logic](NMOS_logic "NMOS logic") after the mid-1970s. nMOS had the advantage that it could run on a single voltage, typically +5V, which simplified the power supply requirements and allowed it to be easily interfaced with the wide variety of +5V [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") (TTL) devices. nMOS had the disadvantage that it was more susceptible to electronic noise generated by slight impurities in the underlying silicon material, and it was not until the mid-1970s that these, sodium in particular, were successfully removed to the required levels. At that time, around 1975, nMOS quickly took over the market.[[2]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-2)

This corresponded with the introduction of new [semiconductor masking](Photomask "Photomask") systems, notably the <Micralign> system from <Perkin-Elmer>. Micralign projected an image of the mask onto the silicon wafer, never touching it directly, which eliminated the previous problems when the mask would be lifted off the surface and take away some of the [photoresist](Photoresist "Photoresist") along with it, ruining the chips on that portion of the wafer.[[3]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-3) By reducing the number of flawed chips, from about 70% to 10%, the cost of complex designs like early microprocessors fell by the same amount. Systems based on contact aligners cost on the order of $300 in single-unit quantities, the [MOS 6502](MOS_6502 "MOS 6502"), designed specifically to take advantage of these improvements, cost only $25.[[4]](Microprocessor_chronology#cite_note-4)

This period also saw considerable experimentation with various [word lengths](Word_length "Word length"). Early on, [4-bit](4-bit_computing "4-bit computing") processors were common, like the Intel 4004, simply because making a wider word length could not be accomplished cost-effectively in the room available on the small wafers of the era, especially when the majority would be defective. As yields improved, wafer sizes grew, and feature size continued to be reduced, more complex [8-bit](8-bit_computing "8-bit computing") designs emerged like the [Intel 8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") and 6502. [16-bit](16-bit_computing "16-bit computing") processors emerged early but were expensive; by the decade's end, low-cost 16-bit designs like the [Zilog Z8000](Zilog_Z8000 "Zilog Z8000") were becoming common.
