| External image | |
| --- | --- |
| [Photo of the interior of a clean room of a 300mm fab](https://www.tsmc.com/img/photoGallery/fabs_in/Fab12inc046.jpg) run by <TSMC> | |


In the [microelectronics](Microelectronics "Microelectronics") industry, a **semiconductor fabrication plant** (commonly called a **fab**; sometimes **foundry**) is a factory for [semiconductor device fabrication](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication").[[1]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-1)

Fabs require many expensive devices to function. Estimates put the cost of building a new fab over one billion [U.S. dollars](United_States_dollars "United States dollars") with values as high as $3–4 billion not being uncommon. <TSMC> invested $9.3 billion in its *Fab15* 300 mm [wafer](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") manufacturing facility in Taiwan.[[2]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-2) The same company estimations suggest that their future fab might cost $20 billion.[[3]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-3) A [foundry model](Foundry_model "Foundry model") emerged in the 1990s: Foundries that produced their own designs were known as [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDMs). Companies that farmed out manufacturing of their designs to foundries were termed [fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company"). Those foundries, which did not create their own designs, were called [pure-play semiconductor foundries](Pure-play_semiconductor_foundry "Pure-play semiconductor foundry").[[4]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-4)

The central part of a fab is the [clean room](Clean_room "Clean room"), an area where the environment is controlled to eliminate all dust, since even a single speck can ruin a microcircuit, which has nanoscale features much smaller than dust particles. The clean room must also be damped against vibration to enable nanometer-scale alignment of machines and must be kept within narrow bands of temperature and humidity. Vibration control may be achieved by using deep piles in the cleanroom's foundation that anchor the cleanroom to the bedrock, careful selection of the construction site, and/or using vibration dampers. Controlling temperature and humidity is critical for minimizing [static electricity](Static_electricity "Static electricity"). Corona discharge sources can also be used to reduce static electricity. Often, a fab will be constructed in the following manner: (from top to bottom): the roof, which may contain air handling equipment that draws, purifies and cools outside air, an air plenum for distributing the air to several floor-mounted [fan filter units](Fan_filter_unit "Fan filter unit"), which are also part of the cleanroom's ceiling, the cleanroom itself, which may or may not have more than one story, [[5]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-5) a return air plenum, the clean subfab that may contain support equipment for the machines in the cleanroom such as chemical delivery, purification, recycling and destruction systems, and the ground floor, that may contain electrical equipment. Fabs also often have some office space.

The clean room is where all fabrication takes place and contains the machinery for integrated circuit production such as [steppers](Stepper "Stepper") and/or scanners for [photolithography](Photolithography "Photolithography"), in addition to [etching](Etching_(microfabrication) "Etching (microfabrication)"), cleaning, [doping](Doping_(semiconductors) "Doping (semiconductors)") and [dicing](Wafer_dicing "Wafer dicing") machines. All these devices are extremely precise and thus extremely expensive. Prices for most common pieces of equipment for the processing of 300 mm wafers range from $700,000 to upwards of $4,000,000 each with a few pieces of equipment reaching as high as $340,000,000 each (e.g. [EUV](Extreme_ultraviolet_lithography "Extreme ultraviolet lithography") scanners). A typical fab will have several hundred equipment items.

## History

Typically an advance in chip-making technology requires a completely new fab to be built. In the past, the equipment to outfit a fab was not very expensive and there were a huge number of smaller fabs producing chips in small quantities. However, the cost of the most up-to-date equipment has since grown to the point where a new fab can cost several billion dollars.

Another side effect of the cost has been the challenge to make use of older fabs. For many companies these older fabs are useful for producing designs for unique markets, such as [embedded processors](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor"), [flash memory](Flash_memory "Flash memory"), and [microcontrollers](Microcontroller "Microcontroller"). However, for companies with more limited product lines, it is often best to either rent out the fab, or close it entirely. This is due to the tendency of the cost of upgrading an existing fab to produce devices requiring newer technology to exceed the cost of a completely new fab.

There has been a trend to produce ever larger [wafers](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)"), so each process step is being performed on more and more chips at once. The goal is to spread production costs (chemicals, fab time) over a larger number of saleable chips. It is impossible (or at least impracticable) to retrofit machinery to handle larger wafers. This is not to say that foundries using smaller wafers are necessarily obsolete; older foundries can be cheaper to operate, have higher yields for simple chips and still be productive.

The industry was aiming to move from the state-of-the-art wafer size 300 mm (12 in) to 450 mm by 2018.[[6]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-6) In March 2014, <Intel> expected 450 mm deployment by 2020.[[7]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-intel450mm-7) But in 2016, corresponding joint research efforts were stopped.[[8]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-8)

Additionally, there is a large push to completely automate the production of semiconductor chips from beginning to end. This is often referred to as the "[lights-out fab](Lights_out_(manufacturing) "Lights out (manufacturing)")" concept.

The International Sematech Manufacturing Initiative (ISMI), an extension of the US consortium <SEMATECH>, is sponsoring the "300 mm Prime" initiative. An important goal of this initiative is to enable fabs to produce greater quantities of smaller chips as a response to shorter lifecycles seen in consumer electronics. The logic is that such a fab can produce smaller lots more easily and can efficiently switch its production to supply chips for a variety of new electronic devices. Another important goal is to reduce the waiting time between processing steps.[[9]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-9)[[10]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-10)

**Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited** (**TSMC**; also called **Taiwan Semiconductor**)[[3]](TSMC#cite_note-3)[[4]](TSMC#cite_note-4) is a [Taiwanese](Taiwan "Taiwan") [multinational](Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation") [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") contract manufacturing and design company. It is the world's most valuable semiconductor company,[[5]](TSMC#cite_note-5) the world's largest [dedicated](Foundry_model#Dedicated_foundry "Foundry model") independent ("[pure-play](Pure_play "Pure play")") [semiconductor foundry](Foundry_(electronics) "Foundry (electronics)"),[[6]](TSMC#cite_note-6) and its country's largest company,[[7]](TSMC#cite_note-7)[[8]](TSMC#cite_note-8) with headquarters and main operations located in the [Hsinchu Science Park](Hsinchu_Science_Park "Hsinchu Science Park") in , . It is majority owned by foreign investors,[[9]](TSMC#cite_note-9) and the [central government of Taiwan](Executive_Yuan "Executive Yuan") is the largest shareholder.[[10]](TSMC#cite_note-10) Founded in Taiwan in 1987 by [Morris Chang](Morris_Chang "Morris Chang"), TSMC was the world's first dedicated semiconductor foundry and has long been the leading company in its field.[[11]](TSMC#cite_note-profile-11)[[12]](TSMC#cite_note-12) When Chang retired in 2018, after 31 years of TSMC leadership, Mark Liu became chairman and C. C. Wei became Chief Executive.[[13]](TSMC#cite_note-13)[[14]](TSMC#cite_note-14) It has been listed on the [Taiwan Stock Exchange](Taiwan_Stock_Exchange "Taiwan Stock Exchange") (TWSE: 2330) since 1993; in 1997 it became the first Taiwanese company to be listed on the [New York Stock Exchange](New_York_Stock_Exchange "New York Stock Exchange") (NYSE: TSM). Since 1994, TSMC has had a [compound annual growth rate](Compound_annual_growth_rate "Compound annual growth rate") (CAGR) of 17.4% in revenue and a CAGR of 16.1% in earnings.[[15]](TSMC#cite_note-15) Most of the leading [fabless](Fabless "Fabless") semiconductor companies such as [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices"), [Apple](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), [ARM](ARM_Holdings "ARM Holdings"), [Broadcom](Broadcom_Inc. "Broadcom Inc."), [Marvell](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group"), , and , are customers of TSMC, as are emerging companies such as [Allwinner Technology](Allwinner_Technology "Allwinner Technology"), , Spectra7, and .[[16]](TSMC#cite_note-16) Leading [programmable logic device](Programmable_logic_device "Programmable logic device") companies and previously also make or made use of TSMC's foundry services.[[17]](TSMC#cite_note-17) Some [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") that have their own [fabrication facilities](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant"), such as [Intel](Intel_Corporation "Intel Corporation"), , and [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"), outsource some of their production to TSMC.[[18]](TSMC#cite_note-18)[[19]](TSMC#cite_note-19) At least one semiconductor company, [LSI](LSI_Corporation "LSI Corporation"), re-sells TSMC wafers through its [ASIC](Application-specific_integrated_circuit "Application-specific integrated circuit") design services and design [IP](Intellectual_property "Intellectual property") portfolio. TSMC has a global capacity of about thirteen million 300 mm-equivalent wafers per year as of 2020 and makes chips for customers with process nodes from 2 microns to [5 nanometres](5_nm_process "5 nm process"). TSMC was the first foundry to market [7-nanometre](7_nm_process "7 nm process") and [5-nanometre](5_nm_process "5 nm process") (used by the 2020 [Apple A14](Apple_A14 "Apple A14") and [M1](Apple_M1 "Apple M1") [SoCs](System_on_a_chip "System on a chip"), the MediaTek [Dimensity 8100](List_of_MediaTek_processors "List of MediaTek processors"), and [AMD Ryzen 7000](List_of_AMD_Ryzen_processors#Raphael_desktop "List of AMD Ryzen processors") series processors) production capabilities, and the first to commercialize [extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography](Extreme_ultraviolet_lithography "Extreme ultraviolet lithography") technology in high volume. ## History In 1986, [Li Kwoh-ting](Li_Kwoh-ting "Li Kwoh-ting"), representing the [Executive Yuan](Executive_Yuan "Executive Yuan"), invited Morris Chang to serve as the president of the [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute") (ITRI). At that time, the Taiwanese government wanted to develop its semiconductor industry, but its high investment and high risk nature made it difficult to find investors. Only was willing to sign a joint venture contract with Taiwan to put up $58 million, transfer its production technology, and license intellectual property in exchange for a 27.5 percent stake in TSMC. The Taiwanese government provided another 48 percent of the startup capital for TSMC and the rest of the capital was raised from wealthy Taiwanese who were “asked” by the government to invest. “What generally happened was that one of the ministers in the government would call a businessman in Taiwan,” Chang explained, “to get him to invest.” The government asked several of the island’s wealthiest families, who owned firms that specialized in plastics, textiles, and chemicals, to put up the money. From day one, TSMC wasn’t really a private business: it was a project of the Taiwanese state.[[20]](TSMC#cite_note-20)[[21]](TSMC#cite_note-21)[[22]](TSMC#cite_note-22) Since then, the company has continued to grow, albeit subject to the cycles of demand. In 2011, the company planned to increase research and development expenditures by almost 39% to [NT$](New_Taiwan_dollar "New Taiwan dollar")50 billion to fend off growing competition.[[23]](TSMC#cite_note-23) The company also planned to expand capacity by 30% in 2011 to meet strong market demand.[[24]](TSMC#cite_note-24) In May 2014, TSMC's board of directors approved capital appropriations of [US$](United_States_dollar "United States dollar")568 million to increase and improve manufacturing capabilities after the company forecast higher than expected demand.[[25]](TSMC#cite_note-Q2_2014_forecast-25) In August 2014, TSMC's board of directors approved additional capital appropriations of US$3 [91012 more characters...]

This article is about the business model for making [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuits "Integrated circuits"). For other uses of the term **foundry**, see [foundry (disambiguation)](Foundry_(disambiguation) "Foundry (disambiguation)").

The **foundry model** is a [microelectronics](Microelectronics "Microelectronics") engineering and manufacturing [business model](Business_model "Business model") consisting of a [semiconductor fabrication plant](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant"), or foundry, and an [integrated circuit design](Integrated_circuit_design "Integrated circuit design") operation, each belonging to separate companies or subsidiaries.[[1]](Foundry_model#cite_note-1)[[2]](Foundry_model#cite_note-2)[[3]](Foundry_model#cite_note-3)[[4]](Foundry_model#cite_note-4)

[Integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDMs) design and manufacture integrated circuits. Many companies, known as [fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company"), only design devices; merchant or [pure play](Pure_play "Pure play") foundries only manufacture devices for other companies, without designing them. Examples of IDMs are <Intel>, [Samsung](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"), and [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"),
examples of pure play foundries are <GlobalFoundries>, <TSMC>, and [UMC](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation"), and examples of fabless companies are [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices"), <Nvidia>, and <Qualcomm>.

Integrated circuit production facilities are expensive to build and maintain. Unless they can be kept at nearly full use, they will become a drain on the [finances](Finances "Finances") of the company that owns them. The foundry [model](Business_model "Business model") uses two methods to avoid these costs: fabless companies avoid costs by not owning such facilities. Merchant foundries, on the other hand, find work from the worldwide pool of fabless companies, through careful [scheduling](Scheduling_(production_processes) "Scheduling (production processes)"), [pricing](Pricing "Pricing"), and contracting, keep their plants in full use.

## History

Companies that both designed and produced the devices were originally responsible for manufacturing microelectronic devices. These manufacturers were involved in both the [research and development](Research_and_development "Research and development") of manufacturing processes and the research and development of [microcircuit](Microcircuit "Microcircuit") design.

The first pure play semiconductor company is the [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation](Taiwan_Semiconductor_Manufacturing_Corporation "Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation"), a [spin-off](Corporate_spin-off "Corporate spin-off") of the government [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute"), which split its design and fabrication divisions in 1987,[[5]](Foundry_model#cite_note-5) a model advocated for by [Carver Mead](Carver_Mead "Carver Mead") in the U.S., but deemed too costly to pursue. The separation of design and fabrication became known as the foundry model, with [fabless manufacturing](Fabless_manufacturing "Fabless manufacturing") outsourcing to [semiconductor foundries](Semiconductor_foundry "Semiconductor foundry").[[6]](Foundry_model#cite_note-Brown-6)

[Fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_companies "Fabless semiconductor companies") do not have any semiconductor fabrication capability; and contract production with a merchant foundry manufacturer. The fabless company concentrates on the research and development of an IC-product; the foundry concentrates on manufacturing and [testing](Test_method "Test method") the physical product. If the foundry does not have any semiconductor design capability, it is a pure-play semiconductor foundry.

An absolute separation into fabless and foundry companies is not necessary. Some companies continue to exist that perform both operations and benefit from the close coupling of their skills. Some companies manufacture some of their own designs and contract out to have others manufactured or designed, in cases where they see [value](Value_(marketing) "Value (marketing)") or seek special skills. The foundry model is a business vision that seeks to optimize productivity.

### MOSIS

The very first merchant foundries were part of the <MOSIS> service. The MOSIS service gave limited production access to designers with limited means, such as students, university researchers, and engineers at small [startups](Startup_company "Startup company").[[7]](Foundry_model#cite_note-BergerLester2015-7) The designer submitted designs, and these submissions were manufactured with the commercial company's extra capacity. Manufacturers could insert some [wafers](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") for a MOSIS design into a collection of their own wafers when a processing step was compatible with both operations. The commercial company (serving as foundry) was already running the process, so they were effectively being paid by MOSIS for something they were already doing. A factory with excess capacity during slow periods could also run MOSIS designs to avoid having expensive [capital](Capital_(economics) "Capital (economics)") equipment stand idle.

Under-use of an expensive manufacturing plant could lead to the financial ruin of the owner, so selling surplus [wafer](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") capacity was a way to maximize the fab's use. Hence, economic factors created a climate where fab operators wanted to sell surplus wafer-manufacturing capacity and designers wanted to purchase manufacturing capacity rather than try to build it.

Although MOSIS opened the doors to some fabless customers, earning additional [revenue](Revenue "Revenue") for the foundry and providing inexpensive service to the customer, running a business around MOSIS production was difficult. The merchant foundries sold wafer capacity on a surplus basis, as a secondary business activity. Services to the customers were secondary to the commercial business, with little [guarantee](Guarantee "Guarantee") of support. The choice of merchant dictated the design, development flow, and available techniques to the fabless customer. Merchant foundries might require [proprietary](Property "Property") and non-portable preparation steps. Foundries concerned with protecting what they considered [trade secrets](Trade_secret "Trade secret") of their [methodologies](Methodologies "Methodologies") might only be willing to release data to designers after an onerous [nondisclosure](Nondisclosure_agreement "Nondisclosure agreement") procedure.

### Dedicated foundry

In 1987, the world's first dedicated merchant foundry opened its doors: [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)](TSMC "TSMC").[[8]](Foundry_model#cite_note-HirakawaLal2013-8) The distinction of 'dedicated' is in reference to the typical merchant foundry of the era, whose primary business activity was building and selling of its own [IC](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit")-products. The dedicated foundry offers several key advantages to its customers: first, it does not sell finished IC-products into the [supply](Supply_(economics) "Supply (economics)") channel; thus a dedicated foundry will never compete directly with its fabless customers (obviating a common concern of fabless companies). Second, the dedicated foundry can scale production capacity to a customer's needs, offering low-quantity [shuttle](Multi-project_wafer_service "Multi-project wafer service") services in addition to full-scale [production](Mass_production "Mass production") lines. Finally, the dedicated foundry offers a "COT-flow" (customer owned tooling) based on industry-standard [EDA](Electronic_design_automation "Electronic design automation") systems, whereas many IDM merchants required its customers to use proprietary (non-portable) development tools. The COT advantage gave the customer complete control over the design process, from concept to final design.

## Foundry sales leaders by year

- **Pure-play semiconductor foundry** is a company that does not offer a significant amount of IC products of its own design, but instead operates [semiconductor fabrication plants](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") focused on producing ICs for other companies.[[9]](Foundry_model#cite_note-9)
- **[Integrated device manufacturer](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDM) semiconductor foundry** is where companies such as Texas Instruments, IBM, and Samsung join in to provide foundry services as long as there is no conflict of interest between relevant parties.

## Financial and IP issues

Like all industries, the semiconductor industry faces upcoming challenges and obstacles.

The cost to stay on the leading edge has steadily increased with each generation of chips. The financial strain is being felt by both large merchant foundries and their fabless customers. The cost of a new foundry exceeds $1 billion. These costs must be passed on to customers. Many merchant foundries have entered into joint ventures with their competitors in an effort to split research and design expenditures and fab-maintenance expenses.

Chip design companies sometimes avoid other companies' patents simply by purchasing the products from a licensed foundry with broad cross-license agreements with the patent owner.[[23]](Foundry_model#cite_note-23)

Stolen design data is also a concern; data is rarely directly copied, because blatant copies are easily identified by distinctive features in the chip,[[24]](Foundry_model#cite_note-24) placed there either for this purpose or as a byproduct of the design process. However, the data including any procedure, process system, method of operation or concept may be sold to a competitor, who may save months or years of tedious [reverse engineering](Reverse_engineering "Reverse engineering").

---

| External image | |
| --- | --- |
| [Photo of the interior of a clean room of a 300mm fab](https://www.tsmc.com/img/photoGallery/fabs_in/Fab12inc046.jpg) run by <TSMC> | |


In the [microelectronics](Microelectronics "Microelectronics") industry, a **semiconductor fabrication plant** (commonly called a **fab**; sometimes **foundry**) is a factory for [semiconductor device fabrication](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication").[[1]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-1)

Fabs require many expensive devices to function. Estimates put the cost of building a new fab over one billion [U.S. dollars](United_States_dollars "United States dollars") with values as high as $3–4 billion not being uncommon. <TSMC> invested $9.3 billion in its *Fab15* 300 mm [wafer](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") manufacturing facility in Taiwan.[[2]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-2) The same company estimations suggest that their future fab might cost $20 billion.[[3]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-3) A [foundry model](Foundry_model "Foundry model") emerged in the 1990s: Foundries that produced their own designs were known as [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDMs). Companies that farmed out manufacturing of their designs to foundries were termed [fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company"). Those foundries, which did not create their own designs, were called [pure-play semiconductor foundries](Pure-play_semiconductor_foundry "Pure-play semiconductor foundry").[[4]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-4)

The central part of a fab is the [clean room](Clean_room "Clean room"), an area where the environment is controlled to eliminate all dust, since even a single speck can ruin a microcircuit, which has nanoscale features much smaller than dust particles. The clean room must also be damped against vibration to enable nanometer-scale alignment of machines and must be kept within narrow bands of temperature and humidity. Vibration control may be achieved by using deep piles in the cleanroom's foundation that anchor the cleanroom to the bedrock, careful selection of the construction site, and/or using vibration dampers. Controlling temperature and humidity is critical for minimizing [static electricity](Static_electricity "Static electricity"). Corona discharge sources can also be used to reduce static electricity. Often, a fab will be constructed in the following manner: (from top to bottom): the roof, which may contain air handling equipment that draws, purifies and cools outside air, an air plenum for distributing the air to several floor-mounted [fan filter units](Fan_filter_unit "Fan filter unit"), which are also part of the cleanroom's ceiling, the cleanroom itself, which may or may not have more than one story, [[5]](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant#cite_note-5) a return air plenum, the clean subfab that may contain support equipment for the machines in the cleanroom such as chemical delivery, purification, recycling and destruction systems, and the ground floor, that may contain electrical equipment. Fabs also often have some office space.

The clean room is where all fabrication takes place and contains the machinery for integrated circuit production such as [steppers](Stepper "Stepper") and/or scanners for [photolithography](Photolithography "Photolithography"), in addition to [etching](Etching_(microfabrication) "Etching (microfabrication)"), cleaning, [doping](Doping_(semiconductors) "Doping (semiconductors)") and [dicing](Wafer_dicing "Wafer dicing") machines. All these devices are extremely precise and thus extremely expensive. Prices for most common pieces of equipment for the processing of 300 mm wafers range from $700,000 to upwards of $4,000,000 each with a few pieces of equipment reaching as high as $340,000,000 each (e.g. [EUV](Extreme_ultraviolet_lithography "Extreme ultraviolet lithography") scanners). A typical fab will have several hundred equipment items.

## History

Typically an advance in chip-making technology requires a completely new fab to be built. In the past, the equipment to outfit a fab was not very expensive and there were a huge number of smaller fabs producing chips in small quantities. title: Moore's second law
---


**Rock's law** or **Moore's second law**, named for [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock") or [Gordon Moore](Gordon_Moore "Gordon Moore"), says that the cost of a [semiconductor chip](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") [fabrication plant](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") doubles every four years.[[1]](Moore's_second_law#cite_note-1) As of 2015, the price had already reached about 14 billion US dollars.[[2]](Moore's_second_law#cite_note-2)

Rock's law can be seen as the economic flip side to [Moore's (first) law](Moore's_law "Moore's law") – that the number of transistors in a dense integrated circuit doubles every two years. The latter is a direct consequence of the ongoing growth of the capital-intensive semiconductor industry— innovative and popular products mean more profits, meaning more capital available to invest in ever higher levels of [large-scale integration](Integrated_circuit#LSI "Integrated circuit"), which in turn leads to the creation of even more innovative products.

The semiconductor industry has always been extremely capital-intensive, with ever-dropping manufacturing [unit costs](Unit_cost "Unit cost"). Thus, the ultimate [limits to growth](Limits_to_growth "Limits to growth") of the industry will constrain the maximum amount of capital that can be invested in new products; at some point, Rock's Law will collide with Moore's Law.[[3]](Moore's_second_law#cite_note-3)[[4]](Moore's_second_law#cite_note-4)[[5]](Moore's_second_law#cite_note-5)

It has been suggested that fabrication plant costs have not increased as quickly as predicted by Rock's law – indeed plateauing in the late 1990s[[6]](Moore's_second_law#cite_note-Ross03-6) – and also that the fabrication plant cost *per transistor* (which has shown a pronounced downward trend[[6]](Moore's_second_law#cite_note-Ross03-6)) may be more relevant as a constraint on Moore's Law.

## See also

- [Semiconductor device fabrication](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication")
- [Fabless manufacturing](Fabless_manufacturing "Fabless manufacturing")
- [Wirth's law](Wirth's_law "Wirth's law"), an analogous law about software complicating over time
- [Semiconductor consolidation](Semiconductor_consolidation "Semiconductor consolidation")

[[9]](Semiconductor_industry#cite_note-9) ## Industry structure The global semiconductor industry is dominated by companies from the [United States](United_States "United States"), , [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea"), and the . Unique features of the industry include continuous growth but in a cyclical pattern with high volatility. While the current 20 year annual average growth of the semiconductor industry is on the order of 13%, this has been accompanied by equally above-average market volatility, which can lead to significant if not dramatic cyclical swings. This has required the need for high degrees of flexibility and innovation in order to constantly adjust to the rapid pace of change in the market as many products embedding semiconductor devices often have a very short life cycle. At the same time, the rate of constant price-performance improvement in the semiconductor industry is staggering. As a consequence, changes in the semiconductor market not only occur extremely rapidly but also anticipate changes in industries evolving at a slower pace. The semiconductor industry is widely recognized as a key driver and technology enabler for the whole electronics value chain.[[10]](Semiconductor_industry#cite_note-10) The industry is based on the [foundry model](Foundry_model "Foundry model"), which consists of [semiconductor fabrication plants](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") (foundries) and integrated circuit design operations, each belonging to separate companies or subsidiaries. Some companies, known as [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer"), both design and manufacture semiconductors. The foundry model has resulted in [consolidation](Semiconductor_consolidation "Semiconductor consolidation") among foundries. The  **semiconductor industry**, including Integrated Circuit (IC) manufacturing, design, and packing, forms a major part of <Taiwan>'s IT industry.[[1]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-emerging-1) Due to its strong capabilities in OEM wafer manufacturing and a complete industry [supply chain](Supply_chain "Supply chain"), Taiwan has been able to distinguish itself as a leading microchip manufacturer and dominate the global marketplace.[[1]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-emerging-1)[[2]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-2) Taiwan’s [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") sector accounted for US$115 billion, around 20 percent of the global semiconductor industry. In sectors such as foundry operations, Taiwanese companies account for 50 percent of the world market, with [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company](TSMC "TSMC") (TSMC) the biggest player in the foundry market.[[3]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-3)

## Overview

<TSMC> and [United Microelectronics Corporation](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation") (UMC) are the two largest contract chipmakers in the world,[[4]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-SCMP_2019-4) while <MediaTek> is the fourth-largest [fabless semiconductor company](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company") globally.[[5]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-5) [ASE Group](ASE_Group "ASE Group") is also the world's largest Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test (OSAT) provider.[[6]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-6)

## History

The Taiwanese semiconductor industry got its start in 1974. In 1976 the government convinced <RCA> to transfer semiconductor technology to <Taiwan>.[[4]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-SCMP_2019-4)

In 1987, TSMC pioneered the fabless foundry model, reshaping the global semiconductor industry.[[7]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-veteran-7)[[8]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-8) From [ITRI](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute")'s first 3-inch wafer fabrication plant built in 1977[[7]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-veteran-7) and the founding of UMC in 1980,[[9]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-9) the industry had developed into a world leader with 40 fabs in operation by 2002.[[1]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-emerging-1) In 2007, the semiconductor industry overtook that of the United States, second only to Japan.[[10]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-10)

The sector output reached US$39 billion in 2009, ranking first in global market share in IC manufacturing, packaging, and testing, and second in IC design.[[7]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-veteran-7) Although the global financial crisis from 2007 to 2010 affected sales and exports,[[11]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-11) the industry has rebounded with companies posting record profits for 2010.[[12]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-12)[[13]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-13) In 2010 Taiwan had the largest share of 300 nm, 90 nm, and 60 nm manufacturing capacities worldwide, and was expected to pass Japan in total IC fab capacity by mid-2011.[[14]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-14)[[15]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-15) By 2020, Taiwan was the unmatched leader of the global semiconductor industry with [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company](TSMC "TSMC") (TSMC) alone accounting for more than 50% of the global market.[[16]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-16)

## Sustainability

The semiconductor industry uses a large portion of the power produced in Taiwan. By 2022 TSMC alone is estimated to consume 7.2% of Taiwan's total power output.[[17]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-17) Due to pressure from customers and government regulations the semiconductor industry has been switching to green power. In July 2020 TSMC signed a 20-year deal with [Ørsted](%C3%98rsted_(company) "Ørsted (company)") to buy the entire production of two offshore wind farms under development off Taiwan's west coast. At the time of its signing it was the largest corporate [green energy](Green_energy "Green energy") order ever made.[[18]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-18) Much of the switch to renewable energy has been mandated by [Apple Inc.](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") whose primary components suppliers are located on Taiwan.[[19]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-19)[[20]](Semiconductor_industry_in_Taiwan#cite_note-20)

The **Chinese semiconductor industry**, including [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") design and manufacturing, forms a major part of mainland China's [information technology](Information_technology "Information technology") industry.

China's semiconductor industry consists of a wide variety of companies, from [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") to [pure-play foundries](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant"), [fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company") and OSAT companies. [Integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDMs) design and manufacture integrated circuits. [Pure-play foundries](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") only manufacture devices for other companies, without designing them, while [fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company") only design devices. Examples of Chinese IDMs are <YMTC> and [CXMT](Changxin_Memory_Technologies "Changxin Memory Technologies"), examples of Chinese pure-play foundries are [SMIC](Semiconductor_Manufacturing_International_Corporation "Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation"), [Hua Hong Semiconductor](Hua_Hong_Semiconductor "Hua Hong Semiconductor") and <Wingtech>, examples of Chinese fabless companies are <Zhaoxin>, <HiSilicon> and <UNISOC>, and examples of Chinese OSAT companies are [JCET](JCET_(company) "JCET (company)"), Huatian Technology and Tongfu Microelectronics.

## Overview

China is currently the world's largest semiconductor market in terms of consumption. In 2020, China represented 53.7% of worldwide chip sales, or $239.45 billion out of $446.1 billion. However, a large percentage are imported from multinational suppliers. In 2020, imports took up 83.38% ($199.7 billion) of total chip sales. In response, the country has launched a number of initiatives to close the gap, including investing $150 billion into its domestic IC industry through avenues like the [National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund](China_Integrated_Circuit_Industry_Investment_Fund "China Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund") (CICF), with a “Made in China 2025” goal of 70% domestic production.[[1]](Semiconductor_industry_in_China#cite_note-semiengineering1-1)[[2]](Semiconductor_industry_in_China#cite_note-semianalysis1-2)

China leads the world in terms of number of new fabs under construction, with 8 out of 19 worldwide in 2021, and 17 fabs in total are expected to start construction from 2021 to 2023. Total installed capacity of Chinese-owned chipmakers will also increase from 2.96 million wafers per month (wpm) in 2020 to 3.572 million wpm in 2021.[[1]](Semiconductor_industry_in_China#cite_note-semiengineering1-1)

Due to the rapid pace of Chinese semiconductor industry advances, on October 7, 2022, the U.S. government announced a major set of export restrictions toward China, with a focus on artificial Intelligence and semiconductor technologies, with the aim of disrupting the development of China's semiconductor industry.[[3]](Semiconductor_industry_in_China#cite_note-3) In January 2023, these export controls were made multilateral with an agreement between the governments of the United States, Japan, and the Netherlands.[[4]](Semiconductor_industry_in_China#cite_note-4) Between October 2022, and May 2023, China's government responded with a diverse set of measures, including filing a suit in the World Trade Organization.[[5]](Semiconductor_industry_in_China#cite_note-5)

## Foreign companies

Main article: [List of semiconductor fabrication plants](List_of_semiconductor_fabrication_plants "List of semiconductor fabrication plants")

There are a large number of foreign semiconductor companies operating fabrication plants and design facilities in China, including the largest companies such as [SK Hynix](SK_Hynix "SK Hynix"), <TSMC>, <Samsung>, [UMC](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation"), [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"), [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology") and until 2021, <Intel>. Currently, the most advanced foreign made node in mainland China is 16 nm manufactured by TSMC in <Nanjing>.

[Samsung](Samsung_Foundry "Samsung Foundry"), who is currently the world's largest producer of NAND flash memory, has two plants in <Xi'an> which accounts for 42.5% percent of its total production capacity, and 15.3% of worldwide NAND production capacity.[[6]](Semiconductor_industry_in_China#cite_note-6)[[7]](Semiconductor_industry_in_China#cite_note-7) It was the company's largest overseas investment in chip production

# Multi-Agent Delegation

When the user asks a complex question, do not attempt to answer it yourself. Break it up into smaller pieces, then use the `fork` tool to delegate each piece to a subagent. You MUST use the `join` tool to retrieve the subagent's result for each subagent you create with `fork`. Each subagent has access to the exact same tools that you do.

If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

## Writing Instructions

## Industry structure

The global semiconductor industry is dominated by companies from the [United States](United_States "United States"), <Taiwan>, [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea"), <Japan> and the <Netherlands>.

Unique features of the industry include continuous growth but in a cyclical pattern with high volatility. While the current 20 year annual average growth of the semiconductor industry is on the order of 13%, this has been accompanied by equally above-average market volatility, which can lead to significant if not dramatic cyclical swings. This has required the need for high degrees of flexibility and innovation in order to constantly adjust to the rapid pace of change in the market as many products embedding semiconductor devices often have a very short life cycle.

At the same time, the rate of constant price-performance improvement in the semiconductor industry is staggering. As a consequence, changes in the semiconductor market not only occur extremely rapidly but also anticipate changes in industries evolving at a slower pace. The semiconductor industry is widely recognized as a key driver and technology enabler for the whole electronics value chain.[[10]](Semiconductor_industry#cite_note-10)

The industry is based on the [foundry model](Foundry_model "Foundry model"), which consists of [semiconductor fabrication plants](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") (foundries) and integrated circuit design operations, each belonging to separate companies or subsidiaries. Some companies, known as [integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer"), both design and manufacture semiconductors. The foundry model has resulted in [consolidation](Semiconductor_consolidation "Semiconductor consolidation") among foundries. As of 2021, only three firms are able to manufacture the most advanced semiconductors: <TSMC> of Taiwan, <Samsung> of South Korea, and <Intel> of the United States.[[11]](Semiconductor_industry#cite_note-Economist2021-11) Part of this is due to the high capital costs of building foundries. TSMC's latest factory, capable of fabricating [3 nm process](3_nm_process "3 nm process") semiconductors and completed in 2020, cost $19.5 billion.[[11]](Semiconductor_industry#cite_note-Economist2021-11)

Intel is considering outsourcing some production to TSMC. It currently can only produce 10 nm semiconductors, while TSMC and Samsung can both produce 5 nm.[[11]](Semiconductor_industry#cite_note-Economist2021-11) <GlobalFoundries>, an American-headquartered firm, uses a 12 nm process for its most advanced chips due to the rapidly increasing development costs of smaller process nodes.[[12]](Semiconductor_industry#cite_note-12)

# Multi-Agent Delegation

When the user asks a complex question, do not attempt to answer it yourself. Break it up into smaller pieces, then use the `fork` tool to delegate each piece to a subagent. You MUST use the `join` tool to retrieve the subagent's result for each subagent you create with `fork`. Each subagent has access to the exact same tools that you do.

If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

## Writing Instructions

The instructions you give to each subagent SHOULD be a smaller piece of the instructions you were given. Do not delegate your full task to a subagent. Subagents do not have access to the information you have retrieved in prior turns or your thoughts. You must provide each subagent with the necessary context it needs in its instructions.

Your instructions to a subagent can be long, up to about 5000 characters. Each subagent is as capable as you are, but starts with a blank slate, so you must provide it specific and detailed information in its instructions.

- Analyze the retrieved page to find the number of stations.
- Implement the `dfs()` function.
- Use the article to list the subway connections.
- Prove Lemma 3.
- Continue searching for the magic number.

**Rapidus Corporation** ([Japanese](Japanese_language "Japanese language"): Rapidus株式会社, [Hepburn](Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *Rapidus <Kabushiki-gaisha>*) is a [semiconductor manufacturer](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication") headquartered in [Chiyoda, Tokyo](Chiyoda%2C_Tokyo "Chiyoda, Tokyo"), <Japan>. Rapidus was established in August 2022 with the support of eight major Japanese companies: <Denso>, <Kioxia>, [MUFG Bank](MUFG_Bank "MUFG Bank"), <NEC>, [NTT](Nippon_Telegraph_and_Telephone "Nippon Telegraph and Telephone"), <SoftBank>, <Sony>, and <Toyota>. The goal of Rapidus is to increase advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity with a [2 nm process](2_nm_process "2 nm process") by 2027.[[2]](Rapidus#cite_note-2)

## Background history

The semiconductor industry in Japan was highly competitive in the 1980s, with a global share reaching 50%.[[3]](Rapidus#cite_note-3) However, the 1986 Japan-United States semiconductor agreement concluded to resolve [trade friction](Japan-United_States_relations "Japan-United States relations") and the rise of [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea") and <Taiwan> gradually reduced competitiveness.[[4]](Rapidus#cite_note-4) In 1999, [Elpida Memory](Micron_Memory_Japan "Micron Memory Japan") was established by integrating the businesses of <Hitachi> and <NEC> for [DRAM](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory"), one of the semiconductors for memory, and later took over the business of [Mitsubishi Electric](Mitsubishi_Electric "Mitsubishi Electric"), and at one point acquired the world's third largest market share in this field. However, management deteriorated due to the [Lehman shock](Bankruptcy_of_Lehman_Brothers "Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers") in 2009 and the subsequent [yen appreciation recession](Endaka "Endaka"), and although support was provided with government funds, it went bankrupt in 2012.[[5]](Rapidus#cite_note-5) Elpida was acquired by [Micron Technology](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology") in 2013,[[6]](Rapidus#cite_note-6) and changed its name to [Micron Memory Japan](Micron_Memory_Japan "Micron Memory Japan") in 2014.[[7]](Rapidus#cite_note-:0-7) Due to international competition from companies including <TSMC>, [Samsung Electronics](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"), and <Intel>, the share of Japanese companies in the semiconductor industry as a whole has fallen to 10% as of 2019.[[8]](Rapidus#cite_note-8)[[9]](Rapidus#cite_note-9)

In May 2022, United States President [Joe Biden](Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") and Japanese Prime Minister [Fumio Kishida](Fumio_Kishida "Fumio Kishida") met in Tokyo and discussed increased collaboration on important technologies, including semiconductors, [nuclear power](Nuclear_power "Nuclear power"), [space exploration](Space_exploration "Space exploration"), [electric batteries](Electric_batteries "Electric batteries"), [critical minerals](List_of_elements_facing_shortage "List of elements facing shortage"), and [supply chains](Supply_chains "Supply chains").[[10]](Rapidus#cite_note-10) The [Second Kishida Cabinet](Second_Kishida_Cabinet "Second Kishida Cabinet")'s basic policy (*[Honebuto no hōshin](Honebuto_no_h%C5%8Dshin "Honebuto no hōshin")*) announced on 7 June 2022 included consideration of support for private companies developing next-generation advanced technologies and the establishment of a design and manufacturing infrastructure for next-generation semiconductors in the latter half of the 2020s. )[[7]](NEC#cite_note-7) NEC spun off its semiconductor business to [Renesas Electronics](Renesas_Electronics "Renesas Electronics") and [Elpida Memory](Elpida_Memory "Elpida Memory"). Once Japan's major electronics company, NEC has largely withdrawn from manufacturing since the beginning of the 21st century.

NEC was #463 on the 2017 Fortune 500 list.[[8]](NEC#cite_note-8) NEC is a member of the [Sumitomo Group](Sumitomo_Group "Sumitomo Group").

## History

### NEC

[Kunihiko Iwadare](Kunihiko_Iwadare "Kunihiko Iwadare") and Takeshiro Maeda established Nippon Electric Limited Partnership on August 31, 1898, by using facilities that they had bought from Miyoshi Electrical Manufacturing Company. Iwadare acted as the representative partner; Maeda handled company sales. [Western Electric](Western_Electric "Western Electric"), which had an interest in the Japanese phone market, was represented by [Walter Tenney Carleton](Walter_Tenney_Carleton "Walter Tenney Carleton").[[9]](NEC#cite_note-9) Carleton was also responsible for the renovation of the Miyoshi facilities.[[10]](NEC#cite_note-10) It was agreed that the partnership would be reorganized as a joint-stock company when the treaty would allow it. On July 17, 1899, the revised treaty between Japan and the United States went into effect. Nippon Electric Company, Limited was organized the same day as Western Electric Company to become the first Japanese [joint-venture](Joint-venture "Joint-venture") with foreign capital.[[11]](NEC#cite_note-11) Iwadare was named managing director. Ernest Clement and Carleton were named as directors. Maeda and Mototeru Fujii were assigned to be auditors. Iwadare, Maeda, and Carleton handled the overall management.[[12]](NEC#cite_note-12)

The company started with the production, sales, and maintenance of telephones and [switches](Switch "Switch"). NEC modernized the production facilities with the construction of the Mita Plant in 1901 at Mita Shikokumachi. It was completed in December 1902.

The Japanese [Ministry of Communications](Ministry_of_Internal_Affairs_and_Communications "Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications") adopted a new technology in 1903: the common battery [switchboard](Telephone_switchboard "Telephone switchboard") supplied by NEC. The common battery switchboards powered the subscriber phone, eliminating the need for a permanent magnet generator in each subscriber's phone. The switchboards were initially imported, but were manufactured locally by 1909.[[13]](NEC#cite_note-13)

NEC started exporting [telephone sets](History_of_the_telephone "History of the telephone") to China in 1904. In 1905, [Iwadare](Kunihiko_Iwadare "Kunihiko Iwadare") visited Western Electric in the U.S. to see their management and production control. On his return to Japan, he discontinued the "oyakata" system of sub-contracting and replaced it with a new system where managers and employees were all direct employees of the company. Inefficiency was also removed from the production process. The company paid higher salaries with incentives for efficiency. New accounting and cost controls were put in place, and time clocks was installed.[[14]](NEC#cite_note-14)

Between 1899 and 1907 the number of telephone subscribers in Japan rose from 35,000 to 95,000.[[15]](NEC#cite_note-15) NEC entered the China market in 1908 with the implementation of the telegraph treaty between Japan and China. They also entered the Korean market, setting up an office in Seoul in January 1908. During the period from 1907 to 1912 sales rose from 1.6 million yen to 2 million yen. The expansion of the Japanese phone service had been a key part of NEC's success during this period.

The Ministry of Communications delayed a third expansion plan of the phone service in March 1913, despite having 120,000 potential telephone subscribers waiting for phone installations. NEC sales fell sixty percent between 1912 and 1915. During the interim, Iwadare started importing appliances, including electric fans, kitchen appliances, washing machines, and vacuum cleaners. Electric fans had never been seen in Japan before. The imports were intended to prop up company sales. In 1916, the government resumed the delayed telephone-expansion plan, adding 75,000 subscribers and 326,000 kilometers of new toll lines. Thanks to this third expansion plan, NEC expanded at a time when much of the rest of the Japanese industry contracted.[[16]](NEC#cite_note-16)

### 1919 to 1938

In 1919, NEC started its first association with [Sumitomo](Sumitomo_Group "Sumitomo Group"), engaging Sumitomo Densen Seizosho to manufacture cables. As part of the venture, NEC provided cable manufacturing equipment to Sumitomo Densen. Rights to Western Electric's duplex cable patents were also transferred to Sumitomo Densen.[[17]](NEC#cite_note-17)

The [Great Kantō earthquake](1923_Great_Kant%C5%8D_earthquake "1923 Great Kantō earthquake") struck Japan in 1923. 140,000 people were killed and 3.4 million were left homeless.[[18]](NEC#cite_note-18) Four of NEC's factories were destroyed, killing 105 of NEC's engineers and workers. Thirteen of Tokyo's telephone offices were destroyed by fire. Telephone and telegraph service was interrupted by damage to telephone cables. In response, the Ministry of Communications accelerated major programs to install automatic telephone switching systems and enter radio broadcasting.[[19]](NEC#cite_note-19)[](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.00148.pdf) The first automatic switching systems were the [Strowger](Strowger_switch "Strowger switch")-type model made by Automatic Telephone Manufacturing Co. (ATM) in the United Kingdom. NEC participated in the installation of the automatic switching systems, ultimately becoming the general sales agent for ATM. NEC developed its own Strowger-type automatic switching system in 1924, the first in Japan. One of the plants almost leveled during the Kanto earthquake, the Mita Plant, was chosen to support expanding production. A new three-story steel-reinforced concrete building was built, starting in 1925. It was modeled after the [Western Electric](Western_Electric "Western Electric") [Hawthorne Works](Hawthorne_Works "Hawthorne Works").

NEC started its radio communications business in 1924. Japan's first radio broadcaster, Radio Tokyo was founded in 1924 and started broadcasting in 1925. NEC imported the broadcasting equipment from Western Electric.[[20]](NEC#cite_note-20) The expansion of radio broadcasting into Osaka and Nagoya marked the emergence of radio as an Industry. NEC established a radio research unit in 1924. NEC started developing electron tubes in 1925. By 1930, they were manufacturing their first 500 W radio transmitter. They provided the Chinese Xinjing station with a 100 kW radio broadcasting system in 1934.

Photo-telegraphic equipment developed by NEC transmitted photos of the accession ceremony of [Emperor Hirohito](Hirohito "Hirohito"). The ceremony was held in <Kyoto> in 1928. The Newspapers [Asahi Shimbun](Asahi_Shimbun "Asahi Shimbun") and [Mainichi Shimbun](Mainichi_Shimbun "Mainichi Shimbun") were competing to cover the ceremony. The Asahi Shimbun was using a <Siemens> device. The Mainichi was planning to use French photo-telegraphic equipment. In the end, both papers acquired and used the NEC product, due to its faster transmission rate and higher picture quality.[[21]](NEC#cite_note-21)

In 1929 Nippon Electric provided Japan's Ministry of Communications with the A-type switching system, the first of these systems to be developed in Japan. Nippon supplied Japan's Ministry of Communications with nonloaded line carrier equipment for long-distance telephone channels in 1937.[[22]](NEC#cite_note-22)

### 1938 to 1945

[World War II](World_War_II "World War II") was described by the company as being the blackest days of its history.[[23]](NEC#cite_note-23) In 1938 the Mita and Tamagawa plants were placed under military control, with direct supervision by military officers. In 1939, Nippon Electric established a research laboratory in the Tamagawa plant. It became the first Japanese company to successfully test microwave multiplex communications.[[24]](NEC#cite_note-24) On December 22, 1941, the enemy property control law was passed. NEC shares owned by International Standard Electric Corporation (ISE), an [ITT](ITT_Corporation "ITT Corporation") subsidiary, and Western Electric affiliate were seized. Capital and technical relations were abruptly severed. The "Munitions Company Law" was passed in October 1943, placing overall control of NEC plants under military jurisdiction.[[25]](NEC#cite_note-25) The Ueno plant was leveled by the military attack in March 1945. Fire bombings in April and May heavily damaged the Tamagawa Plant, reducing its capacity by forty percent. The Okayama Plant was totally destroyed by a bombing attack in June of the same year. At the end of the war, NEC's production had been substantially reduced by damage to its facilities, and by material and personnel shortages.

### 1945 to 1980

After the war, production was slowly returned to civilian use. NEC re-opened its major plants by the end of January 1946.[[26]](NEC#cite_note-fundinguniverse.com-26) NEC began transistor research and development in 1950. It started exporting radio-broadcast equipment to Korea under the first major postwar contract in 1951. NEC received the [Deming Prize](Deming_Prize "Deming Prize") for excellence in quality control in 1952. Computer research and development began in 1954. NEC produced the first [crossbar switching](Crossbar_switch "Crossbar switch") system in Japan. It was installed at Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Public Corporation (currently [Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation](Nippon_Telegraph_and_Telephone "Nippon Telegraph and Telephone"); NTT) in 1956. st postwar overseas joint venture in 1958. They completed the NEAC-1101 and NEAC-1102 computers in the same year. In September 1958, NEC built their first fully transistorized computer, the NEAC-2201, with parts made solely in Japan.[[27]](NEC#cite_note-27) One year later, they demonstrated it at the UNESCO AUTOMATH show in Paris. The company began integrated circuit research and development in 1960. In 1963 NEC started trading as American Depositary Receipts, with ten million shares being sold in the United States.[[28]](NEC#cite_note-28) Nippon Electric New York (now NEC America Inc.) was incorporated in the same year.[[26]](NEC#cite_note-fundinguniverse.com-26)

NEC supplied KDD with submarine cable systems for laying in the Pacific Ocean in 1964. They supplied short-haul 24 channel PCM carrier transmission equipment to NTT in 1965. NEC de Mexico, S. A. de C. V., NEC do Brasil, S. A., NEC Australia Pty. Ltd. were established between 1968 and 1969. NEC supplied Comsat Corporation with the SPADE satellite communications system in 1971. In 1972, Switzerland ordered a NEC satellite communications earth station. The same year, a small transportable satellite communications earth station was set up in China. Shares of NEC common stock were listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange in 1973. NEC also designed an automated broadcasting system for the Japan Broadcasting Corporation in the same year. NEC Electronics (Europe) GmbH was also established. In 1974, the ACOS series computer was introduced. The New Central Research Laboratories were completed in 1975. In 1977, Japan's National Space Development Agency launched the NEC [geostationary meteorological satellite](Geostationary_meteorological_satellite "Geostationary meteorological satellite"), named [Himawari](Himawari_(satellite) "Himawari (satellite)").[[30]](NEC#cite_note-30)

During this period NEC introduced the concept of "C&C", the integration of computers and communications. NEC America Inc. opened a plant in [Dallas, Texas](Dallas%2C_Texas "Dallas, Texas") to manufacture <PABX> and telephone systems in 1978. They also acquired Electronic Arrays, Inc. of <California> the same year to start semiconductor chip production in the United States.[[31]](NEC#cite_note-31)

### 1980 to 2000

In 1980, NEC created the first [digital signal processor](Digital_signal_processor "Digital signal processor"), the NEC µPD7710. NEC Semiconductors (UK) Ltd. was established in 1981, producing [VLSIs](Very-large-scale_integration "Very-large-scale integration") and LSIs. NEC introduced the 8-bit [PC-8800](NEC_PC-8801 "NEC PC-8801") series personal computer in 1981, followed by the 16-bit [PC-9800](NEC_PC-9801 "NEC PC-9801") series in 1982. In 1983 NEC stock was listed on the Basel, Geneva, and Zurich, Switzerland exchanges. NEC quickly became the dominant leader of the Japanese PC industry, holding 80% market share.[[32]](NEC#cite_note-32) NEC changed its English company name to NEC Corporation the same year. NEC Information Systems, Inc. started manufacturing computers and related products in the United States in 1984. NEC also released the [V-series processor](NEC_V20 "NEC V20") the same year. In 1986, NEC delivered its SX-2 supercomputer to the [Houston Advanced Research Center](Houston_Advanced_Research_Center "Houston Advanced Research Center"), [The Woodlands, Texas](The_Woodlands%2C_Texas "The Woodlands, Texas"). In the same year, the NEAX61 digital switching system went into service. In 1987, NEC Technologies (UK) Ltd. was established in the United Kingdom to manufacture [VCRs](VCR "VCR"), printers, and [computer monitors](Computer_monitor "Computer monitor") and mobile telephones for Europe. Also that year, NEC licensed technology from [Hudson Soft](Hudson_Soft "Hudson Soft"), a [video game](Video_game "Video game") manufacturer, to create a [video game console](Video_game_console "Video game console") called the <PC-Engine> (later released in 1989 as the TurboGrafx-16 in the North American market). Its prototype 3D spec successor, the Tetsujin was originally set to be released in 1992, but the lack of completed games pushed the launch date about early 1993, which was planned debut in Japan. While the PC-Engine achieved a considerable following, it has been said that NEC held a much stronger influence on the video game industry through its role as a leading semiconductor manufacturer than through any of its direct video game products.[[33]](NEC#cite_note-33) NEC USA, Inc. was established in 1989 as a holding company for North American operations.

In 1983, NEC Brasil ([pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEC%20Brasil "pt:NEC Brasil")), the Brazilian subsidiary of NEC, was forced to nationalize its corporate stock under orders of the [Brazilian military government](Brazilian_military_government "Brazilian military government"), whereby shareholder control of NEC Brasil was ceded to the private equity group <Brasilinvest> of Brazilian investment banker [Mário Garnero](M%C3%A1rio_Garnero "Mário Garnero"). Since NEC Brasil's foundation in 1968, it had become the major supplier of telecommunications equipment to the Brazilian government.[[34]](NEC#cite_note-CidadãoKane-34) In 1986, the then Minister of Communications [Antônio Carlos Magalhães](Ant%C3%B4nio_Carlos_Magalh%C3%A3es "Antônio Carlos Magalhães") put NEC Brasil in financial difficulties by suspending all government contract payments to the company, whose main client was the federal government.[[34]](NEC#cite_note-CidadãoKane-34) With the subsidiary in crisis, the NEC Corporation in Japan sold NEC Brasil to [Organizações Globo](Organiza%C3%A7%C3%B5es_Globo "Organizações Globo") for only one million [US dollars](United_States_dollar "United States dollar") (US$1,000,000).[[34]](NEC#cite_note-CidadãoKane-34) Shortly thereafter, Magalhães resumed the government contracts and corresponding payments, and NEC Brazil became valued at over 350 million US dollars (US$350,000,000).[[34]](NEC#cite_note-CidadãoKane-34) Suspicions regarding the NEC-Globo deal, which included among other things the unilateral breach of contract by Globo founder [Roberto Marinho](Roberto_Marinho "Roberto Marinho") regarding the management of a regional television station in the Brazilian state of <Bahia>,[[34]](NEC#cite_note-CidadãoKane-34) took to the national stage only in 1992 during the first corruption charges against the impeached Brazilian president [Fernando Collor de Mello](Fernando_Collor_de_Mello "Fernando Collor de Mello"). Organizações Globo subsequently sold their shares in NEC Brazil, which hit their all-time high during the state monopoly years, back to NEC Corporation in 1999 following the break-up and privatization of the Brazilian state-owned telephone monopoly [Telebrás](Telebr%C3%A1s "Telebrás").[[35]](NEC#cite_note-LobFSP-35)

In 1990, the new head office building, known as the "[Super Tower](NEC_Supertower "NEC Supertower")", was completed in [Shiba, Tokyo](Shiba%2C_Tokyo "Shiba, Tokyo"). Additionally, joint-venture agreements were established to manufacture and market digital electronic switching systems and LSIs in China. In 1993 NEC's asynchronous transfer mode (ATM) switching system, the NEAX61 (Nippon Electronic Automatic Exchange) ATM Service Node, went into service in the United States. NEC Europe, Ltd. was established as a holding company for European operations the same year. The NEC C&C Research Laboratories, NEC Europe, Ltd. were opened in Germany in 1994. NEC (China) Co, Ltd. was established as a holding company for Chinese operations in 1996. In 1997 NEC developed 4Gbit DRAM, and their semiconductor group was honored with one of the first Japan Quality Awards. In 1998, NEC opened the world's most advanced semiconductor [R&D](R%26D "R&D") facility.

NEC had been the no. 1 personal computer vendor in Japan during the 1980s, but it faced increasing competition from <Fujitsu>, [Seiko Epson](Seiko_Epson "Seiko Epson") and [IBM Japan](IBM_Japan_Ltd "IBM Japan Ltd"). Nevertheless, by the early 1990s, NEC was still the largest, having well over 50% market share in the Japanese market. Competition heated up later as rival Fujitsu started to aggressively market its computers, which were industry standard ([x86](X86 "X86")) instead of NEC's indigenous models.

In June 1995, NEC purchased the California-based Packard Bell company to produce desktop PCs in a common manufacturing plant for the North American market. As a result, NEC Technologies (USA) was merged with Packard Bell to create Packard Bell NEC Inc. By 1997, NEC's share was reduced to about 35%.[[36]](NEC#cite_note-36)

In decades, NEC released a new console for its predecessor [SuperGrafx](PC_Engine_SuperGrafx "PC Engine SuperGrafx"), the Japan-only <PC-FX>, a <32-bit> system with a tower-like design; it enjoyed a small but steady stream of games until 1998, when NEC finally abandoned the video games industry.

NEC also supplied rival <Nintendo> with the <RISC>-based CPU, V810 (same one used in the PC-FX) for the [Virtual Boy](Virtual_Boy "Virtual Boy")[[37]](NEC#cite_note-37) and [VR4300](R4300i "R4300i") CPU for the [Nintendo 64](Nintendo_64 "Nintendo 64"), released in 1995–1996, and both <SNK> updated VR4300 CPU (64-bit MIPS III) on [Hyper Neo Geo 64](Hyper_Neo_Geo_64 "Hyper Neo Geo 64"),[[38]](NEC#cite_note-38) as well as to former rival Sega with a version of its <PowerVR> 2 GPU for the <Dreamcast>, released in 1997–1998. After working the previous chipset on the system. NEC supplied Bandai's <WonderSwan> handheld console, which was originally developed by Gunpei Yokoi, with the [V30 MZ](NEC_V20#Variants_and_successors "NEC V20") CPU.[[39]](NEC#cite_note-39)[[40]](NEC#cite_note-40) In the 2000s, NEC manufactured dynamic RAM process chips and produced for the <GameCube> GPU, Flipper, a graphics card development by <ArtX>.[[41]](NEC#cite_note-41)[[42]](NEC#cite_note-42)[[43]](NEC#cite_note-43)[[44]](NEC#cite_note-44)

The **history of computing hardware** starting at 1960 is marked by the conversion from [vacuum tube](Vacuum_tube "Vacuum tube") to [solid-state](Solid-state_electronics "Solid-state electronics") devices such as [transistors](Transistor "Transistor") and then [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") (IC) chips. Around 1953 to 1959, discrete transistors started being considered sufficiently reliable and economical that they made further vacuum tube computers [uncompetitive](Competition_(economics) "Competition (economics)"). [Metal–oxide–semiconductor](Metal%E2%80%93oxide%E2%80%93semiconductor "Metal–oxide–semiconductor") (MOS) [large-scale integration](Large-scale_integration "Large-scale integration") (LSI) technology subsequently led to the development of [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") in the mid-to-late 1960s and then the [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") in the early 1970s. This led to primary [computer memory](Computer_memory "Computer memory") moving away from [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory") devices to solid-state static and dynamic semiconductor memory, which greatly reduced the cost, size, and power consumption of computers. These advances led to the miniaturized [personal computer](Personal_computer "Personal computer") (PC) in the 1970s, starting with [home computers](Home_computer "Home computer") and [desktop computers](Desktop_computer "Desktop computer"), followed by [laptops](Laptop "Laptop") and then [mobile computers](Mobile_computer "Mobile computer") over the next several decades.

## Second generation

See also: [List of transistorized computers](List_of_transistorized_computers "List of transistorized computers") and [Transistor computer](Transistor_computer "Transistor computer")

For the purposes of this article, the term "second generation" refers to computers using discrete transistors, even when the vendors referred to them as "third-generation". By 1960 transistorized computers were replacing vacuum tube computers, offering lower cost, higher speeds, and reduced power consumption. The marketplace was dominated by *IBM and the seven dwarfs*:

- <IBM>
- The <BUNCH>
  * [Burroughs](Burroughs_Corporation "Burroughs Corporation")
  * <UNIVAC>
  * [NCR](NCR_Corporation "NCR Corporation")
  * [Control Data Corporation](Control_Data_Corporation "Control Data Corporation") (CDC)
  * <Honeywell>
- [General Electric](General_Electric "General Electric")
- <RCA>.


Some examples of 1960s second generation computers from those vendors are:

- the [IBM 1401](IBM_1401 "IBM 1401"), the [IBM 7090/7094](IBM_7090 "IBM 7090"), and the [IBM System/360](IBM_System/360 "IBM System/360");
- the [Burroughs 5000 series](Burroughs_Large_Systems#B5000 "Burroughs Large Systems");
- the [UNIVAC 1107](UNIVAC_1107 "UNIVAC 1107");
- the [NCR 315](NCR_315 "NCR 315");
- the [CDC 1604](CDC_1604 "CDC 1604") and the [CDC 3000 series](CDC_3000_series "CDC 3000 series");
- the [Honeywell 200](Honeywell_200 "Honeywell 200"), Honeywell 400, and [Honeywell 800](Honeywell_800 "Honeywell 800");
- the [GE-400 series](GE-400_series "GE-400 series") and the [GE-600 series](GE-600_series "GE-600 series");
- the RCA 301, 3301 and the [Spectra 70](RCA_Spectra_70 "RCA Spectra 70") series.


However, some smaller companies made significant contributions. Also, towards the end of the second generation [Digital Equipment Corporation](Digital_Equipment_Corporation "Digital Equipment Corporation") (DEC) was a serious contender in the small and medium machine marketplace.

Meanwhile, second-generation computers were also being developed in the USSR as, e.g., the [Razdan](Razdan_(computer) "Razdan (computer)") family of general-purpose digital computers created at the [Yerevan Computer Research and Development Institute](Yerevan_Computer_Research_and_Development_Institute "Yerevan Computer Research and Development Institute").

The second-generation computer architectures initially varied; they included character-based [decimal computers](Decimal_computer "Decimal computer"), [sign-magnitude](Sign-magnitude "Sign-magnitude") decimal computers with a 10-digit word, sign-magnitude binary computers, and [ones' complement](Ones'_complement "Ones' complement")
