### Psychology

The [Rashomon effect](Rashomon_effect "Rashomon effect") is where the same event is given contradictory interpretations by different individuals involved. The concept originates from [Akira Kurosawa](Akira_Kurosawa "Akira Kurosawa")'s 1950 film *<Rashomon>*, where a murder is described in four mutually contradictory ways by its four witnesses.[[33]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-33)

## Technology in the Empire of Japan (1868–1945)

For the first twenty years in the [Meiji era](Meiji_(era) "Meiji (era)"), patents and inventions failed to attract much public attention. From the time of the [Russo-Japanese War](Russo-Japanese_War "Russo-Japanese War"), largely through the action of the body known as the Imperial Invention Association, invention has been encouraged by the Government. With the outbreak of the [First World War](First_World_War "First World War"), imported manufactured goods were cut off, as was the inflow of foreign technology, and, as a consequence, a number of new industries, especially in the heavy and chemical sectors, were set up. Existing firms also took advantage of the opportunity for technical development and thepenetration of new markets. Several such companies were able to overcome the difficulties posed by economic depression and severe international competition. In 1935, at a time Japan experienced state of the art modernization entitled [Shōwa Modan](Sh%C5%8Dwa_Modan "Shōwa Modan"), the country ranked only behind the [United States](United_States "United States") and <Germany> in the number of patents granted.[[34]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-34)[[35]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:4-35)

### Agriculture

**Vertical rice polishing machine**

The [rice polishing machines](Rice_polisher "Rice polisher") used today are based on the vertical power-driven [the milling machine](Milling_(machining) "Milling (machining)"), which was invented by Riichi Satake (the founder of [Satake Corporation](Satake_Corporation "Satake Corporation") 株式会社サタケ) in 1930. The condition of the rice after milling, the extent of the milling, and damage to the rice grains during the process affects every link in the production chain. Rice could now be polished more efficiently. The abrasive action of the vertical polishing machine reduced the number of broken grains and made polishing more even, making it possible to produce highly polished rice. Unlike the previous horizontal polishing machines, which are used for table rice, the vertical design used gravity to drop the rice through the center chamber, which was outfitted with a center grindstone coated with carborundum. Horizontal polishing machines have the rice grains rub each other, but the vertical Satake type polished the grain with the abrasive center roller to achieve a 40 percent polishing ration, removing 50 percent of the rice grain, revolutionizing the rice milling system and became the standard, resulting in more uniform, finely polished grains that didn't chip or crack.[[36]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-36)[[37]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-37)

### Batteries

**Dry cell**

The world's first [dry-battery](Dry_cell "Dry cell") was invented during the [Meiji Era](Meiji_(era) "Meiji (era)"). The inventor was Yai Sakizou. Unfortunately, the company Yai founded no longer exists.[[38]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:5-38) An award was granted for a dry cell battery by Yai at the 1903 [fifth National Industrial Exhibition](Fifth_National_Industrial_Exhibition "Fifth National Industrial Exhibition") ( 第5回内国勧業博覧会 ) in <Osaka>, Japan. It seems that his award was given in recognition of the fact that his battery was already being exported to foreign countries.[[39]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:7-39)

**Reactive lead oxides production method**

In 1920[, Genzo Shimadzu](Shimadzu "Shimadzu") invents "reactive lead oxides production method". Genzo's invention of the reactive lead powder manufacturing method in 1920 revolutionized the quality and cost of lead powder used in storage batteries. The manufactured lead powder was also used in anti-rust paints, which was even used on the Tokyo Skytree tower completed in 2012. For that invention, Genzo Jr. was selected as one of Japan's ten greatest inventors. He directed the company's efforts toward the development, independently, of a lead-powder production method, which was subsequently named the 'Production Method for Positive Response Lead Powder.' This was a simple and inexpensive method of industrial production, whereby a lump of lead was placed in a revolving iron drum while air was blown in. The ensuing oxidation of the lump of lead, and its breakdown into lead particles by the friction of the revolving drum, produced the positively charged lead powder. In addition to patenting various processes in Japan, Shimadzu registered patents in the major foreign countries. There were enquiries also concerning the implementation of patents for the Shimadzu production method in the US, Britain, Italy, Belgium, Sweden,Canada Australia and France, attesting to the strong international interest in this technology. At this point, however, Shimadzu became entangled in a patent dispute in the USA. In June 1932, the [US Supreme Court](Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") pronounced its final verdict and established the patent rights for the Shimadzu technology. Following this victory, implementation of patent rights were finalized in the US, Britain, and France; that is, contracts were concluded successively in these countries. A contract for the acquisition by Ost Lurgi of the Shimadzu technology option was signed in Frankfurt am Main on 1 June 1926. Fritz Haber was also present at this meeting. The company, Ost Lurgi located in Berlin, was established in March 1926 as a joint venture of <Mitsubishi>, <Metallgesellschaft> and [Degussa AG](Degussa_AG "Degussa AG"). The initiator of the establishing Ost Lurgi was [Fritz Haber](Fritz_Haber "Fritz Haber"), inventor of the [Haber Bosch process](Haber_process "Haber process"), who visited Japan in 1924, he thought highly of the standard of Japanese technology and originated a number of proposals for technico-industrial cooperation between Germany and Japan. One of his idealistic proposals gave rise to the establishment contract of Ost Lurgi. The purpose of Ost Lurgi was to transfer Japanese technology to Germany, but negotiations were drawn out, since the parties could not agree on conditions.[[40]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-40)[[41]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-41)[[42]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-42)[[35]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:4-35)

### Telecommunications

**Cathode ray tube (CRT)**

In 1924, [Kenjiro Takayanagi](Kenjiro_Takayanagi "Kenjiro Takayanagi") began a research program on [electronic television](Electronic_television "Electronic television"). In 1925, he demonstrated a [cathode ray tube](Cathode_ray_tube "Cathode ray tube") (CRT) television with thermal electron emission.[[43]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-ieee-tv-43)

The first observation of interaction between meteors and radio propagation was reported by [Hantaro Nagaoka](Hantaro_Nagaoka "Hantaro Nagaoka") in 1929.[[50]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-50)

Yagi antenna

The [Yagi-Uda antenna](Yagi%E2%80%93Uda_antenna "Yagi–Uda antenna") was invented in 1926 by [Shintaro Uda](Shintaro_Uda "Shintaro Uda") of [Tohoku Imperial University](Tohoku_University "Tohoku University"), <Sendai>, Japan, with the collaboration of [Hidetsugu Yagi](Hidetsugu_Yagi "Hidetsugu Yagi"), also of Tohoku Imperial University. Yagi published the first English-language reference on the antenna in a 1928 survey article on short wave research in Japan and it came to be associated with his name. However, Yagi always acknowledged Uda's principal contribution to the design, and the proper name for the antenna is, as above, the Yagi-Uda antenna (or array).[[51]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-51)

**NE-style phototelegraphy**

Phototelegraphic equipment invented by [Yasujiro Niwa](Yasujiro_Niwa "Yasujiro Niwa") that became the foundation of [mechanical televisions](Mechanical_television "Mechanical television") and [FAX machines](Fax "Fax") in Japan. In November 1928, when [Emperor Hirohito](Hirohito "Hirohito")'s Imperial Accession Ceremony was held, newspaper companies that had mulled over ways to deliver papers with photos (The first photo-telegraph to be sent using a leased line) of the ceremony throughout the nation as quickly as possible employed this phototelegraphic equipment with great success. In general use, the NEC-style photo-telegraph was used to send information such as pictures and handwriting.[[52]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:13-52)

**Non-loaded Cable**

The vital technology in Japan's effort to build a strategic communications link between the home islands and Manchukuo. The importance of this technological invention was not limited to <Manchuria>, it was the technological equivalent in Japan's new empire-building endeavor to the [gutta-percha submarine cable](Gutta_Percha_Company "Gutta Percha Company") in the creation of the [British empire](British_Empire "British Empire"). In the meantime, NLC would be heralded as a quintessential "Japanese-style technology" and a milestone in modern Japan's quest for technological autonomy. Even decades later, many in Japan were still convinced that "consistently in every step from invention to application, it was literally a domestically produced technology, worthy of international pride" and the development of NLC was "clearly the starting point of the leap forward of our telecommunications technology to the world’s top level". In 1936, the Japanese government adopted non-loaded cable for the new Japan–Manchukuo cable network as well as for the long-distance communications networks in Japan, thus establishing the supremacy of the new technology in Japan. In the same year, [Shigeyoshi Matsumae](Shigeyoshi_Matsumae "Shigeyoshi Matsumae") (松前重義 1901–1991) was awarded the Asano Prize by Japan's Association of Electrical Engineering for his ground-breaking contribution to the development of telecommunications technology. Named after one of Japan's first electrical engineers, who oversaw the laying of the submarine cable to <Taiwan>, the prize of 1,000 yen further consolidated the reputation of NLC as well as that of its chief inventor. Later that year, Matsumae received his doctoral degree from Tōhoku Imperial University. the NLC technology was "the greatest invention in Japan’s telecommunications industry". Now recognized as Japan's unique contribution to the field of [telephone](Telephone "Telephone") transmission.[[53]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-53)

### Electronics

Digital circuits

From 1934 to 1936, <NEC> engineer Akira Nakashima introduced [switching circuit theory](Switching_circuit_theory "Switching circuit theory") in a series of papers showing that [two-valued](Two-element_Boolean_algebra "Two-element Boolean algebra") [Boolean algebra](Boolean_algebra "Boolean algebra"), which he discovered independently, can describe the operation of switching circuits. Nakashima's switching circuit theory used [digital electronics](Digital_electronics "Digital electronics") for Boolean algebraic operations.[[54]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:14-54)[[55]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-ipsj-switch-55)[[16]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-historical-16)[[17]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-Stanković-Astola_2008-17) Nakashima's work was later cited and elaborated on in [Claude Shannon](Claude_Shannon "Claude Shannon")'s seminal 1938 paper "[A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits](A_Symbolic_Analysis_of_Relay_and_Switching_Circuits "A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits")".[[16]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-historical-16) Nakashima laid the foundations for [digital system](Digital_system "Digital system") design with his switching circuit theory, using a form of Boolean algebra as a way to analyze and design circuits by [algebraic](Algebra "Algebra") means in terms of [logic gates](Logic_gate "Logic gate"). His switching circuit theory provided the mathematical foundations and tools for digital system design in almost all areas of modern technology, and was the basis for [digital electronics](Digital_electronics "Digital electronics") and [computer theory](Computer_science "Computer science").[[17]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-Stanković-Astola_2008-17)[[55]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-ipsj-switch-55)

Nakashima's work on switching circuit theory was further advanced by [Claude Shannon](Claude_Shannon "Claude Shannon") in the United States during the late 1930s to 1940s,[[17]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-Stanković-Astola_2008-17)[[55]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-ipsj-switch-55) and by Goto Mochinori in Japan during the 1940s.[[56]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-mark1-56)[[57]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-dawn-57)

**Screen grid valve**

The first true screen-grid valve, with a screen grid designed for this purpose, was patented by Hiroshi Ando in 1919.[[58]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-58)

### Instruments

**Electronic organ**

[Yamaha](Yamaha_Corporation "Yamaha Corporation") engineer Mr. Yamashita invented the [Yamaha Magna Organ](Yamaha_Magna_Organ "Yamaha Magna Organ") in 1935. It was an [electrostatic reed organ](Electrostatic_reed_organ "Electrostatic reed organ"), a multi-timbral keyboard instrument based on electrically blown [free reeds](Free_reed "Free reed") with [pickups](Pickup_(music_technology) "Pickup (music technology)").[[59]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:17-59)[[60]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:18-60)

### Lighting

**Double-coil bulb**

In 1921, Junichi Miura created the first double-coil bulb using a coiled coil tungsten filament while working for <Hakunetsusha> (a predecessor of <Toshiba>). At the time, machinery to mass-produce coiled coil filaments did not exist, however Hakunetsusha developed a method to mass-produce coiled coil filaments by 1936.[[61]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-61)

### Metallurgy/Materials

**KS steel**

Magnetic resistant steel that is three times more resistant than tungsten steel, invented by [Kotaro Honda](Kotaro_Honda "Kotaro Honda").[[62]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-62) Honda's discovery formed an important basis for Japan's world-leading position in this field. Always been interested in [magnetism](Magnetism "Magnetism"), and after returning from studying at [Göttingen University](University_of_G%C3%B6ttingen "University of Göttingen") in <Germany>, he became a professor of [Tohoku University](Tohoku_University "Tohoku University") in 1911. It was at Tohoku University that he invented cobalt steel. Later, he recalled the way he created this world-class material:

```
"The structure of the alloy (cobalt steel) was basically created in my brain. It was not created merely by chance or by accident. Japanese researchers would do well to learn from my example."
```
The [cobalt steel](High-speed_steel "High-speed steel") was named 'KS steel' in Japan, since these were the initials of Sumitomo Kichizaemon, the family head of the [Sumitomo](Sumitomo_Group "Sumitomo Group") zaibatsu, who had donated generous funds for this research. In 1918, Sumitomo Steel Casting succeeded in producing KS steel commercially. This steel, although very expensive, was extremely advanced, and was widely exported to Europe and the United States. In the same year, the Institute of Iron and Steel Research (later known as the Institute of Metal Research), the first public research institute for metals, was founded at Tohoku University, and it became the centre for metal research in Japan.[[63]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-:1-63)

**MKM steel**

MKM steel, an alloy containing nickel and aluminum, was developed in 1931 by the Japanese metallurgist [Tokushichi Mishima](Tokuhichi_Mishima "Tokuhichi Mishima").[[64]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-64)[[65]](History_of_science_and_technology_in_Japan#cite_note-65)

kugawa_shogunate "Tokugawa shogunate") enacted a policy of national seclusion known as *[sakoku](Sakoku "Sakoku")* (literally, "chained country"). Foreigners were barred from setting foot in Japan save for limited contact with the Dutch and Chinese at <Nagasaki>, Christianity was banned, and Catholic missionaries were expelled. Japanese citizens were also forbidden to leave Japan in most cases.

There were occasional minor contacts. For example, in 1785 an ship owned and commanded by an Irishman, [John O'Donnell](John_O'Donnell_(merchant) "John O'Donnell (merchant)"), docked at Baltimore and reportedly had ethnically Japanese sailors as part of its crew.[[13]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-13) And in 1791, two American ships commanded by the American explorer [John Kendrick](John_Kendrick_(American_sea_captain) "John Kendrick (American sea captain)") stopped for 11 days on [Kii Ōshima](Kii_%C5%8Cshima "Kii Ōshima") island, south of the [Kii Peninsula](Kii_Peninsula "Kii Peninsula"). He is the first American to visit Japan, but there is no Japanese account of his visit.[[14]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-14)

In the early 1800s American whaling vessels operating in the North Pacific whaling grounds routinely sought to land in Japan to gather firewood and fresh water, but were routinely turned away or even driven off with cannon fire. Meanwhile, the U.S. government increasingly cast its eyes on Japan as a possible coaling station for the U.S. Navy and a stopping point for U.S. merchants engaged in the lucrative [China trade](Old_China_Trade "Old China Trade"). In 1846, Commander [James Biddle](James_Biddle_(commodore) "James Biddle (commodore)") was dispatched to Japan by Washington with orders to open trade, anchoring himself in [Tokyo Bay](Tokyo_Bay "Tokyo Bay") with two ships, one of which was armed with seventy-two cannons. However, Japanese representatives refused to negotiate, and he returned home empty-handed.[[15]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-15)

### Perry Expedition 1853–1854

Main article: [Perry Expedition](Perry_Expedition "Perry Expedition")

In 1848, Captain [James Glynn](James_Glynn "James Glynn") sailed to [Nagasaki](Nagasaki%2C_Nagasaki "Nagasaki, Nagasaki"), which led to the first successful negotiation by an American with *sakoku* Japan. Glynn recommended to the Congress that any negotiations to open up Japan should be backed up by a demonstration of force; this paved the way for the 1853–1854 expedition of US Navy Commodore [Matthew Perry](Matthew_C._Perry "Matthew C. Perry").[[16]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-16)

The Perry Expedition (Japanese: 黒船来航, kurofune raikō, "Arrival of the Black Ships") lasted from 1853 to 1854. It was a significant diplomatic and military undertaking of the United States Navy towards the Tokugawa Shogunate in Japan. The expedition involved two separate voyages by American warships with objectives such as exploration, surveying, and establishing diplomatic relations and trade agreements with countries in the region. The primary aim of the mission was to establish contact with the Japanese government and open up Japanese ports to American trade, which was a top priority. Under the command of Commodore Matthew Calbraith Perry, who received orders from [President Millard Fillmore](Presidency_of_Millard_Fillmore "Presidency of Millard Fillmore"), the expedition aimed to end Japan's 220-year-old policy of isolation by utilizing gunboat diplomacy if necessary. As a result, the Perry Expedition played a crucial role in establishing diplomatic relations between Japan and the western Great Powers, leading to the collapse of the Tokugawa shogunate and the restoration of the Emperor in the [Meiji Restoration](Meiji_Restoration "Meiji Restoration") of 1868. Furthermore, Japan's growing trade relationships with the world after the expedition resulted in the rise of Japonisme, a cultural trend where Japanese culture influenced art in Europe and America.[[17]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-17)

In 1852, American Commodore [Matthew C. Perry](Matthew_C._Perry "Matthew C. Perry") embarked from Norfolk, Virginia, for Japan, in command of a squadron tasked with negotiating a trade treaty with Japan.[[18]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-18) Aboard a black-hulled steam frigate, he ported [*Mississippi*](USS_Mississippi_(1841) "USS Mississippi (1841)"), [*Plymouth*](USS_Plymouth_(1844) "USS Plymouth (1844)"), [*Saratoga*](USS_Saratoga_(1842) "USS Saratoga (1842)"), and [*Susquehanna*](USS_Susquehanna_(1847) "USS Susquehanna (1847)") at Uraga Harbor near <Edo> (present-day Tokyo) on July 8, 1853, and he was met by representatives of the [Tokugawa Shogunate](Tokugawa_Shogunate "Tokugawa Shogunate"). They told him to proceed to [Nagasaki](Nagasaki%2C_Nagasaki "Nagasaki, Nagasaki"), where the sakoku laws allowed limited trade by the Dutch. Perry refused to leave, and he demanded permission to present a letter from President Fillmore, threatening force if he was denied. Japan had shunned modern technology for centuries, and the Japanese military would not be able to resist Perry's ships; these "[Black Ships](Black_Ships "Black Ships")" would later become a symbol of threatening Western technology in Japan.[[19]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-19) The Dutch behind the scenes smoothed the American treaty process with the Tokugawa shogunate.[[20]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-20) Perry returned in March 1854 with twice as many ships, finding that the delegates had prepared a treaty embodying virtually all the demands in Fillmore's letter; Perry signed the [U.S.-Japan Treaty of Peace and Amity](Convention_of_Kanagawa "Convention of Kanagawa") on March 31, 1854, and returned home a hero.[[21]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-21)

Perry had a missionary vision to bring an American presence to Japan. His goal was to open commerce and more profoundly to introduce Western morals and values. The treaty gave priority to American interests over Japan's. Perry's forceful opening of Japan was used before 1945 to rouse Japanese resentment against the United States and the West; an unintended consequence was to facilitate Japanese militarism.[[22]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-22)

### Harris treaty of 1858

[Townsend Harris](Townsend_Harris "Townsend Harris") (1804–1878) served 1856–1861 as the first American diplomat after Perry left.[[23]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-23) He won the confidence of the Japanese leaders, who asked his advice on how to deal with Europeans. In 1858, Harris successfully concluded a full trade treaty with Japan, remembered in the United States as the "[Harris Treaty of 1858](Treaty_of_Amity_and_Commerce_(United_States%E2%80%93Japan) "Treaty of Amity and Commerce (United States–Japan)")." Via the new treaty, Harris obtained the privilege of Americans to reside in Japan in five "treaty ports" and travel in designated areas. The treaty also banned the opium trade, established extremely low tariffs favorable to American merchants, and guaranteed [extraterritoriality](Extraterritoriality "Extraterritoriality") for American citizens in Japan. Following the conclusion of the Harris Treaty, other western powers, including Great Britain, France, the Netherlands, and Russia, rushed to secure "[unequal treaties](Unequal_treaty "Unequal treaty")" of their own from Japan; these treaties closely followed the American model and granted similar rights to treaty ports and extraterritoriality. The extreme one-sidedness of the new treaties caused significant domestic unrest within Japan, and contributed to the collapse of the 250-year-old [Tokugawa Shogunate](Tokugawa_Shogunate "Tokugawa Shogunate") just ten years later.[[24]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaFeber199721–23-24)

### Japanese Embassy to the United States

Main article: [Japanese Embassy to the United States (1860)](Japanese_Embassy_to_the_United_States_(1860) "Japanese Embassy to the United States (1860)")

Two years later, the Shōgun sent [*Kanrin Maru*](Japanese_warship_Kanrin_Maru "Japanese warship Kanrin Maru") on a mission to the United States, intending to display Japan's mastery of Western navigation techniques and naval engineering. On January 19, 1860, *Kanrin Maru* left the [Uraga Channel](Uraga_Channel "Uraga Channel") for [San Francisco](San_Francisco "San Francisco"). The delegation included [Katsu Kaishu](Katsu_Kaishu "Katsu Kaishu") as ship captain, [Nakahama Manjirō](Nakahama_Manjir%C5%8D "Nakahama Manjirō") and [Fukuzawa Yukichi](Fukuzawa_Yukichi "Fukuzawa Yukichi"). From San Francisco, the embassy continued to [Washington](Washington%2C_DC "Washington, DC") via <Panama> on American vessels.

Japan's official objective with this mission was to send its first embassy to the United States and to ratify the new Treaty of Friendship, Commerce, and Navigation between the two governments. The *Kanrin Maru* delegates also tried to revise some of the [unequal clauses](Unequal_treaty "Unequal treaty") in [Perry](Matthew_C._Perry "Matthew C. Perry")'s treaties; they were unsuccessful.

Townsend Harris returned to the United States in 1861 after five years as the main U.S. diplomat in Japan. Harris was succeeded by [Robert H. Pruyn](Robert_H._Pruyn "Robert H. Pruyn"), a New York politician who was a close friend and ally of Secretary of State [William Henry Seward](William_Henry_Seward "William Henry Seward"). Pruyn served from 1862 to 1865[[25]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-25) and oversaw successful negotiations following the [Shimonoseki bombardment](Bombardment_of_Shimonoseki "Bombardment of Shimonoseki").[[26]](Japan%E2%80%93United_States_relations#cite_note-26)

Based on my searches through Wikipedia, I've found substantial information about NEC's semiconductor business in the 1980s. Here's a comprehensive summary:

## NEC's Semiconductor Business in the 1980s

### Overall Market Position

**NEC was the world's largest semiconductor company** by annual revenue from **1985 to 1992** during this period. This was part of the broader Japanese semiconductor industry dominance, which held approximately **50% of global semiconductor market share** in the 1980s.

### Key Products and Operations

**Memory Chips (DRAM):**
- NEC was a major producer of DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) chips
- In 1997, NEC developed 4Gbit DRAM
- In 1999, NEC's DRAM business was merged with Hitachi's to form **Elpida Memory**, which later became one of the world's top DRAM manufacturers before its bankruptcy in 2012

**Microprocessors:**
- **1980**: NEC created the first digital signal processor, the **NEC µPD7710**
- **1984**: Introduced the **NEC V20** microprocessor (an Intel 8088 clone with enhanced features)
- **1986-1989**: Released the V-series processors:
  - NEC V60 (1986) - 16/32-bit processor at 16 MHz
  - NEC V70 (1987) - 32-bit processor at 20/25 MHz
  - NEC V80 (1989) - 32-bit processor at 25/33 MHz

**LSI/VLSI Products:**
- The **NEC µCOM series** of 4-bit, 8-bit, and 16-bit microprocessors/microcontrollers manufactured throughout the 1970s and 1980s
- Production of VLSIs (Very-Large-Scale Integration) and LSIs (Large-Scale Integration)

### Manufacturing and International Operations

**1978**: NEC acquired Electronic Arrays, Inc. of California to start semiconductor chip production in the United States

**1981**: Established **NEC Semiconductors (UK) Ltd.** to produce VLSIs and LSIs for the European market

**1987**: NEC Technologies (UK) Ltd. was established to manufacture various electronics for Europe

### Market Context and Challenges

**1986 Japan-United States Semiconductor Agreement**: This trade agreement was signed to resolve trade friction between Japan and the U.S., as Japanese companies (including NEC) had achieved dominant global market positions. This agreement, combined with the rise of South Korean and Taiwanese competitors, gradually reduced Japanese competitiveness in subsequent years.

### Legacy

NEC's semiconductor business was eventually spun off to form **Renesas Electronics** (for logic chips) and **Elpida Memory** (for DRAM). NEC's manufacturing operations have since been largely scaled back, though the company has maintained some semiconductor involvement through these entities.

### Manufacturing Facilities

While specific production volume data is not available in Wikipedia sources, NEC operated multiple fabrication plants and had established itself as a world-class semiconductor manufacturer with both domestic Japanese facilities and international operations in the U.S. and Europe by the late 1980s.

Rapidus was established in August 2022 with the support of eight major Japanese companies: <Denso>, <Kioxia>, [MUFG Bank](MUFG_Bank "MUFG Bank"), <NEC>, [NTT](Nippon_Telegraph_and_Telephone "Nippon Telegraph and Telephone"), <SoftBank>, <Sony>, and <Toyota>. The goal of Rapidus is to increase advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity with a [2 nm process](2_nm_process "2 nm process") by 2027.[[2]](Rapidus#cite_note-2)

**Spansion Inc.** was an [American](United_States "United States")-based company that designed, developed, and manufactured [flash memory](Flash_memory "Flash memory"), [microcontrollers](Microcontrollers "Microcontrollers"), mixed-signal and analog products, and system-on-chip (SoC) solutions.[[1]](Spansion#cite_note-Reuters-1)[[2]](Spansion#cite_note-EcoRam-2) The company had more than 3,700 employees in 2014 and is headquartered in [Sunnyvale, California](Sunnyvale%2C_California "Sunnyvale, California"). Spansion is a former joint-venture between <AMD> and <Fujitsu>.[[3]](Spansion#cite_note-Chin-3) In August 2013, Spansion closed the acquisition of the Microcontroller and Analog Business of Fujitsu Semiconductor Limited.[[4]](Spansion#cite_note-4)

Spansion had more than 10,000 customers worldwide. Its products were used in the following markets: automotive electronics, home appliance, peripheral computing equipment, consumer equipment, industrial, and networking.[[1]](Spansion#cite_note-Reuters-1)

In 1993, AMD introduced the first of the <Am486> family of processors,[[16]](AMD#cite_note-history-16) which proved popular with a large number of [original equipment manufacturers](Original_equipment_manufacturer "Original equipment manufacturer"), including <Compaq>, which signed an exclusive agreement using the Am486.[[8]](AMD#cite_note-directory-8)[[102]](AMD#cite_note-102)[[103]](AMD#cite_note-103) The <Am5x86>, another Am486-based processor, was released in November 1995, and continued AMD's success as a fast, cost-effective processor.[[104]](AMD#cite_note-104)[[105]](AMD#cite_note-105)

Finally, in an agreement effective 1996, AMD received the rights to the microcode in Intel's x386 and x486 processor families, but not the rights to the microcode in the following generations of processors.[[106]](AMD#cite_note-106)[[107]](AMD#cite_note-107)

#### K5, K6, Athlon, Duron, and Sempron

Main articles: [AMD K5](AMD_K5 "AMD K5"), [AMD K6](AMD_K6 "AMD K6"), <Athlon>, <Duron>, and <Sempron>

AMD's first in-house x86 processor was the [K5](AMD_K5 "AMD K5"), launched in 1996.[[108]](AMD#cite_note-CPU-INFO_K5-108) The "K" in its name was a reference to <Kryptonite>, the only substance known to harm comic book character <Superman>. This itself was a reference to Intel's hegemony over the market, i.e., an anthropomorphization of them as Superman.[[109]](AMD#cite_note-Forbes-Chip-Names-109) The number "5" was a reference to the fifth generation of x86 processors; rival Intel had previously introduced its line of fifth-generation x86 processors as <Pentium> because the U.S. Trademark and Patent Office had ruled that mere numbers could not be trademarked.[[110]](AMD#cite_note-newyorker-110)

In 1996, AMD purchased <NexGen>, specifically for the rights to their Nx series of x86-compatible processors. AMD gave the NexGen design team their own building, left them alone, and gave them time and money to rework the Nx686. The result was the [K6](AMD_K6 "AMD K6") processor, introduced in 1997. Although it was based on [Socket 7](Socket_7 "Socket 7"), variants such as <K6-III>/450 were faster than Intel's [Pentium II](Pentium_II "Pentium II") (sixth-generation processor).

The K7 was AMD's seventh-generation x86 processor, making its debut under the brand name <Athlon> on June 23, 1999. Unlike previous AMD processors, it could not be used on the same motherboards as Intel's, due to licensing issues surrounding Intel's [Slot 1](Slot_1 "Slot 1") connector, and instead used a [Slot A](Slot_A "Slot A") connector, referenced to the [Alpha](DEC_Alpha "DEC Alpha") processor bus. The <Duron> was a lower-cost and limited version of the Athlon (64KB instead of 256KB L2 cache) in a 462-pin [socketed](CPU_socket "CPU socket") [PGA](Pin_grid_array "Pin grid array") (socket A) or soldered directly onto the motherboard. <Sempron> was released as a lower-cost Athlon XP, replacing Duron in the [socket A](Socket_A "Socket A") PGA era. It has since been migrated upward to all new sockets, up to <AM3>.

On October 9, 2001, the [Athlon XP](Athlon_XP "Athlon XP") was released. On February 10, 2003, the Athlon XP with 512KB L2 Cache was released.[[111]](AMD#cite_note-The_AMD_Athlon_XP_Processor_with_512KB_L2_Cache-111)

The technology was initially launched as the <Opteron> server-oriented processor on April 22, 2003.[[112]](AMD#cite_note-112) Shortly thereafter, it was incorporated into a product for desktop PCs, branded [Athlon 64](Athlon_64 "Athlon 64").[[113]](AMD#cite_note-113)

On April 21, 2005, AMD released the first [dual-core](Multi-core_processor "Multi-core processor") <Opteron>, an x86-based server CPU.[[114]](AMD#cite_note-114) A month later, it released the [Athlon 64 X2](Athlon_64_X2 "Athlon 64 X2"), the first desktop-based [dual-core processor](Multi-core_(computing) "Multi-core (computing)") family.[[115]](AMD#cite_note-115) In May 2007, AMD abandoned the string "64" in its dual-core desktop product branding, becoming Athlon X2, downplaying the significance of [64-bit computing](X86-64 "X86-64") in its processors. Further updates involved improvements to the microarchitecture, and a shift of the target market from mainstream desktop systems to value dual-core desktop systems. In 2008, AMD started to release dual-core Sempron processors exclusively in China, branded as the Sempron 2000 series, with lower HyperTransport speed and smaller L2 cache. AMD completed its dual-core product portfolio for each market segment.

In September 2007, AMD released the first server Opteron [K10](AMD_K10 "AMD K10") processors,[[116]](AMD#cite_note-116) followed in November by the [Phenom](AMD_Phenom "AMD Phenom") processor for desktop. K10 processors came in dual-core, [triple-core](Multi-core "Multi-core"),[[117]](AMD#cite_note-117) and [quad-core](Multi-core "Multi-core") versions, with all cores on a single die. AMD released a new platform codenamed "[Spider](AMD_Spider "AMD Spider")", which used the new Phenom processor, as well as an R770 GPU and a 790 GX/FX chipset from the [AMD 700 chipset series](AMD_700_chipset_series "AMD 700 chipset series").[[118]](AMD#cite_note-hothardware-118) However, AMD built the Spider at <65nm>, which was uncompetitive with Intel's smaller and more power-efficient <45nm>.

In January 2009, AMD released a new processor line dubbed [Phenom II](Phenom_II "Phenom II"), a refresh of the original [Phenom](AMD_Phenom "AMD Phenom") built using the 45 nm process.[[119]](AMD#cite_note-anandtech3512-119) AMD's new platform, codenamed "[Dragon](AMD_Dragon "AMD Dragon")", used the new Phenom II processor, and an [ATI](ATI_(brand) "ATI (brand)") R770 GPU from the [R700](Radeon_R700 "Radeon R700") GPU family, as well as a 790 GX/FX chipset from the [AMD 700 chipset series](AMD_700_chipset_series "AMD 700 chipset series").[[120]](AMD#cite_note-120) The Phenom II came in dual-core, triple-core and quad-core variants, all using the same die, with cores disabled for the triple-core and dual-core versions. The Phenom II resolved issues that the original Phenom had, including a low clock speed, a small L3 cache, and a <Cool'n'Quiet> bug that decreased performance. The Phenom II cost less but was not performance-competitive with Intel's mid-to-high-range [Core 2](Core_2 "Core 2") Quads. The Phenom II also enhanced its predecessor's memory controller, allowing it to use <DDR3> in a new native socket <AM3>, while maintaining backward compatibility with [AM2+](AM2%2B "AM2+"), the socket used for the Phenom, and allowing the use of the [DDR2](DDR2_SDRAM "DDR2 SDRAM") memory that was used with the platform.

In April 2010, AMD released a new Phenom II Hexa-core (6-core) processor codenamed "[Thuban](Phenom_X6 "Phenom X6")".[[121]](AMD#cite_note-121) This was a totally new die based on the hexa-core "Istanbul" <Opteron> processor. It included AMD's "turbo core" technology, which allows the processor to automatically switch from 6 cores to 3 faster cores when more pure speed is needed.

The [Magny Cours](List_of_AMD_Opteron_microprocessors "List of AMD Opteron microprocessors") and [Lisbon](List_of_AMD_Opteron_microprocessors "List of AMD Opteron microprocessors") server parts were released in 2010.[[122]](AMD#cite_note-Opteron6100Series-122) The Magny Cours part came in 8 to 12 cores and the Lisbon part in 4 and 6 core parts. Magny Cours is focused on performance while the Lisbon part is focused on high performance per watt. Magny Cours is an MCM ([multi-chip module](Multi-chip_module "Multi-chip module")) with two hexa-core "Istanbul" <Opteron> parts. This will use a new [socket G34](Socket_G34 "Socket G34") for dual and quad-socket processors and thus will be marketed as Opteron 61xx series processors. Lisbon uses [socket C32](Socket_C32 "Socket C32") certified for dual-socket use or single socket use only and thus will be marketed as Opteron 41xx processors. Both will be built on a [45 nm](45_nm "45 nm") [SOI](Silicon_on_insulator "Silicon on insulator") process.

#### Fusion becomes the AMD APU

Main articles: [AMD APU](AMD_APU "AMD APU") and [AMD mobile platform](AMD_mobile_platform "AMD mobile platform")

Following AMD's 2006 acquisition of Canadian graphics company [ATI Technologies](ATI_Technologies "ATI Technologies"), an initiative codenamed *Fusion* was announced to integrate a <CPU> and <GPU> together on some of AMD's microprocessors, including a built in [PCI Express](PCI_Express "PCI Express") link to accommodate separate PCI Express peripherals, eliminating the [northbridge](Northbridge_(computing) "Northbridge (computing)") chip from the motherboard. The initiative intended to move some of the processing originally done on the CPU (e.g. [floating-point unit](Floating-point_unit "Floating-point unit") operations) to the GPU, which is better optimized for some calculations. The Fusion was later renamed the [AMD APU](AMD_APU "AMD APU") (Accelerated Processing Unit).[[123]](AMD#cite_note-APU-123)

Llano was AMD's first APU built for laptops. Llano was the second APU released,[[124]](AMD#cite_note-Hruska-124) targeted at the mainstream market.[[123]](AMD#cite_note-APU-123) It incorporated a CPU and GPU on the same die, as well as northbridge functions, and used "[Socket FM1](Socket_FM1 "Socket FM1")" with <DDR3> memory. The CPU part of the processor was based on the [Phenom II](Phenom_II "Phenom II") "Deneb" processor. AMD suffered an unexpected decrease in revenue based on production problems for the Llano.[[125]](AMD#cite_note-125) More AMD APUs for laptops running Windows 7 and Windows 8 OS are being used commonly. These include AMD's price-point APUs, the E1 and E2, and their mainstream competitors with Intel's [Core i](Core_i "Core i")-series: The Vision A- series, the A standing for accelerated. These range from the lower-performance A4 chipset to the A6, A8, and A10. These all incorporate next-generation Radeon graphics cards, with the A4 utilizing the base Radeon HD chip and the rest using a Radeon R4 graphics card, with the exception of the highest-model A10 (A10-7300) which uses an R6 graphics card.

#### New microarchitectures

##### High-power, high-performance Bulldozer cores

Main articles: [Bulldozer microarchitecture](Bulldozer_(microarchitecture) "Bulldozer (microarchitecture)"), [Piledriver microarchitecture](Piledriver_(microarchitecture) "Piledriver (microarchitecture)"), [Steamroller microarchitecture](Steamroller_(microarchitecture) "Steamroller (microarchitecture)"), and [Excavator microarchitecture](Excavator_(microarchitecture) "Excavator (microarchitecture)")

Bulldozer was AMD's microarchitecture codename for server and desktop [AMD FX](AMD_FX "AMD FX") processors, first released on October 12, 2011. This [family 15h microarchitecture](Zen_4 "Zen 4") is the successor to the [family 10h (K10)](AMD_10h "AMD 10h") microarchitecture design. Bulldozer was a clean-sheet design, not a development of earlier processors.[[126]](AMD#cite_note-126) The core was specifically aimed at 10–125 W [TDP](Thermal_Design_Power "Thermal Design Power") computing products. AMD claimed dramatic performance-per-watt efficiency improvements in [high-performance computing](High-performance_computing "High-performance computing") (HPC) applications with Bulldozer cores. While hopes were high that Bulldozer would bring AMD to be performance-competitive with Intel once more, most benchmarks were disappointing. In some cases the new Bulldozer products were slower than the K10 models they were built to replace.[[127]](AMD#cite_note-127)[[128]](AMD#cite_note-128)[[129]](AMD#cite_note-129)

The [Piledriver microarchitecture](Piledriver_(microarchitecture) "Piledriver (microarchitecture)") was the 2012 successor to Bulldozer, increasing clock speeds and performance relative to its predecessor.[[130]](AMD#cite_note-130) Piledriver would be released in AMD FX, APU, and Opteron product lines.[[131]](AMD#cite_note-131)[[132]](AMD#cite_note-132)[[133]](AMD#cite_note-133)[[134]](AMD#cite_note-134) Piledriver was subsequently followed by the [Steamroller microarchitecture](Steamroller_(microarchitecture) "Steamroller (microarchitecture)") in 2013. Used exclusively in AMD's APUs, Steamroller focused on greater parallelism.[[135]](AMD#cite_note-anandtech-kaveri-review-135)[[136]](AMD#cite_note-136)

In 2015, the [Excavator microarchitecture](Excavator_(microarchitecture) "Excavator (microarchitecture)") replaced Piledriver.[[137]](AMD#cite_note-PCWorld-137) Expected to be the last microarchitecture of the Bulldozer series,[[138]](AMD#cite_note-138)[[139]](AMD#cite_note-139) Excavator focused on improved power efficiency.[[140]](AMD#cite_note-140)

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Intel](Timeline_of_Intel "Timeline of Intel").

### Origins

Intel was incorporated in [Mountain View, California](Mountain_View%2C_California "Mountain View, California"), on July 18, 1968, by [Gordon E. Moore](Gordon_E._Moore "Gordon E. Moore") (known for "[Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law")"), a [chemist](Chemist "Chemist"), [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce"), a physicist and co-inventor of the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") and [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock"), an investor and [venture capitalist](Venture_capital "Venture capital")[[35]](Intel#cite_note-35)[[36]](Intel#cite_note-36)[[37]](Intel#cite_note-37) Moore and Noyce had left [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") and were part of the "[traitorous eight](Traitorous_eight "Traitorous eight")". There were originally 500,000 shares outstanding of which Dr. Noyce bought 245,000 shares, Dr. Moore 245,000 shares, and Mr. Rock 10,000 shares; all at $1 per share. Rock offered $2,500,000 of convertible debentures to a limited group of private investors (equivalent to $21 million in 2022), convertible at $5 per share.[[38]](Intel#cite_note-38)[[39]](Intel#cite_note-39) Just 2 years later, Intel became a [public company](Public_company "Public company") via an [initial public offering](Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO), raising $6.8 million ($23.50 per share).[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) Intel's third employee was [Andy Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove"),[[note 1]](Intel#cite_note-41) a [chemical engineer](Chemical_engineer "Chemical engineer"), who later ran the company through much of the 1980s and the high-growth 1990s.

In deciding on a name, Moore and Noyce quickly rejected "Moore Noyce",[[41]](Intel#cite_note-42) near [homophone](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/homophone "wikt:homophone") for "more noise" – an ill-suited name for an [electronics](Electronics "Electronics") company, since [noise in electronics](Electronic_noise "Electronic noise") is usually undesirable and typically associated with bad [interference](Electromagnetic_interference "Electromagnetic interference"). Instead, they founded the company as **NM Electronics** (or **MN Electronics**) on July 18, 1968, but by the end of the month had changed the name to **Intel** which stood for **Int**egrated **El**ectronics.[[note 2]](Intel#cite_note-48) Since "Intel" was already trademarked by the hotel chain Intelco, they had to buy the rights for the name.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[47]](Intel#cite_note-49)

### Early history

At its founding, Intel was distinguished by its ability to make [logic circuits](Logic_circuit "Logic circuit") using [semiconductor devices](Semiconductor_device "Semiconductor device"). The founders' goal was the [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") market, widely predicted to replace [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory"). Its first product, a quick entry into the small, high-speed memory market in 1969, was the 3101 [Schottky TTL](Schottky_transistor "Schottky transistor") [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") 64-bit [static random-access memory](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") (SRAM), which was nearly twice as fast as earlier Schottky diode implementations by Fairchild and the Electrotechnical Laboratory in [Tsukuba, Japan](Tsukuba%2C_Ibaraki "Tsukuba, Ibaraki").[[48]](Intel#cite_note-50)[[49]](Intel#cite_note-51) In the same year, Intel also produced the 3301 Schottky bipolar 1024-bit [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM)[[50]](Intel#cite_note-52) and the first commercial [metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor](MOSFET "MOSFET") (MOSFET) [silicon gate](Silicon_gate "Silicon gate") SRAM chip, the 256-bit 1101.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[52]](Intel#cite_note-54)

While the 1101 was a significant advance, its complex static [cell structure](Memory_cell_(computing) "Memory cell (computing)") made it too slow and costly for [mainframe](Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") memories. The three-[transistor](Transistor "Transistor") cell implemented in the first commercially available [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM), the [1103](Intel_1103 "Intel 1103") released in 1970, solved these issues. The 1103 was the bestselling semiconductor memory chip in the world by 1972, as it replaced core memory in many applications.[[53]](Intel#cite_note-55)[[54]](Intel#cite_note-Bellis-56) Intel's business grew during the 1970s as it expanded and improved its manufacturing processes and produced a wider range of [products](Product_(business) "Product (business)"), still dominated by various memory devices.

Intel created the [first commercially available microprocessor (Intel 4004)](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") in 1971.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) The microprocessor represented a notable advance in the technology of integrated circuitry, as it miniaturized the central processing unit of a computer, which then made it possible for small machines to perform calculations that in the past only very large machines could do. Considerable technological innovation was needed before the microprocessor could actually become the basis of what was first known as a "mini computer" and then known as a "personal computer".[[55]](Intel#cite_note-57) Intel also created one of the first [microcomputers](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1973.[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[56]](Intel#cite_note-Intellec-1973-58)

The K5 was an ambitious design, closer to a Pentium Pro than a Pentium regarding technical solutions and internal architecture. However, the final product was closer to the Pentium regarding performance, although faster clock-for-clock compared to the Pentium. ## Technical details The K5 was based upon an internal highly parallel processor architecture with an x86 decoding front-end.[[1]](AMD_K5#cite_note-1) The K5 offered good x86 compatibility and the in-house-developed test suite proved invaluable on later projects. All models had 4.3 million [transistors](Transistor "Transistor"), with five integer units that could process instructions [out of order](Out-of-order_execution "Out-of-order execution") and one floating-point unit. It had a 16 KB four-way [set-associative](CPU_cache#Associativity "CPU cache") instruction cache and an 8 KB data cache. The floating-point divide and square-root microcode were mechanically proven.[[3]](AMD_K5#cite_note-3)[[4]](AMD_K5#cite_note-4) The floating-point transcendental instructions were implemented in hardware and were faithful to true mathematical results for all operands.[[5]](AMD_K5#cite_note-5) ## Performance The K5 project represented an early chance for AMD to take technical leadership from Intel. Although the chip addressed the right design concepts, the actual engineering implementation had its issues. The low clock rates were, in part, due to AMD's limitations as a "cutting edge" manufacturing company at the time, and in part due to the design itself, which had many levels of logic for the process technology of the day, hampering clock scaling. Additionally, while the K5's floating-point performance was regarded as superior to that of the [Cyrix 6x86](Cyrix_6x86 "Cyrix 6x86"), it was slower than that of the Pentium, although offering more reliable transcendental function results. Because it was late to market and did not meet performance expectations, the K5 never gained the acceptance among large computer manufacturers that the earlier and later [AMD K6](AMD_K6 "AMD K6") enjoyed. ## Features ## Models Main article: [List of AMD K5 processors](List_of_AMD_K5_processors "List of AMD K5 processors") There were two revisions of the K5 architecture, internally called the **SSA/5** and the **5k86**, both released with the K5 label. The original set of "SSA/5" CPUs had its branch prediction unit disabled and additional internal waitstates added; these issues were remedied with the "5k86", resulting in up to 30% better performance clock for clock.[[6]](AMD_K5#cite_note-6)[[7]](AMD_K5#cite_note-7) The "SSA/5" line ran from 75 to 100 MHz; the "5k86" line ran from 90 to 133 MHz. [Zen](Zen_(microarchitecture) "Zen (microarchitecture)") is a new architecture for x86-64 based <Ryzen> series of CPUs and APUs, introduced in 2017 by AMD and built from the ground up by a team led by [Jim Keller](Jim_Keller_(engineer) "Jim Keller (engineer)"), beginning with his arrival in 2012, and [taping out](Tape-out "Tape-out") before his departure in September 2015. One of AMD's primary goals with Zen was an [IPC](Instructions_per_cycle "Instructions per cycle") increase of at least 40%, however in February 2017 AMD announced that they had actually achieved a 52% increase.[[167]](AMD#cite_note-167) Processors made on the Zen architecture are built on the 14 nm FinFET node and have a renewed focus on single-core performance and [HSA](Heterogeneous_System_Architecture "Heterogeneous System Architecture") compatibility.[[168]](AMD#cite_note-168) Previous processors from AMD were either built in the 32 nm process ("Bulldozer" and "Piledriver" CPUs) or the 28 nm process ("Steamroller" and "Excavator" APUs). Because of this, Zen is much more energy efficient. The Zen architecture is the first to encompass CPUs and APUs from AMD built for a single socket (Socket AM4). Also new for this architecture is the implementation of [simultaneous multithreading](Simultaneous_multithreading "Simultaneous multithreading") (SMT) technology, something Intel has had for years on some of their processors with their proprietary [hyper-threading](Hyper-threading "Hyper-threading") implementation of SMT. This is a departure from the "[Clustered MultiThreading](Clustered_multi-thread "Clustered multi-thread")" design introduced with the Bulldozer architecture. Zen also has support for [DDR4](DDR4_SDRAM "DDR4 SDRAM") memory. AMD released the Zen-based high-end Ryzen 7 "Summit Ridge" series CPUs on March 2, 2017,[[169]](AMD#cite_note-169) mid-range Ryzen 5 series CPUs on April 11, 2017, and entry level Ryzen 3 series CPUs on July 27, 2017.[[170]](AMD#cite_note-zen_ars-170) AMD later released the <Epyc> line of Zen derived server processors for 1P and 2P systems.[[171]](AMD#cite_note-171) In October 2017, AMD released Zen-based APUs as Ryzen Mobile, incorporating [Vega](Graphics_Core_Next#GCN_5th_Generation_(Vega) "Graphics Core Next") graphics cores.[[172]](AMD#cite_note-RM_AT-172) In January 2018 AMD has announced their new lineup plans, with Ryzen 2.[[173]](AMD#cite_note-173) AMD launched CPUs with the [12nm Zen+](Zen%2B "Zen+")[[174]](AMD#cite_note-174) microarchitecture in April 2018, following up with the [7nm Zen 2](Zen_2 "Zen 2") microarchitecture in June 2019, including an update to the Epyc line with new processors using the Zen 2 microarchitecture in August 2019, and Zen 3 slated for release in Q3 2020. As of 2019, AMD's Ryzen processors were reported to outsell Intel's consumer desktop processors.[[175]](AMD#cite_note-175) At CES 2020 AMD announced their Ryzen Mobile 4000, as the first 7 nm x86 mobile processor, the first 7 nm 8-core (also 16-thread) high-performance mobile processor, and the first 8-core (also 16-thread) processor for ultrathin laptops.[[176]](AMD#cite_note-176) This generation is still based on the Zen 2 architecture. In October 2020, AMD announced new processors based on the Zen 3 architecture.[[177]](AMD#cite_note-177) On PassMark's Single thread performance test the Ryzen 5 5600x bested all other CPUs besides the Ryzen 9 5950X.[[178]](AMD#cite_note-178) In August 2022, AMD announced their initial lineup of CPUs based on the new [Zen 4](Zen_4 "Zen 4") architecture.[[179]](AMD#cite_note-179)

The [Steam Deck](Steam_Deck "Steam Deck"),[[180]](AMD#cite_note-180)[[181]](AMD#cite_note-181) [PlayStation 5](PlayStation_5 "PlayStation 5"), [Xbox Series X and Series S](Xbox_Series_X_and_Series_S "Xbox Series X and Series S") all use chips based on the Zen 2 microarchitecture, with proprietary tweaks and different configurations in each system's implementation than AMD sells in its own commercially available APUs.[[182]](AMD#cite_note-182)[[183]](AMD#cite_note-183)

Paul Galvin wanted a brand name for Galvin Manufacturing Corporation's new car radio, and created the name "Motorola" by linking "motor" (for motorcar) with "ola" (from <Victrola>), which was also a popular ending for many companies at the time, e.g. <Moviola>, <Crayola>.[[10]](Motorola#cite_note-10) The company sold its first Motorola branded radio on June 23, 1930, to H.C. Wall of Fort Wayne, Indiana, for $30.[[11]](Motorola#cite_note-11) The Motorola brand name became so well known that Galvin Manufacturing Corporation later changed its name to Motorola, Inc., in 1947.[[4]](Motorola#cite_note-:3-4)[[3]](Motorola#cite_note-:2-3)

Galvin Manufacturing Corporation began selling Motorola car-radio receivers to police departments and municipalities in November 1930. **Freescale Semiconductor, Inc.** was an American [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") manufacturer. It was created by the divestiture of the Semiconductor Products Sector of <Motorola> in 2004. Freescale focused their [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") products on the automotive, [embedded](Embedded_system "Embedded system") and communications markets. It was bought by a private investor group in 2006, and subsequently merged into [NXP Semiconductors](NXP_Semiconductors "NXP Semiconductors") in 2015.[[2]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-2)

## History

### Divesture from Motorola and first IPO

As of 2003, Motorola Semiconductor Products Sector earned US$5.0 [billion](Billion "Billion") in semiconductor sales in 2002 (out of US$27 billion sales for all of Motorola).[[3]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-3)

Motorola announced that their semiconductor division would be divested on October 6, 2003, to create Freescale.

Freescale completed its [Initial public offering](Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO) on July 16, 2004, at a price of US$13. In its announcement, it estimated the stock price to be US$17.50- 19.50 but following a cooling of the market towards tech stocks, it lowered its price to US$13. Existing shareholders of Motorola stock received 0.110415 shares of Freescale stock for every share of Motorola stock as a dividend which was distributed on December 2, 2004.[[4]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-4)

### Buyout

On September 15, 2006, Freescale agreed to accept a [buyout](Buyout "Buyout") for the sum of $17.6 billion ($40 per share) by a consortium led by the [Blackstone Group](Blackstone_Group "Blackstone Group"). Share prices of $13 at the July 2004 IPO had risen to $39.35 in afterhours trading that Friday when the news, rumored that week, broke. A special shareholders meeting on November 13, 2006, voted to accept the buyout offer. The purchase, which closed on December 1, 2006, is reportedly the largest private buyout of a technology company and one of the ten largest buyouts of all time.[[5]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-5)[[6]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-6)[[7]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-7)[[8]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-8)

### Second IPO

Freescale filed to go public again on February 11, 2011, and completed its IPO on May 26, 2011. Freescale was traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the [ticker symbol](Ticker_symbol "Ticker symbol") FSL. At the time of the IPO, the company had $7.6 billion in outstanding debt on its books,[[9]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-Freescale_Debt-9) and the company was investigated for misconduct related to this IPO.[[10]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-10)

### MH370

On March 8, 2014, Freescale announced that 20 of its employees were lost aboard [Malaysia Airlines Flight 370](Malaysia_Airlines_Flight_370 "Malaysia Airlines Flight 370").[[11]](Freescale_Semiconductor#cite_note-11)

## Products

**Samsung Group**,[[3]](Samsung#cite_note-3) or simply **Samsung** ([Korean](Korean_language "Korean language"): 삼성; [RR](Revised_Romanization_of_Korean "Revised Romanization of Korean"): *samseong* [samsʌŋ]) (stylized as **SΛMSUNG**), is a South Korean [multinational](Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation") manufacturing [conglomerate](Conglomerate_(company) "Conglomerate (company)") headquartered in Samsung Digital City, <Suwon>, South Korea.[[1]](Samsung#cite_note-samsung.co.kr-1) It comprises numerous affiliated businesses,[[1]](Samsung#cite_note-samsung.co.kr-1) most of them united under the Samsung brand, and is the largest South Korean *[chaebol](Chaebol "Chaebol")* (business conglomerate). As of 2020, Samsung has the eighth highest global [brand value](Brand_valuation "Brand valuation").[[4]](Samsung#cite_note-4)

Samsung was founded by [Lee Byung-chul](Lee_Byung-chul "Lee Byung-chul") in 1938 as a [trading company](Trading_company "Trading company"). Over the next three decades, the group diversified into areas including food processing, textiles, insurance, securities, and retail. Samsung entered the [electronics industry](Electronics_industry "Electronics industry") in the late 1960s and the construction and shipbuilding industries in the mid-1970s; these areas would drive its subsequent growth. Following Lee's death in 1987, Samsung was separated into five business groups – Samsung Group, <Shinsegae> Group, [CJ Group](CJ_Group "CJ Group") and <Hansol> Group, and [JoongAng](JoongAng_Ilbo "JoongAng Ilbo") Group.

Notable Samsung industrial affiliates include [Samsung Electronics](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics") (the world's largest [information technology company](List_of_largest_technology_companies_by_revenue "List of largest technology companies by revenue"), [consumer electronics maker](Consumer_electronics "Consumer electronics") and [chipmaker](Semiconductor_industry "Semiconductor industry") measured by 2017 revenues),[[5]](Samsung#cite_note-5)[[6]](Samsung#cite_note-6) [Samsung Heavy Industries](Samsung_Heavy_Industries "Samsung Heavy Industries") (the world's second largest [shipbuilder](Shipbuilding "Shipbuilding") measured by 2010 revenues),[[7]](Samsung#cite_note-7) and [Samsung Engineering](Samsung_Engineering "Samsung Engineering") and [Samsung C&T Corporation](Samsung_C%26T_Corporation "Samsung C&T Corporation") (respectively the world's 13th and 36th largest construction companies).[[8]](Samsung#cite_note-8) Other notable subsidiaries include [Samsung Life Insurance](Samsung_Life_Insurance "Samsung Life Insurance") (the world's 14th largest life insurance company),[[9]](Samsung#cite_note-9) Samsung Everland (operator of [Everland Resort](Everland_Resort "Everland Resort"), the oldest [theme park](Theme_park "Theme park") in South Korea)[[10]](Samsung#cite_note-10) and [Cheil Worldwide](Cheil_Worldwide "Cheil Worldwide") (the world's 15th largest advertising agency, as measured by 2012 revenues).[[11]](Samsung#cite_note-11)[[12]](Samsung#cite_note-12)

## Etymology

According to Samsung's founder, the meaning of the [Korean](Korean_language "Korean language") [hanja](Hanja "Hanja") word *Samsung* ([三](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/三 "wikt:三")[星](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/星 "wikt:星")) is "three stars". The word "three" represents something "big, numerous and powerful",[[13]](Samsung#cite_note-13) while "stars" means "everlasting" or "eternal", like stars in the sky.[[14]](Samsung#cite_note-14)[[15]](Samsung#cite_note-15)

## History

### 1938–1970

In 1938, during [Japanese-ruled Korea](Korea_under_Japanese_rule "Korea under Japanese rule"), [Lee Byung-chul](Lee_Byung-chul "Lee Byung-chul") (1910–1987) of a large landowning family in the [Uiryeong](Uiryeong_County "Uiryeong County") county moved to nearby <Daegu> city and founded Mitsuboshi Trading Company (株式会社三星商会 (*Kabushiki gaisha Mitsuboshi Shōkai*)), or *Samsung Sanghoe* (주식회사 삼성상회). Samsung started out as a small trading company with forty employees located in Su-dong (now Ingyo-dong).[[16]](Samsung#cite_note-Samsung-16) It dealt in dried-fish,[[16]](Samsung#cite_note-Samsung-16) locally-grown groceries and noodles. The company prospered and Lee moved its head office to Seoul in 1947. When the [Korean War](Korean_War "Korean War") broke out, he was forced to leave Seoul. He started a [sugar refinery](Sugar_refinery "Sugar refinery") in <Busan> named [*Cheil Jedang*](CJ_Group "CJ Group"). In 1954, Lee founded [*Cheil Mojik*](Cheil_Industries "Cheil Industries") and built the plant in Chimsan-dong, <Daegu>. It was the largest woollen mill ever in the country.

Samsung diversified into many different areas. Lee sought to establish Samsung as a leader in a wide range of industries. Samsung moved into lines of business such as insurance, securities, and retail.

<Samsung>, a Korean electronics company, began producing [semiconductors](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") in 1974 and has grown to become one of the largest semiconductor fabricators in the world. In the decades following Samsung's entrance into semiconductor fabrication, many of its workers developed serious illnesses, including leukemia, lymphoma, and [multiple sclerosis (MS)](Multiple_sclerosis "Multiple sclerosis"). Beginning in 2007, the families of the impacted workers, with the help of a variety of domestic and international organizations, organized and mobilized against Samsung in the form of various protests and legal challenges. This organized opposition lasted for over a decade and largely concluded upon the signing of a binding settlement agreement between Samsung and the relevant opposition leader. Additionally, Samsung issued a public apology[[1]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-1) and acceptance responsibility for causing an increased risk of serious illness in its semiconductor factories.

## Background

Samsung first entered the semiconductor fabrication business in 1974 by [acquiring Korea Semiconductors](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics").[[2]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-2) By 1993, Samsung was the world's largest producer of memory chips, and it has retained that title ever since.[[3]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-3)

The semiconductor fabrication process necessitates the use of a variety of chemicals and carcinogenic substances. At various points in the process, workers are required to dip components in chemical baths, utilize X-ray radiation, and engage in various other production techniques that expose them to potentially harmful chemicals.[[4]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:0-4)

In the 1980s and 1990s, the semiconductor industry was subject a variety of criticisms for creating potential health hazards in their fabrication facilities.[[5]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:4-5) A number of Samsung's US-based competitors were found to have statistically greater serious illness incidence rates among their semiconductor workforces, which led to increased monitoring, safety standards, and protection for semiconductor workers in the US and many other countries.[[4]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:0-4) Samsung, however, has historically declined to release the relevant health data and information on the environment in its semiconductor plants. This decision has been facilitated by the South Korean government's regulations protecting trade secrets that have allowed the company to withhold relevant information, such as the types of chemicals used in semiconductor production, despite numerous attempts to have it made public.[[6]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:5-6)

Studies and reports released decades after Samsung's entry into semiconductor fabrication showed that the company has a long history of questionable health and safety practices.[[7]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-7) It was discovered that Samsung semiconductor workers' exposure to radiation was significantly beyond the acceptable levels recognized by US regulators.[[8]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:1-8) Moreover, it was found that Samsung neglected to actually check the chemical composition of substances used in its semiconductor fabrication process, and that the company failed to conduct exposure assessments for 71% of chemicals utilized in production.[[8]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:1-8) Other investigations suggested the company continued to use harmful substances even after stating it would no longer use them. For example, internal documents showed that Samsung was using TCE, a known toxic substance, as recently as 2010 despite the company publicly stating it had not been a part of the fabrication process since 1995.[[4]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:0-4)

As such, there have been a great deal of cases of serious illness being developed in Samsung's manufacturing workforce over the decades after it first entered the semiconductor market. However, prior to the organization of an opposition movement, no court in South Korea had ordered Samsung to pay compensation for causing illness in any of its workers.

shio Iue"), the founder of <Sanyo>, played a role as an advisor to [Lee Byung-chul](Lee_Byung-chul "Lee Byung-chul"), Samsung's founder, who was a novice in the electronics business. December the same year, Samsung Electric established a joint venture named Samsung-Sanyo Electric with <Sanyo> and [Sumitomo Corporation](Sumitomo_Corporation "Sumitomo Corporation"). This is the direct predecessor of today's Samsung Electronics.[[32]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-32)

The joint venture's early products were electronic and electrical appliances including televisions, [calculators](Calculator "Calculator"), [refrigerators](Refrigerator "Refrigerator"), air conditioners, and washing machines. In 1970, Samsung established the joint venture Samsung-NEC with Japan's <NEC> Corporation and [Sumitomo Corporation](Sumitomo_Corporation "Sumitomo Corporation") to manufacture [home appliances](Home_appliances "Home appliances") and [audiovisual devices](Professional_audiovisual_industry "Professional audiovisual industry"). Samsung-NEC later became Samsung SDI, the group's display and battery business unit. In 1973, Samsung and Sanyo created Samsung-Sanyo Parts, the predecessor of [Samsung Electro-Mechanics](Samsung_Electro-Mechanics "Samsung Electro-Mechanics"). By 1981, Samsung Electric had manufactured over 10 million [black-and-white televisions](Black_and_white_television "Black and white television").

In 1974, Samsung Group expanded into the [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") business by acquiring Korea Semiconductor, which was on the verge of bankruptcy whilst building one of the first chip-making facilities in the country at the time. Soon after, Korea Telecommunications, an electronic switching system producer and a Samsung Group company, took over the semiconductor business and became Samsung Semiconductor & Communications.[[33]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-33)

In February 1983, Lee, along with the board of the Samsung industry and corporation agreement and help by sponsoring the event, made an announcement later dubbed the "Tokyo declaration", in which he declared that Samsung intended to become a [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM) vendor. One year later, Samsung announced that it successfully developed a 64 [kb](Kilobit "Kilobit") DRAM, reducing the technological gap between the companies from [first-world](First_World "First World") countries and the young electronics maker from more than a decade to approximately four years. In the process, Samsung used technologies imported from [Micron Technology](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology") of the U.S for the development of DRAM and [Sharp Corporation](Sharp_Corporation "Sharp Corporation") of Japan for its [SRAM](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") and [ROM](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory").[[34]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-34) In 1988, Samsung Electric Industries merged with Samsung Semiconductor & Communications to form Samsung Electronics,[[35]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-35) as before that, they had not been one company and had not been a leading corporation together, but they were not rivals, as they had been in talks for a time until they finally merged.

In the 1980s and early 1990s, Samsung sold personal computers under the Leading Technology brand. However, the equipment was manufactured by Samsung, and the FCC filings from this period typically refer to Samsung products.[[36]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-36)

### 1988–1995: consumer struggles

In 1988, Samsung Electronics launched its first mobile phone in the South Korean market.[[37]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-Michell1-37) Sales were initially poor, and by the early 1990s, Motorola held a market share of over 60 percent in the country's mobile phone market compared to just 10 percent for Samsung.[[37]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-Michell1-37) Samsung's mobile phone division also struggled with poor quality and inferior products until the mid-1990s, and exit from the sector was a frequent topic of discussion within the company.[[38]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-38)

### 1995–2008: component manufacturing and design strategy

Lee Kun-Hee decided that Samsung needed to change its strategy. The company shelved the production of many under-selling product lines and instead pursued a process of designing and manufacturing components and investing in new technologies for other companies. In addition, Samsung outlined a 10-year plan to shrug off its image as a "budget brand" and to challenge [Sony](Sony_Corporation "Sony Corporation") as the world's largest consumer electronics manufacturer. It was hoped that, in this way, Samsung would gain an understanding of how products are made and give a technological lead sometime in the future. This patient [vertical integration](Vertical_integration "Vertical integration") strategy of manufacturing components has borne fruit for Samsung in the late 2000s.[[39]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-businessweek-39)

A complementary brand leadership strategy was also initiated by chairman Lee when he declared 1996 to be the "Year of Design Revolution" at Samsung. His objective was to build Samsung design capabilities as a competitive asset and transform the company into a global brand-design leader. However, this effort required major changes in corporate culture, processes, and systems. By integrating a comprehensive [design management](Design_management "Design management") system and strategy into the corporate culture, Samsung was successful in developing an award-winning product design portfolio by the late 1990s, resulting in significant brand equity growth.[[40]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-Samsung3B-40)[[41]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-Nussbaum,_B._1997-41)[[42]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-Samsung4B-42)

As Samsung shifted away from consumer markets, the company devised a plan to sponsor major sporting events. One such sponsorship was for the [1998 Winter Olympics](1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics") held in [Nagano](Nagano_(city) "Nagano (city)"), Japan.[[43]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-43)

As a [chaebol](Chaebol "Chaebol"), Samsung Group wielded wealth that allowed the company to invest and develop new technology rather than build products at a level that would not have a detrimental impact on Samsung's finances.[[44]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-44)

Samsung had a number of technological breakthroughs, particularly in the field of memory which are commonplace in most electrical products today. This includes the world's first 64MB DRAM in 1992, 256 MB DRAM in 1994, and 1GB DRAM in 1996.[[45]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-45) In 2004, Samsung developed the world's first 8GB [NAND flash](NAND_flash "NAND flash") memory chip, and a manufacturing deal was struck with Apple in 2005. A deal to supply Apple with memory chips was sealed in 2005, and Samsung remains a key supplier of Apple components as of October 2013, manufacturing the [A7](Apple_A7 "Apple A7") processors inside the [iPhone 5S](IPhone_5S "IPhone 5S") model.[[46]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-samsungsupplier-46)[[47]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-Bloom-47)

### 2008–present: recent developments

From 2000 to 2003, Samsung posted [net earnings](Net_income "Net income") higher than five-percent; this was at a time when 16 out of the 30 top South Korean companies ceased operating in the wake of the unprecedented crisis.[[48]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-48)[[49]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-49)

In 2005, Samsung Electronics surpassed its Japanese rival <Sony> for the first time to become the world's twentieth-largest and most popular consumer brand, as measured by Interbrand.[[50]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-50)

In 2007, Samsung Electronics became the world's second-largest smartphone manufacturer, overtaking Motorola for the first time.[[51]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-51) In 2009, Samsung achieved total revenues of US$117.4 billion, overtaking Hewlett-Packard to become the world's largest technology company measured by sales.[[52]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-st-52)

In 2009 and 2010, the US and EU fined the company, along with eight other memory chip manufacturers, for its part in a price-fixing scheme that occurred between 1999 and 2002. **Lee Kun-hee** ([Korean](Korean_language "Korean language"): 이건희; <Hanja>: 李健熙, Korean: [iːɡʌnɣi]; 9 January 1942 – 25 October 2020) was a South Korean business magnate who served as the chairman of [Samsung Group](Samsung "Samsung") from 1987 to 2008, and again from 2010 until his death in 2020. He is also credited with the transformation of Samsung to one of the world's largest business entities that engages in semiconductors, smartphones, electronics, shipbuilding, construction, and other businesses. Since Lee Kun-hee became the chairman of Samsung, the company became the world's largest manufacturer of smartphones, memory chips, and appliances. He was the third son of Samsung founder [Lee Byung-chul](Lee_Byung-chul "Lee Byung-chul"). With an estimated net worth of US$21 billion at the time of his death,[[1]](Lee_Kun-hee#cite_note-Forbes_profile-1) he was the richest person in South Korea, a position that he had held since 2007.

He was convicted twice, once in 1996 and subsequently in 2008, for corruption and tax evasion charges, but was pardoned on both instances. In 2014, Lee was named the world's 35th most powerful person and the most powerful Korean by *Forbes*'s [list of the world's most powerful people](Forbes_list_of_The_World's_Most_Powerful_People "Forbes list of The World's Most Powerful People") along with his son, [Lee Jae-yong](Lee_Jae-yong_(businessman) "Lee Jae-yong (businessman)").[[2]](Lee_Kun-hee#cite_note-2)

"Washington, D.C."), but did not get a degree.[[5]](Lee_Kun-hee#cite_note-:0-5)[[6]](Lee_Kun-hee#cite_note-:1-6)

Prosecutors requested that Lee be sentenced to seven years in prison and fined 350 billion won (approximately US$312 million). In 1973, Samsung and Sanyo created Samsung-Sanyo Parts, the predecessor of [Samsung Electro-Mechanics](Samsung_Electro-Mechanics "Samsung Electro-Mechanics"). # Multi-Agent Delegation

When the user asks a complex question, do not attempt to answer it yourself. Break it up into smaller pieces, then use the `fork` tool to delegate each piece to a subagent. You MUST use the `join` tool to retrieve the subagent's result for each subagent you create with `fork`. Each subagent has access to the exact same tools that you do.

If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

## Writing Instructions
