### Hakunetsusha (Tokyo Denki)

**Hakunetsusha** (白熱舎) was a company established by Shōichi Miyoshi and Fujioka Ichisuke, two of Japan's industrial pioneers during the Tokugawa / [Edo period](Edo_period "Edo period"). It specialized in the manufacture of light bulbs.

The company was established in 1890 and started out by selling bulbs using bamboo filaments. However, following the opening up of trade with the West through the [Unequal treaty](Unequal_treaty "Unequal treaty"), <Hakunetsusha> met with fierce competition from imports. Its bulb cost about 60 percent more than the imports and the quality was poorer. The company managed to survive with the booms after the [First Sino-Japanese War](First_Sino-Japanese_War "First Sino-Japanese War") of 1894–95 and the [Russo-Japanese War](Russo-Japanese_War "Russo-Japanese War") of 1904–05, but afterward its financial position was precarious.

In 1905 the company was renamed [Tokyo Denki](Tokyo_Denki "Tokyo Denki") (Tokyo Electric) and entered into a financial and technological collaboration with [General Electric](General_Electric "General Electric") of the US. General Electric acquired 51 percent share of ownership, sent a vice president, and provided the technology for bulb-making. Production equipment was bought from GE and Tokyo Denki soon started selling its products with GE's trademark.

### 1939 to 2000

Toshiba was founded in 1939 by the merger of Shibaura Seisakusho[[20]](Toshiba#cite_note-20) and Tokyo Denki. The merger of Shibaura and Tokyo Denki created a new company called Tokyo Shibaura Denki (Tokyo Shibaura Electric) ([**東**京](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/東京 "wikt:東京") [**芝**浦](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/芝浦 "wikt:芝浦") [電気](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/電気 "wikt:電気")). It was soon nicknamed Toshiba, but it was not until 1978 that the company was officially renamed Toshiba Corporation.

The group expanded rapidly, driven by a combination of organic growth and by acquisitions, buying heavy engineering, and primary industry firms in the 1940s and 1950s. Groups created include [Toshiba Music Industries/Toshiba EMI](EMI_Music_Japan "EMI Music Japan") (1960), Toshiba International Corporation (the 1970s) Toshiba Electrical Equipment (1974), Toshiba Chemical (1974), Toshiba Lighting and Technology (1989), Toshiba America Information Systems (1989) and Toshiba Carrier Corporation (1999).

Toshiba is responsible for a number of Japanese firsts, including radar (1912), the TAC digital computer (1954), transistor television, color CRTs[[21]](Toshiba#cite_note-21) and microwave oven (1959), [color video phone](Videophone "Videophone") (1971), Japanese [word processor](Word_processor "Word processor") (1978), MRI system (1982), laptop personal computer (1986), NAND EEPROM (1991), DVD (1995), the [Libretto](Libretto_(notebook) "Libretto (notebook)") sub-notebook personal computer (1996) and [HD DVD](HD_DVD "HD DVD") (2005).

In 1977, Toshiba acquired the Brazilian company Semp (Sociedade Eletromercantil Paulista), subsequently forming Semp Toshiba through the combination of the two companies' South American operations.

In 1987, Tocibai Machine, a subsidiary of Toshiba, was accused of illegally selling CNC [milling machines](Milling_machine "Milling machine") used to produce very quiet [submarine](Submarine "Submarine") propellers to the [Soviet Union](Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") in violation of the <CoCom> agreement, an international [embargo](Embargo "Embargo") on certain countries to <COMECON> countries. The [Toshiba-Kongsberg scandal](Toshiba-Kongsberg_scandal "Toshiba-Kongsberg scandal") involved a subsidiary of Toshiba and the Norwegian company [Kongsberg Vaapenfabrikk](Kongsberg_Defence_%26_Aerospace "Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace"). The incident strained relations between the [United States](United_States "United States") and <Japan>, and resulted in the arrest and prosecution of two senior executives, as well as the imposition of [sanctions](Economic_sanctions "Economic sanctions") on the company by both countries.[[24]](Toshiba#cite_note-24) Senator [John Heinz](John_Heinz "John Heinz") of Pennsylvania said "What Toshiba and Kongsberg did was ransom the security of the United States for $517 million."

The contract ended in 2008, ending seven years of OEM production with Orion.

In December 2004, Toshiba quietly announced it would discontinue manufacturing traditional in-house [cathode-ray tube](Cathode-ray_tube "Cathode-ray tube") (CRT) televisions. In 2005, Matsushita Toshiba Picture Display Co. Ltd. (a joint venture between <Panasonic> and Toshiba created in 2002[[25]](Toshiba#cite_note-25)) stopped production of CRTs at its factory in Horseheads, New York. A year later, in 2006, it stopped production at its Malaysian factory, following heavy losses.[[26]](Toshiba#cite_note-26)[[27]](Toshiba#cite_note-27)[[28]](Toshiba#cite_note-28) In 2006, Toshiba terminated sales of CRT TVs in Japan[[29]](Toshiba#cite_note-29) and production of in-house plasma TVs. To ensure its future competitiveness in the flat-panel digital television and display market, Toshiba has made a considerable investment in a new kind of display technology called [SED](Surface-conduction_electron-emitter_display "Surface-conduction electron-emitter display"). This technology, however, was never sold to the public, as it was not price-competitive with LCDs. Toshiba sold its share in SED Inc. to [Canon](Canon_Inc. "Canon Inc.") after Nano-Proprietary, which owns several patents related to SED technology, claimed SED Inc. was not a subsidiary of Canon.[[30]](Toshiba#cite_note-30) Before [World War II](World_War_II "World War II"), Toshiba was a member of the [Mitsui Group](Mitsui "Mitsui") [zaibatsu](Zaibatsu "Zaibatsu") ([family-controlled](Family_business "Family business") [vertical monopoly](Vertical_monopoly "Vertical monopoly")). On 30 June 2020, Sharp exercised its option to acquire the remaining 19.9% percent of Dynabook shares from Toshiba.[[97]](Toshiba#cite_note-:3-97)

In May 2019, Toshiba announced that it would put non-Japanese investors on its board for the first time in nearly 80 years.[[98]](Toshiba#cite_note-98) In November, the company transferred its logistics service business to SBS Group.[[99]](Toshiba#cite_note-99)

In January 2020, Toshiba unveiled its plan to launch quantum cryptography services by September the same year.[[5]](Toshiba#cite_note-quantumToshiba-5) It also announced a number of other technologies waiting for commercialization, including an affordable solid-state <Lidar> based on [silicon photomultiplier](Silicon_photomultiplier "Silicon photomultiplier"), high-capacity [hydrogen fuel cells](Hydrogen_fuel_cells "Hydrogen fuel cells"),[[100]](Toshiba#cite_note-100)[[101]](Toshiba#cite_note-101) and a proprietary [computer algorithm](Algorithm "Algorithm") named *Simulated Bifurcation Algorithm* that mimics [quantum computing](Quantum_computing "Quantum computing"), of which it plans to sell access to other parties such as financial institutions, social networking services, etc. The company claims the algorithm running on a desktop PC at room temperature environment is capable of surpassing the performance of similar algorithms running on existing [supercomputers](Supercomputer "Supercomputer"), even that of laser-based quantum computer when a specialized setting is given.[[102]](Toshiba#cite_note-102) It has been added to quantum computing services offered by major cloud platforms including [Microsoft Azure](Microsoft_Azure "Microsoft Azure").[[103]](Toshiba#cite_note-103)

In October 2020, Toshiba made a decision to pull out of the system [LSI](Integrated_circuit#LSI "Integrated circuit") business citing mounted losses while reportedly mulling on the sale of its semiconductor fabs as well.[[104]](Toshiba#cite_note-104)[[105]](Toshiba#cite_note-105) In April 2021, [CVC Capital Partners](CVC_Capital_Partners "CVC Capital Partners") made a takeover offer.[[106]](Toshiba#cite_note-106)

On 12 November 2021, Toshiba announced that it would split into three separate companies. Two of the companies will respectively focus on infrastructure and electronic devices; the third, which will retain the Toshiba name, would manage the 40.6% stake in <Kioxia> and all other remaining assets. The company expects to complete the plan by March 2024.[[12]](Toshiba#cite_note-Breakup_-_WSJ-12) Toshiba announced in February 2022 that it plans to split into two companies instead after the original proposal proved unpopular with shareholders.[[107]](Toshiba#cite_note-107)

## Operations

See also: [List of Toshiba subsidiaries](List_of_Toshiba_subsidiaries "List of Toshiba subsidiaries")

- The Toshiba research and development facility in [Kawasaki, Kanagawa](Kawasaki%2C_Kanagawa "Kawasaki, Kanagawa"), Japan

- Toshiba Europe offices in <Neuss>, <Germany>

- Toshiba Canada offices

As of 2012, Toshiba had 39 R&D facilities worldwide, which employed around 4,180 people,[[108]](Toshiba#cite_note-annrepop2012-108) and was organized into four main business groupings: the Digital Products Group, the Electronic Devices Group, the Home Appliances Group and the Social Infrastructure Group.[[108]](Toshiba#cite_note-annrepop2012-108) In the year ended 31 March 2012, Toshiba had total revenues of ¥6,100.3 billion, of which 25.2 percent was generated by the Digital Products Group, 24.5 percent by the Electronic Devices Group, 8.7 percent by the Home Appliances Group, 36.6 percent by the Social Infrastructure Group and 5 percent by other activities. In the same year, 45 percent of Toshiba's sales were generated in Japan and 55 percent in the rest of the world.[[108]](Toshiba#cite_note-annrepop2012-108)

Toshiba invested a total of ¥319.9 billion in R&D in the year ended 31 March 2012, equivalent to 5.2 percent of sales.[[108]](Toshiba#cite_note-annrepop2012-108) Toshiba registered a total of 2,483 patents in the United States in 2011, the fifth-largest number of any company (after <IBM>, [Samsung Electronics](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"), [Canon](Canon_Inc. "Canon Inc.") and <Panasonic>).[[108]](Toshiba#cite_note-annrepop2012-108)

Toshiba had around 141,256 employees as of 31 March 2018.[[109]](Toshiba#cite_note-corporatedata-109)

## Products, services, and standards

Toshiba has had a range of products and services, including air conditioners,[[110]](Toshiba#cite_note-tceh-110) consumer electronics (including televisions and DVD and Blu-ray players),[[111]](Toshiba#cite_note-dps-111) control systems (including air-traffic control systems, railway systems, security systems and traffic control systems),[[112]](Toshiba#cite_note-sisc-112) electronic point of sale equipment,[[113]](Toshiba#cite_note-tec-113) elevators and escalators,[[114]](Toshiba#cite_note-114) home appliances (including refrigerators and washing machines),[[110]](Toshiba#cite_note-tceh-110) IT services,[[115]](Toshiba#cite_note-115) lighting,[[110]](Toshiba#cite_note-tceh-110)[[116]](Toshiba#cite_note-116) materials and electronic components,[[117]](Toshiba#cite_note-117) medical equipment (including CT and MRI scanners, ultrasound equipment and X-ray equipment),[[118]](Toshiba#cite_note-118) office equipment,[[113]](Toshiba#cite_note-tec-113)[[119]](Toshiba#cite_note-119) business telecommunication equipment[[120]](Toshiba#cite_note-120) personal computers,[[111]](Toshiba#cite_note-dps-111) semiconductors,[[121]](Toshiba#cite_note-121) power systems (including electricity turbines, fuel cells and nuclear reactors)[[122]](Toshiba#cite_note-122) power transmission and distribution systems,[[112]](Toshiba#cite_note-sisc-112) and TFT displays.[[123]](Toshiba#cite_note-123)

### HD DVD

Main article: [HD DVD](HD_DVD "HD DVD")

HD DVD logo

Toshiba had played a critical role in the development and proliferation of <DVD>.[[124]](Toshiba#cite_note-124) On 19 February 2008, Toshiba announced that it would be discontinuing its HD DVD storage format, the successor of DVD, following defeat in [a format war](High-definition_optical_disc_format_war "High-definition optical disc format war") against [Blu-ray](Blu-ray_Disc "Blu-ray Disc").[[125]](Toshiba#cite_note-125) The HD DVD format had failed after most of the major US film studios backed the Blu-ray format, which was developed by <Sony>, Panasonic, <Philips> and [Pioneer Corporation](Pioneer_Corporation "Pioneer Corporation"). Conceding the abandonment of HD DVD, Toshiba's president, [Atsutoshi Nishida](Atsutoshi_Nishida "Atsutoshi Nishida") said "We concluded that a swift decision would be best [and] if we had continued, that would have created problems for consumers, and we simply had no chance to win".[[126]](Toshiba#cite_note-126)

Toshiba continued to supply retailers with machines until the end of March 2008, and continued to provide technical support to the estimated one million people worldwide who owned HD DVD players and recorders. Toshiba announced a new line of stand-alone Blu-ray players as well as drives for PCs and laptops, and subsequently joined the BDA, the industry body which oversees the development of the Blu-ray format.[[127]](Toshiba#cite_note-127)

### REGZA

REGZA wordmark

REGZA (**R**eal **E**xpression **G**uaranteed by Ama**z**ing **A**rchitecture) is a unified television brand owned and manufactured by Toshiba. In 2010 REGZA name disappeared from the North American market, and from March 2015[[128]](Toshiba#cite_note-128) new TVs carrying the Toshiba name are designed and produced by [Compal Electronics](Compal_Electronics "Compal Electronics"), a Taiwanese company, to which Toshiba has licensed its name. This system supports 3D capability without glasses (utilizing an integral imaging system of 9 parallax images with a vertical lenticular sheet). The retail product was released in December 2010.[[129]](Toshiba#cite_note-129)

[4K Ultra HD](4K_resolution "4K resolution") (3840×2160p) televisions provides four times the resolution of 1080p Full HD televisions. Toshiba's 4K HD LED televisions are powered by a CEVO 4K Quad + dual-core processor.[[130]](Toshiba#cite_note-130)

### Laptops

Main article: [Dynabook Inc.](Dynabook_Inc. "Dynabook Inc.")

In 1985, Toshiba released the [T1100](Toshiba_T1100 "Toshiba T1100"), the world's first commercially accepted [laptop PC](Laptop "Laptop").[[11]](Toshiba#cite_note-:2-11)

In October 2014, Toshiba released the <Chromebook> 2, a new version with a thinner profile and a much-improved display. ### Flash memory

In the 1980s, a Toshiba team led by [Fujio Masuoka](Fujio_Masuoka "Fujio Masuoka") invented [flash memory](Flash_memory "Flash memory"), both NOR and NAND types. In March 2015, Toshiba announced the development of the first 48-layer, three-dimensional flash memory. The new flash memory is based on a vertical stacking technology that Toshiba calls BiCS (Bit Cost Scaling), stores two bits of data per transistor, and can store 128Gbits (16GB) per chip. s Incorporated** (**TI**) is an American technology company headquartered in <Dallas>, <Texas>, that designs and manufactures [semiconductors](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") and various [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit"), which it sells to electronics designers and [manufacturers](Manufacturer "Manufacturer") globally.[[5]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-5) It is one of the top 10 semiconductor companies worldwide based on [sales](Sales "Sales") volume.[[6]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-6) The company's focus is on developing [analog chips](Analog_chip "Analog chip") and [embedded processors](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor"), which account for more than 80% of its revenue.[[7]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ReferenceA-7) TI also produces TI [digital light processing](Digital_Light_Processing "Digital Light Processing") technology and education technology[[7]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ReferenceA-7) products including [calculators](Calculator "Calculator"), [microcontrollers](Microcontroller "Microcontroller"), and [multi-core processors](Multi-core_processor "Multi-core processor"). The company holds 45,000 patents worldwide as of 2016.[[8]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-8)

Texas Instruments emerged in 1951 after a reorganization of [Geophysical Service Incorporated](Geophysical_Service_Incorporated "Geophysical Service Incorporated"), a company founded in 1930 that manufactured equipment for use in the seismic industry, as well as defense electronics.[[9]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-9) TI produced the world's first commercial [silicon transistor](Silicon_transistor "Silicon transistor") in 1954,[[10]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-10) and the same year designed and manufactured the first [transistor radio](Transistor_radio "Transistor radio"). [Jack Kilby](Jack_Kilby "Jack Kilby") invented the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") in 1958 while working at TI's Central Research Labs. TI also invented the hand-held [calculator](Calculator "Calculator") in 1967, and introduced the first single-chip microcontroller in 1970, which combined all the elements of computing onto one piece of silicon.[[11]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-:0-11)

In 1987, TI invented the [digital light processing device](Digital_Light_Processing "Digital Light Processing") (also known as the DLP chip), which serves as the foundation for the company's DLP technology and DLP Cinema.[[11]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-:0-11) TI released the popular <TI-81> calculator in 1990, which made it a leader in the graphing calculator industry. Its defense business was sold to [Raytheon Company](Raytheon_Company "Raytheon Company") in 1997; this allowed TI to strengthen its focus on digital solutions.[[12]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-12) After the acquisition of [National Semiconductor](National_Semiconductor "National Semiconductor") in 2011, the company had a combined portfolio of 45,000 analog products and customer design tools.[[13]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-13) In the stock market, Texas Instruments is often regarded as an indicator for the semiconductor and electronics industry as a whole, since the company sells to more than 100,000 customers.[[14]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-14)[[15]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-15)[[16]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ED-16)

## History

Texas Instruments was founded by [Cecil H. Green](Cecil_H._Green "Cecil H. Green"), [J. Erik Jonsson](J._Erik_Jonsson "J. Erik Jonsson"), [Eugene McDermott](Eugene_McDermott "Eugene McDermott"), and [Patrick E. Haggerty](Patrick_E._Haggerty "Patrick E. Haggerty") in 1951. McDermott was one of the original founders of [Geophysical Service](Geophysical_Service_Incorporated "Geophysical Service Incorporated") Inc. (GSI) in 1930. McDermott, Green, and Jonsson were GSI employees who purchased the company in 1941. In November 1945, Patrick Haggerty was hired as general manager of the Laboratory and Manufacturing (L&M) division, which focused on electronic equipment.[[17]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-17) By 1951, the L&M division, with its defense contracts, was growing faster than GSI's geophysical division. The company was reorganized and initially renamed General Instruments Inc. Because a firm named [General Instrument](General_Instrument "General Instrument") already existed, the company was renamed Texas Instruments that same year. From 1956 to 1961, [Fred Agnich](Fred_Agnich "Fred Agnich") of Dallas, later a [Republican](Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") member of the [Texas House of Representatives](Texas_House_of_Representatives "Texas House of Representatives"), was the Texas Instruments president. Geophysical Service, Inc. became a subsidiary of Texas Instruments. Early in 1988, most of GSI was sold to the <Halliburton> Company.
> Texas Instruments exists to create, make, and market useful products and services to satisfy the needs of its customers throughout the world.[[18]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-Innovation-18)
>
> — Patrick Haggerty, Texas Instruments Statement of Purpose

### Geophysical Service Incorporated

In 1930, [J. Clarence Karcher](J._Clarence_Karcher "J. Clarence Karcher") and Eugene McDermott founded Geophysical Service, an early provider of [seismic exploration](Reflection_seismology "Reflection seismology") services to the petroleum industry. In 1939, the company reorganized as Coronado Corp,[[19]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-19) an oil company with Geophysical Service Inc (GSI), now as a subsidiary. On December 6, 1941, McDermott along with three other GSI employees, J. Erik Jonsson, Cecil H. Green, and H. B. Peacock purchased GSI. During World War II, GSI expanded its services to include [electronics](Electronics "Electronics") for the [U.S. Army](United_States_Army "United States Army"), [Army Signal Corps](United_States_Army_Signal_Corps "United States Army Signal Corps"), and [U.S. Navy](United_States_Navy "United States Navy"). In 1951, the company changed its name to Texas Instruments, spun off to build seismographs for oil explorations[[20]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TIcalcsMedium-20) and with GSI becoming a wholly owned subsidiary of the new company.

An early success story for TI-GSI came in 1965 when GSI was able (under a [Top Secret](Security_clearance "Security clearance") government contract) to monitor the [Soviet Union](Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")'s underground [nuclear weapons](Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") [testing](Nuclear_testing "Nuclear testing") under the ocean in [Vela Uniform](Vela_Uniform "Vela Uniform"), a subset of [Project Vela](Project_Vela "Project Vela"), to verify compliance of the [Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty](Partial_Nuclear_Test_Ban_Treaty "Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty").[[21]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-21)

Texas Instruments also continued to manufacture equipment for use in the seismic industry, and GSI continued to provide seismic services. After selling (and repurchasing) GSI, TI finally sold the company to <Halliburton> in 1988, after which sale GSI ceased to exist as a separate entity.

### Semiconductors

In early 1952, Texas Instruments purchased a patent license to produce germanium transistors from [Western Electric](Western_Electric "Western Electric"), the manufacturing arm of AT&T, for $25,000, beginning production by the end of the year. Haggerty brought [Gordon Teal](Gordon_Teal "Gordon Teal") to the company due to his expertise in growing semiconductor crystals while at [Bell Telephone Laboratories](Bell_Telephone_Laboratories "Bell Telephone Laboratories"). Teal's first assignment was to direct TI's research laboratory. At the end of 1952, Texas Instruments announced that it had expanded to 2,000 employees and $17 million in sales.[[22]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-22)

Among his new hires was [Willis Adcock](Willis_Adcock "Willis Adcock"), who joined TI early in 1953. Adcock, who like Teal was a [physical chemist](Physical_chemist "Physical chemist"), began leading a small research group focused on the task of fabricating grown-junction, [silicon](Silicon "Silicon"), single-crystal, small-signal transistors.[[23]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-transistor-23) Adcock later became the first TI Principal Fellow.[[24]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-Tribute-24)

#### First silicon transistor and integrated circuits

In January 1954, [Morris Tanenbaum](Morris_Tanenbaum "Morris Tanenbaum") at Bell Telephone Laboratories created the first workable silicon transistor.[[23]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-transistor-23) This work was reported in the spring of 1954, at the IRE off-the-record conference on solid-state devices, and was later published in the *Journal of Applied Physics*. Working independently in April 1954, Gordon Teal at TI created the first commercial silicon transistor and tested it on April 14, 1954. On May 10, 1954, at the Institute of Radio Engineers National Conference on Airborne Electronics in Dayton, Ohio, Teal presented a paper: "Some Recent Developments in Silicon and Germanium Materials and Devices".[[25]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-25)

In 1954, Texas Instruments designed and manufactured the first [transistor radio](Transistor_radio "Transistor radio"). The [Regency TR-1](Regency_TR-1 "Regency TR-1") used germanium transistors, as silicon transistors were much more expensive at the time. #### Standard TTL

The [7400 series](7400_series "7400 series") of [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") chips, developed by Texas Instruments in the 1960s, popularized the use of integrated circuits in computer logic. The military-grade version of this was the 5400 series.[[33]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-33)

#### Microprocessor

Texas Instruments invented the hand-held [calculator](Calculator "Calculator") (a prototype called "[Cal Tech](Cal_Tech_(calculator) "Cal Tech (calculator)")") in 1967 and the single-chip [microcomputer](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1971, was assigned the first patent on a single-chip [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") (invented by Gary Boone) on September 4, 1973.[[34]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-34) This was disputed by Gilbert Hyatt, formerly of the Micro Computer Company, in August 1990, when he was awarded a patent superseding TI's. This was overturned on June 19, 1996, in favor of TI[[35]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-35) (note: <Intel> is usually given credit with Texas Instruments for the almost-simultaneous invention of the microprocessor).

#### First speech synthesis chip

In 1978, Texas Instruments introduced the first single-chip [linear predictive coding](Linear_predictive_coding "Linear predictive coding") [speech synthesizer](Speech_synthesizer "Speech synthesizer").[[36]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-36) In 1976, TI began a feasibility study of memory-intensive applications for bubble memory then being developed. They soon focused on speech applications. This resulted in the development the TMC0280 one-chip linear predictive coding speech synthesizer, which was the first time a single silicon chip had electronically replicated the human voice.[[37]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TITimeLine-37)[[38]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-38) This was used in several TI commercial products beginning with [Speak & Spell](Speak_%26_Spell_(toy) "Speak & Spell (toy)"), which was introduced at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in June 1978. In 2001, TI left the speech synthesis business, selling it to Sensory Inc. of Santa Clara, California.[[39]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TI_will_exit_dedicated_speech-synthesis_chips,_transfer_products_to_Sensory-39)

### Consumer electronics and computers

In May 1954, Texas Instruments designed and built a prototype of the world's first [transistor radio](Transistor_radio "Transistor radio"), and, through a partnership with Industrial Development Engineering Associates of Indianapolis, Indiana, the 100% solid-state radio was sold to the public beginning in October of that year.[[40]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-40)

In the 1960s, company president Pat Haggerty had a team that included Jack Kilby to work on a handheld calculator project. Kilby and two other colleagues created the Cal-Tech, a three-pound battery-powered calculator that could do basic math and fit six-digit numbers on its display. This 4.25 x 6.15 x 1.75 inch calculator's processor would originate the vast majority of Texas Instruments’ revenue.[[20]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TIcalcsMedium-20)

In 1973, the handheld calculator SR-10 (named after [slide rule](Slide_rule "Slide rule")) and in 1974, the handheld scientific calculator [SR-50](TI_SR-50 "TI SR-50") were issued by TI. Both had red LED-segments numeric displays. The optical design of the SR-50 is somewhat similar to the <HP-35> edited by <Hewlett-Packard> before in early 1972, but buttons for the operations "+", "–", ... are in the right of the number block and the decimal point lies between two neighboring digits.

TI continued to be active in the consumer electronics market through the 1970s and 1980s. Early on, this also included two digital clock models – one for desk and the other a bedside alarm. From this sprang what became the Time Products Division, which made LED watches. Though these LED watches enjoyed early commercial success due to excellent quality, it was short-lived due to poor battery life. LEDs were replaced with LCD watches for a short time, but these could not compete because of styling issues, excessive makes and models, and price points. The watches were manufactured in <Dallas> and then [Lubbock, Texas](Lubbock%2C_Texas "Lubbock, Texas"). Several spin-offs of the [Speak & Spell](Speak_%26_Spell_(toy) "Speak & Spell (toy)"), such as the [Speak & Read](Speak_%26_Read "Speak & Read") and [Speak & Math](Speak_%26_Math "Speak & Math"), were introduced soon thereafter.[[41]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-41)

In 1979, TI entered the [home computer](Home_computer "Home computer") market with the [TI-99/4](TI-99/4A "TI-99/4A"), a competitor to such entries as the [Apple II](Apple_II_series "Apple II series"), <TRS-80>, and the later [Atari 400/800](Atari_8-bit_family "Atari 8-bit family") series and <VIC-20>. By late 1982, TI was dominating the U.S. home computer market, shipping 5,000 computers a day from their factory in Lubbock.[[42]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-death_1984_04_texasmonthly-42) It discontinued the <TI-99/4A> (1981), the sequel to the 99/4, in late 1983 amid an intense [price war](North_American_video_game_crash_of_1983 "North American video game crash of 1983") waged primarily against Commodore. At the 1983 Winter CES, TI showed models 99/2 and the [Compact Computer 40 (CC-40)](Compact_Computer_40 "Compact Computer 40"), the latter aimed at professional users. The [TI Professional](Texas_Instruments_Professional_Portable_Computer "Texas Instruments Professional Portable Computer") (1983) ultimately joined the ranks of the many unsuccessful <DOS> and [x86](X86 "X86")-based—but [non-compatible](PC_compatible "PC compatible")[[43]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-Inc.1984-43)—competitors to the [IBM PC](IBM_Personal_Computer "IBM Personal Computer") (the founders of <Compaq>, an early leader in PC compatibles, all came from TI). The company for years successfully made and sold PC-compatible laptops before withdrawing from the market and selling its product line to [Acer](Acer_Inc. "Acer Inc.") in 1998.[[44]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-44)

### Defense electronics

TI entered the [defense](Defense_(military) "Defense (military)") electronics market in 1942 with submarine detection equipment,[[45]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-45) based on the seismic exploration technology previously developed for the oil industry. The division responsible for these products was known at different times as the Laboratory & Manufacturing Division, the Apparatus Division, the Equipment Group, and the Defense Systems & Electronics Group (DSEG).

During the early 1980s, TI instituted a quality program which included [Juran](Joseph_M._Juran "Joseph M. Juran") training, as well as promoting [statistical process control](Statistical_process_control "Statistical process control"), [Taguchi methods](Taguchi_methods "Taguchi methods"), and [Design for Six Sigma](Design_for_Six_Sigma "Design for Six Sigma"). In the late '80s, the company, along with [Eastman Kodak](Eastman_Kodak "Eastman Kodak") and [Allied Signal](Allied_Signal "Allied Signal"), began involvement with <Motorola>, institutionalizing Motorola's [Six Sigma](Six_Sigma "Six Sigma") methodology.[[46]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-46) Motorola, which originally developed the Six Sigma methodology, began this work in 1982. In 1992, the DSEG division[[47]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-47) of Texas Instruments' quality-improvement efforts were rewarded by winning the [Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award](Malcolm_Baldrige_National_Quality_Award "Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award") for manufacturing.

TI developed the AAA-4 [infrared search and track](Infrared_search_and_track "Infrared search and track") device in the late '50s and early '60s for the [F-4B Phantom](F-4B_Phantom "F-4B Phantom")[[48]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweetmanBonds1987526-48) for passive scanning of jet-engine emissions, but it possessed limited capabilities and was eliminated on F-4Ds and later models.[[49]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-FOOTNOTESweetmanBonds1987552-49)

In 1956, TI began research on [infrared](Infrared "Infrared") technology that led to several line scanner contracts and with the addition of a second scan mirror the invention of the first [forward looking infrared](Forward_looking_infrared "Forward looking infrared") (FLIR) in 1963 with production beginning in 1966. In 1972, TI invented the common module FLIR[[50]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-50) concept, greatly reducing cost and allowing reuse of common components.

TI went on to produce side-looking radar systems, the first [terrain-following radar](Terrain_following_radar "Terrain following radar") and surveillance radar systems for both the military and FAA. TI demonstrated the first solid-state radar called Molecular Electronics for Radar Applications.[[51]](Texas_Instrument

When again the US government forced Raytheon to divest itself of a duplicate capability, the company kept the TI IR systems business and the Hughes detector business. As a result of these acquisitions, these former arch rivals of TI systems and Hughes detectors work together.[[59]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-59)

Immediately after acquisition, DSEG was known as Raytheon TI Systems (RTIS).[[60]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-60) It is now fully integrated into Raytheon and this designation no longer exists.

### Artificial intelligence

TI was active in the area of [artificial intelligence](Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") in the 1980s. In addition to ongoing developments in speech and signal processing and recognition, it developed and sold the [Explorer](TI_Explorer "TI Explorer") computer family of [Lisp machines](Lisp_machine "Lisp machine"). For the Explorer, a special 32-bit Lisp microprocessor was developed, which was used in the Explorer II and the TI MicroExplorer (a Lisp Machine on a <NuBus> board for the Apple <Macintosh>). AI application software developed by TI for the Explorer included the gate assignment system for United Airlines, [described as](http://articles.latimes.com/1989-11-07/business/fi-1112_1_expert-system) "an artificial intelligence program that captures the combined experience and knowledge of a half-dozen United operations experts." In software for the PC, they introduced "Personal Consultant", a rule-based [expert system](Expert_system "Expert system") development tool and runtime engine, followed by "Personal Consultant Plus" written in the Lisp-like language from MIT known as [Scheme](Scheme_(programming_language) "Scheme (programming language)"), and the natural language menu system NLMenu.[[61]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-61)

### Sensors and controls

TI was a major [original-equipment manufacturer](Original_equipment_manufacturer "Original equipment manufacturer") of [sensor](Sensor "Sensor"), control, protection, and <RFID> products for the automotive, appliance, aircraft, and other industries. The Sensors & Controls division was headquartered in [Attleboro, Massachusetts](Attleboro%2C_Massachusetts "Attleboro, Massachusetts").

By the mid-1980s, industrial computers known as PLC's (programmable logic controllers) were separated from Sensors & Controls as the Industrial Systems Division, which was sold in the early 1990s to Siemens.

In 2006, [Bain Capital LLC](Bain_Capital_LLC "Bain Capital LLC"), a private equity firm, purchased the Sensors & Controls division for $3.0 billion in cash.[[62]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-62) The RFID portion of the division remained part of TI, transferring to the Application Specific Products business unit of the Semiconductor division, with the newly formed independent company based in Attleboro taking the name Sensata Technologies.[[63]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-63)

In 1997, TI sold its software division, along with its main products such as the [CA Gen](CA_Gen "CA Gen"), to [Sterling Software](Sterling_Software "Sterling Software"), which is now part of [Computer Associates](Computer_Associates "Computer Associates"). However, TI still owns small pieces of software, such as the software for calculators such as the [TI Interactive!](TI_Interactive! "TI Interactive!").[[64]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-64) TI also creates a significant amount of target software for its digital signal processors, along with host-based tools for creating DSP applications.[[65]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-65)

### TI.com

In 2000, Texas Instruments first implemented an e-commerce platform on TI.com as a way to sell its Code Composer Studio™ software tool directly to customers. With TI.com, purchase managers and design engineers have access to TI products that are immediately available for shipping. The platform has grown to include tens of thousands of TI analog and embedded processing products. In 2020, TI added several features, including full and custom quantity reels, multiple payment options, lines of credit, and flat-rate shipping.

On August 6, 1999, TI announced the restatement of its results for parts of 1998 and the first quarter of 1999 after a review by the [Securities and Exchange Commission](Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "Securities and Exchange Commission") over the timing of charges for a plant closing and writedown.[[66]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-66)

## Divisions

Today, TI is made up of four divisions: [analog products](Analog_electronics "Analog electronics"), [embedded processors](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor"), [digital light processing](Digital_light_processing "Digital light processing"), and [educational technology](Educational_technology "Educational technology").[[69]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ti.com-69)

As of January 2021, the industrial market accounts for 41 percent of the company's annual revenue while the automotive market accounts for 21 percent.[[16]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ED-16)

### Other businesses

TI's remaining businesses consisting of DLP products (primarily used in projectors to create high-definition images), calculators and certain custom semiconductors known as application-specific integrated circuits.

#### DLP Products

DLP is a trademark under which Texas Instruments sells technology regarding TVs, video projectors, and [digital cinema](Digital_cinema "Digital cinema"). On February 2, 2000, Philippe Binant, technical manager of Digital Cinema Project at [Gaumont](Gaumont_Film_Company "Gaumont Film Company") in France, realized the first digital cinema projection in Europe with the DLP CINEMA technology developed by TI DLP technology enables a diverse range of display and advanced light control applications spanning industrial, enterprise, automotive, and consumer market segments.

Custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs)

The ASICs business develops more complex integrated-circuit solutions for clients on a custom basis.

#### Educational technology

TI has produced educational toys for children, including the [Little Professor](Little_Professor "Little Professor") in 1976 and <Dataman> in 1977.[[70]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-70)[[71]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-71)

TI produces a range of calculators, with the <TI-30> being one of the most popular early [calculators](Calculator "Calculator"). TI has also developed a line of [graphing calculators](Graphing_calculator "Graphing calculator"), the first being the <TI-81>, and most popular being the [TI-83 Plus](TI-83_Plus "TI-83 Plus") (with the [TI-84 Plus](TI-84_Plus "TI-84 Plus") being an updated equivalent).

Many TI calculators are still sold without graphing capabilities.[[72]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-72) The TI-30 has been replaced by the [TI-30X IIS](TI-30 "TI-30"). Also, some financial calculators are for sale on the TI website.

In 2007, TI released the <TI-Nspire> family of calculators and computer software that has similar capabilities to the calculators.

Less than 3% of Texas Instruments’ overall revenue comes from calculators, part of the $1.43 billion revenue in the "Other" section in the company's 2018 annual report. Nevertheless, the calculators are a lucrative product. For example, estimates have a $15 to $20 cost to produce TI-84 Plus which likely has a profit margin of at least 50%.

Throughout the 1980s, Texas Instruments worked closely with National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) to develop a calculator to become the educational standard. In 1986, Connecticut School Board became the first to require a graphing calculator on state-mandated exams. Chicago Public Schools gave a free calculator to every student, beginning in the fourth grade, in 1988. New York required the calculator in 1992 for its Regents exams after first allowing it the previous year. The College Board required calculators on the Advanced Placement tests in 1993 and allowed calculators on the SAT a year later. Texas Instruments provides free services to the College Board, which administers AP tests and the SAT, and also has a group called Teachers Teaching for Technology (T3), which educates teachers on how to use its calculators.[[20]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TIcalcsMedium-20)

#### TI calculator community

In the 1990s, with the advent of TI's graphing calculator series, programming became popular among some students. The TI-8x series of calculators (beginning with the TI-81) came with a built-in [BASIC](TI-BASIC "TI-BASIC") interpreter, through which simple programs could be created. The TI-83 was the first in the series to receive native assembly.[[73]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-73) Around the same time that these programs were first being written, programmers began creating websites to host their work, along with tutorials and other calculator-relevant information. This led to the formation of TI calculator [webrings](Webrings "Webrings") and eventually a few large communities, including ticalc.org.[[74]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-74)[[75]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-75)[[76]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-root.cz-76)

The TI community reached the height of its popularity in the early 2000s, with many new websites and programming groups being started. In fact, the aforementioned community sites were exploding with activity, with close to 100 programs being uploaded daily by users of the sites. Also, a competition existed between both sites to be the top site in the community, which helped increase interest and activity in the community.

One of the common unifying forces that has united the community over the years has been the rather contentious relationship with TI regarding control over its graphing calculators. TI graphing calculators generally fall into two distinct groups—the older ones powered by the [Zilog Z80](Zilog_Z80 "Zilog Z80") and the newer ones running on the [Motorola 68000](Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") series.[[76]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-root.cz-76) Both lines of calculators are locked by TI with checks in the hardware and through the signing of software to disable use of custom operating systems. However, users discovered the keys and published them in 2009. TI responded by sending invalid <DMCA> [takedown notices](Takedown_notice "Takedown notice"), causing the [Texas Instruments signing key controversy](Texas_Instruments_signing_key_controversy "Texas Instruments signing key controversy").[[77]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-77)

## History

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Intel](Timeline_of_Intel "Timeline of Intel").

### Origins

Intel was incorporated in [Mountain View, California](Mountain_View%2C_California "Mountain View, California"), on July 18, 1968, by [Gordon E. Moore](Gordon_E._Moore "Gordon E. Moore") (known for "[Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law")"), a [chemist](Chemist "Chemist"), [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce"), a physicist and co-inventor of the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") and [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock"), an investor and [venture capitalist](Venture_capital "Venture capital")[[35]](Intel#cite_note-35)[[36]](Intel#cite_note-36)[[37]](Intel#cite_note-37) Moore and Noyce had left [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") and were part of the "[traitorous eight](Traitorous_eight "Traitorous eight")". There were originally 500,000 shares outstanding of which Dr. Noyce bought 245,000 shares, Dr. Moore 245,000 shares, and Mr. Rock 10,000 shares; all at $1 per share. Rock offered $2,500,000 of convertible debentures to a limited group of private investors (equivalent to $21 million in 2022), convertible at $5 per share.[[38]](Intel#cite_note-38)[[39]](Intel#cite_note-39) Just 2 years later, Intel became a [public company](Public_company "Public company") via an [initial public offering](Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO), raising $6.8 million ($23.50 per share).[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) Intel's third employee was [Andy Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove"),[[note 1]](Intel#cite_note-41) a [chemical engineer](Chemical_engineer "Chemical engineer"), who later ran the company through much of the 1980s and the high-growth 1990s.

In deciding on a name, Moore and Noyce quickly rejected "Moore Noyce",[[41]](Intel#cite_note-42) near [homophone](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/homophone "wikt:homophone") for "more noise" – an ill-suited name for an [electronics](Electronics "Electronics") company, since [noise in electronics](Electronic_noise "Electronic noise") is usually undesirable and typically associated with bad [interference](Electromagnetic_interference "Electromagnetic interference"). Instead, they founded the company as **NM Electronics** (or **MN Electronics**) on July 18, 1968, but by the end of the month had changed the name to **Intel** which stood for **Int**egrated **El**ectronics.[[note 2]](Intel#cite_note-48) Since "Intel" was already trademarked by the hotel chain Intelco, they had to buy the rights for the name.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[47]](Intel#cite_note-49)

### Early history

At its founding, Intel was distinguished by its ability to make [logic circuits](Logic_circuit "Logic circuit") using [semiconductor devices](Semiconductor_device "Semiconductor device"). The founders' goal was the [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") market, widely predicted to replace [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory"). Its first product, a quick entry into the small, high-speed memory market in 1969, was the 3101 [Schottky TTL](Schottky_transistor "Schottky transistor") [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") 64-bit [static random-access memory](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") (SRAM), which was nearly twice as fast as earlier Schottky diode implementations by Fairchild and the Electrotechnical Laboratory in [Tsukuba, Japan](Tsukuba%2C_Ibaraki "Tsukuba, Ibaraki").[[48]](Intel#cite_note-50)[[49]](Intel#cite_note-51) In the same year, Intel also produced the 3301 Schottky bipolar 1024-bit [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM)[[50]](Intel#cite_note-52) and the first commercial [metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor](MOSFET "MOSFET") (MOSFET) [silicon gate](Silicon_gate "Silicon gate") SRAM chip, the 256-bit 1101.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[52]](Intel#cite_note-54)

While the 1101 was a significant advance, its complex static [cell structure](Memory_cell_(computing) "Memory cell (computing)") made it too slow and costly for [mainframe](Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") memories. The three-[transistor](Transistor "Transistor") cell implemented in the first commercially available [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM), the [1103](Intel_1103 "Intel 1103") released in 1970, solved these issues. The 1103 was the bestselling semiconductor memory chip in the world by 1972, as it replaced core memory in many applications.[[53]](Intel#cite_note-55)[[54]](Intel#cite_note-Bellis-56) Intel's business grew during the 1970s as it expanded and improved its manufacturing processes and produced a wider range of [products](Product_(business) "Product (business)"), still dominated by various memory devices.

Intel created the [first commercially available microprocessor (Intel 4004)](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") in 1971.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) The microprocessor represented a notable advance in the technology of integrated circuitry, as it miniaturized the central processing unit of a computer, which then made it possible for small machines to perform calculations that in the past only very large machines could do. Considerable technological innovation was needed before the microprocessor could actually become the basis of what was first known as a "mini computer" and then known as a "personal computer".[[55]](Intel#cite_note-57) Intel also created one of the first [microcomputers](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1973.[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[56]](Intel#cite_note-Intellec-1973-58)

72, in <Malaysia>, which would host multiple Intel operations, before opening assembly facilities and semiconductor plants in <Singapore> and <Jerusalem> in the early 1980s, and manufacturing and development centers in China, India, and Costa Rica in the 1990s.[[57]](Intel#cite_note-59) By the early 1980s, its business was dominated by [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM) chips. However, increased competition from Japanese semiconductor manufacturers had, by 1983, dramatically reduced the profitability of this market. The growing success of the <IBM> personal computer, based on an Intel microprocessor, was among factors that convinced Gordon Moore (CEO since 1975) to shift the company's focus to microprocessors and to change fundamental aspects of that business model. Moore's decision to sole-source Intel's 386 chip played into the company's continuing success.

By the end of the 1980s, buoyed by its fortuitous position as microprocessor supplier to IBM and IBM's competitors within the rapidly growing [personal computer market](IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible"), Intel embarked on a 10-year period of unprecedented growth as the primary (and most profitable) hardware supplier to the PC industry, part of the winning 'Wintel' combination. Moore handed over his position as CEO to Andy Grove in 1987. By launching its Intel Inside [marketing campaign](Marketing_campaign "Marketing campaign") in 1991, Intel was able to associate [brand loyalty](Brand_loyalty "Brand loyalty") with consumer selection, so that by the end of the 1990s, its line of <Pentium> processors had become a household name.

### Challenges to dominance (2000s)

After 2000, growth in demand for high-end microprocessors slowed. Competitors, most notably <AMD> (Intel's largest competitor in its primary [x86](X86 "X86") architecture market), garnered significant market share, initially in low-end and mid-range processors but ultimately across the product range, and Intel's dominant position in its core market was greatly reduced,[[58]](Intel#cite_note-Wong-60) mostly due to controversial <NetBurst> microarchitecture. In the early 2000s then-CEO, [Craig Barrett](Craig_Barrett_(businessman) "Craig Barrett (businessman)") attempted to diversify the company's business beyond semiconductors, but few of these activities were ultimately successful.

#### Litigation

Intel had also for a number of years been embroiled in litigation. US law did not initially recognize [intellectual property rights](Intellectual_property_rights "Intellectual property rights") related to microprocessor [topology](Topology_(electrical_circuits) "Topology (electrical circuits)") (circuit layouts), until the [Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984](Semiconductor_Chip_Protection_Act_of_1984 "Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984"), a law sought by Intel and the [Semiconductor Industry Association](Semiconductor_Industry_Association "Semiconductor Industry Association") (SIA).[[59]](Intel#cite_note-61) During the late 1980s and 1990s (after this law was passed), Intel also sued companies that tried to develop competitor chips to the [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386") <CPU>.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) The lawsuits were noted to significantly burden the competition with legal bills, even if Intel lost the suits.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) <Antitrust> allegations had been simmering since the early 1990s and had been the cause of one [lawsuit](Lawsuit "Lawsuit") against Intel in 1991. In 2004 and 2005, AMD brought [further claims](Intel_Corp._v._Advanced_Micro_Devices%2C_Inc. "Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.") against Intel related to [unfair competition](Unfair_competition "Unfair competition").

### Reorganization and success with Intel Core (2005–2015)

In 2005, CEO [Paul Otellini](Paul_Otellini "Paul Otellini") reorganized the company to refocus its core processor and chipset business on platforms (enterprise, digital home, digital health, and mobility).

On June 6, 2005, [Steve Jobs](Steve_Jobs "Steve Jobs"), then CEO of [Apple](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), announced that Apple would be using Intel's x86 processors for its <Macintosh> computers, switching from the <PowerPC> architecture developed by the [AIM alliance](AIM_alliance "AIM alliance").[[61]](Intel#cite_note-auto2-63) This was seen as win for Intel;[[62]](Intel#cite_note-auto1-64) An analyst called the move "risky" and "foolish", as Intel's current offerings at the time were considered to be behind those of AMD and IBM.[[63]](Intel#cite_note-Computerworld1-65)

In 2006, Intel unveiled its [Core microarchitecture](Core_(microarchitecture) "Core (microarchitecture)") to widespread critical acclaim; the product range was perceived as an exceptional leap in processor performance that at a stroke regained much of its leadership of the field.[[64]](Intel#cite_note-66)[[65]](Intel#cite_note-67) In 2008, Intel had another "tick" when it introduced the Penryn microarchitecture, fabricated using the 45 nm process node. Later that year, Intel released a processor with the [Nehalem](Nehalem_(microarchitecture) "Nehalem (microarchitecture)") architecture to positive reception.[[66]](Intel#cite_note-68)

On June 27, 2006, the sale of Intel's <XScale> assets was announced. Intel agreed to sell the XScale processor business to [Marvell Technology Group](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group") for an estimated $600 million and the assumption of unspecified liabilities. The move was intended to permit Intel to focus its resources on its core x86 and server businesses, and the [acquisition](Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions") completed on November 9, 2006.[[67]](Intel#cite_note-XScale-69)

In 2008, Intel spun off key assets of a solar startup business effort to form an independent company, SpectraWatt Inc. In 2011, SpectraWatt filed for bankruptcy.[[68]](Intel#cite_note-eetimes1-70)

In February 2011, Intel began to build a new microprocessor manufacturing facility in [Chandler, Arizona](Chandler%2C_Arizona "Chandler, Arizona"), completed in 2013 at a cost of $5 billion.[[69]](Intel#cite_note-71) The building is now the 10 nm-certified Fab 42 and is connected to the other Fabs (12, 22, 32) on Ocotillo Campus via an enclosed bridge known as the Link.[[70]](Intel#cite_note-72)[[71]](Intel#cite_note-73)[[72]](Intel#cite_note-74)[[73]](Intel#cite_note-75) The company produces three-quarters of its products in the United States, although three-quarters of its revenue come from overseas.[[74]](Intel#cite_note-76)

The [Alliance for Affordable Internet](Alliance_for_Affordable_Internet "Alliance for Affordable Internet") (A4AI) was launched in October 2013 and Intel is part of the coalition of public and private organizations that also includes <Facebook>, <Google>, and <Microsoft>. Led by [Sir Tim Berners-Lee](Tim_Berners-Lee "Tim Berners-Lee"), the A4AI seeks to make Internet access more affordable so that access is broadened in the developing world, where only 31% of people are online. Google will help to decrease Internet access prices so that they fall below the UN Broadband Commission's worldwide target of 5% of monthly income.[[75]](Intel#cite_note-77)

#### Attempts at entering the smartphone market

In April 2011, Intel began a pilot project with [ZTE Corporation](ZTE_Corporation "ZTE Corporation") to produce smartphones using the [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processor for China's domestic market. In December 2011, Intel announced that it reorganized several of its business units into a new mobile and communications group[[76]](Intel#cite_note-78) that would be responsible for the company's smartphone, tablet, and wireless efforts. Intel planned to introduce Medfield – a processor for tablets and smartphones – to the market in 2012, as an effort to compete with Arm.[[77]](Intel#cite_note-79) As a 32-nanometer processor, Medfield is designed to be energy-efficient, which is one of the core features in Arm's chips.[[78]](Intel#cite_note-autogenerated12-80)

At the Intel Developers Forum (IDF) 2011 in San Francisco, Intel's partnership with Google was announced. In January 2012, Google announced Android 2.3, supporting Intel's Atom microprocessor.[[79]](Intel#cite_note-81)[[80]](Intel#cite_note-82)[[81]](Intel#cite_note-83) In 2013, Intel's Kirk Skaugen said that Intel's exclusive focus on Microsoft platforms was a thing of the past and that they would now support all "tier-one operating systems" such as Linux, Android, iOS, and Chrome.[[82]](Intel#cite_note-84)

In 2014, Intel cut thousands of employees in response to "evolving market trends",[[83]](Intel#cite_note-85) and offered to subsidize manufacturers for the extra costs involved in using Intel chips in their tablets. In April 2016, Intel cancelled the <SoFIA> platform and the Broxton Atom SoC for smartphones,[[84]](Intel#cite_note-86)[[85]](Intel#cite_note-87)[[86]](Intel#cite_note-88)[[87]](Intel#cite_note-89) effectively leaving the smartphone market.[[88]](Intel#cite_note-MyUser_Theverge.com_June_1_2016c-90)[[89]](Intel#cite_note-verge2-91)

#### Intel custom foundry

Finding itself with excess fab capacity after the failure of the <Ultrabook> to gain market traction and with PC sales declining, in 2013 Intel reached a [foundry](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") agreement to produce chips for <Altera> using a 14nm process. General Manager of Intel's custom foundry division Sunit Rikhi indicated that Intel would pursue further such deals in the future.[[90]](Intel#cite_note-92) This was after poor sales of [Windows 8](Windows_8 "Windows 8") hardware caused a major retrenchment for most of the major semiconductor manufacturers, except for Qualcomm, which continued to see healthy purchases from its largest customer, Apple.[[91]](Intel#cite_note-93)

#### 10 nm process node issues

While Intel originally planned to introduce 10 nm products in 2016, it later became apparent that there were manufacturing issues with the node.[[97]](Intel#cite_note-99) The first microprocessor under that node, [Cannon Lake](Cannon_Lake_(microarchitecture) "Cannon Lake (microarchitecture)") (marketed as 8th generation Core), was released in small quantities in 2018.[[98]](Intel#cite_note-Cutress-100)[[99]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_discontinues_Cannon_Lake_NUC-101) The company first delayed the mass production of their 10 nm products to 2017.[[100]](Intel#cite_note-102)[[101]](Intel#cite_note-103) They later delayed mass production to 2018,[[102]](Intel#cite_note-104) and then to 2019. Despite rumors of the process being cancelled,[[103]](Intel#cite_note-105) Intel finally introduced mass-produced 10 nm 10th generation Intel Core mobile processors (codenamed "[Ice Lake](Ice_Lake_(microprocessor) "Ice Lake (microprocessor)")") in September 2019.[[104]](Intel#cite_note-106)

Intel later acknowledged that their strategy to shrink to 10 nm was too aggressive.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)[[105]](Intel#cite_note-107) While other foundries used up to four steps in 10 nm or 7 nm processes, the company's 10 nm process required up to five or six multi-pattern steps.[[106]](Intel#cite_note-108) In addition, Intel's 10 nm process is denser than its counterpart processes from other foundries.[[107]](Intel#cite_note-109)[[108]](Intel#cite_note-110) Since Intel's microarchitecture and process node development were coupled, processor development stagnated.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)

In early January 2018, it was reported that all [Intel processors](Intel_CPUs "Intel CPUs") made since 1995,[[109]](Intel#cite_note-111) excluding [Intel Itanium](Intel_Itanium "Intel Itanium") and pre-2013 [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processors, have been subject to two security flaws dubbed [Meltdown](Meltdown_(security_vulnerability) "Meltdown (security vulnerability)") and [Spectre](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)").[[110]](Intel#cite_note-112)[[111]](Intel#cite_note-wiredflaw-113) It is believed that "hundreds of millions" of systems could be affected by these flaws.[[112]](Intel#cite_note-telegraph2018flaw-114)[[113]](Intel#cite_note-115) More security flaws were disclosed on May 3, 2018,[[114]](Intel#cite_note-116) on August 14, 2018, on January 18, 2019, and on March 5, 2020.[[115]](Intel#cite_note-ZDNET-20200305-117)[[116]](Intel#cite_note-AT-20200305-118)[[117]](Intel#cite_note-EG-20200306-119)[[118]](Intel#cite_note-INTEL-20200211-120)

## Product and market history

In 1983, at the dawn of the personal computer era, Intel's profits came under increased pressure from Japanese memory-chip manufacturers, and then-president Andy Grove focused the company on microprocessors. Grove described this transition in the book *[Only the Paranoid Survive](Only_the_Paranoid_Survive "Only the Paranoid Survive")*. A key element of his plan was the notion, then considered radical, of becoming the single source for successors to the popular [8086](Intel_8086 "Intel 8086") microprocessor.

Until then, the manufacture of complex integrated circuits was not reliable enough for customers to depend on a single supplier, but Grove began producing processors in three geographically distinct factories, and ceased licensing the chip designs to competitors such as [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices").[[140]](Intel#cite_note-142) When the PC industry boomed in the late 1980s and 1990s, Intel was one of the primary beneficiaries.

### Early x86 processors and the IBM PC

Despite the ultimate importance of the microprocessor, the [4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") and its successors the [8008](Intel_8008 "Intel 8008") and the [8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") were never major revenue contributors at Intel. As the next processor, the [8086](Intel_8086 "Intel 8086") (and its variant the 8088) was completed in 1978, Intel embarked on a major marketing and sales campaign for that chip nicknamed "Operation Crush", and intended to win as many customers for the processor as possible. One design win was the newly created [IBM PC](IBM_PC "IBM PC") division, though the importance of this was not fully realized at the time.

<IBM> introduced its personal computer in 1981, and it was rapidly successful. In 1982, Intel created the [80286](Intel_80286 "Intel 80286") microprocessor, which, two years later, was used in the [IBM PC/AT](IBM_Personal_Computer/AT "IBM Personal Computer/AT"). <Compaq>, the first IBM PC "clone" manufacturer, produced a desktop system based on the faster 80286 processor in 1985 and in 1986 quickly followed with the first [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386")-based system, beating IBM and establishing a competitive market for PC-compatible systems and setting up Intel as a key component supplier.

In 1975, the company had started a project to develop a highly advanced 32-bit microprocessor, finally released in 1981 as the [Intel iAPX 432](Intel_iAPX_432 "Intel iAPX 432"). The project was too ambitious and the processor was never able to meet its performance objectives, and it failed in the marketplace. Intel extended the [x86 architecture](X86 "X86") to 32 bits instead.[[141]](Intel#cite_note-143)[[142]](Intel#cite_note-144)

#### 386 microprocessor

During this period [Andrew Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove") dramatically redirected the company, closing much of its <DRAM> business and directing resources to the [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") business. Of perhaps greater importance was his decision to "single-source" the 386 microprocessor. Prior to this, microprocessor manufacturing was in its infancy, and manufacturing problems frequently reduced or stopped production, interrupting supplies to customers. To mitigate this risk, these customers typically insisted that multiple manufacturers produce chips they could use to ensure a consistent supply. The 8080 and 8086-series microprocessors were produced by several companies, notably AMD, with which Intel had a technology-sharing contract.

Grove made the decision not to license the 386 design to other manufacturers, instead, producing it in three geographically distinct factories: [Santa Clara](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California"), California; [Hillsboro](Hillsboro%2C_Oregon "Hillsboro, Oregon"), Oregon; and [Chandler](Chandler%2C_Arizona "Chandler, Arizona"), a suburb of [Phoenix](Phoenix%2C_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"), Arizona. He convinced customers that this would ensure consistent delivery. In doing this, Intel breached its contract with AMD, which sued and was paid millions of dollars in damages but could not manufacture new Intel CPU designs any longer. (Instead, AMD started to develop and manufacture its own competing x86 designs.)

As the success of <Compaq>'s [Deskpro 386](Compaq_Deskpro_386 "Compaq Deskpro 386") established the 386 as the dominant CPU choice, Intel achieved a position of near-exclusive dominance as its supplier. Profits from this funded rapid development of both higher-performance chip designs and higher-performance manufacturing capabilities, propelling Intel to a position of unquestioned leadership by the early 1990s.

#### 486, Pentium, and Itanium

Intel introduced the [486](Intel_80486 "Intel 80486") microprocessor in 1989, and in 1990 established a second design team, designing the processors code-named "[P5](P5_(microarchitecture) "P5 (microarchitecture)")" and "[P6](P6_(microarchitecture) "P6 (microarchitecture)")" in parallel and committing to a major new processor every two years, versus the four or more years such designs had previously taken. Engineers [Vinod Dham](Vinod_Dham "Vinod Dham") and [Rajeev Chandrasekhar](Rajeev_Chandrasekhar "Rajeev Chandrasekhar") (Member of Parliament, India) were key figures on the core team that invented the 486 chip and later, Intel's signature Pentium chip. The P5 project was earlier known as "Operation Bicycle", referring to the cycles of the processor through two parallel execution pipelines. The P5 was introduced in 1993 as the Intel <Pentium>, substituting a registered trademark name for the former part number (numbers, such as 486, cannot be legally registered as trademarks in the United States). The P6 followed in 1995 as the [Pentium Pro](Pentium_Pro "Pentium Pro") and improved into the [Pentium II](Pentium_II "Pentium II") in 1997. New architectures were developed alternately in [Santa Clara, California](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California") and [Hillsboro, Oregon](Hillsboro%2C_Oregon "Hillsboro, Oregon").

The Santa Clara design team embarked in 1993 on a successor to the [x86 architecture](X86 "X86"), codenamed "P7". The first attempt was dropped a year later but quickly revived in a cooperative program with <Hewlett-Packard> engineers, though Intel soon took over primary design responsibility. The resulting implementation of the [IA-64](Itanium "Itanium") 64-bit architecture was the <Itanium>, finally introduced in June 2001. The Itanium's performance running legacy x86 code did not meet expectations, and it failed to compete effectively with [x86-64](X86-64 "X86-64"), which was AMD's 64-bit extension of the 32-bit x86 architecture (Intel uses the name **Intel 64**, previously **EM64T**). In 2017, Intel announced that the [Itanium 9700 series (Kittson)](Kittson_(processor) "Kittson (processor)") would be the last Itanium chips produced.[[143]](Intel#cite_note-Davis_2017-145)[[144]](Intel#cite_note-IA-PCWorld-146)

The Hillsboro team designed the [Willamette](Pentium_4#Willamette "Pentium 4") processors (initially code-named P68), which were marketed as the Pentium 4.

During this period, Intel undertook two major supporting advertising campaigns. The first campaign, the 1991 "Intel Inside" marketing and branding campaign, is widely known and has become synonymous with Intel itself. The idea of "[ingredient branding](Ingredient_branding "Ingredient branding")" was new at the time, with only <NutraSweet> and a few others making attempts to do so.[[145]](Intel#cite_note-147) One of the key architects of the marketing team was the head of the microprocessor division, [David House](David_House_(computer_designer) "David House (computer designer)").[[146]](Intel#cite_note-148) He coined the slogan "Intel Inside".[[147]](Intel#cite_note-149) This campaign established Intel, which had been a component supplier little-known outside the PC industry, as a household name.

The second campaign, Intel's Systems Group, which began in the early 1990s, showcased manufacturing of PC [motherboards](Motherboard "Motherboard"), the main board component of a personal computer, and the one into which the processor (CPU) and memory (RAM) chips are plugged.[[148]](Intel#cite_note-150) The Systems Group campaign was lesser known than the Intel Inside campaign.

Shortly after, Intel began manufacturing fully configured "[white box](White_box_(computer_hardware) "White box (computer hardware)")" systems for the dozens of PC clone companies that rapidly sprang up. At its peak in the mid-1990s, Intel manufactured over 15% of all PCs, making it the third-largest supplier at the time.

During the 1990s, [Intel Architecture Labs](Intel_Architecture_Labs "Intel Architecture Labs") (IAL) was responsible for many of the hardware innovations for the PC, including the [PCI](Conventional_PCI "Conventional PCI") Bus, the [PCI Express](PCI_Express "PCI Express") (PCIe) bus, and [Universal Serial Bus](Universal_Serial_Bus "Universal Serial Bus") (USB). IAL's software efforts met with a more mixed fate; its video and graphics software was important in the development of software digital video, but later its efforts were largely overshadowed by competition from <Microsoft>. The competition between Intel and Microsoft was revealed in testimony by then IAL Vice-president [Steven McGeady](Steven_McGeady "Steven McGeady") at the [Microsoft antitrust trial](United_States_v._Microsoft_Corp._(2001) "United States v. Microsoft Corp. (2001)") (*United States v. Microsoft Corp.*).
