Intel changed its position and offered to replace every chip, quickly putting in place a large end-user [support](Technical_support "Technical support") organization. This resulted in a $475 million charge against Intel's 1994 [revenue](Revenue "Revenue").[[151]](Intel#cite_note-153) Dr. Nicely later learned that Intel had discovered the FDIV bug in its own testing a few months before him (but had decided not to inform customers).[[152]](Intel#cite_note-154)

The "Pentium flaw" incident, Intel's response to it, and the surrounding media coverage propelled Intel from being a technology supplier generally unknown to most computer users to a household name. Dovetailing with an uptick in the "Intel Inside" campaign, the episode is considered to have been a positive event for Intel, changing some of its business practices to be more end-user focused and generating substantial public awareness, while avoiding a lasting negative impression.[[153]](Intel#cite_note-155)

### Intel Core

Main article: [Intel Core](Intel_Core "Intel Core")

The Intel Core line originated from the original Core brand, with the release of the [32-bit](32-bit_computing "32-bit computing") *[Yonah](Yonah_(microprocessor) "Yonah (microprocessor)")* <CPU>, Intel's first [dual-core](Dual-core "Dual-core") mobile (low-power) processor. Derived from the [Pentium M](Pentium_M "Pentium M"), the processor family used an enhanced version of the P6 microarchitecture. Its successor, the [Core 2](Intel_Core_2 "Intel Core 2") family, was released on July 27, 2006. This was based on the Intel [Core microarchitecture](Intel_Core_(microarchitecture) "Intel Core (microarchitecture)"), and was a 64-bit design.[[154]](Intel#cite_note-156) Instead of focusing on higher clock rates, the Core microarchitecture emphasized power efficiency and a return to lower clock speeds.[[155]](Intel#cite_note-157) It also provided more efficient decoding stages, execution units, [caches](CPU_cache "CPU cache"), and [buses](Bus_(computing) "Bus (computing)"), reducing the [power consumption](Electric_energy_consumption "Electric energy consumption") of Core 2-branded CPUs while increasing their processing capacity.

In November 2008, Intel released the first generation Core processors based on the [Nehalem microarchitecture](Nehalem_(microarchitecture) "Nehalem (microarchitecture)"). Intel also introduced a new naming scheme, with the three variants now named Core i3, i5, and i7 (as well as i9 from 7th generation onwards). Unlike the previous naming scheme, these names no longer correspond to specific technical features. It was succeeded by the [Westmere microarchitecture](Westmere_(microarchitecture) "Westmere (microarchitecture)") in 2010, with a die shrink to 32 nm and included Intel HD Graphics.

In 2011, Intel released the [Sandy Bridge](Sandy_Bridge "Sandy Bridge")-based 2nd generation Core processor family. This generation featured an 11% performance increase over Nehalem.[[156]](Intel#cite_note-158) It was succeeded by [Ivy Bridge](Ivy_Bridge_(microarchitecture) "Ivy Bridge (microarchitecture)")-based 3rd generation Core, introduced at the 2012 Intel Developer Forum.[[157]](Intel#cite_note-159) Ivy Bridge featured a die shrink to [22 nm](22_nm_process "22 nm process"), and supported both DDR3 memory and DDR3L chips.

Intel continued its [tick-tock](Tick%E2%80%93tock_model "Tick–tock model") model of a microarchitecture change followed by a die shrink until the 6th generation Core family based on the [Skylake](Skylake_(microarchitecture) "Skylake (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture. This model was deprecated in 2016, with the release of the seventh generation Core family based on [Kaby Lake](Kaby_Lake "Kaby Lake"), ushering in the [process–architecture–optimization model](Process%E2%80%93architecture%E2%80%93optimization_model "Process–architecture–optimization model").[[158]](Intel#cite_note-anandtech-pao-160) From 2016 until 2021, Intel later released more optimizations on the Skylake microarchitecture with [Kaby Lake R](Kaby_Lake "Kaby Lake"), [Amber Lake](Amber_Lake_(microarchitecture) "Amber Lake (microarchitecture)"), [Whiskey Lake](Whiskey_Lake_(microprocessor) "Whiskey Lake (microprocessor)"), [Coffee Lake](Coffee_Lake "Coffee Lake"), [Coffee Lake R](Coffee_Lake_Refresh "Coffee Lake Refresh"), and [Comet Lake](Comet_Lake_(microprocessor) "Comet Lake (microprocessor)").[[159]](Intel#cite_note-161)[[160]](Intel#cite_note-162)[[161]](Intel#cite_note-163)[[162]](Intel#cite_note-164) Intel struggled to shrink their process node from [14 nm](14_nm_process "14 nm process") to [10 nm](10_nm_process "10 nm process"), with the first microarchitecture under that node, [Cannon Lake](Cannon_Lake_(microarchitecture) "Cannon Lake (microarchitecture)") (marketed as 8th generation Core), only being released in small quantities in 2018.[[98]](Intel#cite_note-Cutress-100)[[99]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_discontinues_Cannon_Lake_NUC-101)

In 2019, Intel released the 10th generation of Core processors, codenamed "Amber Lake", "Comet Lake", and "[Ice Lake](Ice_Lake_(microprocessor) "Ice Lake (microprocessor)")". Ice Lake, based on the [Sunny Cove](Sunny_Cove "Sunny Cove") microarchitecture, was produced on the 10 nm process and was limited to low-power mobile processors. Both Amber Lake and Comet Lake were based on a refined 14 nm node, with the latter being used for desktop and high performance mobile products and the former used for low-power mobile products.

In September 2020, 11th generation Core mobile processors, codenamed [Tiger Lake](Tiger_Lake_(microprocessor) "Tiger Lake (microprocessor)"), were launched.[[163]](Intel#cite_note-:13-165) Tiger Lake is based on the Willow Cove microarchitecture and a refined 10 nm node.[[164]](Intel#cite_note-166) Intel later released 11th generation Core desktop processors (codenamed "[Rocket Lake](Rocket_Lake "Rocket Lake")"), fabricated using Intel's 14 nm process and based on the [Cypress Cove](Cypress_Cove_(microarchitecture) "Cypress Cove (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture,[[165]](Intel#cite_note-anandtech-167) on March 30, 2021.[[166]](Intel#cite_note-168) It replaced Comet Lake desktop processors. All 11th generation Core processors feature new integrated graphics based on the [Intel Xe](Intel_Xe "Intel Xe") microarchitecture.[[167]](Intel#cite_note-169)

Both desktop and mobile products were unified under a single process node with the release of 12th generation Intel Core processors (codenamed "[Alder Lake](Alder_Lake_(microprocessor) "Alder Lake (microprocessor)")") in late 2021.[[168]](Intel#cite_note-:02-170)[[169]](Intel#cite_note-171) This generation will be fabricated using Intel's 7 nm process, called Intel 7, for both desktop and mobile processors, and is based on a [hybrid architecture](Heterogeneous_computing "Heterogeneous computing") utilizing high-performance [Golden Cove](Golden_Cove_(microarchitecture) "Golden Cove (microarchitecture)") cores and high-efficiency [Gracemont](Gracemont_(microarchitecture) "Gracemont (microarchitecture)") (Atom) cores.[[168]](Intel#cite_note-:02-170)

#### Meltdown, Spectre, and other security vulnerabilities

Main article: [Transient execution CPU vulnerability](Transient_execution_CPU_vulnerability "Transient execution CPU vulnerability")

In early January 2018, it was reported that all [Intel processors](Intel_CPUs "Intel CPUs") made since 1995[[170]](Intel#cite_note-172)[[112]](Intel#cite_note-telegraph2018flaw-114) (besides [Intel Itanium](Intel_Itanium "Intel Itanium") and pre-2013 [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom")) have been subject to two security flaws dubbed [Meltdown](Meltdown_(security_vulnerability) "Meltdown (security vulnerability)") and [Spectre](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)").[[171]](Intel#cite_note-173)[[111]](Intel#cite_note-wiredflaw-113)

The impact on performance resulting from software patches is "workload-dependent". Several procedures to help protect home computers and related devices from the Spectre and Meltdown security vulnerabilities have been published.[[172]](Intel#cite_note-NYT-20180104-174)[[173]](Intel#cite_note-FM-20180105-175)[[174]](Intel#cite_note-PCW-20180104-176)[[175]](Intel#cite_note-CNET-20180104-177) Spectre patches have been reported to significantly slow down performance, especially on older computers; on the newer 8th generation Core platforms, benchmark performance drops of 2–14 percent have been measured.[[121]](Intel#cite_note-PCW-20180109-123) Meltdown patches may also produce performance loss.[[122]](Intel#cite_note-NYT-20180103-124)[[123]](Intel#cite_note-bbcflaw-125)[[124]](Intel#cite_note-TV-20180104-126) It is believed that "hundreds of millions" of systems could be affected by these flaws.[[112]](Intel#cite_n

") microprocessor family.[[29]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen50-29) When Intel began installing [microcode](Microcode "Microcode") in its microprocessors in 1976, it entered into a [cross-licensing](Cross-licensing "Cross-licensing") agreement with AMD, which was granted a copyright license to the microcode in its microprocessors and peripherals, effective October 1976.[[25]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen55-25)[[31]](AMD#cite_note-31)[[32]](AMD#cite_note-32)[[33]](AMD#cite_note-justia1994-33)[[34]](AMD#cite_note-sec1996-34)

In 1977, AMD entered into a joint venture with <Siemens>, a German engineering conglomerate wishing to enhance its technology expertise and enter the American market.[[35]](AMD#cite_note-malerba-35) Siemens purchased 20% of AMD's stock, giving the company an infusion of cash to increase its product lines.[[35]](AMD#cite_note-malerba-35)[[36]](AMD#cite_note-36)[[37]](AMD#cite_note-37) The two companies also jointly established Advanced Micro Computers (AMC), located in Silicon Valley and in Germany, allowing AMD to enter the [microcomputer](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") development and manufacturing field,[[35]](AMD#cite_note-malerba-35)[[38]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen60-38)[[39]](AMD#cite_note-39)[[40]](AMD#cite_note-40) in particular based on AMD's second-source <Zilog> <Z8000> microprocessors.[[41]](AMD#cite_note-freiberger-41)[[42]](AMD#cite_note-42) When the two companies' vision for Advanced Micro Computers diverged, AMD bought out Siemens' stake in the American division in 1979.[[43]](AMD#cite_note-43)[[44]](AMD#cite_note-44) AMD closed Advanced Micro Computers in late 1981 after switching focus to manufacturing second-source Intel x86 microprocessors.[[41]](AMD#cite_note-freiberger-41)[[45]](AMD#cite_note-swaine-45)[[46]](AMD#cite_note-46)

Total sales in [fiscal year](Fiscal_year "Fiscal year") 1978 topped $100 million,[[38]](AMD#cite_note-rodengen60-38) and in 1979, AMD debuted on the [New York Stock Exchange](New_York_Stock_Exchange "New York Stock Exchange").[[16]](AMD#cite_note-history-16) In 1979, production also began on AMD's new [semiconductor fabrication plant](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") in [Austin, Texas](Austin%2C_Texas "Austin, Texas");[[16]](AMD#cite_note-history-16) the company already had overseas assembly facilities in <Penang> and <Manila>,[[47]](AMD#cite_note-47) and began construction on a fabrication plant in [San Antonio](San_Antonio "San Antonio") in 1981.[[48]](AMD#cite_note-HittC26-48) In 1980, AMD began supplying semiconductor products for telecommunications, an industry undergoing rapid expansion and innovation.[[49]](AMD#cite_note-49)

### Technology exchange agreement with Intel

<Intel> had introduced the first [x86](X86 "X86") microprocessors in 1978.[[50]](AMD#cite_note-50) In 1981, <IBM> created its [PC](IBM_Personal_Computer "IBM Personal Computer"), and wanted Intel's x86 processors, but only under the condition that Intel also provide a [second-source](Second-source "Second-source") manufacturer for its patented x86 microprocessors.[[11]](AMD#cite_note-singer-11) Intel and AMD entered into a 10-year technology exchange agreement, first signed in October 1981[[45]](AMD#cite_note-swaine-45)[[51]](AMD#cite_note-51) and formally executed in February 1982.[[34]](AMD#cite_note-sec1996-34) The terms of the agreement were that each company could acquire the right to become a second-source manufacturer of semiconductor products developed by the other; that is, each party could "earn" the right to manufacture and sell a product developed by the other, if agreed to, by exchanging the manufacturing rights to a product of equivalent technical complexity. The technical information and licenses needed to make and sell a part would be exchanged for a royalty to the developing company.[[33]](AMD#cite_note-justia1994-33) The 1982 agreement also extended the 1976 AMD–Intel cross-licensing agreement through 1995.[[33]](AMD#cite_note-justia1994-33)[[34]](AMD#cite_note-sec1996-34) The agreement included the right to invoke arbitration of disagreements, and after five years the right of either party to end the agreement with one year's notice.[[33]](AMD#cite_note-justia1994-33) The main result of the 1982 agreement was that AMD became a second-source manufacturer of Intel's x86 microprocessors and related chips, and Intel provided AMD with database tapes for its <8086>, <80186>, and <80286> chips.[[34]](AMD#cite_note-sec1996-34) However, in the event of a bankruptcy or takeover of AMD, the cross-licensing agreement would be effectively canceled.[[52]](AMD#cite_note-52)

Beginning in 1982, AMD began volume-producing second-source Intel-licensed 8086, 8088, 80186, and 80188 processors, and by 1984, its own <Am286> clone of Intel's 80286 processor, for the rapidly growing market of IBM PCs and [IBM clones](IBM_clone "IBM clone").[[11]](AMD#cite_note-singer-11)[[53]](AMD#cite_note-53) It also continued its successful concentration on proprietary [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") chips.[[54]](AMD#cite_note-54)

The company continued to spend greatly on research and development,[[55]](AMD#cite_note-55) and created the world's first 512K <EPROM> in 1984.[[56]](AMD#cite_note-56) That year, AMD was listed in the book *The 100 Best Companies to Work for in America*,[[48]](AMD#cite_note-HittC26-48)[[57]](AMD#cite_note-57) and later made the [*Fortune* 500](Fortune_500 "Fortune 500") list for the first time in 1985.[[58]](AMD#cite_note-58)[[59]](AMD#cite_note-59)

By mid-1985, the microchip market experienced a severe downturn, mainly due to long-term aggressive trade practices ([dumping](Dumping_(pricing_policy) "Dumping (pricing policy)")) from Japan, but also due to a crowded and non-innovative chip market in the United States.[[60]](AMD#cite_note-60) AMD rode out the mid-1980s crisis by aggressively innovating and modernizing,[[61]](AMD#cite_note-61) devising the Liberty Chip program of designing and manufacturing one new chip or chipset per week for 52 weeks in [fiscal year](Fiscal_year "Fiscal year") 1986,[[48]](AMD#cite_note-HittC26-48)[[62]](AMD#cite_note-62) and by heavily lobbying the U.S. government until sanctions and restrictions were put in place to prevent predatory Japanese pricing.[[63]](AMD#cite_note-63) During this time, AMD withdrew from the <DRAM> market,[[64]](AMD#cite_note-64) and made some headway into the <CMOS> market, which it had lagged in entering, having focused instead on bipolar chips.[[65]](AMD#cite_note-65)

AMD had some success in the mid-1980s with the AMD7910 and AMD7911 "World Chip" [FSK](Frequency-shift_keying "Frequency-shift keying") modem, one of the first multi-standard devices that covered both Bell and [CCITT](ITU-T "ITU-T") tones at up to 1200 baud half duplex or 300/300 full duplex.[[66]](AMD#cite_note-66) Beginning in 1986, AMD embraced the perceived shift toward <RISC> with their own [AMD Am29000](AMD_Am29000 "AMD Am29000") (29k) processor;[[67]](AMD#cite_note-67) the 29k survived as an [embedded processor](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor").[[68]](AMD#cite_note-68)[[69]](AMD#cite_note-69) The company also increased its <EPROM> memory market share in the late 1980s.[[70]](AMD#cite_note-70) Throughout the 1980s, AMD was a second-source supplier of Intel x86 processors. In 1991, it introduced its own 386-compatible <Am386>, an AMD-designed chip. Creating its own chips, AMD began to compete directly with Intel.[[71]](AMD#cite_note-71)

AMD had a large, successful [flash memory](Flash_memory "Flash memory") business, even during the [dotcom bust](Dotcom_bust "Dotcom bust").[[72]](AMD#cite_note-72) In 2003, to divest some manufacturing and aid its overall cash flow, which was under duress from aggressive microprocessor competition from Intel, AMD spun off its flash memory business and manufacturing into <Spansion>, a joint venture with <Fujitsu>, which had been co-manufacturing flash memory with AMD since 1993.[[73]](AMD#cite_note-73)[[74]](AMD#cite_note-74) In December 2005, AMD divested itself of Spansion to focus on the microprocessor market, and Spansion went public in an IPO.[[75]](AMD#cite_note-75)

On July 24, 2006, AMD announced its acquisition of the Canadian 3D graphics card company [ATI Technologies](ATI_Technologies "ATI Technologies"). AMD paid $4.3 billion and 58 million shares of its [capital stock](Capital_stock "Capital stock"), for a total of approximately $5.4 billion. The transaction was completed on October 25, 2006.[[76]](AMD#cite_note-76) On August 30, 2010, AMD announced that it would retire the ATI brand name for its graphics chipsets in favor of the AMD brand name.[[77]](AMD#cite_note-77)[[78]](AMD#cite_note-78)

In October 2008, AMD announced plans to spin off manufacturing operations in the form of [GlobalFoundries Inc.](GlobalFoundries "GlobalFoundries"), a multibillion-dollar joint venture with [Advanced Technology Investment Co.](Advanced_Technology_Investment_Company "Advanced Technology Investment Company"), an investment company formed by the government of [Abu Dhabi](Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"). The partnership and spin-off gave AMD an infusion of cash and allowed it to focus solely on chip design.[[79]](AMD#cite_note-79) To assure the Abu Dhabi investors of the new venture's success, AMD's CEO [Hector Ruiz](Hector_Ruiz "Hector Ruiz") stepped down in July 2008, while remaining executive chairman, in preparation for becoming chairman of GlobalFoundries in March 2009.[[80]](AMD#cite_note-80)[[81]](AMD#cite_note-81) President and COO [Dirk Meyer](Dirk_Meyer "Dirk Meyer") became AMD's CEO.[[82]](AMD#cite_note-82) Recessionary losses necessitated AMD cutting 1,100 jobs in 2009.[[83]](AMD#cite_note-83)

TSMC and the rest of the foundry industry are exposed to the [cyclical industrial dynamics](Cyclical_industrial_dynamics "Cyclical industrial dynamics") of the semiconductor industry. TSMC must ensure its production capacity to meet strong customer demand during upturns. However, during downturns, it must contend with excess capacity because of weak demand and the high fixed costs associated with its manufacturing facilities.[[73]](TSMC#cite_note-Morningstar_mobile_chips_article-73) As a result, the company's financial results tend to fluctuate with a cycle time of a few years. This is more apparent in earnings than revenues because of the general trend of revenue and capacity growth. TSMC's business has generally also been seasonal, with a peak in Q3 and a low in Q1.

In 2014, TSMC was at the forefront of the foundry industry for high-performance, low-power applications,[[74]](TSMC#cite_note-EE_Times_Q1_2014_results_article-74)[[75]](TSMC#cite_note-SimmTester_28nm_article-75) leading major smartphone chip companies such as Qualcomm,[[76]](TSMC#cite_note-76)[[77]](TSMC#cite_note-TSMC_banking_on_28nm-77) Mediatek[[77]](TSMC#cite_note-TSMC_banking_on_28nm-77)[[78]](TSMC#cite_note-DigiTimes_MediaTek_GlobalFoundries-78) and Apple[[30]](TSMC#cite_note-TechNews_Apple_A8_article-30)[[32]](TSMC#cite_note-Taipei_Times_Apple_article-32) to place an increasing amount of orders.[[74]](TSMC#cite_note-EE_Times_Q1_2014_results_article-74) While the competitors in the foundry industry (primarily <GlobalFoundries> and [United Microelectronics Corporation](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation")) have encountered difficulties ramping leading-edge 28 nm capacity,[[78]](TSMC#cite_note-DigiTimes_MediaTek_GlobalFoundries-78) the leading [Integrated Device Manufacturers](Integrated_Device_Manufacturer "Integrated Device Manufacturer") such as <Samsung> and <Intel> that seek to offer foundry capacity to third parties were also unable to match the requirements for advanced mobile applications.[[75]](TSMC#cite_note-SimmTester_28nm_article-75)

For most of 2014, TSMC saw a continuing increase in revenues due to increased demand, primarily due to chips for smartphone applications. TSMC raised its financial guidance in March 2014 and posted 'unseasonably strong' first-quarter results.[[25]](TSMC#cite_note-Q2_2014_forecast-25)[[79]](TSMC#cite_note-79) For Q2 2014, revenues came in at NT$183 billion, with 28 nm technology business growing more than 30% from the previous quarter.[[80]](TSMC#cite_note-80) Lead times for chip orders at TSMC increased due to a tight capacity situation, putting fabless chip companies at risk of not meeting their sales expectations or shipment schedules,[[81]](TSMC#cite_note-81) and in August 2014 it was reported that TSMC's production capacity for the fourth quarter of 2014 was already almost fully booked, a scenario that had not occurred for many years, which was described as being due to a ripple-effect due to TSMC landing CPU orders from Apple.[[82]](TSMC#cite_note-82)

However, monthly sales for 2014 peaked in October, decreasing by 10% in November due to cautious inventory adjustment actions taken by some of its customers.[[83]](TSMC#cite_note-Taipei_Times_2014-12-11-83) TSMC's revenue for 2014 saw growth of 28% over the previous year, while TSMC forecasted that revenue for 2015 would grow by 15 to 20 percent from 2014, thanks to strong demand for its 20 nm process, new 16 nm FinFET process technology as well as continuing demand for 28 nm, and demand for less advanced chip fabrication in its 200mm fabs.[[83]](TSMC#cite_note-Taipei_Times_2014-12-11-83)

## Technologies

TSMC's N7+ is the first commercially available extreme-ultraviolet lithographic process in the semiconductor industry.[[84]](TSMC#cite_note-84) It uses ultraviolet patterning and enables more acute circuits to be implemented on the silicon. N7+ offers a 15–20% higher transistor density and 10% reduction in power consumption than previous technology.[[85]](TSMC#cite_note-85)[[86]](TSMC#cite_note-86) The N7 achieved the fastest ever volume time to market, faster than 10 nm and 16 nm.[[87]](TSMC#cite_note-87)

The N5 iteration doubles transistor density and improves performance by an additional 15%.[[88]](TSMC#cite_note-88)[[89]](TSMC#cite_note-89)

### WaferTech subsidiary

WaferTech, a subsidiary of TSMC, is a [pure-play semiconductor foundry](Pure-play_semiconductor_foundry "Pure-play semiconductor foundry") employing 1,100 workers, located in [Camas, Washington](Camas%2C_Washington "Camas, Washington"), United States, the second-largest pure-play foundry in the United States. The largest is GlobalFoundries Fab 8 in [Malta, New York](Malta%2C_New_York "Malta, New York"), which employs over 3,000 workers with over 278,709 m2 (3,000,000 sq ft) under one roof.

WaferTech was established in June 1996 as a joint venture with TSMC, <Altera>, [Analog Devices](Analog_Devices "Analog Devices"), and ISSI as key partners. The four companies and minor individual investors placed US$1.2 billion into this venture, which was at the time the single largest startup investment in the state of Washington. The company started production in July 1998 in its 200mm semiconductor fabrication plant. Its first product was a 0.35 micrometer part for Altera.

TSMC bought out the joint venture partners in 2000 and acquired full control, operating it as a fully owned subsidiary.[[118]](TSMC#cite_note-118)

WaferTech is based in [Camas](Camas%2C_Washington "Camas, Washington"), 32 km (20 mi) outside [Portland](Portland%2C_Oregon "Portland, Oregon"), Oregon. The WaferTech campus contains a 9.3 ha (23 acres) complex housed on 105 ha (260 acres). The main fabrication facility consists of a 12,000 m2 (130,000 sq ft) 200mm wafer fabrication plant.[[119]](TSMC#cite_note-119)

In 2015, Dr. Tsung Kuo was named company president and fab director of WaferTech.[[120]](TSMC#cite_note-120)

### Germany

In August 2023, TSMC committed 3.5 billion Euros to a 10+ billion Euro factory in Dresden, Germany, with participation of [Robert Bosch GmbH](Robert_Bosch_GmbH "Robert Bosch GmbH"), [Infineon Technologies](Infineon_Technologies "Infineon Technologies") and [NXP Semiconductors](NXP_Semiconductors "NXP Semiconductors") and a 5 billion Euro subsidy from the German government, in exchange for a 70% majority in the resulting European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC).[[121]](TSMC#cite_note-121)[[122]](TSMC#cite_note-122)[[123]](TSMC#cite_note-123)[[124]](TSMC#cite_note-124)

This article is about the business model for making [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuits "Integrated circuits"). For other uses of the term **foundry**, see [foundry (disambiguation)](Foundry_(disambiguation) "Foundry (disambiguation)").

The **foundry model** is a [microelectronics](Microelectronics "Microelectronics") engineering and manufacturing [business model](Business_model "Business model") consisting of a [semiconductor fabrication plant](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant"), or foundry, and an [integrated circuit design](Integrated_circuit_design "Integrated circuit design") operation, each belonging to separate companies or subsidiaries.[[1]](Foundry_model#cite_note-1)[[2]](Foundry_model#cite_note-2)[[3]](Foundry_model#cite_note-3)[[4]](Foundry_model#cite_note-4)

[Integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDMs) design and manufacture integrated circuits. Many companies, known as [fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company"), only design devices; merchant or [pure play](Pure_play "Pure play") foundries only manufacture devices for other companies, without designing them. Examples of IDMs are <Intel>, [Samsung](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"), and [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"),
examples of pure play foundries are <GlobalFoundries>, <TSMC>, and [UMC](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation"), and examples of fabless companies are [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices"), <Nvidia>, and <Qualcomm>.

Integrated circuit production facilities are expensive to build and maintain. Unless they can be kept at nearly full use, they will become a drain on the [finances](Finances "Finances") of the company that owns them. The foundry [model](Business_model "Business model") uses two methods to avoid these costs: fabless companies avoid costs by not owning such facilities. Merchant foundries, on the other hand, find work from the worldwide pool of fabless companies, through careful [scheduling](Scheduling_(production_processes) "Scheduling (production processes)"), [pricing](Pricing "Pricing"), and contracting, keep their plants in full use.

## History

Companies that both designed and produced the devices were originally responsible for manufacturing microelectronic devices. These manufacturers were involved in both the [research and development](Research_and_development "Research and development") of manufacturing processes and the research and development of [microcircuit](Microcircuit "Microcircuit") design.

The first pure play semiconductor company is the [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation](Taiwan_Semiconductor_Manufacturing_Corporation "Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation"), a [spin-off](Corporate_spin-off "Corporate spin-off") of the government [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute"), which split its design and fabrication divisions in 1987,[[5]](Foundry_model#cite_note-5) a model advocated for by [Carver Mead](Carver_Mead "Carver Mead") in the U.S., but deemed too costly to pursue. The separation of design and fabrication became known as the foundry model, with [fabless manufacturing](Fabless_manufacturing "Fabless manufacturing") outsourcing to [semiconductor foundries](Semiconductor_foundry "Semiconductor foundry").[[6]](Foundry_model#cite_note-Brown-6)

[Fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_companies "Fabless semiconductor companies") do not have any semiconductor fabrication capability; and contract production with a merchant foundry manufacturer. The fabless company concentrates on the research and development of an IC-product; the foundry concentrates on manufacturing and [testing](Test_method "Test method") the physical product. If the foundry does not have any semiconductor design capability, it is a pure-play semiconductor foundry.

An absolute separation into fabless and foundry companies is not necessary. Some companies continue to exist that perform both operations and benefit from the close coupling of their skills. Some companies manufacture some of their own designs and contract out to have others manufactured or designed, in cases where they see [value](Value_(marketing) "Value (marketing)") or seek special skills. The foundry model is a business vision that seeks to optimize productivity.

### MOSIS

The very first merchant foundries were part of the <MOSIS> service. The MOSIS service gave limited production access to designers with limited means, such as students, university researchers, and engineers at small [startups](Startup_company "Startup company").[[7]](Foundry_model#cite_note-BergerLester2015-7) The designer submitted designs, and these submissions were manufactured with the commercial company's extra capacity. Manufacturers could insert some [wafers](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") for a MOSIS design into a collection of their own wafers when a processing step was compatible with both operations. The commercial company (serving as foundry) was already running the process, so they were effectively being paid by MOSIS for something they were already doing. A factory with excess capacity during slow periods could also run MOSIS designs to avoid having expensive [capital](Capital_(economics) "Capital (economics)") equipment stand idle.

Under-use of an expensive manufacturing plant could lead to the financial ruin of the owner, so selling surplus [wafer](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") capacity was a way to maximize the fab's use. Hence, economic factors created a climate where fab operators wanted to sell surplus wafer-manufacturing capacity and designers wanted to purchase manufacturing capacity rather than try to build it.

Although MOSIS opened the doors to some fabless customers, earning additional [revenue](Revenue "Revenue") for the foundry and providing inexpensive service to the customer, running a business around MOSIS production was difficult. The merchant foundries sold wafer capacity on a surplus basis, as a secondary business activity. Services to the customers were secondary to the commercial business, with little [guarantee](Guarantee "Guarantee") of support. The choice of merchant dictated the design, development flow, and available techniques to the fabless customer. Merchant foundries might require [proprietary](Property "Property") and non-portable preparation steps. Key clients like Apple, Qualcomm, and MediaTek were instrumental in driving demand across these technology nodes, particularly for 28nm mobile applications.

Based on my comprehensive research of Wikipedia, here is a detailed summary of TSMC's manufacturing capacity, production volumes, and market position during the 2010s (2010-2019):

## TSMC: Manufacturing Capacity, Production Volumes & Market Position (2010-2019)

### **Fabrication Plants**

During the 2010s, TSMC operated multiple fabrication facilities:

**300mm Wafer Fabs (12-inch):**
- **Fab 12A** (Hsinchu) - Phases 1, 2, 4-7 operational (TSMC headquarters)
- **Fab 14** (Shanhua District, Tainan) - Phases 1-7 operational, phase 8 under construction
- **Fab 15** (Taichung) - Phases 1-7 operational; **US$9.4 billion investment announced in July 2010**, expected to manufacture over **100,000 wafers/month**
- **Fab 16** (Nanjing, China) - 300mm wafer facility
- **Fab 18** (Anding District, Tainan) - Phases 1-8 operational
- **Fab 11** (Camas, Washington) - WaferTech subsidiary (200mm), acquired completely in 2000

**200mm Wafer Fabs:**
- Fab 3, 5, 6, 8, 10 (various locations in Taiwan and China)
- SSMC (Singapore) - Joint venture with Philips/NXP

### **Monthly Wafer Capacity & Growth**

- **2011**: TSMC planned to **expand capacity by 30%** to meet strong market demand
- **2014**: Production capacity for Q4 2014 was **almost fully booked** - a scenario not seen for many years
- WaferTech (Washington): 12,000 m² 200mm wafer fabrication plant
- The Central Taiwan Science Park Fab 15 investment (US$9.4 billion, 2010) was projected to add **over 100,000 wafers per month**

### **Revenue Performance (2010-2019)**

**Yearly Revenues (in million NT$):**
| Year | Revenue (NT$ million) |
|------|----------------------|
| 2010 | 419,538 |
| 2011 | 427,081 |
| 2012 | 506,754 |
| 2013 | 597,024 |
| 2014 | 762,806 |
| 2015 | 843,497 |
| 2016 | 947,938 |
| 2017 | 977,477 |
| 2018 | 1,031,474 |
| 2019 | 1,069,985 |

**Key Revenue Milestones:**
- 2014: **28% growth** over 2013 (forecast 15-20% growth for 2015)
- By 2019: Revenue exceeded **NT$1 trillion** for the first time

**Quarterly Growth (millions NT$):**
- Q1 2012: 105,615 → Q4 2019: 317,237
- **Q2 2014**: NT$183 billion, with 28nm technology business growing **>30%** from previous quarter

### **Market Share in Semiconductor Foundry Services**

- **55.9% market share** in 2017 (according to TrendForce)
- TSMC was recognized as the **world's largest dedicated independent (pure-play) semiconductor foundry**
- Competitors struggling: GlobalFoundries and UMC encountered difficulties ramping leading-edge 28nm capacity
- Samsung and Intel, despite offering foundry services, were unable to match TSMC's advanced mobile application requirements

### **Key Technology Nodes Introduced (2010-2019)**

| Year | Technology Node | Features |
|------|----------------|----------|
| 2010-2012 | **40nm** | General-purpose, low-power, ultra-low power options |
| 2012-2013 | **28nm** | HP, HPM, HPC, HPL, LP, HPC+, ULP with HKMG |
| 2014-2015 | **20nm** | Advanced node expansion |
| 2015-2016 | **16nm FinFET** | FF, FF+, FFC variants |
| 2016-2017 | **12nm** | Enhanced version of 16nm (FFC, FFN) |
| 2017-2018 | **10nm FinFET** | FF variant |
| 2018-2019 | **7nm FinFET** | FF, FF+, FFP, HPC variants |
| 2019 | **N7+ (7nm EUV)** | First commercially available EUV process, 15-20% higher transistor density, 10% power reduction |

### **Capital Expenditures & Capacity Expansion**

- **2010**: US$9.4 billion for Fab 15 (Central Taiwan Science Park)
- **2011**: Land acquisition from Powerchip Semiconductor for **NT$2.9 billion** (US$96 million) to build two additional 300mm fabs (Fab 12B)
- **May 2014**: Capital appropriations of **US$568 million** to increase manufacturing capabilities
- **August 2014**: Additional capital appropriations of **US$3.05 billion**
- **2014**: 30% capacity expansion planned to meet strong market demand

### **Major Customers (2010-2019)**

**Key Fabless Semiconductor Customers:**
- **Apple** - Most important customer as of 2014
  - 2011: A5 and A6 SoCs for iPad and iPhone
  - 2014: A8 and A8X SoCs
  - 2015: A9 SoC (shared with Samsung), A9X exclusively
- **Qualcomm** - Snapdragon 800 processor (2013), 28HPM technology
- **MediaTek** - Multiple 28nm chip orders
- **NVIDIA** - Custom GPU chips
- **AMD** - Various products
- **ARM** - Partner on 10nm FinFET processors (2014)
- **Xilinx** - Programmable logic devices
- **NXP, STMicroelectronics, Texas Instruments** - Some production outsourcing

### **Significant Capacity Expansions (2010-2019)**

1. **2010**: US$9.4 billion Fab 15 in Central Taiwan Science Park
2. **2011**: Acquisition of Powerchip Semiconductor land for NT$2.9 billion
3. **2011**: 30% capacity expansion to meet strong demand
4. **2014**: US$568M + US$3.05B in capital appropriations
5. **2014**: Q4 production capacity "almost fully booked"
6. **2016**: Fab 14 phase 8 under construction
7. **2019**: N7+ EUV process technology in high-volume production

### **Key Achievements During the 2010s**

- **Leading 28nm production** while competitors struggled with ramp-up
- **First company** to achieve mass production at multiple advanced nodes (20nm, 16nm, 10nm, 7nm)
- **First commercially available EUV lithography process** (N7+ in 2019)
- **Market dominance**: Maintained 50%+ foundry market share throughout the decade
- **Revenue growth**: CAGR of 17.4% in revenue from 1994-2020, with strong performance throughout the 2010s
- **Technology leadership**: Fastest time-to-market for 7nm vs. 10nm and 16nm

### **Market Position Summary**

Through the 2010s, TSMC solidified its position as the **dominant pure-play foundry** globally, maintaining what was referred to as an "almost monopoly" position with over **55% market share** by 2017. The company's ability to deliver advanced process nodes ahead of competitors, combined with strong customer relationships (especially with Apple) and massive capacity expansions, made TSMC the go-to manufacturing partner for virtually all major fabless semiconductor companies during this transformative decade in the industry.

#### Fab 1

Fab 1, located in <Dresden>, Germany, is a 364,512 m2 plant which was transferred to GlobalFoundries on its inception: Fab 36 and Fab 38 were renamed Module 1 and Module 2, respectively. Each module can produce 25,000 300 mm diameter wafers per month.[[8]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-300mm-8)[[54]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-54)

Module 1 is a 300 mm wafer production facility. It is capable of manufacturing wafers at 40 nm, 28 nm BULK and 22 nm FDSOI. Module 2 was originally named "(AMD) Fab 30" and was a 200 mm fab producing 30,000 Wafer Outs Per Month, but has now been converted into a 300 mm wafer fab. Together with other clean room extensions like the Annex they have a maximum full capacity of 80,000 of 300 mm wafers/month (180,000 200 mm wafers/month equivalent), using technologies of [45 nm](45_nm "45 nm") and below.

he original Zen and the Zen+ CPUs are of a monolithic design which were produced at Global Foundries Malta Facilities in [Malta, NY](Malta%2C_New_York "Malta, New York"). Going forward AMD will pursue a multiple Chiplet Design with the Zen 2 microprocessor. The Zen 2 will consist of a 14/12 nm manufactured IO die surrounded by a number of 7 nm Core dies. When Global Foundries announced the suspension of 7 nm operations AMD executed a shift in plans transferring production of the 7 nm core dies to TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Corporation). There was speculation in some quarters as to where manufacture of the Core Dies would take place. In AMD's 2018 fourth quarter financial conference call which took place on January 29, 2019, AMD CEO Lisa Su announced the WSA (Wafer Supply Agreement) governing production and acquisition by AMD from GlobalFoundries had been amended for the seventh time. The amendment stated AMD would continue to procure 12 nm node and above from Global Foundries while giving AMD latitude to purchase 7 nm node manufactured wafers from any source free from paying any royalties. The agreement will run through 2024 and ensures that Global Foundries will have work for its Malta plant for that time period. Pricing commitments for Wafers runs through 2021 when it is likely the WSA will be amended again.[[59]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-59)

#### Accreditation as a Trusted Supplier

In May 2023, the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD), through the Defense Microelectronics Activity (DMEA), Trusted Access Program Office (TAPO), accredited GlobalFoundries' advanced manufacturing facility in Malta, New York, as a Category 1A Trusted Supplier. This accreditation enables GlobalFoundries to manufacture secure semiconductors for a wide range of critical aerospace and defense applications.[[60]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-60)

#### Fab 10

Fab 10,[[61]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-globalfoundries.com-61) located in [East Fishkill, New York](East_Fishkill%2C_New_York "East Fishkill, New York"), United States, was previously known as IBM Building 323. It became part of GlobalFoundries operations with the acquisition of [IBM Microelectronics](IBM_Microelectronics "IBM Microelectronics"). It currently manufactures technology down to the 14 nm node. In April 2019, it was announced that this fab has been sold to [ON Semiconductor](ON_Semiconductor "ON Semiconductor") for $430m. The facility will be transferred over within three years.[[62]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-OnSemi-62)

On February 10, 2023, onsemi successfully completed its acquisition of GF's 300 mm East Fishkill, New York site and fabrication facility.[[63]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-63)

### 200 mm fabrication facilities

All 200 mm fabs except Fab 9 are located in <Singapore>, and originally owned by [Chartered Semiconductor](Chartered_Semiconductor "Chartered Semiconductor").

#### Fab 2

Fab 2, located in Woodlands, Singapore. This fab is capable of manufacturing wafers at 600 to 350 nm for use in selected automotive IC products, High Voltage power management IC and Mixed-signal products.

#### Fab 3/5

Fab 3/5, located in Woodlands, Singapore. This fab is capable of manufacturing wafers at 350 to 180 nm for use in high voltage IC's for small panel display drivers and mobile power management modules.

#### Fab 3E

Fab 3E, located in Tampines, Singapore. This fab produces [180 nm](180_nm "180 nm") wafers for use in selected automotive IC products, High Voltage power management IC and Mixed-Signal products with embedded non-volatile memory technology.

In January 2019 GlobalFoundries announced that it had agreed to sell its Fab 3E in Singapore to [Vanguard International Semiconductor Corporation](Vanguard_International_Semiconductor_Corporation "Vanguard International Semiconductor Corporation") with transfer of ownership set to be completed on December 31, 2019.

#### Fab 6

Fab 6 located in Woodlands, Singapore, is a copper fabrication facility that is capable of manufacturing integrated CMOS and RFCMOS products for applications such as <Wi-Fi> & <Bluetooth> devices at [180](180_nm "180 nm") to 110 nm processes. The facility was later converted to 300mm and merged with Fab 7, a facility for manufacturing products based on the 300 nm node.

#### Fab 9

Fab 9,[[61]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-globalfoundries.com-61) located in the village of [Essex Junction, Vermont](Essex_Junction%2C_Vermont "Essex Junction, Vermont"), United States, near Vermont's largest city of [Burlington](Burlington%2C_Vermont "Burlington, Vermont"), became part of GlobalFoundries operations with the acquisition of IBM Microelectronics. The fab manufactures technologies down to the 90 nm node and is the largest private employer within the state of Vermont. The site also hosted a captive [mask shop](Mask_shop "Mask shop"), with development efforts down to the [7 nanometer](7_nanometer "7 nanometer") node, until it was sold to Toppan in 2019.[[64]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-64)

## Mergers and acquisitions

### Chartered Semiconductor

The majority investor of GlobalFoundries, Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Investment Co., announced on September 6, 2009, that it has agreed to acquire Singapore-based [Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd.](Chartered_Semiconductor_Manufacturing "Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing"), for a total of $3.9 billion, with Chartered's operations being folded into GlobalFoundries.[[65]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-65)

Chartered Semiconductor is a member of the Common Platform, <IBM>'s semiconductor technology alliance. GlobalFoundries is a JDA partner of Common Platform Technology Alliance.

### IBM Microelectronics

Further information: [IBM Microelectronics § 2015 sale to GlobalFoundries](IBM_Microelectronics#2015_sale_to_GlobalFoundries "IBM Microelectronics")

In October 2014, GlobalFoundries received US$1.5 billion from IBM to accept taking over [IBM Microelectronics](IBM_Microelectronics "IBM Microelectronics"), including a 200 mm fab (now Fab 9) in Essex Junction, Vermont, and a 300 mm fab (now Fab 10) in East Fishkill, New York. As part of the agreement, GlobalFoundries will be the sole provider of IBM's server processor chips for the next 10 years. The deal closed on July 1, 2015.[[66]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-66) IBM-India employees who moved over to GlobalFoundries as part of the acquisition are now part of its Bangalore office.[[67]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-67)

In April 2019 [ON Semiconductor](ON_Semiconductor "ON Semiconductor") and GlobalFoundries announced a $430 million agreement to transfer ownership of GlobalFoundries 300mm Fab 10 in East Fishkill, New York, to ON Semiconductor.[[68]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-68)

In 2021 and 2023, GlobalFoundries sued IBM over [intellectual property](Intellectual_property "Intellectual property") disputes involving the latter's agreements with <Intel> and <Rapidus>.[[69]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-69)

## Process technologies

GlobalFoundries' [22 nm](22_nm "22 nm") FD-SOI process is [second-sourced](Second_source "Second source") from <STMicroelectronics>.[[70]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-st22fdsoi-70) STMicroelectronics signed a sourcing and licensing agreement with Samsung for the same technology later.[[71]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-ss28fdsoi-71)

GlobalFoundries' [14 nm](14_nm "14 nm") 14LPP <FinFET> process is [second-sourced](Second_source "Second source") from [Samsung Electronics](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"). GlobalFoundries' 12 nm FinFET nodes are based on Samsung's 14 nm 14LPP process.[[21]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-:0-21)

**United Microelectronics Corporation** (**UMC**; [Chinese](Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 聯華電子; [pinyin](Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Liánhuá Diànzǐ*) is a Taiwanese company based in <Hsinchu>, <Taiwan>. It was founded as Taiwan's first [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") company in 1980 as a spin-off of the government-sponsored [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute") (ITRI).[[4]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-overview-4)

## Overview

UMC is best known for its semiconductor foundry business, manufacturing [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") [wafers](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") for [fabless](Fabless "Fabless") semiconductor companies. In this role, UMC is ranked behind competitor <TSMC>. It has four 300 mm fabs, one in Taiwan, one in Singapore, one in China, and one in Japan.[[4]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-overview-4)

UMC is listed on the [Taiwan Stock Exchange](Taiwan_Stock_Exchange "Taiwan Stock Exchange") as [2303](https://finance.yahoo.com/q?m=TW&s=2303.TW). UMC has 12 manufacturing facilities worldwide, employing approximately 19,500 people.

UMC is a significant supplier to the automotive industry.[[5]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-5)

## History

- On May 22, 1980, UMC was spun off from the [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute") and was formally established as the first private integrated circuit company in Taiwan.
- 1983: TMC starts a joint research project with US-based [Vitelic](Mosel_Vitelic_Inc "Mosel Vitelic Inc").
- 1985
  * UMC was officially listed on the [Taiwan Stock Exchange](Taiwan_Stock_Exchange "Taiwan Stock Exchange") (code: 2303). It was the first listed semiconductor company in Taiwan. At that time, [Morris Chang](Morris_Chang "Morris Chang") was its chairman.
  * UMC sets up a subsidiary, **Unicorn Microelectronics Corporation** (also abbreviated UMC), in Silicon Valley to improve access to technology, signing joint research agreements with Mosel (later Mosel Vitelic) and Quasel.
- 1995: UMC decided to transform from an IDM company with its own products to a professional pure-play foundry.
- 1996: Spun off its IC design units to establish <MediaTek>, Novatek, ITE Technology, [Faraday Technology](Faraday_Technology "Faraday Technology"), AMIC Technology, and Davicom.
- 1999: Fab 12A 12-inch wafer fab in [Tainan Science Park](Tainan_Science_Park "Tainan Science Park") was officially established.
- 2000:
  * Lists on the [New York Stock Exchange](New_York_Stock_Exchange "New York Stock Exchange") (code: UMC) as Taiwan's first semiconductor company to do so.[[6]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-6)
  * Produces the first chips using copper process technology and the first 0.13 micron ICs in the semiconductor industry.
- 2004: 12-inch wafer fab in Singapore enters mass production.
- 2008: Listed as a constituent stock on the [Dow Jones Sustainability Index](Dow_Jones_Sustainability_Index "Dow Jones Sustainability Index") (DJSI) for the first time.[[7]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-7)
- 2010: 30th anniversary of the company.
- 2013: Fully acquires "**[Hejian Technology](Hejian_Technology "Hejian Technology") Wafer Fab**" in Suzhou, <China>.
- 2015: USCXM 12-inch wafer fab located in Xiamen, Fujian Province, China was officially established.[[8]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-8)
- 2017: 28 nm mass production begins at USCXM in Xiamen, China.
- 2019: Fully acquired Japan-based Mie Fujitsu Semiconductor.[[9]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-9)[[10]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-10)[[11]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-11)
- 2020: Reached a plea agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice to resolve a 2018 trade secrets case.[[12]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-businesswire.com-12)


### U.S. Indictment and guilty plea

The [United States Department of Justice](United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") indicted UMC and Chinese firm [Fujian Jinhua](Fujian_Jinhua_Integrated_Circuit "Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit") in 2018, alleging that they conspired to steal intellectual property from U.S. company [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology").[[13]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-13)[[14]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-:1-14) In October 2020, UMC and the U.S. Department of Justice reached a plea agreement, with UMC pleading guilty to one count of receiving and possessing a stolen trade secret and agreeing to pay a fine of $60 million. UMC’s plea and Plea Agreement resolved the 2018 trade secrets case brought against UMC by the U.S. Department of Justice. As part of the Plea Agreement, DOJ agreed to dismiss the original indictment against UMC, including allegations of conspiracy to commit economic espionage and conspiracy to steal multiple trade secrets from Micron Technology, Inc. (“Micron”), patent-related allegations, and alleged damages and penalties of $400 million USD to $8.75 billion. The one trade secret at issue in the guilty plea and Plea Agreement related to older technology that had been in mass production worldwide for several years. DOJ also dismissed a related civil case against UMC. Aside from the fine amount, UMC has no further financial obligations to DOJ. The Plea Agreement also provides that UMC will cooperate with DOJ and will be subject to a three-year term of non-supervised probation.[[12]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-businesswire.com-12)

(circa) 25,000 (2022) | | Website | [www.amd.com](https://www.amd.com/) | | **Footnotes / references** [[1]](AMD#cite_note-10K-1) | | **Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.**, commonly abbreviated as **AMD**, is an American multinational [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") company based in [Santa Clara, California](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California"), that develops [computer processors](Processor_(computing) "Processor (computing)") and related technologies for business and consumer markets. The company was founded in 1969 by [Jerry Sanders](Jerry_Sanders_(businessman) "Jerry Sanders (businessman)") and a group of other technology professionals. AMD's early products were primarily memory chips and other components for computers. The company later expanded into the microprocessor market, competing with , its main rival in the industry. In the early 2000s, AMD experienced significant growth and success, thanks in part to its strong position in the PC market and the success of its and processors. However, the company faced challenges in the late 2000s and early 2010s, as it struggled to keep up with Intel in the race to produce faster and more powerful processors. In the late 2010s, AMD regained some of its market share thanks to the success of its processors which are now widely regarded as superior to Intel products in business applications including cloud applications. AMD's processors are used in a wide range of computing devices, including personal computers, servers, laptops, and gaming consoles. While it initially manufactured its own processors, the company later outsourced its manufacturing, a practice known as going [fabless](Fabless_manufacturing "Fabless manufacturing"), after was spun off in 2009. AMD's main products include [microprocessors](Microprocessor "Microprocessor"), [motherboard](Motherboard "Motherboard") [chipsets](Chipset "Chipset"), [embedded processors](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor"), [graphics processors](Graphics_processing_unit "Graphics processing unit"), and [FPGAs](FPGA "FPGA") for [servers](Server_(computing) "Server (computing)"), [workstations](Workstation "Workstation"), personal computers, and [embedded system](Embedded_system "Embedded system") applications. ### Technology exchange agreement with Intel

<Intel> had introduced the first [x86](X86 "X86") microprocessors in 1978.[[50]](AMD#cite_note-50) In 1981, <IBM> created its [PC](IBM_Personal_Computer "IBM Personal Computer"), and wanted Intel's x86 processors, but only under the condition that Intel also provide a [second-source](Second-source "Second-source") manufacturer for its patented x86 microprocessors.[[11]](AMD#cite_note-singer-11) Intel and AMD entered into a 10-year technology exchange agreement, first signed in October 1981[[45]](AMD#cite_note-swaine-45)[[51]](AMD#cite_note-51) and formally executed in February 1982.[[34]](AMD#cite_note-sec1996-34) The terms of the agreement were that each company could acquire the right to become a second-source manufacturer of semiconductor products developed by the other; that is, each party could "earn" the right to manufacture and sell a product developed by the other, if agreed to, by exchanging the manufacturing rights to a product of equivalent technical complexity. The technical information and licenses needed to make and sell a part would be exchanged for a royalty to the developing company.[[33]](AMD#cite_note-justia1994-33) The 1982 agreement also extended the 1976 AMD–Intel cross-licensing agreement through 1995.[[33]](AMD#cite_note-justia1994-33)[[34]](AMD#cite_note-sec1996-34) The agreement included the right to invoke arbitration of disagreements, and after five years the right of either party to end the agreement with one year's notice.[[33]](AMD#cite_note-justia1994-33) The main result of the 1982 agreement was that AMD became a second-source manufacturer of Intel's x86 microprocessors and related chips, and Intel provided AMD with database tapes for its <8086>, <80186>, and <80286> chips.[[34]](AMD#cite_note-sec1996-34) However, in the event of a bankruptcy or takeover of AMD, the cross-licensing agreement would be effectively canceled.[[52]](AMD#cite_note-52)

Beginning in 1982, AMD began volume-producing second-source Intel-licensed 8086, 8088, 80186, and 80188 processors, and by 1984, its own <Am286> clone of Intel's 80286 processor, for the rapidly growing market of IBM PCs and [IBM clones](IBM_clone "IBM clone").[[11]](AMD#cite_note-singer-11)[[53]](AMD#cite_note-53) It also continued its successful concentration on proprietary [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") chips.[[54]](AMD#cite_note-54)

The company continued to spend greatly on research and development,[[55]](AMD#cite_note-55) and created the world's first 512K <EPROM> in 1984.[[56]](AMD#cite_note-56) That year, AMD was listed in the book *The 100 Best Companies to Work for in America*,[[48]](AMD#cite_note-HittC26-48)[[57]](AMD#cite_note-57) and later made the [*Fortune* 500](Fortune_500 "Fortune 500") list for the first time in 1985.[[58]](AMD#cite_note-58)[[59]](AMD#cite_note-59)

By mid-1985, the microchip market experienced a severe downturn, mainly due to long-term aggressive trade practices ([dumping](Dumping_(pricing_policy) "Dumping (pricing policy)")) from Japan, but also due to a crowded and non-innovative chip market in the United States.[[60]](AMD#cite_note-60) AMD rode out the mid-1980s crisis by aggressively innovating and modernizing,[[61]](AMD#cite_note-61) devising the Liberty Chip program of designing and manufacturing one new chip or chipset per week for 52 weeks in [fiscal year](Fiscal_year "Fiscal year") 1986,[[48]](AMD#cite_note-HittC26-48)[[62]](AMD#cite_note-62) and by heavily lobbying the U.S. government until sanctions and restrictions were put in place to prevent predatory Japanese pricing.[[63]](AMD#cite_note-63) During this time, AMD withdrew from the <DRAM> market,[[64]](AMD#cite_note-64) and made some headway into the <CMOS> market, which it had lagged in entering, having focused instead on bipolar chips.[[65]](AMD#cite_note-65)

AMD had some success in the mid-1980s with the AMD7910 and AMD7911 "World Chip" [FSK](Frequency-shift_keying "Frequency-shift keying") modem, one of the first multi-standard devices that covered both Bell and [CCITT](ITU-T "ITU-T") tones at up to 1200 baud half duplex or 300/300 full duplex.[[66]](AMD#cite_note-66) Beginning in 1986, AMD embraced the perceived shift toward <RISC> with their own [AMD Am29000](AMD_Am29000 "AMD Am29000") (29k) processor;[[67]](AMD#cite_note-67) the 29k survived as an [embedded processor](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor").[[68]](AMD#cite_note-68)[[69]](AMD#cite_note-69) The company also increased its <EPROM> memory market share in the late 1980s.[[70]](AMD#cite_note-70) Throughout the 1980s, AMD was a second-source supplier of Intel x86 processors. In 1991, it introduced its own 386-compatible <Am386>, an AMD-designed chip. Creating its own chips, AMD began to compete directly with Intel.[[71]](AMD#cite_note-71)

AMD had a large, successful [flash memory](Flash_memory "Flash memory") business, even during the [dotcom bust](Dotcom_bust "Dotcom bust").[[72]](AMD#cite_note-72) In 2003, to divest some manufacturing and aid its overall cash flow, which was under duress from aggressive microprocessor competition from Intel, AMD spun off its flash memory business and manufacturing into <Spansion>, a joint venture with <Fujitsu>, which had been co-manufacturing flash memory with AMD since 1993.[[73]](AMD#cite_note-73)[[74]](AMD#cite_note-74) In December 2005, AMD divested itself of Spansion to focus on the microprocessor market, and Spansion went public in an IPO.[[75]](AMD#cite_note-75)

### Acquisition of ATI, spin-off of GlobalFoundries, and acquisition of Xilinx

On July 24, 2006, AMD announced its acquisition of the Canadian 3D graphics card company [ATI Technologies](ATI_Technologies "ATI Technologies"). AMD paid $4.3 billion and 58 million shares of its [capital stock](Capital_stock "Capital stock"), for a total of approximately $5.4 billion. The transaction was completed on October 25, 2006.[[76]](AMD#cite_note-76) On August 30, 2010, AMD announced that it would retire the ATI brand name for its graphics chipsets in favor of the AMD brand name.[[77]](AMD#cite_note-77)[[78]](AMD#cite_note-78)

In October 2008, AMD announced plans to spin off manufacturing operations in the form of [GlobalFoundries Inc.](GlobalFoundries "GlobalFoundries"), a multibillion-dollar joint venture with [Advanced Technology Investment Co.](Advanced_Technology_Investment_Company "Advanced Technology Investment Company"), an investment company formed by the government of [Abu Dhabi](Abu_Dhabi "Abu Dhabi"). The partnership and spin-off gave AMD an infusion of cash and allowed it to focus solely on chip design.[[79]](AMD#cite_note-79) To assure the Abu Dhabi investors of the new venture's success, AMD's CEO [Hector Ruiz](Hector_Ruiz "Hector Ruiz") stepped down in July 2008, while remaining executive chairman, in preparation for becoming chairman of GlobalFoundries in March 2009.[[80]](AMD#cite_note-80)[[81]](AMD#cite_note-81) President and COO [Dirk Meyer](Dirk_Meyer "Dirk Meyer") became AMD's CEO.[[82]](AMD#cite_note-82) Recessionary losses necessitated AMD cutting 1,100 jobs in 2009.[[83]](AMD#cite_note-83)

In August 2011, AMD announced that former <Lenovo> executive [Rory Read](Rory_Read "Rory Read") would be joining the company as CEO, replacing Meyer.[[84]](AMD#cite_note-84) In November 2011, AMD announced plans to lay off more than 10% (1,400) of its employees from across all divisions worldwide.[[85]](AMD#cite_note-85) In October 2012, it announced plans to lay off an additional 15% of its workforce to reduce costs in the face of declining sales revenue.[[86]](AMD#cite_note-king2012-86)

AMD acquired the low-power server manufacturer <SeaMicro> in early 2012, with an eye to bringing out an <Arm64> server chip.[[87]](AMD#cite_note-vance2012-87)

On October 8, 2014, AMD announced that Rory Read had stepped down after three years as president and chief executive officer.[[88]](AMD#cite_note-wsj.com-88) He was succeeded by [Lisa Su](Lisa_Su "Lisa Su"), a key lieutenant who had been serving as chief operating officer since June.[[89]](AMD#cite_note-89)

On October 16, 2014, AMD announced a new restructuring plan along with its Q3 results. Effective July 1, 2014, AMD reorganized into two business groups: Computing and Graphics, which primarily includes desktop and notebook processors and chipsets, discrete GPUs, and professional graphics; and Enterprise, Embedded, and Semi-Custom, which primarily includes server and embedded processors, dense servers, semi-custom SoC products (including [solutions for gaming consoles](AMD#Partnerships)), engineering services, and royalties. As part of this restructuring, AMD announced that 7% of its global workforce would be laid off by the end of 2014.[[90]](AMD#cite_note-90)

After the GlobalFoundries spin-off and subsequent layoffs, AMD was left with significant vacant space at 1 AMD Place, its aging Sunnyvale headquarters office complex. In August 2016, AMD's 47 years in Sunnyvale came to a close when it signed a lease with the [Irvine Company](Irvine_Company "Irvine Company") for a new 220,000 sq. ft. headquarters building in Santa Clara.[[91]](AMD#cite_note-DonatoWeinstein-91) AMD's new location at Santa Clara Square faces the headquarters of archrival Intel across the [Bayshore Freeway](Bayshore_Freeway "Bayshore Freeway") and [San Tomas Aquino Creek](San_Tomas_Aquino_Creek "San Tomas Aquino Creek"). Around the same time, AMD also agreed to sell 1 AMD Place to the Irvine Company.[[92]](AMD#cite_note-SVBJ-92) In April 2019, the Irvine Company secured approval from the Sunnyvale City Council of its plans to demolish 1 AMD Place and redevelop the entire 32-acre site into townhomes and apartments.[[92]](AMD#cite_note-SVBJ-92)

In October 2020, AMD announced that it was acquiring <Xilinx> in an all-stock transaction. The acquisition was completed in February 2022, with an estimated acquisition price of $50 billion.[[93]](AMD#cite_note-93)[[94]](AMD#cite_note-94)

#### K5, K6, Athlon, Duron, and Sempron

Main articles: [AMD K5](AMD_K5 "AMD K5"), [AMD K6](AMD_K6 "AMD K6"), <Athlon>, <Duron>, and <Sempron>

AMD's first in-house x86 processor was the [K5](AMD_K5 "AMD K5"), launched in 1996.[[108]](AMD#cite_note-CPU-INFO_K5-108) The "K" in its name was a reference to <Kryptonite>, the only substance known to harm comic book character <Superman>. This itself was a reference to Intel's hegemony over the market, i.e., an anthropomorphization of them as Superman.[[109]](AMD#cite_note-Forbes-Chip-Names-109) The number "5" was a reference to the fifth generation of x86 processors; rival Intel had previously introduced its line of fifth-generation x86 processors as <Pentium> because the U.S. Trademark and Patent Office had ruled that mere numbers could not be trademarked.[[110]](AMD#cite_note-newyorker-110)

In 1996, AMD purchased <NexGen>, specifically for the rights to their Nx series of x86-compatible processors. AMD gave the NexGen design team their own building, left them alone, and gave them time and money to rework the Nx686. The result was the [K6](AMD_K6 "AMD K6") processor, introduced in 1997. Although it was based on [Socket 7](Socket_7 "Socket 7"), variants such as <K6-III>/450 were faster than Intel's [Pentium II](Pentium_II "Pentium II") (sixth-generation processor).

The K7 was AMD's seventh-generation x86 processor, making its debut under the brand name <Athlon> on June 23, 1999. Unlike previous AMD processors, it could not be used on the same motherboards as Intel's, due to licensing issues surrounding Intel's [Slot 1](Slot_1 "Slot 1") connector, and instead used a [Slot A](Slot_A "Slot A") connector, referenced to the [Alpha](DEC_Alpha "DEC Alpha") processor bus. The <Duron> was a lower-cost and limited version of the Athlon (64KB instead of 256KB L2 cache) in a 462-pin [socketed](CPU_socket "CPU socket") [PGA](Pin_grid_array "Pin grid array") (socket A) or soldered directly onto the motherboard. <Sempron> was released as a lower-cost Athlon XP, replacing Duron in the [socket A](Socket_A "Socket A") PGA era. It has since been migrated upward to all new sockets, up to <AM3>.

On October 9, 2001, the [Athlon XP](Athlon_XP "Athlon XP") was released. On February 10, 2003, the Athlon XP with 512KB L2 Cache was released.[[111]](AMD#cite_note-The_AMD_Athlon_XP_Processor_with_512KB_L2_Cache-111)

#### Athlon 64, Opteron and Phenom

Main articles: [Athlon 64](Athlon_64 "Athlon 64"), <Opteron>, and [Phenom](AMD_Phenom "AMD Phenom")

The K8 was a major revision of the K7 architecture, with the most notable features being the addition of a [64-bit](64-bit_computing "64-bit computing") extension to the x86 instruction set (called [x86-64](X86-64 "X86-64"), AMD64, or x64), the incorporation of an on-chip memory controller, and the implementation of an extremely high-performance point-to-point interconnect called <HyperTransport>, as part of the [Direct Connect Architecture](Direct_Connect_Architecture "Direct Connect Architecture"). The technology was initially launched as the <Opteron> server-oriented processor on April 22, 2003.[[112]](AMD#cite_note-112) Shortly thereafter, it was incorporated into a product for desktop PCs, branded [Athlon 64](Athlon_64 "Athlon 64").[[113]](AMD#cite_note-113)

On April 21, 2005, AMD released the first [dual-core](Multi-core_processor "Multi-core processor") <Opteron>, an x86-based server CPU.[[114]](AMD#cite_note-114) A month later, it released the [Athlon 64 X2](Athlon_64_X2 "Athlon 64 X2"), the first desktop-based [dual-core processor](Multi-core_(computing) "Multi-core (computing)") family.[[115]](AMD#cite_note-115) In May 2007, AMD abandoned the string "64" in its dual-core desktop product branding, becoming Athlon X2, downplaying the significance of [64-bit computing](X86-64 "X86-64") in its processors. Further updates involved improvements to the microarchitecture, and a shift of the target market from mainstream desktop systems to value dual-core desktop systems. In 2008, AMD started to release dual-core Sempron processors exclusively in China, branded as the Sempron 2000 series, with lower HyperTransport speed and smaller L2 cache. AMD completed its dual-core product portfolio for each market segment.

In September 2007, AMD released the first server Opteron [K10](AMD_K10 "AMD K10") processors,[[116]](AMD#cite_note-116) followed in November by the [Phenom](AMD_Phenom "AMD Phenom") processor for desktop. K10 processors came in dual-core, [triple-core](Multi-core "Multi-core"),[[117]](AMD#cite_note-117) and [quad-core](Multi-core "Multi-core") versions, with all cores on a single die. AMD released a new platform codenamed "[Spider](AMD_Spider "AMD Spider")", which used the new Phenom processor, as well as an R770 GPU and a 790 GX/FX chipset from the [AMD 700 chipset series](AMD_700_chipset_series "AMD 700 chipset series").[[118]](AMD#cite_note-hothardware-118) However, AMD built the Spider at <65nm>, which was uncompetitive with Intel's smaller and more power-efficient <45nm>.

In January 2009, AMD released a new processor line dubbed [Phenom II](Phenom_II "Phenom II"), a refresh of the original [Phenom](AMD_Phenom "AMD Phenom") built using the 45 nm process.[[119]](AMD#cite_note-anandtech3512-119) AMD's new platform, codenamed "[Dragon](AMD_Dragon "AMD Dragon")", used the new Phenom II processor, and an [ATI](ATI_(brand) "ATI (brand)") R770 GPU from the [R700](Radeon_R700 "Radeon R700") GPU family, as well as a 790 GX/FX chipset from the [AMD 700 chipset series](AMD_700_chipset_series "AMD 700 chipset series").[[120]](AMD#cite_note-120) The Phenom II came in dual-core, triple-core and quad-core variants, all using the same die, with cores disabled for the triple-core and dual-core versions. The Phenom II resolved issues that the original Phenom had, including a low clock speed, a small L3 cache, and a <Cool'n'Quiet> bug that decreased performance. The Phenom II cost less but was not performance-competitive with Intel's mid-to-high-range [Core 2](Core_2 "Core 2") Quads. The Phenom II also enhanced its predecessor's memory controller, allowing it to use <DDR3> in a new native socket <AM3>, while maintaining backward compatibility with [AM2+](AM2%2B "AM2+"), the socket used for the Phenom, and allowing the use of the [DDR2](DDR2_SDRAM "DDR2 SDRAM") memory that was used with the platform.

In April 2010, AMD released a new Phenom II Hexa-core (6-core) processor codenamed "[Thuban](Phenom_X6 "Phenom X6")".[[121]](AMD#cite_note-121) This was a totally new die based on the hexa-core "Istanbul" <Opteron> processor. It included AMD's "turbo core" technology, which allows the processor to automatically switch from 6 cores to 3 faster cores when more pure speed is needed.

The [Magny Cours](List_of_AMD_Opteron_microprocessors "List of AMD Opteron microprocessors") and [Lisbon](List_of_AMD_Opteron_microprocessors "List of AMD Opteron microprocessors") server parts were released in 2010.[[122]](AMD#cite_note-Opteron6100Series-122) The Magny Cours part came in 8 to 12 cores and the Lisbon part in 4 and 6 core parts. Magny Cours is focused on performance while the Lisbon part is focused on high performance per watt. Magny Cours is an MCM ([multi-chip module](Multi-chip_module "Multi-chip module")) with two hexa-core "Istanbul" <Opteron> parts. This will use a new [socket G34](Socket_G34 "Socket G34") for dual and quad-socket processors and thus will be marketed as Opteron 61xx series processors. Lisbon uses [socket C32](Socket_C32 "Socket C32") certified for dual-socket use or single socket use only and thus will be marketed as Opteron 41xx processors. Both will be built on a [45 nm](45_nm "45 nm") [SOI](Silicon_on_insulator "Silicon on insulator") process.

#### Fusion becomes the AMD APU

Main articles: [AMD APU](AMD_APU "AMD APU") and [AMD mobile platform](AMD_mobile_platform "AMD mobile platform")

Following AMD's 2006 acquisition of Canadian graphics company [ATI Technologies](ATI_Technologies "ATI Technologies"), an initiative codenamed *Fusion* was announced to integrate a <CPU> and <GPU> together on some of AMD's microprocessors, including a built in [PCI Express](PCI_Express "PCI Express") link to accommodate separate PCI Express peripherals, eliminating the [northbridge](Northbridge_(computing) "Northbridge (computing)") chip from the motherboard. The initiative intended to move some of the processing originally done on the CPU (e.g. [floating-point unit](Floating-point_unit "Floating-point unit") operations) to the GPU, which is better optimized for some calculations. The Fusion was later renamed the [AMD APU](AMD_APU "AMD APU") (Accelerated Processing Unit).[[123]](AMD#cite_note-APU-123)

Llano was AMD's first APU built for laptops. Llano was the second APU released,[[124]](AMD#cite_note-Hruska-124) targeted at the mainstream market.[[123]](AMD#cite_note-APU-123) It incorporated a CPU and GPU on the same die, as well as northbridge functions, and used "[Socket FM1](Socket_FM1 "Socket FM1")" with <DDR3> memory. The CPU part of the processor was based on the [Phenom II](Phenom_II "Phenom II") "Deneb" processor. AMD suffered an unexpected decrease in revenue based on production problems for the Llano.[[125]](AMD#cite_note-125) More AMD APUs for laptops running Windows 7 and Windows 8 OS are being used commonly. These include AMD's price-point APUs, the E1 and E2, and their mainstream competitors with Intel's [Core i](Core_i "Core i")-series: The Vision A- series, the A standing for accelerated. These range from the lower-performance A4 chipset to the A6, A8, and A10. These all incorporate next-generation Radeon graphics cards, with the A4 utilizing the base Radeon HD chip and the rest using a Radeon R4 graphics card, with the exception of the highest-model A10 (A10-7300) which uses an R6 graphics card.

#### New microarchitectures

##### High-power, high-performance Bulldozer cores

Main articles: [Bulldozer microarchitecture](Bulldozer_(microarchitecture) "Bulldozer (microarchitecture)"), [Piledriver microarchitecture](Piledriver_(microarchitecture) "Piledriver (microarchitecture)"), [Steamroller microarchitecture](Steamroller_(microarchitecture) "Steamroller (microarchitecture)"), and [Excavator microarchitecture](Excavator_(microarchitecture) "Excavator (microarchitecture)")

Bulldozer was AMD's microarchitecture codename for server and desktop [AMD FX](AMD_FX "AMD FX") processors, first released on October 12, 2011. This [family 15h microarchitecture](Zen_4 "Zen 4") is the successor to the [family 10h (K10)](AMD_10h "AMD 10h") microarchitecture design. Bulldozer was a clean-sheet design, not a development of earlier processors.[[126]](AMD#cite_note-126) The core was specifically aimed at 10–125 W [TDP](Thermal_Design_Power "Thermal Design Power") computing products. AMD claimed dramatic performance-per-watt efficiency improvements in [high-performance computing](High-performance_computing "High-performance computing") (HPC) applications with Bulldozer cores. While hopes were high that Bulldozer would bring AMD to be performance-competitive with Intel once more, most benchmarks were disappointing. In some cases the new Bulldozer products were slower than the K10 models they were built to replace.[[127]](AMD#cite_note-127)[[128]](AMD#cite_note-128)[[129]](AMD#cite_note-129)

The [Piledriver microarchitecture](Piledriver_(microarchitecture) "Piledriver (microarchitecture)") was the 2012 successor to Bulldozer, increasing clock speeds and performance relative to its predecessor.[[130]](AMD#cite_note-130) Piledriver would be released in AMD FX, APU, and Opteron product lines.[[131]](AMD#cite_note-131)[[132]](AMD#cite_note-132)[[133]](AMD#cite_note-133)[[134]](AMD#cite_note-134) Piledriver was subsequently followed by the [Steamroller microarchitecture](Steamroller_(microarchitecture) "Steamroller (microarchitecture)") in 2013. Used exclusively in AMD's APUs, Steamroller focused on greater parallelism.[[135]](AMD#cite_note-anandtech-kaveri-review-135)[[136]](AMD#cite_note-136)

In 2015, the [Excavator microarchitecture](Excavator_(microarchitecture) "Excavator (microarchitecture)") replaced Piledriver.[[137]](AMD#cite_note-PCWorld-137) Expected to be the last microarchitecture of the Bulldozer series,[[138]](AMD#cite_note-138)[[139]](AMD#cite_note-139) Excavator focused on improved power efficiency.[[140]](AMD#cite_note-140)

Main articles: [Bobcat microarchitecture](Bobcat_(microarchitecture) "Bobcat (microarchitecture)"), [Jaguar microarchitecture](Jaguar_(microarchitecture) "Jaguar (microarchitecture)"), and [Puma microarchitecture](Puma_(microarchitecture) "Puma (microarchitecture)")
