## Divisions

Today, TI is made up of four divisions: [analog products](Analog_electronics "Analog electronics"), [embedded processors](Embedded_processor "Embedded processor"), [digital light processing](Digital_light_processing "Digital light processing"), and [educational technology](Educational_technology "Educational technology").[[69]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ti.com-69)

As of January 2021, the industrial market accounts for 41 percent of the company's annual revenue while the automotive market accounts for 21 percent.[[16]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-ED-16)

### Other businesses

TI's remaining businesses consisting of DLP products (primarily used in projectors to create high-definition images), calculators and certain custom semiconductors known as application-specific integrated circuits.

#### DLP Products

DLP is a trademark under which Texas Instruments sells technology regarding TVs, video projectors, and [digital cinema](Digital_cinema "Digital cinema"). On February 2, 2000, Philippe Binant, technical manager of Digital Cinema Project at [Gaumont](Gaumont_Film_Company "Gaumont Film Company") in France, realized the first digital cinema projection in Europe with the DLP CINEMA technology developed by TI DLP technology enables a diverse range of display and advanced light control applications spanning industrial, enterprise, automotive, and consumer market segments.

Custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs)

The ASICs business develops more complex integrated-circuit solutions for clients on a custom basis.

#### Educational technology

TI has produced educational toys for children, including the [Little Professor](Little_Professor "Little Professor") in 1976 and <Dataman> in 1977.[[70]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-70)[[71]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-71)

TI produces a range of calculators, with the <TI-30> being one of the most popular early [calculators](Calculator "Calculator"). TI has also developed a line of [graphing calculators](Graphing_calculator "Graphing calculator"), the first being the <TI-81>, and most popular being the [TI-83 Plus](TI-83_Plus "TI-83 Plus") (with the [TI-84 Plus](TI-84_Plus "TI-84 Plus") being an updated equivalent).

Many TI calculators are still sold without graphing capabilities.[[72]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-72) The TI-30 has been replaced by the [TI-30X IIS](TI-30 "TI-30"). Also, some financial calculators are for sale on the TI website.

In 2007, TI released the <TI-Nspire> family of calculators and computer software that has similar capabilities to the calculators.

Less than 3% of Texas Instruments’ overall revenue comes from calculators, part of the $1.43 billion revenue in the "Other" section in the company's 2018 annual report. Nevertheless, the calculators are a lucrative product. For example, estimates have a $15 to $20 cost to produce TI-84 Plus which likely has a profit margin of at least 50%.

Throughout the 1980s, Texas Instruments worked closely with National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) to develop a calculator to become the educational standard. In 1986, Connecticut School Board became the first to require a graphing calculator on state-mandated exams. Chicago Public Schools gave a free calculator to every student, beginning in the fourth grade, in 1988. New York required the calculator in 1992 for its Regents exams after first allowing it the previous year. The College Board required calculators on the Advanced Placement tests in 1993 and allowed calculators on the SAT a year later. Texas Instruments provides free services to the College Board, which administers AP tests and the SAT, and also has a group called Teachers Teaching for Technology (T3), which educates teachers on how to use its calculators.[[20]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TIcalcsMedium-20)

#### TI calculator community

In the 1990s, with the advent of TI's graphing calculator series, programming became popular among some students. The TI-8x series of calculators (beginning with the TI-81) came with a built-in [BASIC](TI-BASIC "TI-BASIC") interpreter, through which simple programs could be created. The TI-83 was the first in the series to receive native assembly.[[73]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-73) Around the same time that these programs were first being written, programmers began creating websites to host their work, along with tutorials and other calculator-relevant information. This led to the formation of TI calculator [webrings](Webrings "Webrings") and eventually a few large communities, including ticalc.org.[[74]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-74)[[75]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-75)[[76]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-root.cz-76)

The TI community reached the height of its popularity in the early 2000s, with many new websites and programming groups being started. In fact, the aforementioned community sites were exploding with activity, with close to 100 programs being uploaded daily by users of the sites. Also, a competition existed between both sites to be the top site in the community, which helped increase interest and activity in the community.

One of the common unifying forces that has united the community over the years has been the rather contentious relationship with TI regarding control over its graphing calculators. TI graphing calculators generally fall into two distinct groups—the older ones powered by the [Zilog Z80](Zilog_Z80 "Zilog Z80") and the newer ones running on the [Motorola 68000](Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") series.[[76]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-root.cz-76) Both lines of calculators are locked by TI with checks in the hardware and through the signing of software to disable use of custom operating systems. However, users discovered the keys and published them in 2009. TI responded by sending invalid <DMCA> [takedown notices](Takedown_notice "Takedown notice"), causing the [Texas Instruments signing key controversy](Texas_Instruments_signing_key_controversy "Texas Instruments signing key controversy").[[77]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-77)

Adcock, who like Teal was a [physical chemist](Physical_chemist "Physical chemist"), began leading a small research group focused on the task of fabricating grown-junction, [silicon](Silicon "Silicon"), single-crystal, small-signal transistors.[[23]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-transistor-23) Adcock later became the first TI Principal Fellow.[[24]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-Tribute-24)

#### First silicon transistor and integrated circuits

In January 1954, [Morris Tanenbaum](Morris_Tanenbaum "Morris Tanenbaum") at Bell Telephone Laboratories created the first workable silicon transistor.[[23]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-transistor-23) This work was reported in the spring of 1954, at the IRE off-the-record conference on solid-state devices, and was later published in the *Journal of Applied Physics*. Working independently in April 1954, Gordon Teal at TI created the first commercial silicon transistor and tested it on April 14, 1954. On May 10, 1954, at the Institute of Radio Engineers National Conference on Airborne Electronics in Dayton, Ohio, Teal presented a paper: "Some Recent Developments in Silicon and Germanium Materials and Devices".[[25]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-25)

In 1954, Texas Instruments designed and manufactured the first [transistor radio](Transistor_radio "Transistor radio"). The [Regency TR-1](Regency_TR-1 "Regency TR-1") used germanium transistors, as silicon transistors were much more expensive at the time. This was an effort by Haggerty to increase market demand for transistors.

[Jack Kilby](Jack_Kilby "Jack Kilby"), an employee at TI, invented the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") in 1958.[[26]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-26) Kilby recorded his initial ideas concerning the integrated circuit in July 1958, and successfully demonstrated the world's first working integrated circuit on September 12, 1958.[[27]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-27) Six months later, [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce") of [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") (who went on to co-found <Intel>) independently developed the integrated circuit with integrated interconnect, and is also considered an inventor of the integrated circuit.[[28]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-28) In 1969, Kilby was awarded the National Medal of Science, and in 1982 he was inducted into the National Inventor's Hall of Fame.[[29]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-29) Kilby also won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for his part of the invention of the integrated circuit.[[30]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-30) Noyce's chip, made at Fairchild, was made of silicon, while Kilby's chip was made of [germanium](Germanium "Germanium"). In 2008, TI named its new development laboratory "Kilby Labs" after Jack Kilby.[[31]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-31)

In 2011, Intel, Samsung, LG, ST-Ericsson, Huawei's HiSilicon Technologies subsidiary, Via Telecom, and three other undisclosed chipmakers licensed the C2C link specification developed by Arteris Inc. and Texas Instruments.[[32]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-32)

#### Standard TTL

The [7400 series](7400_series "7400 series") of [transistor-transistor logic](Transistor-transistor_logic "Transistor-transistor logic") chips, developed by Texas Instruments in the 1960s, popularized the use of integrated circuits in computer logic. The military-grade version of this was the 5400 series.[[33]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-33)

#### Microprocessor

Texas Instruments invented the hand-held [calculator](Calculator "Calculator") (a prototype called "[Cal Tech](Cal_Tech_(calculator) "Cal Tech (calculator)")") in 1967 and the single-chip [microcomputer](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1971, was assigned the first patent on a single-chip [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") (invented by Gary Boone) on September 4, 1973.[[34]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-34) This was disputed by Gilbert Hyatt, formerly of the Micro Computer Company, in August 1990, when he was awarded a patent superseding TI's. This was overturned on June 19, 1996, in favor of TI[[35]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-35) (note: <Intel> is usually given credit with Texas Instruments for the almost-simultaneous invention of the microprocessor).

#### First speech synthesis chip

In 1978, Texas Instruments introduced the first single-chip [linear predictive coding](Linear_predictive_coding "Linear predictive coding") [speech synthesizer](Speech_synthesizer "Speech synthesizer").[[36]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-36) In 1976, TI began a feasibility study of memory-intensive applications for bubble memory then being developed. They soon focused on speech applications. This resulted in the development the TMC0280 one-chip linear predictive coding speech synthesizer, which was the first time a single silicon chip had electronically replicated the human voice.[[37]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TITimeLine-37)[[38]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-38) This was used in several TI commercial products beginning with [Speak & Spell](Speak_%26_Spell_(toy) "Speak & Spell (toy)"), which was introduced at the Summer Consumer Electronics Show in June 1978. In 2001, TI left the speech synthesis business, selling it to Sensory Inc. of Santa Clara, California.[[39]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TI_will_exit_dedicated_speech-synthesis_chips,_transfer_products_to_Sensory-39)

### Consumer electronics and computers

In May 1954, Texas Instruments designed and built a prototype of the world's first [transistor radio](Transistor_radio "Transistor radio"), and, through a partnership with Industrial Development Engineering Associates of Indianapolis, Indiana, the 100% solid-state radio was sold to the public beginning in October of that year.[[40]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-40)

In the 1960s, company president Pat Haggerty had a team that included Jack Kilby to work on a handheld calculator project. Kilby and two other colleagues created the Cal-Tech, a three-pound battery-powered calculator that could do basic math and fit six-digit numbers on its display. This 4.25 x 6.15 x 1.75 inch calculator's processor would originate the vast majority of Texas Instruments’ revenue.[[20]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-TIcalcsMedium-20)

In 1973, the handheld calculator SR-10 (named after [slide rule](Slide_rule "Slide rule")) and in 1974, the handheld scientific calculator [SR-50](TI_SR-50 "TI SR-50") were issued by TI. Both had red LED-segments numeric displays. The optical design of the SR-50 is somewhat similar to the <HP-35> edited by <Hewlett-Packard> before in early 1972, but buttons for the operations "+", "–", ... are in the right of the number block and the decimal point lies between two neighboring digits.

TI continued to be active in the consumer electronics market through the 1970s and 1980s. Early on, this also included two digital clock models – one for desk and the other a bedside alarm. From this sprang what became the Time Products Division, which made LED watches. Though these LED watches enjoyed early commercial success due to excellent quality, it was short-lived due to poor battery life. LEDs were replaced with LCD watches for a short time, but these could not compete because of styling issues, excessive makes and models, and price points. The watches were manufactured in <Dallas> and then [Lubbock, Texas](Lubbock%2C_Texas "Lubbock, Texas"). Several spin-offs of the [Speak & Spell](Speak_%26_Spell_(toy) "Speak & Spell (toy)"), such as the [Speak & Read](Speak_%26_Read "Speak & Read") and [Speak & Math](Speak_%26_Math "Speak & Math"), were introduced soon thereafter.[[41]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-41)

In 1979, TI entered the [home computer](Home_computer "Home computer") market with the [TI-99/4](TI-99/4A "TI-99/4A"), a competitor to such entries as the [Apple II](Apple_II_series "Apple II series"), <TRS-80>, and the later [Atari 400/800](Atari_8-bit_family "Atari 8-bit family") series and <VIC-20>. By late 1982, TI was dominating the U.S. home computer market, shipping 5,000 computers a day from their factory in Lubbock.[[42]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-death_1984_04_texasmonthly-42) It discontinued the <TI-99/4A> (1981), the sequel to the 99/4, in late 1983 amid an intense [price war](North_American_video_game_crash_of_1983 "North American video game crash of 1983") waged primarily against Commodore. At the 1983 Winter CES, TI showed models 99/2 and the [Compact Computer 40 (CC-40)](Compact_Computer_40 "Compact Computer 40"), the latter aimed at professional users. The [TI Professional](Texas_Instruments_Professional_Portable_Computer "Texas Instruments Professional Portable Computer") (1983) ultimately joined the ranks of the many unsuccessful <DOS> and [x86](X86 "X86")-based—but [non-compatible](PC_compatible "PC compatible")[[43]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-Inc.1984-43)—competitors to the [IBM PC](IBM_Personal_Computer "IBM Personal Computer") (the founders of <Compaq>, an early leader in PC compatibles, all came from TI). The company for years successfully made and sold PC-compatible laptops before withdrawing from the market and selling its product line to [Acer](Acer_Inc. "Acer Inc.") in 1998.[[44]](Texas_Instruments#cite_note-44)

### Defense electronics

**Texas Instruments TMS320** is a blanket name for a series of [digital signal processors](Digital_signal_processor "Digital signal processor") (DSPs) from [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"). It was introduced on April 8, 1983 through the TMS32010 processor, which was then the fastest DSP on the market.

The processor is available in many different variants, some with [fixed-point arithmetic](Fixed-point_arithmetic "Fixed-point arithmetic") and some with [floating point arithmetic](Floating_point "Floating point"). The TMS320 processors were [fabricated](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication") on [MOS integrated circuit](MOS_integrated_circuit "MOS integrated circuit") chips, including both [NMOS](NMOS_logic "NMOS logic") and <CMOS> variants. The floating point DSP TMS320C3x, which exploits [delayed branch logic](Delayed_branch_logic "Delayed branch logic"), has as many as three [delay slots](Branch_delay_slot "Branch delay slot").

The flexibility of this line of processors has led to it being used not merely as a co-processor for [digital signal processing](Digital_signal_processing "Digital signal processing") but also as a main CPU. Newer implementations support standard IEEE <JTAG> control for boundary scan and/or in-circuit debugging.

The original TMS32010 and its subsequent variants is an example of a CPU with a [modified Harvard architecture](Modified_Harvard_architecture "Modified Harvard architecture"), which features separate address spaces for instruction and data memory but the ability to read data values from instruction memory. The TMS32010 featured a fast [multiply-and-accumulate](Multiply%E2%80%93accumulate "Multiply–accumulate") operation useful in both DSP applications as well as transformations used in computer graphics. The graphics controller card for the [Apollo Computer](Apollo_Computer "Apollo Computer") DN570 Workstation, released in 1985, was based on the TMS32010 and could transform 20,000 2D vectors every second.

## Variants

The TMS320 architecture has been around for a while so a number of product variants have developed. The product codes used by Texas Instruments after the first TMS32010 processor have involved a very popular series of processor named TMS320Cabcd where *a* is the main series, *b* the generation and *cd* is some custom number for a minor sub-variant.

For this reason people working with DSPs often abbreviate a processor as "C5x" when the actual name is something like TMS320C5510, since all products obviously have the name "TMS320" and all processors with "C5" in the name are [code compatible](Binary_code_compatibility "Binary code compatibility") and share the same basic features. Sometimes you will even hear people talking about "C55x" and similar subgroupings, since processors in the same series and same generation are even more similar.

The TMS320 processors are [fabricated](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication") on [MOS integrated circuit](MOS_integrated_circuit "MOS integrated circuit") chips, including both [NMOS](NMOS_logic "NMOS logic") and <CMOS> variants.[[1]](Texas_Instruments_TMS320#cite_note-1)

### Legacy series

- TMS320C1x, first generation 16-bit [fixed-point](Fixed-point_arithmetic "Fixed-point arithmetic") DSPs. All processors in these series are code-compatible with the TMS32010.
  * TMS32010, the very first processor in the first series introduced in 1983, using external memory
  * TMS320M10, the same processor but with an internal [ROM](Read_only_memory "Read only memory") of 3 KB
  * TMS320C10, TMS320C15, TMS320C25, etc.
- TMS320C3x, 32-bit floating point
  * TMS320C30, 27 to 50 MHz, 8 KB internal SRAM, 5 Volt.
  * TMS320C31, 27 to 60 MHz, 8 KB internal SRAM, 5 Volt, subset of TMS320C30 by removing 2nd serial port, removing 2nd memory bus, replacing user ROM with factory ROM bootloader.
  * TMS320LC31, 33 to 40 MHz, 3.3 Volt version of TMS320C31.
  * TMS320C32, 40 to 60 MHz, 2 KB internal SRAM, 5 Volt, adds 2nd DMA coprocessor, changes external memory bus to allow 8/16/32-bit wide memory access where as other C3x parts are 32-bit only.
  * TMS320VC33, 60 to 75 MHz, 136 KB internal SRAM, 3.3 Volt I/O with 1.8 Volt Core, superset of TMS320C31 by adding 128KB internal SRAM.
- TMS320C4x, 32-bit floating point
  * TMS320C40, 40/50/60/80 MHz, cycle time 50/40/33/25 ns, <CMOS>[[2]](Texas_Instruments_TMS320#cite_note-2)
  * TMS320C44, subset of TMS320C40
- TMS320C8x, multiprocessor chip[[3]](Texas_Instruments_TMS320#cite_note-3)
  * TMS320C80 MVP (multimedia video processor) has a 32 bit floating-point "master processor" and four 32-bit fixed-point "slave processors". In many ways the [Cell microprocessor](Cell_microprocessor "Cell microprocessor") followed this design approach.


### C2000 series

- C2000 microcontroller family consists of 32-bit microcontrollers with performance integrated peripherals designed for real-time control applications. C2000 consists of 5 sub-families: the newer C28x + ARM Cortex M3 series, C28x Delfino floating-point series, C28x Piccolo series, C28x fixed-point series, and C240x, an older 16-bit line that is no longer recommended for new development. The C2000 series is notable for its high performance set of on-chip control peripherals including [PWM](Pulse-width_modulation "Pulse-width modulation"), [ADC](Analog-to-digital_converter "Analog-to-digital converter"), [quadrature encoder](Quadrature_encoder "Quadrature encoder") modules, and capture modules. The series also contains support for [I²C](I%C2%B2C "I²C"), [SPI](Serial_Peripheral_Interface_Bus "Serial Peripheral Interface Bus"), serial (SCI), [CAN](CAN_bus "CAN bus"), [watchdog](Watchdog_timer "Watchdog timer"), McBSP, external memory interface and GPIO. Due to features like PWM waveform synchronization with the ADC unit, the C2000 line is well suited to many real-time control applications. The C2000 family is used for applications like motor drive and control, industrial automation, solar and other renewable energy, server farms, digital power, [power-line communications](Power-line_communication "Power-line communication"), and lighting. A line of low cost kits are available for key applications including motor control, digital power, solar, and LED lighting.


### C5000 series

- TMS320C54x 16-bit fixed-point DSP, 6 stage pipeline with in-order-execution of opcodes, parallel load/store on arithmetic operations, multiply accumulate and other DSP enhancements. Internal multi-port memory. no cache unit.[[4]](Texas_Instruments_TMS320#cite_note-4)
  * A popular choice for <2G> Software defined cellphone radios, particularly <GSM>, circa late 1990s when many <Nokia> and <Ericsson> cellphones made use of the C54x.
  * At the time, desire to improve the user interface of cellphones led to the adoption of <ARM7> as a general-purpose processor for user interface and control, off-loading this function from the DSP. This ultimately led to the creation of a dual core ARM7+C54x DSP, which later evolved into the OMAP product line.
- TMS320C55x generation – fixed-point, runs C54x code but adds more internal parallelism (another ALU, dual MAC, more memory bandwidth) and registers, while supporting much lower power operation.
  * Today, most C55x DSPs are sold as discrete chips
  * [OMAP1](OMAP "OMAP") chips combine an <ARM9> (ARMv5TEJ) with a C55x series DSP.
  * [OMAP2420](OMAP "OMAP") chips combine an <ARM11> (ARMv6) with a C55x series DSP.


### C6000 series

- TMS320 C6000 series, or TMS320C6x: <VLIW>-based DSPs
  * TMS320C62x fixed-point – 2000 MIPS/1.9 [W](Watt "Watt")
  * TMS320C67x floating point – code compatible with TMS320C62x
  * TMS320C64x fixed-point – code compatible with TMS320C62x
  * TMS320C67x+ floating point – architectural update of TMS320C67x
  * TMS320C64x+ fixed-point – major architectural update of TMS320C64x
  * TMS320C674x fixed- and floating point – merger of C64x+ and C67x+
  * TMS320C66x fixed- and floating point – backwards compatible with C674x
- Other parts with C6000 series DSPs include
  * [DaVinci](Texas_Instruments_DaVinci "Texas Instruments DaVinci") chips include one or both of an <ARM9> and a C64x+ or C674x DSP
  * [OMAP-L13x](OMAP "OMAP") chips include an <ARM9> (ARMv5TEJ) and a C674x fixed and floating point DSP
  * [OMAP243x](OMAP "OMAP") chips combine an <ARM11> (ARMv6) with a C64x series DSP
  * [OMAP3](OMAP "OMAP") chips include an ARM Cortex-A8 (ARMv7) with a C64x+ DSP
  * [OMAP4 and OMAP5](OMAP "OMAP") chips include an ARM Cortex-A9 or A15 (ARMv7) with a custom C64x+ derivative known as Tesla (or C64T)


### C7000 series

The C7000 series was released in early 2020, but cores are not available individually. As of August 2023, they are only available bundled inside other SOCs, such as the [TDA4VM](https://www.ti.com/product/TDA4VM), which features a C71x DSP.

### DaVinci series

- The [DaVinci series](Texas_Instruments_DaVinci "Texas Instruments DaVinci") started with [systems-on-a-chip](System-on-a-chip "System-on-a-chip") using an embedded C6000 series (C64x+) DSP, <ARM9> application processors, and Digital Media peripherals. There are variants without ARMs, and without DSPs. Their marketing focuses on their video processing capabilities. Original chips supported NTSC and PAL, while newer ones support HDTV.


### OMAP variants

- <OMAP> variants also have an [ARM](ARM_architecture "ARM architecture") processor in the same chip; see the main article on [Texas Instruments OMAP](Texas_Instruments_OMAP "Texas Instruments OMAP"). (There are also OMAP processors with other secondary processors, so these are not necessarily DSPs.)


### DA variants

- DA variants (target "Digital audio")
  * DA25x is an [ARM](ARM_architecture "ARM architecture") processor and a C55x core. It has some on

The **TMS1000** is a family of [microcontrollers](Microcontroller "Microcontroller") introduced by [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") in 1974.[[1]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-1)[[2]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-2)[[3]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-3)

It combined a 4-bit [central processor unit](Central_processor_unit "Central processor unit"), read-only memory (ROM), random access memory (RAM), and input/output (I/O) lines as a complete "computer on a chip". It was intended for [embedded systems](Embedded_system "Embedded system") in automobiles, appliances, games, and measurement instruments.

It was the first high-volume commercial microcontroller (As described later, the predecessor TMS0100 series may not be regarded as microcontrollers). In 1974, chips in this family could be purchased in volume for around $2 each.[[4]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-RZ09-4) By 1979 about 26 million parts in this family were sold every year.[[5]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-5)

The TMS 1000 was used in Texas Instruments' own [*Speak & Spell*](Speak_%26_Spell_(toy) "Speak & Spell (toy)") educational toy,[[4]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-RZ09-4) the [Big Trak](Big_Trak "Big Trak") programmable toy vehicle and in the electronic game [Simon](Simon_(game) "Simon (game)").[[6]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-6)

## History

### TMS 0100 series

The [Smithsonian Institution](Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution") says [TI](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments") engineers Gary Boone and Michael Cochran succeeded in creating the first microcontroller (also called a microcomputer) in 1971. The TMS1802NC was a single-chip microcontroller which was announced September 17, 1971 and implemented a four-function calculator. The TMS1802NC, despite its designation, was not part of the TMS 1000 series; it was later redesignated TMS0102 as part of the TMS 0100 series,[[7]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-ti_calc_chips-7) which was used in the TI Datamath calculator and the [Sinclair Executive](Sinclair_Executive "Sinclair Executive") calculator.[[8]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-8)

The TMS0100 series may not be considered microcontrollers.[[9]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-9) This is because it cannot be used for purposes other than calculators, and cannot execute user-created programs.

### TMS 1000 series

The later TMS 1000 series went on the market in 1974. TI stressed the 4-bit TMS 1000 for use in pre-programmed embedded applications.[[10]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-10)[[11]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-11)[[12]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-12)[[13]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-13)[[14]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-14)

A computer-on-a-chip combines the microprocessor core (CPU), memory, and I/O ([input/output](Input/output "Input/output")) lines onto one [chip](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit"). The computer-on-a-chip patent, called the "microcomputer patent" at the time, [U.S. Patent 4,074,351](https://patents.google.com/patent/US4074351), was awarded to Gary Boone and Michael J. Cochran of TI. Aside from this patent, the standard meaning of [microcomputer](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") is a computer using one or more microprocessors as its CPU(s), while the concept defined in the patent is more akin to a microcontroller.

## Description

|
| --- |
*TMS1000 registers*

| - 09 08 07 06 05 04 03 02 01 00 *(bit position)* - A accumulator - X Y mem pointer - page add program ctr next instruction - page buff subroutine ret long branch/return - **Branch status flags** - [C](Carry_flag "Carry flag") [S](Carry_flag "Carry flag") call latch/branch |


The TMS1000 family eventually included variants in both the original [PMOS](PMOS_logic "PMOS logic") logic and also in [NMOS](NMOS_logic "NMOS logic") and <CMOS>. Product variations included different sizes of ROM and RAM, different I/O counts, and ROMless versions intended for development or for use with external ROM. The original TMS1000 had 1024 x 8 bits of ROM, 64 x 4 bits of RAM, and 23 input/output lines.

The TMS1000 family used [mask-programmed ROM](Mask_ROM "Mask ROM"). Once the user had a debugged program ready to be committed to production, it would send the program to Texas Instruments who would then make a special mask to program the on-chip ROM. The ROM could not be altered in the field; the contents were fixed by the patterns laid down on the chip by the manufacturer. While this process had a high initial cost, the production cost was very low, making it suitable for high volume products (say, more than a few thousand items sold per year).

All internal data paths of the processor were 4 bits wide. Program ROM and data RAM were separately addressed as in a [Harvard architecture](Harvard_architecture "Harvard architecture"); this became a typical characteristic of microcontrollers by many other manufacturers.

The [ALU](Arithmetic_logic_unit "Arithmetic logic unit") had a carry flag to indicate overflow and facilitate multiple precision arithmetic. On-chip RAM was addressed by X and Y registers, where Y had 4 bits and X had either 2 or 3 bits depending on the size of RAM on the part. The program counter was 6 bits wide, with "page" and "chapter" registers to address up to 2 KB of ROM program memory.

No stack was provided, but a register was provided to store the program counter and carry flag to allow for one level of [subroutine](Subroutine "Subroutine") (some members of the family allowed for 2 or 3 levels). No interrupt facility was provided.

Some models had as few as 4 I/O lines because they had no on-chip ROM and the limited number of package pins were needed to access off-chip program memory. One version had special outputs for driving a [vacuum fluorescent display](Vacuum_fluorescent_display "Vacuum fluorescent display"), and a [programmable logic array](Programmable_logic_array "Programmable logic array") useful for driving [seven segment displays](Seven_segment_display "Seven segment display"). Four input lines were provided for purposes such as sensing keyboard inputs, and a varying number of output lines were provided to control external devices, or to scan the rows of a keyboard.

PMOS versions ran on -9 or -15 volts and consumed around 6 mA, Output logic levels were therefore not compatible with [TTL logic](TTL_logic "TTL logic"). The NMOS and CMOS parts ran on a TTL-style +5 volts and could interoperate with 5 volt logic.

Instruction sets varied slightly by model, with 43 instructions in the basic set and 54 available in some family members; instructions were 8 bits long. [BCD](Binary-coded_decimal "Binary-coded decimal") arithmetic instructions were provided, but no instructions were available for logical AND or OR of registers.

Each instruction took between 10 and 15 microseconds to execute on the NMOS and PMOS parts, but some CMOS parts could be run as fast as 6 microseconds. The internal oscillator gave an effective clock speed of around 0.3 megahertz.

The TMS1000 parts were packaged in through-hole [dual in-line packages](Dual_in-line_package "Dual in-line package") with 28 or 40 pins, but some models for prototyping were in 64-pin packages. All versions had a temperature range of 0 to 70 degrees C.

Since these were intended as single-chip embedded systems, no special support chips [UARTs](UART "UART"), etc. were specifically made in the TMS 1000 family.[[15]](Texas_Instruments_TMS1000#cite_note-15)

Based on my comprehensive search of Wikipedia, I found substantial information about Texas Instruments' activities in the 1990s, though specific quantitative data on production volumes and exact market share percentages for that decade is not available in Wikipedia articles. Here's what I found:

## Texas Instruments in the 1990s: Key Information

### **DSP (Digital Signal Processor) Business**
- **TMS320 Series**: TI's TMS320 DSP family, introduced in 1983, was the dominant force during the 1990s
- The **TMS320C54x** 16-bit fixed-point DSP became very popular in the **late 1990s** for 2G software-defined cellphone radios, particularly used by **Nokia and Ericsson** in their GSM phones
- TI made several strategic DSP acquisitions in the late 1990s to strengthen its position:
  - **1998**: Acquired GO DSP
  - **1999**: Acquired Libit Signal Processing Ltd. (Israel) for ~$365 million
  - **1999**: Acquired Butterfly VLSI, Ltd. for ~$50 million
  - **1999**: Acquired Telogy Networks for $457 million

### **Microcontroller Production**
- TI invented the **first single-chip microcontroller in 1970**
- The TMS1000 family (introduced 1974) sold approximately 26 million units annually by 1979 (though this is from the 1970s, not the 1990s)
- TI continued producing microcontrollers throughout the 1990s as part of what would become their "embedded processors" division

### **Overall Semiconductor Market Position**
- TI is noted as "one of the **top 10 semiconductor companies worldwide** based on sales volume" (Wikipedia states this generally, not 1990s-specific)
- **1997**: TI sold its defense business to **Raytheon**, allowing the company to "strengthen its focus on digital solutions"
- **1999**: TI announced restatement of results for parts of 1998 and Q1 1999 after SEC review

### **1990s Financial Context**
From acquisition data and financial information:
- The company made significant semiconductor-related acquisitions throughout the late 1990s
- **2005** revenue: ~$12.3 billion (first year with available financial data in the article)
- By the end of the 1990s, TI was transitioning toward its modern focus on **analog chips and embedded processors** (which today accounts for 80%+ of revenue)

### **Additional 1990s Business Activities**
- **1990**: TI released the TI-81 calculator, becoming a leader in the graphing calculator industry
- **1996**: Acquired Tartan, Inc.
- **1997**: Acquired Amati Communications for $395 million
- **1998**: Acquired standard logic product lines from Harris Semiconductor (including CD4000, HC4xxx, HCT, FCT, and ACT product families)

## Limitations
Unfortunately, Wikipedia articles don't contain the specific quantitative data you requested about:
- Exact DSP sales figures in dollars for the 1990s
- Specific microcontroller production volumes for the 1990s
- Exact market share percentages during 1990-1999

This type of historical market data would typically be found in:
- Industry analyst reports from Gartner/DataQuest from the 1990s
- TI's annual reports/10-K filings from that era (available on SEC EDGAR)
- Business history books focusing on the semiconductor industry

In deciding on a name, Moore and Noyce quickly rejected "Moore Noyce",[[41]](Intel#cite_note-42) near [homophone](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/homophone "wikt:homophone") for "more noise" – an ill-suited name for an [electronics](Electronics "Electronics") company, since [noise in electronics](Electronic_noise "Electronic noise") is usually undesirable and typically associated with bad [interference](Electromagnetic_interference "Electromagnetic interference"). Instead, they founded the company as **NM Electronics** (or **MN Electronics**) on July 18, 1968, but by the end of the month had changed the name to **Intel** which stood for **Int**egrated **El**ectronics.[[note 2]](Intel#cite_note-48) Since "Intel" was already trademarked by the hotel chain Intelco, they had to buy the rights for the name.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[47]](Intel#cite_note-49)

### Early history

At its founding, Intel was distinguished by its ability to make [logic circuits](Logic_circuit "Logic circuit") using [semiconductor devices](Semiconductor_device "Semiconductor device"). The founders' goal was the [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") market, widely predicted to replace [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory"). Its first product, a quick entry into the small, high-speed memory market in 1969, was the 3101 [Schottky TTL](Schottky_transistor "Schottky transistor") [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") 64-bit [static random-access memory](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") (SRAM), which was nearly twice as fast as earlier Schottky diode implementations by Fairchild and the Electrotechnical Laboratory in [Tsukuba, Japan](Tsukuba%2C_Ibaraki "Tsukuba, Ibaraki").[[48]](Intel#cite_note-50)[[49]](Intel#cite_note-51) In the same year, Intel also produced the 3301 Schottky bipolar 1024-bit [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM)[[50]](Intel#cite_note-52) and the first commercial [metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor](MOSFET "MOSFET") (MOSFET) [silicon gate](Silicon_gate "Silicon gate") SRAM chip, the 256-bit 1101.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[52]](Intel#cite_note-54)

While the 1101 was a significant advance, its complex static [cell structure](Memory_cell_(computing) "Memory cell (computing)") made it too slow and costly for [mainframe](Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") memories. The three-[transistor](Transistor "Transistor") cell implemented in the first commercially available [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM), the [1103](Intel_1103 "Intel 1103") released in 1970, solved these issues. The 1103 was the bestselling semiconductor memory chip in the world by 1972, as it replaced core memory in many applications.[[53]](Intel#cite_note-55)[[54]](Intel#cite_note-Bellis-56) Intel's business grew during the 1970s as it expanded and improved its manufacturing processes and produced a wider range of [products](Product_(business) "Product (business)"), still dominated by various memory devices.

Intel created the [first commercially available microprocessor (Intel 4004)](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") in 1971.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) The microprocessor represented a notable advance in the technology of integrated circuitry, as it miniaturized the central processing unit of a computer, which then made it possible for small machines to perform calculations that in the past only very large machines could do. Considerable technological innovation was needed before the microprocessor could actually become the basis of what was first known as a "mini computer" and then known as a "personal computer".[[55]](Intel#cite_note-57) Intel also created one of the first [microcomputers](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1973.[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[56]](Intel#cite_note-Intellec-1973-58)

Intel opened its first international manufacturing facility in 1972, in <Malaysia>, which would host multiple Intel operations, before opening assembly facilities and semiconductor plants in <Singapore> and <Jerusalem> in the early 1980s, and manufacturing and development centers in China, India, and Costa Rica in the 1990s.[[57]](Intel#cite_note-59) By the early 1980s, its business was dominated by [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM) chips. However, increased competition from Japanese semiconductor manufacturers had, by 1983, dramatically reduced the profitability of this market. The growing success of the <IBM> personal computer, based on an Intel microprocessor, was among factors that convinced Gordon Moore (CEO since 1975) to shift the company's focus to microprocessors and to change fundamental aspects of that business model. Moore's decision to sole-source Intel's 386 chip played into the company's continuing success.

By the end of the 1980s, buoyed by its fortuitous position as microprocessor supplier to IBM and IBM's competitors within the rapidly growing [personal computer market](IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible"), Intel embarked on a 10-year period of unprecedented growth as the primary (and most profitable) hardware supplier to the PC industry, part of the winning 'Wintel' combination. Moore handed over his position as CEO to Andy Grove in 1987. By launching its Intel Inside [marketing campaign](Marketing_campaign "Marketing campaign") in 1991, Intel was able to associate [brand loyalty](Brand_loyalty "Brand loyalty") with consumer selection, so that by the end of the 1990s, its line of <Pentium> processors had become a household name.

### Challenges to dominance (2000s)

After 2000, growth in demand for high-end microprocessors slowed. Competitors, most notably <AMD> (Intel's largest competitor in its primary [x86](X86 "X86") architecture market), garnered significant market share, initially in low-end and mid-range processors but ultimately across the product range, and Intel's dominant position in its core market was greatly reduced,[[58]](Intel#cite_note-Wong-60) mostly due to controversial <NetBurst> microarchitecture. In the early 2000s then-CEO, [Craig Barrett](Craig_Barrett_(businessman) "Craig Barrett (businessman)") attempted to diversify the company's business beyond semiconductors, but few of these activities were ultimately successful.

**Robert Norton Noyce** (December 12, 1927 – June 3, 1990), nicknamed "the Mayor of Silicon Valley", was an American physicist and entrepreneur who co-founded [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") in 1957 and [Intel Corporation](Intel_Corporation "Intel Corporation") in 1968. He was also credited with the realization of the first [monolithic integrated circuit](Monolithic_integrated_circuit "Monolithic integrated circuit") or microchip, which fueled the [personal computer revolution](Personal_computer_revolution "Personal computer revolution") and gave [Silicon Valley](Silicon_Valley "Silicon Valley") its name.[[nb 1]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-1)[[1]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Lécuyer,129-2)

## Early life

Noyce was born on December 12, 1927, in [Burlington, Iowa](Burlington%2C_Iowa "Burlington, Iowa")[[2]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Jones86-3)[[3]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Jones142-4)[[4]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,10-5)[[5]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Burt71-6)[[6]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Welles_Gaylord,130-7) the third of four sons[[4]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,10-5) of the Rev. Ralph Brewster Noyce.[[7]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Jones625-8) His father graduated from [Doane College](Doane_College "Doane College"), [Oberlin College](Oberlin_College "Oberlin College"), and the [Chicago Theological Seminary](Chicago_Theological_Seminary "Chicago Theological Seminary") and was also nominated for a [Rhodes Scholarship](Rhodes_Scholarship "Rhodes Scholarship").[[8]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,14-9)

His mother, Harriet May Norton, was the daughter of the Rev. Milton J. Norton, a [Congregational](Congregational_church "Congregational church") [clergyman](Clergy "Clergy"), and Louise Hill. She was a graduate of Oberlin College and prior to her marriage, she had dreams of becoming a missionary.[[9]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,9-10) Journalist [Tom Wolfe](Tom_Wolfe "Tom Wolfe") described her as "an intelligent woman with a commanding will".[[10]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Wolfe1-11)

Noyce had three siblings: Donald Sterling Noyce, Gaylord Brewster Noyce and Ralph Harold Noyce.[[4]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,10-5)[[11]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,12-12) His brother Donald would go on to become a respected professor and associate dean of undergraduate affairs in the [UC Berkeley College of Chemistry](UC_Berkeley_College_of_Chemistry "UC Berkeley College of Chemistry"); Robert later created the Donald Sterling Noyce Prize to reward excellence in undergraduate teaching at [Berkeley](Berkeley_High_School_(California) "Berkeley High School (California)").[[12]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-13) His brother Gaylord would go on to become a respected professor of [practical theology](Practical_theology "Practical theology") and dean of students at [Yale Divinity School](Yale_Divinity_School "Yale Divinity School"); in 1961, while a young professor, he was arrested for being one of the [Freedom Riders](Freedom_Riders "Freedom Riders") of the [civil rights movement](Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement").[[13]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-14)

Noyce's earliest childhood memory involved beating his father at [ping pong](Table_tennis "Table tennis") and feeling shocked when his mother reacted to the news of his victory with a distracted "Wasn't that nice of Daddy to let you win?" Even at the age of five, Noyce felt offended by the notion of intentionally losing. "That's not the game", he sulked to his mother. "If you're going to play, play to win!"[[11]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,12-12)

When Noyce was twelve years old in the summer of 1940, he and his brother built a boy-sized aircraft, which they used to fly from the roof of the Grinnell College stables. Later he built a radio from scratch and motorized his sled by welding a propeller and a motor from an old washing machine to the back of it.[[14]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,7-15) His parents were both religious but Noyce became an agnostic and irreligious in later life.[[15]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-16)

## Education

Noyce grew up in [Grinnell, Iowa](Grinnell%2C_Iowa "Grinnell, Iowa"). While in high school, he exhibited a talent for mathematics and science and took the [Grinnell College](Grinnell_College "Grinnell College") freshman physics course in his senior year. He graduated from Grinnell High School in 1945 and entered Grinnell College in the fall of that year. He was the star diver on the 1947 [Midwest Conference](Midwest_Conference "Midwest Conference") Championship swim team.[[10]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Wolfe1-11) While at Grinnell College, Noyce sang, played the oboe and acted. In Noyce's junior year, he got in trouble for stealing a 25-pound pig from the Grinnell mayor's farm and roasting it at a school [luau](Luau "Luau"). The mayor wrote to his parents stating that “In the agricultural state of Iowa, stealing a domestic animal is a felony which carries a minimum penalty of a year in prison and a fine of one dollar.” Noyce faced expulsion from school but [Grant Gale](Grant_Gale "Grant Gale"), Noyce's physics professor and president of the college, did not want to lose a student with Noyce's potential. They compromised with the mayor so that Grinnell would compensate him for the pig, and suspend Noyce for one semester. He returned in February 1949.[[16]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-17) He graduated [Phi Beta Kappa](Phi_Beta_Kappa "Phi Beta Kappa") with a BA in [physics](Physics "Physics") and [mathematics](Mathematics "Mathematics") in 1949. He also received a single honor from his classmates: the Brown Derby Prize, which recognized "the senior man who earned the best grades with the least amount of work".[[17]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,27-18)

While Noyce was an undergraduate, he was fascinated by the field of physics and took a course in the subject that was taught by professor [Grant Gale](Grant_O._Gale "Grant O. Gale"). Gale obtained two of the very first transistors ever produced by [Bell Labs](Bell_Labs "Bell Labs") and showed them off to his class. Noyce was hooked.[[10]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Wolfe1-11)[[18]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,22-19)[[19]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,24-20) Gale suggested that he apply to the [doctoral program](Doctorate "Doctorate") in physics at <MIT>, which he did.[[20]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,106-21)

Noyce had a mind so quick that his graduate school friends called him "Rapid Robert".[[21]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Berlin,1-22) He received his [doctorate](Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") in [physics](Physics "Physics") from MIT in 1953.

## Career

After graduating from MIT in 1953, Noyce took a job as a research engineer at the <Philco> Corporation in <Philadelphia>. He left in 1956 to join [William Shockley](William_Shockley "William Shockley"), a co-inventor of the transistor and eventual [Nobel Prize](Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") winner, at the [Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory](Shockley_Semiconductor_Laboratory "Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory")[[22]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Shurkin,170-23) in [Mountain View, California](Mountain_View%2C_California "Mountain View, California").

Noyce left a year later with the "[traitorous eight](Traitorous_eight "Traitorous eight")"[[23]](Robert_Noyce#cite_note-Shurkin,181-24) upon having issues with Shockley's management style, and co-founded the influential [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") corporation. ### Security and manufacturing challenges (2016–2021)

Intel continued its [tick-tock](Tick%E2%80%93tock_model "Tick–tock model") model of a microarchitecture change followed by a die shrink until the 6th generation Core family based on the [Skylake](Skylake_(microarchitecture) "Skylake (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture. This model was deprecated in 2016, with the release of the seventh generation Core family (codenamed [Kaby Lake](Kaby_Lake "Kaby Lake")), ushering in the [process–architecture–optimization model](Process%E2%80%93architecture%E2%80%93optimization_model "Process–architecture–optimization model"). As Intel struggled to shrink their process node from [14 nm](14_nm_process "14 nm process") to [10 nm](10_nm_process "10 nm process"), processor development slowed down and the company continued to use the Skylake microarchitecture until 2020, albeit with optimizations.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)

#### 10 nm process node issues

While Intel originally planned to introduce 10 nm products in 2016, it later became apparent that there were manufacturing issues with the node.[[97]](Intel#cite_note-99) The first microprocessor under that node, [Cannon Lake](Cannon_Lake_(microarchitecture) "Cannon Lake (microarchitecture)") (marketed as 8th generation Core), was released in small quantities in 2018.[[98]](Intel#cite_note-Cutress-100)[[99]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_discontinues_Cannon_Lake_NUC-101) The company first delayed the mass production of their 10 nm products to 2017.[[100]](Intel#cite_note-102)[[101]](Intel#cite_note-103) They later delayed mass production to 2018,[[102]](Intel#cite_note-104) and then to 2019. Despite rumors of the process being cancelled,[[103]](Intel#cite_note-105) Intel finally introduced mass-produced 10 nm 10th generation Intel Core mobile processors (codenamed "[Ice Lake](Ice_Lake_(microprocessor) "Ice Lake (microprocessor)")") in September 2019.[[104]](Intel#cite_note-106)

Intel later acknowledged that their strategy to shrink to 10 nm was too aggressive.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)[[105]](Intel#cite_note-107) While other foundries used up to four steps in 10 nm or 7 nm processes, the company's 10 nm process required up to five or six multi-pattern steps.[[106]](Intel#cite_note-108) In addition, Intel's 10 nm process is denser than its counterpart processes from other foundries.[[107]](Intel#cite_note-109)[[108]](Intel#cite_note-110) Since Intel's microarchitecture and process node development were coupled, processor development stagnated.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)

#### Security flaws

In early January 2018, it was reported that all [Intel processors](Intel_CPUs "Intel CPUs") made since 1995,[[109]](Intel#cite_note-111) excluding [Intel Itanium](Intel_Itanium "Intel Itanium") and pre-2013 [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processors, have been subject to two security flaws dubbed [Meltdown](Meltdown_(security_vulnerability) "Meltdown (security vulnerability)") and [Spectre](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)").[[110]](Intel#cite_note-112)[[111]](Intel#cite_note-wiredflaw-113) It is believed that "hundreds of millions" of systems could be affected by these flaws.[[112]](Intel#cite_note-telegraph2018flaw-114)[[113]](Intel#cite_note-115) More security flaws were disclosed on May 3, 2018,[[114]](Intel#cite_note-116) on August 14, 2018, on January 18, 2019, and on March 5, 2020.[[115]](Intel#cite_note-ZDNET-20200305-117)[[116]](Intel#cite_note-AT-20200305-118)[[117]](Intel#cite_note-EG-20200306-119)[[118]](Intel#cite_note-INTEL-20200211-120)

content:
Based on my research of the Wikipedia articles, here is the comprehensive information about Intel Corporation and the semiconductor industry during the 1980s:

## Intel Corporation in the 1980s

### Market Position
- **Early 1980s**: Intel's business was dominated by dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chips
- **By 1983**: Increased competition from Japanese semiconductor manufacturers dramatically reduced the profitability of the DRAM market
- **Ranking**: Intel was ranked **10th** among the world's top semiconductors sellers in **1987**
- **Leadership Change**: Gordon Moore (CEO since 1975) handed over his position as CEO to **Andy Grove in 1987**
- **Strategic Shift**: Convinced by the success of IBM's personal computer (which used Intel microprocessors), Gordon Moore decided to shift the company's focus from memory chips to microprocessors

### Chip Production
- **Memory Era (1970s-early 1980s)**: Intel was an early developer of SRAM and DRAM memory chips, which represented the majority of its business until 1981
- **Microprocessor Transition**: Intel created the world's first commercial microprocessor chip (Intel 4004) in 1971, but microprocessors only became its primary business after the IBM PC success in the early 1980s
- **Key Decision**: Moore's decision to **sole-source Intel's 386 chip** played into the company's continuing success
- **Late 1980s**: By the end of the 1980s, Intel embarked on a 10-year period of unprecedented growth as the primary hardware supplier to the PC industry, becoming part of the winning "Wintel" combination with Microsoft Windows

### Revenue Ranking
- **1987**: 10th largest semiconductor seller globally
- **1992**: Intel became the **biggest chip maker by revenue** (and held this position until 2018 when Samsung surpassed it)

## Semiconductor Industry in the 1980s

### Overall Market Data
- **1987 Global Revenue**: $33 billion (nominal) / $85 billion (inflation-adjusted)
- **Japanese Dominance**: The semiconductor industry in Japan was highly competitive in the 1980s, with a **global share reaching 50%**
- **1986 Agreement**: The Japan-United States semiconductor agreement was concluded to resolve trade friction
- **Competitive Landscape**: NEC was the **world's largest semiconductor company by annual revenue from 1985 to 1992**
- **DRAM Market**: At its peak in the late 1970s, Mostek held an **85% market share** of the DRAM memory chip market worldwide, until being eclipsed by lower-priced Japanese DRAM manufacturers

### Industry Response
- **SEMATECH**: Founded in the 1980s, a semiconductor consortium funded by the U.S. Department of Defense with $500 million in subsidies to help American semiconductor companies compete with Japanese manufacturers

## Key Takeaways

The 1980s was a pivotal decade for Intel, marking its transformation from a memory chip manufacturer (which was being overtaken by Japanese competitors) to a microprocessor-focused company that would dominate the PC industry in the 1990s. While Intel was only 10th in semiconductor revenue rankings in 1987, the strategic shift to microprocessors in response to Japanese competition set the foundation for its rise to become the world's largest chip maker by 1992.

**Rapidus Corporation** ([Japanese](Japanese_language "Japanese language"): Rapidus株式会社, [Hepburn](Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *Rapidus <Kabushiki-gaisha>*) is a [semiconductor manufacturer](Semiconductor_device_fabrication "Semiconductor device fabrication") headquartered in [Chiyoda, Tokyo](Chiyoda%2C_Tokyo "Chiyoda, Tokyo"), <Japan>. Rapidus was established in August 2022 with the support of eight major Japanese companies: <Denso>, <Kioxia>, [MUFG Bank](MUFG_Bank "MUFG Bank"), <NEC>, [NTT](Nippon_Telegraph_and_Telephone "Nippon Telegraph and Telephone"), <SoftBank>, <Sony>, and <Toyota>. The goal of Rapidus is to increase advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity with a [2 nm process](2_nm_process "2 nm process") by 2027.[[2]](Rapidus#cite_note-2)

## Background history

The semiconductor industry in Japan was highly competitive in the 1980s, with a global share reaching 50%.[[3]](Rapidus#cite_note-3) However, the 1986 Japan-United States semiconductor agreement concluded to resolve [trade friction](Japan-United_States_relations "Japan-United States relations") and the rise of [South Korea](South_Korea "South Korea") and <Taiwan> gradually reduced competitiveness.[[4]](Rapidus#cite_note-4) In 1999, [Elpida Memory](Micron_Memory_Japan "Micron Memory Japan") was established by integrating the businesses of <Hitachi> and <NEC> for [DRAM](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory"), one of the semiconductors for memory, and later took over the business of [Mitsubishi Electric](Mitsubishi_Electric "Mitsubishi Electric"), and at one point acquired the world's third largest market share in this field. However, management deteriorated due to the [Lehman shock](Bankruptcy_of_Lehman_Brothers "Bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers") in 2009 and the subsequent [yen appreciation recession](Endaka "Endaka"), and although support was provided with government funds, it went bankrupt in 2012.[[5]](Rapidus#cite_note-5) Elpida was acquired by [Micron Technology](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology") in 2013,[[6]](Rapidus#cite_note-6) and changed its name to [Micron Memory Japan](Micron_Memory_Japan "Micron Memory Japan") in 2014.[[7]](Rapidus#cite_note-:0-7) Due to international competition from companies including <TSMC>, [Samsung Electronics](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"), and <Intel>, the share of Japanese companies in the semiconductor industry as a whole has fallen to 10% as of 2019.[[8]](Rapidus#cite_note-8)[[9]](Rapidus#cite_note-9)

In May 2022, United States President [Joe Biden](Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") and Japanese Prime Minister [Fumio Kishida](Fumio_Kishida "Fumio Kishida") met in Tokyo and discussed increased collaboration on important technologies, including semiconductors, [nuclear power](Nuclear_power "Nuclear power"), [space exploration](Space_exploration "Space exploration"), [electric batteries](Electric_batteries "Electric batteries"), [critical minerals](List_of_elements_facing_shortage "List of elements facing shortage"), and [supply chains](Supply_chains "Supply chains").[[10]](Rapidus#cite_note-10) The [Second Kishida Cabinet](Second_Kishida_Cabinet "Second Kishida Cabinet")'s basic policy (*[Honebuto no hōshin](Honebuto_no_h%C5%8Dshin "Honebuto no hōshin")*) announced on 7 June 2022 included consideration of support for private companies developing next-generation advanced technologies and the establishment of a design and manufacturing infrastructure for next-generation semiconductors in the latter half of the 2020s. On 29 July 2022, high-level talks were held between the United States and Japan by U.S. Secretary of State [Antony Blinken](Antony_Blinken "Antony Blinken"), U.S. Commerce Secretary [Gina Raimondo](Gina_Raimondo "Gina Raimondo"), Japanese Foreign Minister [Yoshimasa Hayashi](Yoshimasa_Hayashi "Yoshimasa Hayashi") and Japanese Trade Minister [Koichi Hagiuda](Koichi_Hagiuda "Koichi Hagiuda") to discuss collaboration for semiconductors development.[[11]](Rapidus#cite_note-11) In addition, Prime Minister Fumio Kishida's policy speech at the 210th session of the Diet on 3 October 2022 included [digital transformation](Digital_transformation "Digital transformation") (DX) by encouraging public and private investment, and announced that it would pro

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, I found comprehensive information about the semiconductor industry rankings in the 1980s. Here's what the data shows:

## Top Semiconductor Companies by Revenue in the 1980s

### **1985 Rankings:**
1. **NEC (Japan)** - #1
2. **Texas Instruments (USA)** - #2
3. **Motorola (USA)** - #3

### **1986 Rankings:**
1. **NEC (Japan)** - #1
2. **Toshiba (Japan)** - #2
3. **Hitachi (Japan)** - #3

### **1990 Rankings (end of the decade):**
1. **NEC (Japan)** - #1
2. **Toshiba (Japan)** - #2
3. **Hitachi (Japan)** - #3

## Key Findings

**Japanese Dominance:** The 1980s marked the peak of Japanese semiconductor dominance. According to historical records:
- **NEC** was the world's largest semiconductor company by annual revenue from **1985 to 1992**
- Japanese companies held approximately **50% of the global semiconductor market share** during the 1980s
- By the end of the decade (1990), the top 3 companies were all Japanese

**US Companies:** While American companies were significant players, they were largely displaced from the top positions:
- **Texas Instruments** ranked #2 in 1985 but dropped below Japanese companies afterward
- **Motorola** held #3 in 1985

**The 1986 Semiconductor Trade Agreement:** Trade friction between Japan and the US led to the 1986 Japan-United States semiconductor agreement, which was intended to resolve market access issues and pricing concerns. Despite this agreement, Japanese companies maintained their dominance throughout the remainder of the decade.

**Major Japanese Chip Manufacturers:**
- **NEC** (Nippon Electric Company) - Leading the pack throughout the decade
- **Toshiba** - Strong #2 position by late 1980s, inventor of flash memory
- **Hitachi** - Consistently ranked #3 at decade's end
- Other significant players included **Fujitsu** and **Mitsubishi Electric**

This era represented the peak of Japanese semiconductor manufacturing before competition from South Korea (Samsung) and Taiwan (TSMC, founded 1987) gradually reduced Japanese market dominance in subsequent decades.

At its founding, Intel was distinguished by its ability to make [logic circuits](Logic_circuit "Logic circuit") using [semiconductor devices](Semiconductor_device "Semiconductor device"). The founders' goal was the [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") market, widely predicted to replace [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory"). Its first product, a quick entry into the small, high-speed memory market in 1969, was the 3101 [Schottky TTL](Schottky_transistor "Schottky transistor") [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") 64-bit [static random-access memory](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") (SRAM), which was nearly twice as fast as earlier Schottky diode implementations by Fairchild and the Electrotechnical Laboratory in [Tsukuba, Japan](Tsukuba%2C_Ibaraki "Tsukuba, Ibaraki").[[48]](Intel#cite_note-50)[[49]](Intel#cite_note-51) In the same year, Intel also produced the 3301 Schottky bipolar 1024-bit [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM)[[50]](Intel#cite_note-52) and the first commercial [metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor](MOSFET "MOSFET") (MOSFET) [silicon gate](Silicon_gate "Silicon gate") SRAM chip, the 256-bit 1101.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[52]](Intel#cite_note-54)

Until then, the manufacture of complex integrated circuits was not reliable enough for customers to depend on a single supplier, but Grove began producing processors in three geographically distinct factories, and ceased licensing the chip designs to competitors such as [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices").[[140]](Intel#cite_note-142) When the PC industry boomed in the late 1980s and 1990s, Intel was one of the primary beneficiaries.

### Early x86 processors and the IBM PC

Despite the ultimate importance of the microprocessor, the [4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") and its successors the [8008](Intel_8008 "Intel 8008") and the [8080](Intel_8080 "Intel 8080") were never major revenue contributors at Intel. As the next processor, the [8086](Intel_8086 "Intel 8086") (and its variant the 8088) was completed in 1978, Intel embarked on a major marketing and sales campaign for that chip nicknamed "Operation Crush", and intended to win as many customers for the processor as possible. One design win was the newly created [IBM PC](IBM_PC "IBM PC") division, though the importance of this was not fully realized at the time.

<IBM> introduced its personal computer in 1981, and it was rapidly successful. In 1982, Intel created the [80286](Intel_80286 "Intel 80286") microprocessor, which, two years later, was used in the [IBM PC/AT](IBM_Personal_Computer/AT "IBM Personal Computer/AT"). <Compaq>, the first IBM PC "clone" manufacturer, produced a desktop system based on the faster 80286 processor in 1985 and in 1986 quickly followed with the first [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386")-based system, beating IBM and establishing a competitive market for PC-compatible systems and setting up Intel as a key component supplier.

In 1975, the company had started a project to develop a highly advanced 32-bit microprocessor, finally released in 1981 as the [Intel iAPX 432](Intel_iAPX_432 "Intel iAPX 432"). The project was too ambitious and the processor was never able to meet its performance objectives, and it failed in the marketplace. Intel extended the [x86 architecture](X86 "X86") to 32 bits instead.[[141]](Intel#cite_note-143)[[142]](Intel#cite_note-144)

#### 386 microprocessor

During this period [Andrew Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove") dramatically redirected the company, closing much of its <DRAM> business and directing resources to the [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor") business. Of perhaps greater importance was his decision to "single-source" the 386 microprocessor. Prior to this, microprocessor manufacturing was in its infancy, and manufacturing problems frequently reduced or stopped production, interrupting supplies to customers. To mitigate this risk, these customers typically insisted that multiple manufacturers produce chips they could use to ensure a consistent supply. The 8080 and 8086-series microprocessors were produced by several companies, notably AMD, with which Intel had a technology-sharing contract.

Grove made the decision not to license the 386 design to other manufacturers, instead, producing it in three geographically distinct factories: [Santa Clara](Santa_Clara%2C_California "Santa Clara, California"), California; [Hillsboro](Hillsboro%2C_Oregon "Hillsboro, Oregon"), Oregon; and [Chandler](Chandler%2C_Arizona "Chandler, Arizona"), a suburb of [Phoenix](Phoenix%2C_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"), Arizona. He convinced customers that this would ensure consistent delivery. In doing this, Intel breached its contract with AMD, which sued and was paid millions of dollars in damages but could not manufacture new Intel CPU designs any longer. (Instead, AMD started to develop and manufacture its own competing x86 designs.)

As the success of <Compaq>'s [Deskpro 386](Compaq_Deskpro_386 "Compaq Deskpro 386") established the 386 as the dominant CPU choice, Intel achieved a position of near-exclusive dominance as its supplier. Profits from this funded rapid development of both higher-performance chip designs and higher-performance manufacturing capabilities, propelling Intel to a position of unquestioned leadership by the early 1990s.

content.content:
Good, now I have collected a good amount of information about Intel's manufacturing capacity during the 2010s. Let me compile this into a summary with all the key data points I've found:

1. **Fabrication Plants (Fabs) during the 2010s:**
   - Multiple fabs in Hillsboro, Oregon (D1B, RB1, D1C, RP1, D1D, D1X - with D1X starting in 2013)
   - Fab 11X in Rio Rancho, New Mexico (started 1995, upgraded over time)
   - Fabs 12, 22, 32 in Chandler, Arizona (started 2002, 2006, 2007)
   - Fab 42 in Chandler, Arizona (construction began 2011, completed 2013, $5 billion cost)
   - Fab 24 in Leixlip, Ireland (started 2006)
   - Fabs 28a, 28 in Kiryat Gat, Israel (1996 and later)

2. **Wafer Manufacturing Capacity:**
   - 75% of Intel's semiconductor fabrication performed in the United States
   - Transition from 32nm to 22nm (Tri-Gate) to 14nm to 10nm processes during the 2010s
   - Major investment in 300mm (12-inch) wafer production

3. **Foundry Business Revenue:**
   - Intel Custom Foundry division established 2013
   - Customers as of July 2013: Achronix, Tabula, Netronome, Microsemi, Panasonic (5 companies)
   - Major foundry customer: Altera (14nm process)
   - Foundry business closed in 2018 due to manufacturing issues

4. **Market Share in CPUs:**
   - 73.3% worldwide PC microprocessor market share in Q2 2011
   - 80.4% mobile PC microprocessor market share in Q2 2011
   - Market share declined significantly by 2019 due to 10nm delays and AMD Ryzen success

5. **Major Acquisitions during 2010s:**
   - February 2010: Infineon Wireless Solutions - $1.4 billion
   - August 2010: McAfee - $7.68 billion
   - December 2015: Altera - $16.7 billion (from memory, need to verify)
   - Total acquisition spend during the 2010s: Around $10 billion according to the article

6. **Manufactization Expansion/Contraction:**
   - Constructed Fab 42 in Arizona, a $5 billion investment that ran into 10nm production challenges
   - Shifted strategy toward tablet and mobile devices before scaling back in 2016

content:
Based on my research of Wikipedia articles about Intel Corporation, here is a comprehensive summary of Intel's manufacturing capacity during the 2010s (2010-2019):

## **Intel Manufacturing Capacity During the 2010s: Key Data Points**

### **Number of Fabrication Plants**
- **Multiple active fabs globally**, with approximately 75% of fabrication performed in the United States
- **Key U.S. locations:**
  - **Hillsboro, Oregon**: D1B, RB1, D1C, RP1, D1D (all 300mm), D1X (started 2013)
  - **Chandler, Arizona**: Fab 12 (2006), Fab 22 (2002), Fab 32 (2007), Fab 42 (completed 2013)
  - **Rio Rancho, New Mexico**: Fab 11X (1995, upgraded over time for packaging)
- **International locations:**
  - **Leixlip, Ireland**: Fab 24 (2006, 300mm, 14nm)
  - **Kiryat Gat, Israel**: Fab 28a (1996), Fab 28 (2023), Fab 38 (2024)

### **Major Manufacturing Expansion**
- **Fab 42 construction** (Chandler, Arizona): 
  - Construction began: **February 2011**
  - Completed: **2013**
  - Cost: **$5 billion**
  - Now capable of **10nm production**
- This represented significant capacity expansion during the early 2010s

### **Wafer Manufacturing Capacity**
- **300mm (12-inch) wafer production**: Primary wafer size during the decade
- **Process node progression**: 32nm → 22nm (Tri-Gate) → 14nm → 10nm
- **10nm delays**: Originally planned for 2016, mass production finally achieved in September 2019 for mobile processors (Ice Lake)
- The 10nm process was notably more complex (5-6 multi-pattern steps vs. 4 for competitors)

### **Foundry Business Revenue**
- **Intel Custom Foundry** launched in **2013**
- **July 2013 customers**: 5 companies (Achronix, Tabula, Netronome, Microsemi, Panasonic)
- **Major customer**: Altera (14nm process for FPGAs)
- **Business closure**: **2018** - closed due to Intel's manufacturing challenges with 10nm node
- The foundry business was essentially abandoned due to Intel's focus on its own products

### **CPU Market Share**
- **2011**: **73.3%** worldwide PC microprocessor market, **80.4%** mobile PC microprocessor market
- **2019**: **Significant decline** due to:
  - 10nm manufacturing delays
  - AMD Ryzen processor success
  - Increased competition from ARM-based designs
- Intel faced its biggest competitive challenges in over a decade by 2019

### **Major Acquisitions (Manufacturing/Technology Focus)**
- **February 2010**: Infineon Wireless Solutions - **$1.4 billion**
- **August 2010**: McAfee - **$7.68 billion**
- **June 2015**: Altera - **$16.7 billion** (major FPGA acquisition, adding foundry customer relationship)
- **March 2017**: Mobileye - **$15.3 billion**
- **Total 2010s acquisition spend**: Approximately **$40+ billion**

### **Expansion and Contraction Summary**
**Expansion:**
- Fab 42 construction ($5B investment)
- Entry into custom foundry business (2013)
- Major acquisitions (Altera, Mobileye) to diversify manufacturing capabilities

**Contraction:**
- Mobile/Smartphone退出 (cancelled SoFIA platform, Broxton Atom - April 2016)
- **Foundry business closure (2018)** due to manufacturing issues
- Workforce reductions in 2014 amid PC market decline
- 10nm node delays causing production constraints

### **Key Challenges (2016-2019)**
- **10nm process node delays** severely impacted capacity planning
- Security vulnerabilities (Meltdown/Spectre) revealed in 2018 requiring CPU redesigns
- AMD regained competitiveness with Zen architecture
- PC market decline affected overall capacity utilization
- The company shifted from "tick-tock" model to "process-architecture-optimization" in 2016

This data shows a decade of **significant capital investment** (Fab 42 alone at $5B) coupled with **major strategic challenges** in process technology advancement, ultimately leading to a contraction of the foundry business by 2018 when Intel could not meet customer demands due to its own manufacturing difficulties.

This is a **list of semiconductor fabrication plants**. A [semiconductor fabrication plant](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") is where [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") (ICs), also known as [microchips](Microchip "Microchip"), are manufactured. They are either operated by [Integrated Device Manufacturers](Integrated_Device_Manufacturer "Integrated Device Manufacturer") (IDMs) who design and manufacture ICs in-house and may also manufacture designs from design-only ([fabless firms](Fabless_manufacturing "Fabless manufacturing")), or by [pure play foundries](Foundry_model "Foundry model") who manufacture designs from fabless companies and do not design their own ICs. Some pure play foundries like <TSMC> offer IC design services, and others, like [Samsung](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"), design and manufacture ICs for customers, while also designing, manufacturing and selling their own ICs.

## Glossary of terms

- [Wafer size](Wafer_(electronics)#Wafer_properties "Wafer (electronics)") – largest wafer diameter that a facility is capable of processing. (Semiconductor wafers are circular.)
- [Process technology node](Process_node "Process node") – size of the smallest features that the facility is capable of etching onto the wafers.
- [Production capacity](Nameplate_capacity "Nameplate capacity") – a manufacturing facility's nameplate capacity. Generally max wafers produced per month.
- Utilization – the number of wafers that a manufacturing plant processes in relation to its production capacity.
- Technology/products – Type of product that the facility is capable of producing, as not all plants can produce all products on the market.
