While reducing the thickness substantially, the company maintained the performance of previous models, including Full HD 1080p resolution, 120 Hz refresh rate, and 5000:1 contrast ratio.[[115]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-115) On 6 September 2013, Samsung launched its 55-inch curved OLED TV (model KE55S9C) in the United Kingdom with John Lewis.[[116]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-116)

In October 2013, Samsung disseminated a press release for its curved display technology with the [Galaxy Round](Samsung_Galaxy_Round "Samsung Galaxy Round") smartphone model. The press release described the product as the "world's first commercialized full HD Super AMOLED flexible display". The manufacturer explains that users can check information such as time and battery life when the home screen is off, and can receive information from the screen by tilting the device.[[117]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-117)

In 2020, Samsung Display said it was exiting the LCD business.[[118]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-118)

### Mobile and smart phones

Main article: [Samsung Galaxy](Samsung_Galaxy "Samsung Galaxy")

See also: [Samsung Anycall](Samsung_Anycall "Samsung Anycall")

Samsung's mobile cell business began with a [car phone](Car_phone "Car phone") in 1984, while its first handheld mobile phone called the SH-100 was made in 1988.[[119]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-:2-119) It expanded to other markets during the 1990s. Its first smartphone was the [Samsung SPH-i300](Samsung_SPH-i300 "Samsung SPH-i300") in 2001. During the early 2000s Samsung popularised the [clamshell](Clamshell_design "Clamshell design") ("flip phone") design,[[120]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-120) and the [SGH-T100](Samsung_SGH-T100 "Samsung SGH-T100") was the first ever "true color" mobile phone and the firm's first to sell over 10 million handsets.[[121]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-121)[[119]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-:2-119) In the mid-2000s the <SGH-D500> popularised the [slider](Slide_(form) "Slide (form)") form factor,[[122]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-122) and later slider products such as the [E250](Samsung_SGH-E250 "Samsung SGH-E250") were hits.[[123]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-123) In 2006 Samsung's [X820](Samsung_SGH-X820 "Samsung SGH-X820") with a depth of 6.9 mm was the thinnest phone, and for many years its successor U100 would remain the skinniest at just 5.9 mm.[[124]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-124) In 2007 it launched the slate style touchscreen phone [F700](Samsung_Ultra_Smart_F700 "Samsung Ultra Smart F700") which would precede its increasingly relevant touch phones such as [Tocco](Samsung_F480_Tocco "Samsung F480 Tocco") and [Omnia](Samsung_i900_Omnia "Samsung i900 Omnia"). Samsung overtook declining <Motorola> to become the world's second largest mobile phone marker during 2007.[[125]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-125)

Presently, Samsung's flagship mobile handset line is the [Samsung Galaxy S series](Samsung_Galaxy_S_series "Samsung Galaxy S series") of smartphones, which many consider a direct competitor of the Apple [iPhone](IPhone "IPhone").[[126]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-126) It was initially launched in Singapore, Malaysia and South Korea in June 2010,[[127]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-127)[[128]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-128)[[129]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-129) followed by the United States in July. It sold more than one million units within the first 45 days on sale in the United States.[[130]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-130)

While many other handset manufacturers focused on one or two operating systems, Samsung for a time used several of them: <Symbian>, [Windows Phone](Windows_Phone "Windows Phone"), Linux-based [LiMo](LiMo_Platform "LiMo Platform"), and Samsung's proprietary <TouchWiz>, [Bada](Bada_(operating_system) "Bada (operating system)") and <Tizen>.[[131]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-131) By 2013 Samsung had dropped all operating systems except Android phone and Windows Phone. That year Samsung released at least 43 Android phones or tablets and two Windows Phones.[[132]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-132)

At the end of the third quarter of 2010, the company had surpassed the 70 million unit mark in shipped phones, giving it a global market share of 22 percent, trailing <Nokia> by 12 percent.[[133]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-133)[[134]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-134) Overall, the company sold 280 million mobile phones in 2010, corresponding to a market share of 20.2 percent.[[135]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-135) The company overtook Apple in worldwide smartphone sales during the third quarter 2011, with a total market share of 23.8 percent, compared to Apple's 14.6 percent share.[[136]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-136) Samsung became the world's largest smartphone manufacturer in 2012, with the sales of 95 million in the first quarter.[[137]](Samsung_Electronics#cite_note-137)

## Samsung Electronics Semiconductor Division - 2010s Manufacturing Capacity Summary

### Number of Semiconductor Fabs
- **Xi'an China facility**: The company's flagship NAND flash facility, operational since 2014, produces approximately **40% of Samsung's NAND flash memory chips**. This represents one of the company's major manufacturing locations during the 2010s.
- Samsung Electronics operates multiple semiconductor fabrication facilities globally, including the large-scale "Samsung Digital City" complex in Suwon, South Korea, with additional sites in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.

### Memory Chip Capacity & Technology Milestones (2010-2019)

**Process Technology Progression:**
- **2010**: World-first mass production of 30nm-class DRAM and 20nm-class NAND flash; began 20nm-class semiconductor manufacturing process
- **2013**: 10nm-class FinFET process initiated; V-NAND flash memory introduced (3D NAND technology)
- **2016**: HBM2 (High Bandwidth Memory 2) introduced
- **2018**: 7nm FinFET nodes began production; GDDR6 memory introduced
- **Late 2018**: First 5nm nodes started production
- **2020**: Plans to mass-produce 5nm chips using EUV (Extreme ultraviolet lithography)

### Foundry Capacity
- The foundry business was established as a **strategic growth pillar** beginning in **2006**
- Samsung is unique as both an integrated device manufacturer (IDM) and a foundry serving fabless companies
- Positioned to compete with TSMC in advanced process nodes throughout the 2010s

### Revenue from Semiconductor Division
- Samsung became the **world's largest semiconductor company in 2017**, surpassing Intel (the decades-long champion)
- **Memory chips and flexible displays accounted for approximately 68% of Samsung's operating profit in Q4 2016** (a dramatic shift from previous years when smartphones were the main contributor)
- From **1999 to 2009**, Samsung's compound annual growth rate in semiconductor revenues was **13.5%** (compared to Intel's 3.4%)
- In **Q4 2021**, Samsung's chip business was responsible for **nearly two-thirds of the total profit** ($11.5 billion operating profit, up 53% quarter-over-quarter)

### Market Share in DRAM/NAND
- **DRAM Market Share**:
  - Q2 2010: **35% DRAM market share** according to Gartner, cementing Samsung's top position
  - Ranked #1 followed by SK Hynix, Elpida, and Micron
  - Has been the world's largest memory chip manufacturer since 1993

- **NAND Flash Market**:
  - Xi'an facility alone produces 40% of total NAND flash for Samsung
  - V-NAND technology (introduced 2013) became a competitive advantage in 3D NAND market
  - Samsung is the world's largest NAND flash manufacturer throughout the 2010s

| Parameter | Information |

| **Major DRAM Share (2010)** | 35% (Gartner data) |

On August 26, 2019, GlobalFoundries filed [patent infringement](Patent_infringement "Patent infringement") lawsuits against <TSMC> and some of TSMC's customers[[40]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-40) in the US and Germany. GlobalFoundries claims TSMC's 7 nm, 10 nm, 12 nm, 16 nm, and 28 nm nodes have infringed on 16 of its patents. Lawsuits were filed in the [U.S. International Trade Commission](United_States_International_Trade_Commission "United States International Trade Commission"), the [U.S. Federal District Courts](U.S._Federal_District_Court "U.S. Federal District Court") in the Districts of [Delaware](United_States_District_Court_for_the_District_of_Delaware "United States District Court for the District of Delaware"), the [Western District of Texas](United_States_District_Court_for_the_Western_District_of_Texas "United States District Court for the Western District of Texas"), the [Regional Courts](Landgericht_(Germany) "Landgericht (Germany)") of [Düsseldorf](D%C3%BCsseldorf "Düsseldorf"), and <Mannheim> in Germany.[[41]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-41) GlobalFoundries has named 20 defendants: [Apple](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), [Broadcom](Broadcom_Inc. "Broadcom Inc."), <MediaTek>, <Nvidia>, <Qualcomm>, <Xilinx>, Arista, [ASUS](Asus "Asus"), BLU, [Cisco](Cisco_Systems "Cisco Systems"), <Google>, <Hisense>, <Lenovo>, <Motorola>, [TCL](TCL_Corporation "TCL Corporation"), <OnePlus>, [Avnet/EBV](Avnet "Avnet"), <Digi-Key> and [Mouser](Mouser_Electronics "Mouser Electronics").[[42]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-42) On August 27, <TSMC> announced it was reviewing the complaints filed, but are confident that the allegations are baseless and will vigorously defend its proprietary technology.[[43]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-43)

On October 1, 2019, TSMC filed [patent infringement](Patent_infringement "Patent infringement") lawsuits against GlobalFoundries in the US, Germany and Singapore. TSMC claimed GlobalFoundries' 12 nm, 14 nm, 22 nm, 28 nm and 40 nm nodes have infringed on 25 of its patents.[[44]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-44)

On October 29, 2019, TSMC and GlobalFoundries announced a resolution to the dispute. The companies agreed to a new [life-of-patents](Term_of_patent "Term of patent") [cross-license](Cross-licensing "Cross-licensing") for all of their existing semiconductor patents as well as new patents to be filed by the companies in the next ten years.[[45]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-45)[[46]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-46)[[47]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-47)[[48]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-48)[[49]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-49)

### 300 mm fabrication facilities

#### Fab 1

Fab 1, located in <Dresden>, Germany, is a 364,512 m2 plant which was transferred to GlobalFoundries on its inception: Fab 36 and Fab 38 were renamed Module 1 and Module 2, respectively. Each module can produce 25,000 300 mm diameter wafers per month.[[8]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-300mm-8)[[54]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-54)

Module 1 is a 300 mm wafer production facility. It is capable of manufacturing wafers at 40 nm, 28 nm BULK and 22 nm FDSOI. Module 2 was originally named "(AMD) Fab 30" and was a 200 mm fab producing 30,000 Wafer Outs Per Month, but has now been converted into a 300 mm wafer fab. Together with other clean room extensions like the Annex they have a maximum full capacity of 80,000 of 300 mm wafers/month (180,000 200 mm wafers/month equivalent), using technologies of [45 nm](45_nm "45 nm") and below.

In September 2016, GlobalFoundries announced Fab 1 would be refit to produce 12 nm fully depleted [silicon on insulator](Silicon_on_insulator "Silicon on insulator") (FDSOI) products.[[55]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-55) The company expected customer's products would begin to [tape out](Tape_out "Tape out") in the first half of 2019.

#### Fab 7

Fab 7, located in [Woodlands, Singapore](Woodlands%2C_Singapore "Woodlands, Singapore"), is an operational 300 mm Fab, originally owned by [Chartered Semiconductor](Chartered_Semiconductor "Chartered Semiconductor"). It produces wafers at 130 nm to 40 nm on bulk CMOS and SOI processes. It has a maximum full capacity of 50,000 300 mm wafers/month (112,500 200 mm wafers/month equivalent), using [130](130_nm "130 nm") to 40 nm technology.[[8]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-300mm-8)

4/15/2021 Fab 7's target capacity will be expanded to 70–80kpcs/M.

#### Fab 8

Fab 8, located in [Luther Forest Technology Campus](Luther_Forest_Technology_Campus "Luther Forest Technology Campus"), [Saratoga County, New York](Saratoga_County%2C_New_York "Saratoga County, New York"), United States is a 300 mm fab. This fabrication plant was constructed by GF as a green field fab for advanced technologies. It is capable of manufacturing 14 nm node technology. The plant's construction began in July 2009 and the company started mass production in 2012.[[8]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-300mm-8)[[56]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-56) It has a maximum manufacturing capacity of 60,000 of 300 mm wafers/month, or the equivalent of over 135,000 of 200 mm wafers/month. In September 2016, GlobalFoundries announced it would make a multibillion-dollar investment to refit Fab 8 to produce 7 nm <FinFET> parts starting in the second half of 2018.[[57]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-57) The process was planned to initially use [deep ultraviolet lithography](Ultraviolet#Electrical_and_electronics_industry "Ultraviolet"), and eventually transition to [extreme ultraviolet lithography](Extreme_ultraviolet_lithography "Extreme ultraviolet lithography").[[58]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-58)

However, in August 2018, GlobalFoundries made the decision to suspend 7 nm development and planned production, citing the unaffordable costs to outfit Fab 8 for 7 nm production. GlobalFoundries held open the possibility of resuming 7 nm operations in the future if additional resources could be secured. From this decision GlobalFoundries executed a shift in company strategy to focus more effort on FD-SOI manufacturing and R&D. he original Zen and the Zen+ CPUs are of a monolithic design which were produced at Global Foundries Malta Facilities in [Malta, NY](Malta%2C_New_York "Malta, New York"). Going forward AMD will pursue a multiple Chiplet Design with the Zen 2 microprocessor. The Zen 2 will consist of a 14/12 nm manufactured IO die surrounded by a number of 7 nm Core dies. When Global Foundries announced the suspension of 7 nm operations AMD executed a shift in plans transferring production of the 7 nm core dies to TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Corporation). There was speculation in some quarters as to where manufacture of the Core Dies would take place. In AMD's 2018 fourth quarter financial conference call which took place on January 29, 2019, AMD CEO Lisa Su announced the WSA (Wafer Supply Agreement) governing production and acquisition by AMD from GlobalFoundries had been amended for the seventh time. The amendment stated AMD would continue to procure 12 nm node and above from Global Foundries while giving AMD latitude to purchase 7 nm node manufactured wafers from any source free from paying any royalties. The agreement will run through 2024 and ensures that Global Foundries will have work for its Malta plant for that time period. Pricing commitments for Wafers runs through 2021 when it is likely the WSA will be amended again.[[59]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-59)

#### Accreditation as a Trusted Supplier

In May 2023, the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD), through the Defense Microelectronics Activity (DMEA), Trusted Access Program Office (TAPO), accredited GlobalFoundries' advanced manufacturing facility in Malta, New York, as a Category 1A Trusted Supplier. This accreditation enables GlobalFoundries to manufacture secure semiconductors for a wide range of critical aerospace and defense applications.[[60]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-60)

#### Fab 10

Fab 10,[[61]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-globalfoundries.com-61) located in [East Fishkill, New York](East_Fishkill%2C_New_York "East Fishkill, New York"), United States, was previously known as IBM Building 323. It became part of GlobalFoundries operations with the acquisition of [IBM Microelectronics](IBM_Microelectronics "IBM Microelectronics"). It currently manufactures technology down to the 14 nm node. In April 2019, it was announced that this fab has been sold to [ON Semiconductor](ON_Semiconductor "ON Semiconductor") for $430m. The facility will be transferred over within three years.[[62]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-OnSemi-62)

On February 10, 2023, onsemi successfully completed its acquisition of GF's 300 mm East Fishkill, New York site and fabrication facility.[[63]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-63)

### 200 mm fabrication facilities

All 200 mm fabs except Fab 9 are located in <Singapore>, and originally owned by [Chartered Semiconductor](Chartered_Semiconductor "Chartered Semiconductor").

#### Fab 2

Fab 2, located in Woodlands, Singapore. This fab is capable of manufacturing wafers at 600 to 350 nm for use in selected automotive IC products, High Voltage power management IC and Mixed-signal products.

#### Fab 3/5

Fab 3/5, located in Woodlands, Singapore. This fab is capable of manufacturing wafers at 350 to 180 nm for use in high voltage IC's for small panel display drivers and mobile power management modules.

#### Fab 3E

Fab 3E, located in Tampines, Singapore. This fab produces [180 nm](180_nm "180 nm") wafers for use in selected automotive IC products, High Voltage power management IC and Mixed-Signal products with embedded non-volatile memory technology.

In January 2019 GlobalFoundries announced that it had agreed to sell its Fab 3E in Singapore to [Vanguard International Semiconductor Corporation](Vanguard_International_Semiconductor_Corporation "Vanguard International Semiconductor Corporation") with transfer of ownership set to be completed on December 31, 2019.

#### Fab 6

Fab 6 located in Woodlands, Singapore, is a copper fabrication facility that is capable of manufacturing integrated CMOS and RFCMOS products for applications such as <Wi-Fi> & <Bluetooth> devices at [180](180_nm "180 nm") to 110 nm processes. The facility was later converted to 300mm and merged with Fab 7, a facility for manufacturing products based on the 300 nm node.

#### Fab 9

Fab 9,[[61]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-globalfoundries.com-61) located in the village of [Essex Junction, Vermont](Essex_Junction%2C_Vermont "Essex Junction, Vermont"), United States, near Vermont's largest city of [Burlington](Burlington%2C_Vermont "Burlington, Vermont"), became part of GlobalFoundries operations with the acquisition of IBM Microelectronics. The fab manufactures technologies down to the 90 nm node and is the largest private employer within the state of Vermont. The site also hosted a captive [mask shop](Mask_shop "Mask shop"), with development efforts down to the [7 nanometer](7_nanometer "7 nanometer") node, until it was sold to Toppan in 2019.[[64]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-64)

## Mergers and acquisitions

### Chartered Semiconductor

The majority investor of GlobalFoundries, Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Investment Co., announced on September 6, 2009, that it has agreed to acquire Singapore-based [Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd.](Chartered_Semiconductor_Manufacturing "Chartered Semiconductor Manufacturing"), for a total of $3.9 billion, with Chartered's operations being folded into GlobalFoundries.[[65]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-65)

Chartered Semiconductor is a member of the Common Platform, <IBM>'s semiconductor technology alliance. GlobalFoundries is a JDA partner of Common Platform Technology Alliance.

### IBM Microelectronics

Further information: [IBM Microelectronics § 2015 sale to GlobalFoundries](IBM_Microelectronics#2015_sale_to_GlobalFoundries "IBM Microelectronics")

In October 2014, GlobalFoundries received US$1.5 billion from IBM to accept taking over [IBM Microelectronics](IBM_Microelectronics "IBM Microelectronics"), including a 200 mm fab (now Fab 9) in Essex Junction, Vermont, and a 300 mm fab (now Fab 10) in East Fishkill, New York. As part of the agreement, GlobalFoundries will be the sole provider of IBM's server processor chips for the next 10 years. The deal closed on July 1, 2015.[[66]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-66) IBM-India employees who moved over to GlobalFoundries as part of the acquisition are now part of its Bangalore office.[[67]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-67)

In April 2019 [ON Semiconductor](ON_Semiconductor "ON Semiconductor") and GlobalFoundries announced a $430 million agreement to transfer ownership of GlobalFoundries 300mm Fab 10 in East Fishkill, New York, to ON Semiconductor.[[68]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-68)

In 2021 and 2023, GlobalFoundries sued IBM over [intellectual property](Intellectual_property "Intellectual property") disputes involving the latter's agreements with <Intel> and <Rapidus>.[[69]](GlobalFoundries#cite_note-69)

content:
Based on my research of the Wikipedia article for GlobalFoundries, I can now provide you with a comprehensive summary of GlobalFoundries' manufacturing capacity during the 2010s (2010-2019).

## GlobalFoundries Manufacturing Capacity Summary (2010-2019)

### Number of Fabs
- **2009-2010**: Started with AMD's manufacturing facilities plus acquired Chartered Semiconductor (Singapore)
- **2015**: Owned **10 fabrication plants** total
  - Fab 1: Dresden, Germany (300mm)
  - Fabs 2-7: Singapore (200mm and 300mm)
  - Fabs 8-10: Northeast United States (New York, Vermont)
- **2017**: Announced Fab 11 in Chengdu, China ($10B investment planned, abandoned in 2020)
- **2019**: Sold Fab 3E (Singapore, MEMS) to Vanguard International Semiconductor and Fab 10 (New York) to ON Semiconductor

### Wafer Capacity
- **Fab 1 (Dresden, Germany)**: Maximum **80,000 300mm wafers/month** (180,000 200mm equivalent)
- **Fab 7 (Singapore)**: Maximum **50,000 300mm wafers/month** (112,500 200mm equivalent), expanded to 70-80kpcs/M by 2021
- **Fab 8 (Malta, NY)**: Maximum **60,000 300mm wafers/month** (135,000 200mm equivalent)
- **Combined estimated capacity**: 200,000+ 300mm wafers/month at full capacity

### Major Capacity Changes & Strategic Shifts
- **2010**: Finalized integration of Chartered Semiconductor
- **2014**: Acquired IBM Microelectronics ($1.5B from IBM, including Fab 9 in Vermont and Fab 10 in New York)
- **August 2018**: **Cancelled 7nm process development** citing unaffordable costs; shifted strategy to focus on specialized processes
- **2019**: Multiple divestments to exit MEMS business and older 300mm capacity
- **2020**: Abandoned Fab 11 Chengdu, China ($10B investment never brought online)

### Revenue Trends (From article)
- **2022**: Revenue reached $8.1 billion (post-2019 data)
- The article doesn't provide specific 2010s annual revenue figures, but notes the IPO in October 2021 raised ~$2.6 billion (valued company at ~$2.4B)

### Market Share
- **As of 2021**: Fourth-largest semiconductor manufacturer
- **Market position**: Produces chips for **more than 7% of the $86 billion semiconductor manufacturing services industry**

### Major Customers
- **AMD**: Primary customer - wafer supply agreement through 2024 for 12nm node and above (Zen, Threadripper, Epyc CPUs)
- **2019**: Patent dispute lawsuit included 20 defendants: Apple, Broadcom, MediaTek, Nvidia, Qualcomm, Xilinx, Google, Cisco, ASUS, Motorola, Lenovo, and others
- **2023**: Exclusive US semiconductor production deal with General Motors

### Process Technologies During 2010s
- **2012**: 28nm mass production
- **2015**: 14nm FinFET (14LPP) introduced
- **2015**: 22nm FD-SOI introduced
- **2016**: Licensed 14nm FinFET process from Samsung
- **2018**: Developed 12nm node based on Samsung's 14nm process
- **2018**: Suspended 7nm development

### Summary
GlobalFoundries experienced significant expansion in the early-to-mid 2010s through strategic acquisitions (AMD spin-off, Chartered Semiconductor, IBM Microelectronics), reaching 10 fabs by 2015. However, by 2018-2019, the company pivoted away from leading-edge competition, cancelling 7nm development and divesting older capacity. The company established itself as the 4th-largest foundry globally, with ~7% market share, heavily reliant on its AMD partnership for its most advanced manufacturing capacity.

**United Microelectronics Corporation** (**UMC**; [Chinese](Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 聯華電子; [pinyin](Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Liánhuá Diànzǐ*) is a Taiwanese company based in <Hsinchu>, <Taiwan>. It was founded as Taiwan's first [semiconductor](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") company in 1980 as a spin-off of the government-sponsored [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute") (ITRI).[[4]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-overview-4)

## Overview

UMC is best known for its semiconductor foundry business, manufacturing [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") [wafers](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") for [fabless](Fabless "Fabless") semiconductor companies. In this role, UMC is ranked behind competitor <TSMC>. It has four 300 mm fabs, one in Taiwan, one in Singapore, one in China, and one in Japan.[[4]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-overview-4)

UMC is listed on the [Taiwan Stock Exchange](Taiwan_Stock_Exchange "Taiwan Stock Exchange") as [2303](https://finance.yahoo.com/q?m=TW&s=2303.TW). UMC has 12 manufacturing facilities worldwide, employing approximately 19,500 people.

UMC is a significant supplier to the automotive industry.[[5]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-5)

## History

- On May 22, 1980, UMC was spun off from the [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute") and was formally established as the first private integrated circuit company in Taiwan.
- 1983: TMC starts a joint research project with US-based [Vitelic](Mosel_Vitelic_Inc "Mosel Vitelic Inc").
- 1985
  * UMC was officially listed on the [Taiwan Stock Exchange](Taiwan_Stock_Exchange "Taiwan Stock Exchange") (code: 2303). It was the first listed semiconductor company in Taiwan. At that time, [Morris Chang](Morris_Chang "Morris Chang") was its chairman.
  * UMC sets up a subsidiary, **Unicorn Microelectronics Corporation** (also abbreviated UMC), in Silicon Valley to improve access to technology, signing joint research agreements with Mosel (later Mosel Vitelic) and Quasel.
- 1995: UMC decided to transform from an IDM company with its own products to a professional pure-play foundry.
- 1996: Spun off its IC design units to establish <MediaTek>, Novatek, ITE Technology, [Faraday Technology](Faraday_Technology "Faraday Technology"), AMIC Technology, and Davicom.
- 1999: Fab 12A 12-inch wafer fab in [Tainan Science Park](Tainan_Science_Park "Tainan Science Park") was officially established.
- 2000:
  * Lists on the [New York Stock Exchange](New_York_Stock_Exchange "New York Stock Exchange") (code: UMC) as Taiwan's first semiconductor company to do so.[[6]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-6)
  * Produces the first chips using copper process technology and the first 0.13 micron ICs in the semiconductor industry.
- 2004: 12-inch wafer fab in Singapore enters mass production.
- 2008: Listed as a constituent stock on the [Dow Jones Sustainability Index](Dow_Jones_Sustainability_Index "Dow Jones Sustainability Index") (DJSI) for the first time.[[7]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-7)
- 2010: 30th anniversary of the company.
- 2013: Fully acquires "**[Hejian Technology](Hejian_Technology "Hejian Technology") Wafer Fab**" in Suzhou, <China>.
- 2015: USCXM 12-inch wafer fab located in Xiamen, Fujian Province, China was officially established.[[8]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-8)
- 2017: 28 nm mass production begins at USCXM in Xiamen, China.
- 2019: Fully acquired Japan-based Mie Fujitsu Semiconductor.[[9]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-9)[[10]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-10)[[11]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-11)
- 2020: Reached a plea agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice to resolve a 2018 trade secrets case.[[12]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-businesswire.com-12)


### U.S. Indictment and guilty plea

The [United States Department of Justice](United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") indicted UMC and Chinese firm [Fujian Jinhua](Fujian_Jinhua_Integrated_Circuit "Fujian Jinhua Integrated Circuit") in 2018, alleging that they conspired to steal intellectual property from U.S. company [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology").[[13]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-13)[[14]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-:1-14) In October 2020, UMC and the U.S. Department of Justice reached a plea agreement, with UMC pleading guilty to one count of receiving and possessing a stolen trade secret and agreeing to pay a fine of $60 million. UMC’s plea and Plea Agreement resolved the 2018 trade secrets case brought against UMC by the U.S. Department of Justice. As part of the Plea Agreement, DOJ agreed to dismiss the original indictment against UMC, including allegations of conspiracy to commit economic espionage and conspiracy to steal multiple trade secrets from Micron Technology, Inc. (“Micron”), patent-related allegations, and alleged damages and penalties of $400 million USD to $8.75 billion. The one trade secret at issue in the guilty plea and Plea Agreement related to older technology that had been in mass production worldwide for several years. DOJ also dismissed a related civil case against UMC. Aside from the fine amount, UMC has no further financial obligations to DOJ. The Plea Agreement also provides that UMC will cooperate with DOJ and will be subject to a three-year term of non-supervised probation.[[12]](United_Microelectronics_Corporation#cite_note-businesswire.com-12)

This article is about the business model for making [integrated circuits](Integrated_circuits "Integrated circuits"). For other uses of the term **foundry**, see [foundry (disambiguation)](Foundry_(disambiguation) "Foundry (disambiguation)").

The **foundry model** is a [microelectronics](Microelectronics "Microelectronics") engineering and manufacturing [business model](Business_model "Business model") consisting of a [semiconductor fabrication plant](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant"), or foundry, and an [integrated circuit design](Integrated_circuit_design "Integrated circuit design") operation, each belonging to separate companies or subsidiaries.[[1]](Foundry_model#cite_note-1)[[2]](Foundry_model#cite_note-2)[[3]](Foundry_model#cite_note-3)[[4]](Foundry_model#cite_note-4)

[Integrated device manufacturers](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDMs) design and manufacture integrated circuits. Many companies, known as [fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_company "Fabless semiconductor company"), only design devices; merchant or [pure play](Pure_play "Pure play") foundries only manufacture devices for other companies, without designing them. Examples of IDMs are <Intel>, [Samsung](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics"), and [Texas Instruments](Texas_Instruments "Texas Instruments"),
examples of pure play foundries are <GlobalFoundries>, <TSMC>, and [UMC](United_Microelectronics_Corporation "United Microelectronics Corporation"), and examples of fabless companies are [AMD](Advanced_Micro_Devices "Advanced Micro Devices"), <Nvidia>, and <Qualcomm>.

Integrated circuit production facilities are expensive to build and maintain. Unless they can be kept at nearly full use, they will become a drain on the [finances](Finances "Finances") of the company that owns them. The foundry [model](Business_model "Business model") uses two methods to avoid these costs: fabless companies avoid costs by not owning such facilities. Merchant foundries, on the other hand, find work from the worldwide pool of fabless companies, through careful [scheduling](Scheduling_(production_processes) "Scheduling (production processes)"), [pricing](Pricing "Pricing"), and contracting, keep their plants in full use.

## History

Companies that both designed and produced the devices were originally responsible for manufacturing microelectronic devices. These manufacturers were involved in both the [research and development](Research_and_development "Research and development") of manufacturing processes and the research and development of [microcircuit](Microcircuit "Microcircuit") design.

The first pure play semiconductor company is the [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation](Taiwan_Semiconductor_Manufacturing_Corporation "Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation"), a [spin-off](Corporate_spin-off "Corporate spin-off") of the government [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute"), which split its design and fabrication divisions in 1987,[[5]](Foundry_model#cite_note-5) a model advocated for by [Carver Mead](Carver_Mead "Carver Mead") in the U.S., but deemed too costly to pursue. The separation of design and fabrication became known as the foundry model, with [fabless manufacturing](Fabless_manufacturing "Fabless manufacturing") outsourcing to [semiconductor foundries](Semiconductor_foundry "Semiconductor foundry").[[6]](Foundry_model#cite_note-Brown-6)

[Fabless semiconductor companies](Fabless_semiconductor_companies "Fabless semiconductor companies") do not have any semiconductor fabrication capability; and contract production with a merchant foundry manufacturer. The fabless company concentrates on the research and development of an IC-product; the foundry concentrates on manufacturing and [testing](Test_method "Test method") the physical product. If the foundry does not have any semiconductor design capability, it is a pure-play semiconductor foundry.

An absolute separation into fabless and foundry companies is not necessary. Some companies continue to exist that perform both operations and benefit from the close coupling of their skills. Some companies manufacture some of their own designs and contract out to have others manufactured or designed, in cases where they see [value](Value_(marketing) "Value (marketing)") or seek special skills. The foundry model is a business vision that seeks to optimize productivity.

### MOSIS

The very first merchant foundries were part of the <MOSIS> service. The MOSIS service gave limited production access to designers with limited means, such as students, university researchers, and engineers at small [startups](Startup_company "Startup company").[[7]](Foundry_model#cite_note-BergerLester2015-7) The designer submitted designs, and these submissions were manufactured with the commercial company's extra capacity. Manufacturers could insert some [wafers](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") for a MOSIS design into a collection of their own wafers when a processing step was compatible with both operations. The commercial company (serving as foundry) was already running the process, so they were effectively being paid by MOSIS for something they were already doing. A factory with excess capacity during slow periods could also run MOSIS designs to avoid having expensive [capital](Capital_(economics) "Capital (economics)") equipment stand idle.

Under-use of an expensive manufacturing plant could lead to the financial ruin of the owner, so selling surplus [wafer](Wafer_(electronics) "Wafer (electronics)") capacity was a way to maximize the fab's use. Hence, economic factors created a climate where fab operators wanted to sell surplus wafer-manufacturing capacity and designers wanted to purchase manufacturing capacity rather than try to build it.

Although MOSIS opened the doors to some fabless customers, earning additional [revenue](Revenue "Revenue") for the foundry and providing inexpensive service to the customer, running a business around MOSIS production was difficult. The merchant foundries sold wafer capacity on a surplus basis, as a secondary business activity. Services to the customers were secondary to the commercial business, with little [guarantee](Guarantee "Guarantee") of support. The choice of merchant dictated the design, development flow, and available techniques to the fabless customer. Merchant foundries might require [proprietary](Property "Property") and non-portable preparation steps. Foundries concerned with protecting what they considered [trade secrets](Trade_secret "Trade secret") of their [methodologies](Methodologies "Methodologies") might only be willing to release data to designers after an onerous [nondisclosure](Nondisclosure_agreement "Nondisclosure agreement") procedure.

### Dedicated foundry

In 1987, the world's first dedicated merchant foundry opened its doors: [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC)](TSMC "TSMC").[[8]](Foundry_model#cite_note-HirakawaLal2013-8) The distinction of 'dedicated' is in reference to the typical merchant foundry of the era, whose primary business activity was building and selling of its own [IC](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit")-products. The dedicated foundry offers several key advantages to its customers: first, it does not sell finished IC-products into the [supply](Supply_(economics) "Supply (economics)") channel; thus a dedicated foundry will never compete directly with its fabless customers (obviating a common concern of fabless companies). Second, the dedicated foundry can scale production capacity to a customer's needs, offering low-quantity [shuttle](Multi-project_wafer_service "Multi-project wafer service") services in addition to full-scale [production](Mass_production "Mass production") lines. Finally, the dedicated foundry offers a "COT-flow" (customer owned tooling) based on industry-standard [EDA](Electronic_design_automation "Electronic design automation") systems, whereas many IDM merchants required its customers to use proprietary (non-portable) development tools. The COT advantage gave the customer complete control over the design process, from concept to final design.

## Foundry sales leaders by year

- **Pure-play semiconductor foundry** is a company that does not offer a significant amount of IC products of its own design, but instead operates [semiconductor fabrication plants](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") focused on producing ICs for other companies.[[9]](Foundry_model#cite_note-9)
- **[Integrated device manufacturer](Integrated_device_manufacturer "Integrated device manufacturer") (IDM) semiconductor foundry** is where companies such as Texas Instruments, IBM, and Samsung join in to provide foundry services as long as there is no conflict of interest between relevant parties.

TSMC has a global capacity of about thirteen million 300 mm-equivalent wafers per year as of 2020 and makes chips for customers with process nodes from 2 microns to [5 nanometres](5_nm_process "5 nm process"). TSMC was the first foundry to market [7-nanometre](7_nm_process "7 nm process") and [5-nanometre](5_nm_process "5 nm process") (used by the 2020 [Apple A14](Apple_A14 "Apple A14") and [M1](Apple_M1 "Apple M1") [SoCs](System_on_a_chip "System on a chip"), the MediaTek [Dimensity 8100](List_of_MediaTek_processors "List of MediaTek processors"), and [AMD Ryzen 7000](List_of_AMD_Ryzen_processors#Raphael_desktop "List of AMD Ryzen processors") series processors) production capabilities, and the first to commercialize [extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography](Extreme_ultraviolet_lithography "Extreme ultraviolet lithography") technology in high volume.

## History

In 1986, [Li Kwoh-ting](Li_Kwoh-ting "Li Kwoh-ting"), representing the [Executive Yuan](Executive_Yuan "Executive Yuan"), invited Morris Chang to serve as the president of the [Industrial Technology Research Institute](Industrial_Technology_Research_Institute "Industrial Technology Research Institute") (ITRI). At that time, the Taiwanese government wanted to develop its semiconductor industry, but its high investment and high risk nature made it difficult to find investors. Only <Philips> was willing to sign a joint venture contract with Taiwan to put up $58 million, transfer its production technology, and license intellectual property in exchange for a 27.5 percent stake in TSMC. The Taiwanese government provided another 48 percent of the startup capital for TSMC and the rest of the capital was raised from wealthy Taiwanese who were “asked” by the government to invest. “What generally happened was that one of the ministers in the government would call a businessman in Taiwan,” Chang explained, “to get him to invest.” The government asked several of the island’s wealthiest families, who owned firms that specialized in plastics, textiles, and chemicals, to put up the money. From day one, TSMC wasn’t really a private business: it was a project of the Taiwanese state.[[20]](TSMC#cite_note-20)[[21]](TSMC#cite_note-21)[[22]](TSMC#cite_note-22)

Since then, the company has continued to grow, albeit subject to the cycles of demand. In 2011, the company planned to increase research and development expenditures by almost 39% to [NT$](New_Taiwan_dollar "New Taiwan dollar")50 billion to fend off growing competition.[[23]](TSMC#cite_note-23) The company also planned to expand capacity by 30% in 2011 to meet strong market demand.[[24]](TSMC#cite_note-24) In May 2014, TSMC's board of directors approved capital appropriations of [US$](United_States_dollar "United States dollar")568 million to increase and improve manufacturing capabilities after the company forecast higher than expected demand.[[25]](TSMC#cite_note-Q2_2014_forecast-25) In August 2014, TSMC's board of directors approved additional capital appropriations of US$3.05 billion.[[26]](TSMC#cite_note-26)

In 2011, it was reported that TSMC had begun trial production of the [A5](Apple_A5 "Apple A5") SoC and [A6](Apple_A6 "Apple A6") SoCs for Apple's [iPad](IPad "IPad") and [iPhone](IPhone "IPhone") devices.[[27]](TSMC#cite_note-27)[[28]](TSMC#cite_note-28) According to reports,[[29]](TSMC#cite_note-29) in May 2014 Apple sourced its [A8](Apple_A8 "Apple A8") and [A8X](Apple_A8X "Apple A8X") SoCs from TSMC.[[30]](TSMC#cite_note-TechNews_Apple_A8_article-30)[[31]](TSMC#cite_note-CNET_64-bit_processor_article-31) Apple then sourced the [A9](Apple_A9 "Apple A9") SoC with both TSMC and Samsung (to increase volume for [iPhone 6S](IPhone_6S "IPhone 6S") launch) and the [A9X](Apple_A9X "Apple A9X") exclusively with TSMC, thus resolving the issue of sourcing a chip in two different [microarchitecture](Microarchitecture "Microarchitecture") sizes. As of 2014, Apple was TSMC's most important customer.[[31]](TSMC#cite_note-CNET_64-bit_processor_article-31)[[32]](TSMC#cite_note-Taipei_Times_Apple_article-32)

In October 2014, [ARM](ARM_Holdings "ARM Holdings") and TSMC announced a new multi-year agreement for the development of ARM based 10 nm [FinFET](Multigate_device#FinFET "Multigate device") processors.[[33]](TSMC#cite_note-33)

In 2020, TSMC became the first semiconductor company in the world to sign up for the [RE100](The_Climate_Group "The Climate Group") initiative, pledging to use 100% [renewable energy](Renewable_energy "Renewable energy") by 2050.[[34]](TSMC#cite_note-34) TSMC accounts for roughly 5% of the energy consumption in Taiwan, even exceeding that of the capital city Taipei. This initiative was thus expected to accelerate the transformation to renewable energy in the country.[[35]](TSMC#cite_note-35)

For 2020, TSMC had a net income of US$17.60 billion on a consolidated revenue of US$45.51 billion, an increase of 57.5% and 31.4% respectively from the 2019 level of US$11.18 billion net income and US$34.63 billion consolidated revenue.[[36]](TSMC#cite_note-36) Its [market capitalization](Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") was over $550 billion in April 2021. TSMC's revenue in the first quarter of 2020 reached US$10 billion,[[37]](TSMC#cite_note-37) while its market capitalization was US$254 billion.[[38]](TSMC#cite_note-TSM-YahooFinance-38) TSMC's market capitalization reached a value of NT$1.9 trillion (US$63.4 billion) in December 2010.[[39]](TSMC#cite_note-39) It was ranked 70th in the [FT Global 500](FT_Global_500 "FT Global 500") 2013 list of the world's most highly valued companies with a capitalization of US$86.7 billion,[[40]](TSMC#cite_note-40) while reaching US$110 billion in May 2014.[[38]](TSMC#cite_note-TSM-YahooFinance-38) In March 2017, TSMC's market capitalization surpassed that of semiconductor giant <Intel> for the first time, hitting NT$5.14 trillion (US$168.4 billion), with Intel's at US$165.7 billion.[[41]](TSMC#cite_note-41) On 27 June 2020, TSMC briefly became the world's 10th most valuable company, with a market capitalization of US$410 billion.[[42]](TSMC#cite_note-42)

As the risk of a war between Taiwan and the People's Republic of China increases, TSMC and its investors have explored options to mitigate the consequences of such an event. Since the beginning of the 2020s, TSMC has expanded its operations outside of the island of Taiwan, opening new fabs in Japan and the United States, with further plans for expansion into Germany.[[43]](TSMC#cite_note-43) In July 2020, TSMC confirmed it would halt the shipment of silicon wafers to Chinese telecommunications equipment manufacturer <Huawei> and its subsidiary <HiSilicon> by 14 September.[[44]](TSMC#cite_note-44)[[45]](TSMC#cite_note-45)

Based on my research of the Wikipedia articles, I can now summarize UMC's manufacturing capacity during the 2010s (2010-2019).

## UMC Manufacturing Capacity Summary (2010-2019)

### **Manufacturing Facilities**
- **Total fabs**: 12 manufacturing facilities worldwide
- **300mm fabs**: 4 major 300mm wafer fabs (Taiwan, Singapore, China, Japan)
- **Key expansions during the 2010s**:
  - 2013: Fully acquired Hejian Technology Wafer Fab in Suzhou, China
  - 2015: USCXM 12-inch wafer fab established in Xiamen, China
  - 2019: Fully acquired Mie Fujitsu Semiconductor (Japan)

### **Monthly Wafer Capacity** (from Fab list)
Combined capacity across all facilities:
- **300mm (12-inch) fabs**: ~192,000 wafers/month
  - Fab 12A (Tainan, Taiwan): 87,000 wafers/month
  - Fab 12i (Singapore): 53,000 wafers/month
  - Fab 12X (Xiamen, China): 19,000-25,000 wafers/month
  - Fab 12M (Japan): 33,000 wafers/month
- **200mm (8-inch) and smaller fabs**: ~450,000+ wafers/month across 8 facilities
- **Estimated total capacity**: ~600,000+ wafers/month

### **Revenue**
- **2016**: $4,587 million USD
- **2017**: $4,898 million USD
- **2019**: Continued strong performance as 3rd largest pure-play foundry
- **Process node revenue breakdown (2019)**:
  - 14nm-28nm: 12%
  - 28nm-40nm: 26%
  - 40nm-65nm: 14%
  - 65nm-280nm+: 48%

### **Market Share in Foundry Services**
**2017 Pure-Play Foundry Rankings**:
| Rank | Company | Foundry Revenue (2017) |
|------|---------|----------------------|
| 1 | TSMC | $32,040 million |
| 2 | GlobalFoundries | $5,407 million |
| **3** | **UMC** | **$4,898 million** |
| 4 | Samsung (IDM) | $7,398 million |
| 5 | SMIC | $3,099 million |

### **Comparison to TSMC**
| Metric | UMC | TSMC | Ratio |
|--------|-----|------|-------|
| Foundry Revenue (2017) | $4.9B | $32.0B | ~15% of TSMC |
| Market Position | 3rd pure-play | 1st pure-play | Dominated by TSMC |
| Advanced Nodes | Up to 14nm (limited) | 7nm/5nm leaders | Significant gap |
| Global Capacity | ~600K wafers/month | ~13M wafers/year | ~7x smaller |

### **Key Takeaways**
1. UMC consistently ranked **3rd globally** among pure-play foundries throughout the 2010s
2. **Revenue was ~15% of TSMC's** during this period
3. Focused on **mature nodes** (28nm and above) rather than cutting-edge technology
4. Expanded manufacturing footprint in **China** (Suzhou, Xiamen) and **Japan** during the decade
5. Maintained significant capacity on **8-inch and 12-inch mature process nodes** for automotive, industrial, and consumer applications

content:
Based on my research of Wikipedia articles about the semiconductor industry, here's the information about market leaders and production rankings during the 1990s decade:

## Semiconductor Industry Market Leaders and Production Rankings (1990s)

### **Early 1990s: Japanese Dominance**

**Japan** was the dominant force in the semiconductor industry at the start of the 1990s:

- **Japan's Market Share**: Approximately **50% of global semiconductor market share** in the 1980s/early 1990s
- **NEC** was the **world's largest semiconductor company** by annual revenue from **1985 to 1992**
- Other major Japanese semiconductor companies included **Toshiba**, **Hitachi**, and **Fujitsu**

### **Mid to Late 1990s: Shift in Power**

The industry landscape began to shift dramatically during this period:

**Intel's Rise**:
- Intel became the **dominant supplier of PC microprocessors** during the 1990s
- Intel invested heavily in new microprocessor designs, fostering rapid computer industry growth
- Became known as the **"decades-long champion"** of the semiconductor industry
- Intel was a decades-long leader before being briefly surpassed by Samsung (2017-2018)

**NEC's Decline**:
- NEC dropped from #1 to **#2 largest semiconductor company by 1995**
- This marked the beginning of Japan's gradual decline

### **Key Factors in the 1990s Transition**

**1. Japan-United States Semiconductor Agreement (1986)**:
- The agreement resolved trade friction between Japan and the US
- Lead to gradual reduction in Japanese competitiveness

**2. Rise of South Korea and Taiwan**:
- **South Korea**: Companies like **Samsung Electronics** began to emerge as major semiconductor memory manufacturers
- **Taiwan**: TSMC pioneered the **fabless foundry model in 1987**, reshaping the global semiconductor industry structure

### **Industry Structure During the 1990s**

The global semiconductor industry was dominated by companies from:
- **United States** (Intel, Texas Instruments, etc.)
- **Japan** (NEC, Toshiba, Hitachi, etc.)
- **South Korea** (Samsung, Hyundai/Elpida)
- **Taiwan** (UMC, later TSMC)

The 1990s represented a pivotal decade when the semiconductor industry shifted from Japanese memory chip dominance to American microprocessor leadership and the emergence of Korean memory manufacturers and Taiwanese foundries.

<Samsung>, a Korean electronics company, began producing [semiconductors](Semiconductor "Semiconductor") in 1974 and has grown to become one of the largest semiconductor fabricators in the world. In the decades following Samsung's entrance into semiconductor fabrication, many of its workers developed serious illnesses, including leukemia, lymphoma, and [multiple sclerosis (MS)](Multiple_sclerosis "Multiple sclerosis"). Beginning in 2007, the families of the impacted workers, with the help of a variety of domestic and international organizations, organized and mobilized against Samsung in the form of various protests and legal challenges. This organized opposition lasted for over a decade and largely concluded upon the signing of a binding settlement agreement between Samsung and the relevant opposition leader. Additionally, Samsung issued a public apology[[1]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-1) and acceptance responsibility for causing an increased risk of serious illness in its semiconductor factories.

## Background

Samsung first entered the semiconductor fabrication business in 1974 by [acquiring Korea Semiconductors](Samsung_Electronics "Samsung Electronics").[[2]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-2) By 1993, Samsung was the world's largest producer of memory chips, and it has retained that title ever since.[[3]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-3)

The semiconductor fabrication process necessitates the use of a variety of chemicals and carcinogenic substances. At various points in the process, workers are required to dip components in chemical baths, utilize X-ray radiation, and engage in various other production techniques that expose them to potentially harmful chemicals.[[4]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:0-4)

In the 1980s and 1990s, the semiconductor industry was subject a variety of criticisms for creating potential health hazards in their fabrication facilities.[[5]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:4-5) A number of Samsung's US-based competitors were found to have statistically greater serious illness incidence rates among their semiconductor workforces, which led to increased monitoring, safety standards, and protection for semiconductor workers in the US and many other countries.[[4]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:0-4) Samsung, however, has historically declined to release the relevant health data and information on the environment in its semiconductor plants. This decision has been facilitated by the South Korean government's regulations protecting trade secrets that have allowed the company to withhold relevant information, such as the types of chemicals used in semiconductor production, despite numerous attempts to have it made public.[[6]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:5-6)

Studies and reports released decades after Samsung's entry into semiconductor fabrication showed that the company has a long history of questionable health and safety practices.[[7]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-7) It was discovered that Samsung semiconductor workers' exposure to radiation was significantly beyond the acceptable levels recognized by US regulators.[[8]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:1-8) Moreover, it was found that Samsung neglected to actually check the chemical composition of substances used in its semiconductor fabrication process, and that the company failed to conduct exposure assessments for 71% of chemicals utilized in production.[[8]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:1-8) Other investigations suggested the company continued to use harmful substances even after stating it would no longer use them. For example, internal documents showed that Samsung was using TCE, a known toxic substance, as recently as 2010 despite the company publicly stating it had not been a part of the fabrication process since 1995.[[4]](Protests_against_Samsung#cite_note-:0-4)

As such, there have been a great deal of cases of serious illness being developed in Samsung's manufacturing workforce over the decades after it first entered the semiconductor market. However, prior to the organization of an opposition movement, no court in South Korea had ordered Samsung to pay compensation for causing illness in any of its workers.

## Key Findings from Wikipedia

### Becoming #1 Memory Chip Producer in 1993

According to the Wikipedia article "Protests against Samsung":

> **"By 1993, Samsung was the world's largest producer of memory chips, and it has retained that title ever since."**

This is a significant milestone in Samsung's history, marking when the company overtook Japanese competitors to dominate the global memory chip market.

### Samsung's Semiconductor Journey in the 1990s

From the Samsung Electronics Wikipedia article, here are the key production milestones from the 1990s:

**Foundational Years:**
- **1974**: Samsung entered the semiconductor business by acquiring Korea Semiconductors, which was on the verge of bankruptcy
- **1983**: Lee Kun-hee made the "Tokyo Declaration," announcing Samsung's intention to become a DRAM vendor
- **1984**: Samsung successfully developed a 64 kb DRAM, reducing the technological gap from major companies from over a decade to approximately 4 years

**1990s Production Breakthroughs:**
- **1992**: World's first 64MB DRAM
- **1993**: Became the world's largest producer of memory chips
- **1994**: 256 MB DRAM
- **1996**: 1GB DRAM

**Company Evolution:**
- **1988**: Samsung Electric Industries merged with Samsung Semiconductor & Communications to form Samsung Electronics

The article notes that Samsung:
- Is currently the world's largest semiconductor memory manufacturer
- From 2017 to 2018, became the largest semiconductor company in the world, briefly dethroning Intel (the decades-long champion)
- The semiconductor division continues to account for a significant portion of Samsung's operating profits (68% in Q4 2016 according to the article)

Samsung's semiconductor strategy involved vertical integration - manufacturing components for other companies including Apple, Sony, HTC, and Nokia. This strategy was part of a 10-year plan initiated after 1995 to transform Samsung from a "budget brand" into a global design leader while leveraging their component manufacturing capabilities.

Unfortunately, the specific production volume statistics (in terms of units or revenue) from the 1990s are not detailed in the Wikipedia articles I retrieved, though the technological milestones clearly demonstrate Samsung's rapid advancement during that decade.

### Major competitors

Intel's competitors in PC chipsets included <AMD>, [VIA Technologies](VIA_Technologies "VIA Technologies"), [Silicon Integrated Systems](Silicon_Integrated_Systems "Silicon Integrated Systems"), and <Nvidia>. Intel's competitors in networking include [NXP Semiconductors](NXP_Semiconductors "NXP Semiconductors"), <Infineon>, [Broadcom Limited](Broadcom_Limited "Broadcom Limited"), [Marvell Technology Group](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group") and [Applied Micro Circuits Corporation](Applied_Micro_Circuits_Corporation "Applied Micro Circuits Corporation"), and competitors in flash memory included <Spansion>, Samsung Electronics, <Qimonda>, Kioxia, STMicroelectronics, [Micron](Micron_Technology "Micron Technology"), and [SK Hynix](SK_Hynix "SK Hynix").

The only major competitor in the [x86](X86 "X86") processor market is AMD, with which Intel has had full cross-licensing agreements since 1976: each partner can use the other's patented technological innovations without charge after a certain time.[[25]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-AMD_deal_2001-25) However, the cross-licensing agreement is canceled in the event of an AMD bankruptcy or takeover.[[26]](Intel#cite_note-Patent_Cross_License_Agreement-26)

Some smaller competitors, such as VIA Technologies, produce [low-power](Low-power_electronics "Low-power electronics") x86 processors for small factor computers and portable equipment. Moore") (known for "[Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law")"), a [chemist](Chemist "Chemist"), [Robert Noyce](Robert_Noyce "Robert Noyce"), a physicist and co-inventor of the [integrated circuit](Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit") and [Arthur Rock](Arthur_Rock "Arthur Rock"), an investor and [venture capitalist](Venture_capital "Venture capital")[[35]](Intel#cite_note-35)[[36]](Intel#cite_note-36)[[37]](Intel#cite_note-37) Moore and Noyce had left [Fairchild Semiconductor](Fairchild_Semiconductor "Fairchild Semiconductor") and were part of the "[traitorous eight](Traitorous_eight "Traitorous eight")". There were originally 500,000 shares outstanding of which Dr. Noyce bought 245,000 shares, Dr. Moore 245,000 shares, and Mr. Rock 10,000 shares; all at $1 per share. Rock offered $2,500,000 of convertible debentures to a limited group of private investors (equivalent to $21 million in 2022), convertible at $5 per share.[[38]](Intel#cite_note-38)[[39]](Intel#cite_note-39) Just 2 years later, Intel became a [public company](Public_company "Public company") via an [initial public offering](Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") (IPO), raising $6.8 million ($23.50 per share).[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) Intel's third employee was [Andy Grove](Andrew_Grove "Andrew Grove"),[[note 1]](Intel#cite_note-41) a [chemical engineer](Chemical_engineer "Chemical engineer"), who later ran the company through much of the 1980s and the high-growth 1990s.

In deciding on a name, Moore and Noyce quickly rejected "Moore Noyce",[[41]](Intel#cite_note-42) near [homophone](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/homophone "wikt:homophone") for "more noise" – an ill-suited name for an [electronics](Electronics "Electronics") company, since [noise in electronics](Electronic_noise "Electronic noise") is usually undesirable and typically associated with bad [interference](Electromagnetic_interference "Electromagnetic interference"). Instead, they founded the company as **NM Electronics** (or **MN Electronics**) on July 18, 1968, but by the end of the month had changed the name to **Intel** which stood for **Int**egrated **El**ectronics.[[note 2]](Intel#cite_note-48) Since "Intel" was already trademarked by the hotel chain Intelco, they had to buy the rights for the name.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[47]](Intel#cite_note-49)

### Early history

At its founding, Intel was distinguished by its ability to make [logic circuits](Logic_circuit "Logic circuit") using [semiconductor devices](Semiconductor_device "Semiconductor device"). The founders' goal was the [semiconductor memory](Semiconductor_memory "Semiconductor memory") market, widely predicted to replace [magnetic-core memory](Magnetic-core_memory "Magnetic-core memory"). Its first product, a quick entry into the small, high-speed memory market in 1969, was the 3101 [Schottky TTL](Schottky_transistor "Schottky transistor") [bipolar](Bipolar_junction_transistor "Bipolar junction transistor") 64-bit [static random-access memory](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory") (SRAM), which was nearly twice as fast as earlier Schottky diode implementations by Fairchild and the Electrotechnical Laboratory in [Tsukuba, Japan](Tsukuba%2C_Ibaraki "Tsukuba, Ibaraki").[[48]](Intel#cite_note-50)[[49]](Intel#cite_note-51) In the same year, Intel also produced the 3301 Schottky bipolar 1024-bit [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM)[[50]](Intel#cite_note-52) and the first commercial [metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor](MOSFET "MOSFET") (MOSFET) [silicon gate](Silicon_gate "Silicon gate") SRAM chip, the 256-bit 1101.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40)[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[52]](Intel#cite_note-54)

While the 1101 was a significant advance, its complex static [cell structure](Memory_cell_(computing) "Memory cell (computing)") made it too slow and costly for [mainframe](Mainframe_computer "Mainframe computer") memories. The three-[transistor](Transistor "Transistor") cell implemented in the first commercially available [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM), the [1103](Intel_1103 "Intel 1103") released in 1970, solved these issues. The 1103 was the bestselling semiconductor memory chip in the world by 1972, as it replaced core memory in many applications.[[53]](Intel#cite_note-55)[[54]](Intel#cite_note-Bellis-56) Intel's business grew during the 1970s as it expanded and improved its manufacturing processes and produced a wider range of [products](Product_(business) "Product (business)"), still dominated by various memory devices.

Intel created the [first commercially available microprocessor (Intel 4004)](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") in 1971.[[40]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_Museum-40) The microprocessor represented a notable advance in the technology of integrated circuitry, as it miniaturized the central processing unit of a computer, which then made it possible for small machines to perform calculations that in the past only very large machines could do. Considerable technological innovation was needed before the microprocessor could actually become the basis of what was first known as a "mini computer" and then known as a "personal computer".[[55]](Intel#cite_note-57) Intel also created one of the first [microcomputers](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") in 1973.[[51]](Intel#cite_note-Intel-Product-Timeline-53)[[56]](Intel#cite_note-Intellec-1973-58)

72, in <Malaysia>, which would host multiple Intel operations, before opening assembly facilities and semiconductor plants in <Singapore> and <Jerusalem> in the early 1980s, and manufacturing and development centers in China, India, and Costa Rica in the 1990s.[[57]](Intel#cite_note-59) By the early 1980s, its business was dominated by [dynamic random-access memory](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory") (DRAM) chips. However, increased competition from Japanese semiconductor manufacturers had, by 1983, dramatically reduced the profitability of this market. The growing success of the <IBM> personal computer, based on an Intel microprocessor, was among factors that convinced Gordon Moore (CEO since 1975) to shift the company's focus to microprocessors and to change fundamental aspects of that business model. Moore's decision to sole-source Intel's 386 chip played into the company's continuing success.

By the end of the 1980s, buoyed by its fortuitous position as microprocessor supplier to IBM and IBM's competitors within the rapidly growing [personal computer market](IBM_PC_compatible "IBM PC compatible"), Intel embarked on a 10-year period of unprecedented growth as the primary (and most profitable) hardware supplier to the PC industry, part of the winning 'Wintel' combination. Moore handed over his position as CEO to Andy Grove in 1987. By launching its Intel Inside [marketing campaign](Marketing_campaign "Marketing campaign") in 1991, Intel was able to associate [brand loyalty](Brand_loyalty "Brand loyalty") with consumer selection, so that by the end of the 1990s, its line of <Pentium> processors had become a household name.

### Challenges to dominance (2000s)

After 2000, growth in demand for high-end microprocessors slowed. Competitors, most notably <AMD> (Intel's largest competitor in its primary [x86](X86 "X86") architecture market), garnered significant market share, initially in low-end and mid-range processors but ultimately across the product range, and Intel's dominant position in its core market was greatly reduced,[[58]](Intel#cite_note-Wong-60) mostly due to controversial <NetBurst> microarchitecture. In the early 2000s then-CEO, [Craig Barrett](Craig_Barrett_(businessman) "Craig Barrett (businessman)") attempted to diversify the company's business beyond semiconductors, but few of these activities were ultimately successful.

#### Litigation

Intel had also for a number of years been embroiled in litigation. US law did not initially recognize [intellectual property rights](Intellectual_property_rights "Intellectual property rights") related to microprocessor [topology](Topology_(electrical_circuits) "Topology (electrical circuits)") (circuit layouts), until the [Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984](Semiconductor_Chip_Protection_Act_of_1984 "Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984"), a law sought by Intel and the [Semiconductor Industry Association](Semiconductor_Industry_Association "Semiconductor Industry Association") (SIA).[[59]](Intel#cite_note-61) During the late 1980s and 1990s (after this law was passed), Intel also sued companies that tried to develop competitor chips to the [80386](Intel_80386 "Intel 80386") <CPU>.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) The lawsuits were noted to significantly burden the competition with legal bills, even if Intel lost the suits.[[60]](Intel#cite_note-ReferenceA-62) <Antitrust> allegations had been simmering since the early 1990s and had been the cause of one [lawsuit](Lawsuit "Lawsuit") against Intel in 1991. In 2004 and 2005, AMD brought [further claims](Intel_Corp._v._Advanced_Micro_Devices%2C_Inc. "Intel Corp. v. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.") against Intel related to [unfair competition](Unfair_competition "Unfair competition").

### Reorganization and success with Intel Core (2005–2015)

In 2005, CEO [Paul Otellini](Paul_Otellini "Paul Otellini") reorganized the company to refocus its core processor and chipset business on platforms (enterprise, digital home, digital health, and mobility).

On June 6, 2005, [Steve Jobs](Steve_Jobs "Steve Jobs"), then CEO of [Apple](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), announced that Apple would be using Intel's x86 processors for its <Macintosh> computers, switching from the <PowerPC> architecture developed by the [AIM alliance](AIM_alliance "AIM alliance").[[61]](Intel#cite_note-auto2-63) This was seen as win for Intel;[[62]](Intel#cite_note-auto1-64) An analyst called the move "risky" and "foolish", as Intel's current offerings at the time were considered to be behind those of AMD and IBM.[[63]](Intel#cite_note-Computerworld1-65)

In 2006, Intel unveiled its [Core microarchitecture](Core_(microarchitecture) "Core (microarchitecture)") to widespread critical acclaim; the product range was perceived as an exceptional leap in processor performance that at a stroke regained much of its leadership of the field.[[64]](Intel#cite_note-66)[[65]](Intel#cite_note-67) In 2008, Intel had another "tick" when it introduced the Penryn microarchitecture, fabricated using the 45 nm process node. Later that year, Intel released a processor with the [Nehalem](Nehalem_(microarchitecture) "Nehalem (microarchitecture)") architecture to positive reception.[[66]](Intel#cite_note-68)

On June 27, 2006, the sale of Intel's <XScale> assets was announced. Intel agreed to sell the XScale processor business to [Marvell Technology Group](Marvell_Technology_Group "Marvell Technology Group") for an estimated $600 million and the assumption of unspecified liabilities. The move was intended to permit Intel to focus its resources on its core x86 and server businesses, and the [acquisition](Mergers_and_acquisitions "Mergers and acquisitions") completed on November 9, 2006.[[67]](Intel#cite_note-XScale-69)

In 2008, Intel spun off key assets of a solar startup business effort to form an independent company, SpectraWatt Inc. In 2011, SpectraWatt filed for bankruptcy.[[68]](Intel#cite_note-eetimes1-70)

In February 2011, Intel began to build a new microprocessor manufacturing facility in [Chandler, Arizona](Chandler%2C_Arizona "Chandler, Arizona"), completed in 2013 at a cost of $5 billion.[[69]](Intel#cite_note-71) The building is now the 10 nm-certified Fab 42 and is connected to the other Fabs (12, 22, 32) on Ocotillo Campus via an enclosed bridge known as the Link.[[70]](Intel#cite_note-72)[[71]](Intel#cite_note-73)[[72]](Intel#cite_note-74)[[73]](Intel#cite_note-75) The company produces three-quarters of its products in the United States, although three-quarters of its revenue come from overseas.[[74]](Intel#cite_note-76)

The [Alliance for Affordable Internet](Alliance_for_Affordable_Internet "Alliance for Affordable Internet") (A4AI) was launched in October 2013 and Intel is part of the coalition of public and private organizations that also includes <Facebook>, <Google>, and <Microsoft>. Led by [Sir Tim Berners-Lee](Tim_Berners-Lee "Tim Berners-Lee"), the A4AI seeks to make Internet access more affordable so that access is broadened in the developing world, where only 31% of people are online. Google will help to decrease Internet access prices so that they fall below the UN Broadband Commission's worldwide target of 5% of monthly income.[[75]](Intel#cite_note-77)

#### Attempts at entering the smartphone market

In April 2011, Intel began a pilot project with [ZTE Corporation](ZTE_Corporation "ZTE Corporation") to produce smartphones using the [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processor for China's domestic market. In December 2011, Intel announced that it reorganized several of its business units into a new mobile and communications group[[76]](Intel#cite_note-78) that would be responsible for the company's smartphone, tablet, and wireless efforts. Intel planned to introduce Medfield – a processor for tablets and smartphones – to the market in 2012, as an effort to compete with Arm.[[77]](Intel#cite_note-79) As a 32-nanometer processor, Medfield is designed to be energy-efficient, which is one of the core features in Arm's chips.[[78]](Intel#cite_note-autogenerated12-80)

At the Intel Developers Forum (IDF) 2011 in San Francisco, Intel's partnership with Google was announced. In January 2012, Google announced Android 2.3, supporting Intel's Atom microprocessor.[[79]](Intel#cite_note-81)[[80]](Intel#cite_note-82)[[81]](Intel#cite_note-83) In 2013, Intel's Kirk Skaugen said that Intel's exclusive focus on Microsoft platforms was a thing of the past and that they would now support all "tier-one operating systems" such as Linux, Android, iOS, and Chrome.[[82]](Intel#cite_note-84)

In 2014, Intel cut thousands of employees in response to "evolving market trends",[[83]](Intel#cite_note-85) and offered to subsidize manufacturers for the extra costs involved in using Intel chips in their tablets. In April 2016, Intel cancelled the <SoFIA> platform and the Broxton Atom SoC for smartphones,[[84]](Intel#cite_note-86)[[85]](Intel#cite_note-87)[[86]](Intel#cite_note-88)[[87]](Intel#cite_note-89) effectively leaving the smartphone market.[[88]](Intel#cite_note-MyUser_Theverge.com_June_1_2016c-90)[[89]](Intel#cite_note-verge2-91)

#### Intel custom foundry

Finding itself with excess fab capacity after the failure of the <Ultrabook> to gain market traction and with PC sales declining, in 2013 Intel reached a [foundry](Semiconductor_fabrication_plant "Semiconductor fabrication plant") agreement to produce chips for <Altera> using a 14nm process. General Manager of Intel's custom foundry division Sunit Rikhi indicated that Intel would pursue further such deals in the future.[[90]](Intel#cite_note-92) This was after poor sales of [Windows 8](Windows_8 "Windows 8") hardware caused a major retrenchment for most of the major semiconductor manufacturers, except for Qualcomm, which continued to see healthy purchases from its largest customer, Apple.[[91]](Intel#cite_note-93)
