*Intel Custom Foundry* division: <Achronix>, [Tabula](Tabula_(company) "Tabula (company)"), <Netronome>, <Microsemi>, and <Panasonic> –  most are [field-programmable gate array](Field-programmable_gate_array "Field-programmable gate array") (FPGA) makers, but Netronome designs network processors. Only Achronix began shipping chips made by Intel using the 22nm Tri-Gate process.[[92]](Intel#cite_note-94)[[93]](Intel#cite_note-95) Several other customers also exist but were not announced at the time.[[94]](Intel#cite_note-96)

The foundry business was closed in 2018 due to Intel's issues with its manufacturing.[[95]](Intel#cite_note-97)[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98)

### Security and manufacturing challenges (2016–2021)

Intel continued its [tick-tock](Tick%E2%80%93tock_model "Tick–tock model") model of a microarchitecture change followed by a die shrink until the 6th generation Core family based on the [Skylake](Skylake_(microarchitecture) "Skylake (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture. This model was deprecated in 2016, with the release of the seventh generation Core family (codenamed [Kaby Lake](Kaby_Lake "Kaby Lake")), ushering in the [process–architecture–optimization model](Process%E2%80%93architecture%E2%80%93optimization_model "Process–architecture–optimization model"). As Intel struggled to shrink their process node from [14 nm](14_nm_process "14 nm process") to [10 nm](10_nm_process "10 nm process"), processor development slowed down and the company continued to use the Skylake microarchitecture until 2020, albeit with optimizations.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)

#### 10 nm process node issues

While Intel originally planned to introduce 10 nm products in 2016, it later became apparent that there were manufacturing issues with the node.[[97]](Intel#cite_note-99) The first microprocessor under that node, [Cannon Lake](Cannon_Lake_(microarchitecture) "Cannon Lake (microarchitecture)") (marketed as 8th generation Core), was released in small quantities in 2018.[[98]](Intel#cite_note-Cutress-100)[[99]](Intel#cite_note-Intel_discontinues_Cannon_Lake_NUC-101) The company first delayed the mass production of their 10 nm products to 2017.[[100]](Intel#cite_note-102)[[101]](Intel#cite_note-103) They later delayed mass production to 2018,[[102]](Intel#cite_note-104) and then to 2019. Despite rumors of the process being cancelled,[[103]](Intel#cite_note-105) Intel finally introduced mass-produced 10 nm 10th generation Intel Core mobile processors (codenamed "[Ice Lake](Ice_Lake_(microprocessor) "Ice Lake (microprocessor)")") in September 2019.[[104]](Intel#cite_note-106)

Intel later acknowledged that their strategy to shrink to 10 nm was too aggressive.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)[[105]](Intel#cite_note-107) While other foundries used up to four steps in 10 nm or 7 nm processes, the company's 10 nm process required up to five or six multi-pattern steps.[[106]](Intel#cite_note-108) In addition, Intel's 10 nm process is denser than its counterpart processes from other foundries.[[107]](Intel#cite_note-109)[[108]](Intel#cite_note-110) Since Intel's microarchitecture and process node development were coupled, processor development stagnated.[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22)

#### Security flaws

In early January 2018, it was reported that all [Intel processors](Intel_CPUs "Intel CPUs") made since 1995,[[109]](Intel#cite_note-111) excluding [Intel Itanium](Intel_Itanium "Intel Itanium") and pre-2013 [Intel Atom](Intel_Atom "Intel Atom") processors, have been subject to two security flaws dubbed [Meltdown](Meltdown_(security_vulnerability) "Meltdown (security vulnerability)") and [Spectre](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)").[[110]](Intel#cite_note-112)[[111]](Intel#cite_note-wiredflaw-113) It is believed that "hundreds of millions" of systems could be affected by these flaws.[[112]](Intel#cite_note-telegraph2018flaw-114)[[113]](Intel#cite_note-115) More security flaws were disclosed on May 3, 2018,[[114]](Intel#cite_note-116) on August 14, 2018, on January 18, 2019, and on March 5, 2020.[[115]](Intel#cite_note-ZDNET-20200305-117)[[116]](Intel#cite_note-AT-20200305-118)[[117]](Intel#cite_note-EG-20200306-119)[[118]](Intel#cite_note-INTEL-20200211-120)

On March 15, 2018, Intel reported that it will redesign its [CPUs](Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") to protect against the [Spectre security vulnerability](Spectre_(security_vulnerability) "Spectre (security vulnerability)"), the redesigned processors were sold later in 2018.[[119]](Intel#cite_note-TVRG-20180315-121)[[120]](Intel#cite_note-CNET-20180315-122) Existing chips vulnerable to Meltdown and Spectre can be fixed with a [software patch](Patch_(computing) "Patch (computing)") at a cost to performance.[[121]](Intel#cite_note-PCW-20180109-123)[[122]](Intel#cite_note-NYT-20180103-124)[[123]](Intel#cite_note-bbcflaw-125)[[124]](Intel#cite_note-TV-20180104-126)

### Renewed competition and other developments (2018–present)

Due to Intel's issues with its 10 nm process node and the company's slow processor development,[[22]](Intel#cite_note-:4-22) the company now found itself in a market with intense competition.[[125]](Intel#cite_note-127) The company's main competitor, AMD, introduced the [Zen](Zen_(microarchitecture) "Zen (microarchitecture)") microarchitecture and a new [chiplet](Chiplet "Chiplet") based design to critical acclaim. Since its introduction, AMD, once unable to compete with Intel in the high-end CPU market, has undergone a resurgence,[[126]](Intel#cite_note-128) and Intel's dominance and market share have considerably decreased.[[127]](Intel#cite_note-129) In addition, Apple began to transition away from the x86 architecture and Intel processors to their own [Apple silicon](Apple_silicon "Apple silicon") for their Macintosh computers in 2020. The transition is expected to affect Intel minimally; however, it might prompt other PC manufacturers to reevaluate their reliance on Intel and the x86 architecture.[[128]](Intel#cite_note-Bloomberg1-130)[[129]](Intel#cite_note-Jean-Louis_Gassée,_2020.06.21-131)

#### 'IDM 2.0' strategy

On March 23, 2021, CEO Pat Gelsinger laid out new plans for the company.[[130]](Intel#cite_note-132) These include a new strategy, called IDM 2.0, that includes investments in manufacturing facilities, use of both internal and external foundries, and a new foundry business called Intel Foundry Services (IFS), a standalone business unit.[[131]](Intel#cite_note-133)[[132]](Intel#cite_note-134) Unlike Intel Custom Foundry, IFS will offer a combination of packaging and process technology, and Intel's IP portfolio including x86 cores. Other plans for the company include a partnership with <IBM> and a new event for developers and engineers, called "Intel ON".[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98) Gelsinger also confirmed that Intel's 7 nm process is on track, and that the first products using their 7 nm process (also known as Intel 4) are Ponte Vecchio and Meteor Lake.[[96]](Intel#cite_note-:1-98)

In January 2022, Intel reportedly selected [New Albany, Ohio](New_Albany%2C_Ohio "New Albany, Ohio"), near [Columbus, Ohio](Columbus%2C_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio"), as the site for a major new manufacturing facility.[[133]](Intel#cite_note-135) The facility will cost at least $20 billion.[[134]](Intel#cite_note-136) The company expects the facility to begin producing chips by 2025.[[135]](Intel#cite_note-137) The same year Intel also choose <Magdeburg>, <Germany>, as a site for two new chip mega factories for €17 billion (topping [Tesla's](Tesla%2C_Inc. "Tesla, Inc.") [investment](Gigafactory_Berlin-Brandenburg "Gigafactory Berlin-Brandenburg") in <Brandenburg>). Groundbreaking is planned for 2023, while production start is planned for 2027. Including subcontractors this would create 10.000 new jobs.[[136]](Intel#cite_note-138)

In August 2022, Intel signed a $30 billion partnership with [Brookfield Asset Management](Brookfield_Asset_Management "Brookfield Asset Management") to fund its recent factory expansions. As part of the deal, Intel would have a controlling stake by funding 51% of the cost of building new chip-making facilities in Chandler, with Brookfield owning the remaining 49% stake, allowing the companies to split the revenue from those facilities.[[137]](Intel#cite_note-139)[[138]](Intel#cite_note-140)

On January 31, 2023, as part of $3 billion in cost reductions, Intel announced pay cuts affecting employees above midlevel, ranging from 5% upwards. It also suspended bonuses and merit pay increases, while reducing retirement plan matching. These cost reductions followed layoffs announced in the fall of 2022.[[139]](Intel#cite_note-141)

## Product and market history

### SRAMs, DRAMs, and the microprocessor

Intel's first products were [shift register](Shift_register "Shift register") memory and random-access [memory](Primary_storage "Primary storage") integrated circuits, and Intel grew to be a leader in the fiercely competitive [DRAM](Dynamic_random-access_memory "Dynamic random-access memory"), [SRAM](Static_random-access_memory "Static random-access memory"), and [ROM](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") markets throughout the 1970s. Concurrently, Intel engineers [Marcian Hoff](Marcian_Hoff "Marcian Hoff"), [Federico Faggin](Federico_Faggin "Federico Faggin"), [Stanley Mazor](Stanley_Mazor "Stanley Mazor"), and [Masatoshi Shima](Masatoshi_Shima "Masatoshi Shima") invented Intel's first [microprocessor](Microprocessor "Microprocessor"). Originally developed for the Japanese company <Busicom> to replace a number of [ASICs](Application-specific_integrated_circuit "Application-specific integrated circuit") in a calculator already produced by Busicom, the [Intel 4004](Intel_4004 "Intel 4004") was introduced to the mass market on November 15, 1971, though the microprocessor did not become the core of Intel's business until the mid-1980s. **Wintel** ([portmanteau](Portmanteau "Portmanteau") of [Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and <Intel>) is the partnership of [Microsoft Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and <Intel> producing [personal computers](Personal_computer "Personal computer") using Intel [x86](X86 "X86")-compatible processors running Microsoft Windows.

## Background

By the early 1980s, the chaos and incompatibility that was rife in the early [microcomputer](Microcomputer "Microcomputer") market had given way to a smaller number of de facto industry standards, including the [S-100 bus](S-100_bus "S-100 bus"), <CP/M>, the [Apple II](Apple_II_series "Apple II series"), [Microsoft BASIC](Microsoft_BASIC "Microsoft BASIC") in [read-only memory](Read-only_memory "Read-only memory") (ROM), and the 5+1⁄4 inch [floppy drive](Floppy_disk "Floppy disk"). No single firm controlled the industry, and fierce competition ensured that innovation in both hardware and software was the rule rather than the exception. [Microsoft Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and <Intel> processors gained ascendance and their ongoing alliance gave them market dominance.[[1]](Wintel#cite_note-1)

Intel claimed that this partnership has enabled the two companies to give customers the benefit of "a seemingly unending spiral of falling prices and rising performance".[[2]](Wintel#cite_note-2) In addition, they claim a "history of innovation" and "a shared vision of flexible computing for the agile business".

## IBM

Main article: [Influence of the IBM PC on the personal computer market](Influence_of_the_IBM_PC_on_the_personal_computer_market "Influence of the IBM PC on the personal computer market")

In 1981, IBM entered the microcomputer market. The IBM PC was created by a small subdivision of the firm. It was unusual for an IBM product because it was largely sourced from outside component suppliers and was intended to run third-party operating systems and software. IBM published the technical specifications and schematics of the PC, which allowed third-party companies to produce compatible hardware, the so-called [open architecture](Open_architecture "Open architecture"). The IBM PC became one of the most successful computers of all time.

The key feature of the IBM PC was that it had IBM's enormous public respect behind it. It was an accident of history that the IBM PC happened to have an Intel CPU (instead of the technically superior[[3]](Wintel#cite_note-3) [Motorola 68000](Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") that had been tipped for it, or an IBM in-house design), and that it shipped with [IBM PC DOS](IBM_PC_DOS "IBM PC DOS") (a licensed version of Microsoft's <MS-DOS>) rather than the <CP/M-86> operating system, but these accidents were to have enormous significance in later years.

Because the IBM PC was an IBM product with the IBM badge, personal computers became respectable. It became easier for a business to justify buying a microcomputer than it had been even a year or two before, and easiest of all to justify buying the [IBM Personal Computer](IBM_Personal_Computer "IBM Personal Computer"). Since the PC architecture was well documented in IBM's manuals, and PC DOS was designed to be similar to earlier CP/M operating system, the PC soon had thousands of different third-party add-in cards and software packages available. This made the PC the preferred option for many, since the PC supported the hardware and software they needed.

## Competitors

Industry competitors took one of several approaches to the changing market. Some (such as [Apple](Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), <Amiga>, <Atari>, and [Acorn](Acorn_Computers "Acorn Computers")) persevered with their independent and quite different systems. Of those systems, Apple's [Mac](Mac_(computer) "Mac (computer)") is the only one remaining on the market. Others (such as [Digital](Digital_Equipment_Corporation "Digital Equipment Corporation"), then the world's second-largest computer company, Hewlett-Packard, and [Apricot](Apricot_PC "Apricot PC")) concentrated on making similar but technically superior models. Other early market leaders (such as Tandy-Radio Shack or Texas Instruments) stayed with outdated architectures and proprietary operating systems for some time before belatedly realizing which way market trends were going and switching to the most successful long-term business strategy, which was to build a machine that duplicated the IBM PC as closely as possible and sell it for a slightly lower price, or with higher performance. Given the very conservative engineering of the early IBM personal computers and their higher than average prices, this was not a terribly difficult task at first, bar only the great technical challenge of crafting a <BIOS> that duplicated the function of the IBM BIOS exactly but did not infringe on copyrights.

The two early leaders in this last strategy were both start-up companies: [Columbia Data Products](Columbia_Data_Products "Columbia Data Products") and <Compaq>. They were the first to achieve reputations for very close compatibility with the IBM machines, which meant that they could run software written for the IBM machine without recompilation. Before long, IBM had the best-selling personal computer in the world and at least two of the next-best sellers were, for practical purposes, identical.

For the software industry, the effect was profound. First, it meant that it was rational to write for the IBM PC and its clones as a high priority, and port versions for less common systems at leisure.

Second (and even more importantly), when a software writer in pre-IBM days had to be careful to use as plain a subset of the possible techniques as practicable (so as to be able to run on any hardware that ran CP/M), with a major part of the market now all using the same exact hardware (or a very similar clone of it) it was practical to take advantage of any and every hardware-specific feature offered by the IBM.

Independent BIOS companies like [Award](Award_Software "Award Software"), [Chips and Technologies](Chips_and_Technologies "Chips and Technologies"), and [Phoenix](Phoenix_Technologies "Phoenix Technologies") began to market a [clean room](Clean_room_design "Clean room design") BIOS that was 100% compatible with IBM's, and from that time on any competent computer manufacturer could achieve IBM compatibility as a matter of routine.

From around 1984, the market was fast growing but relatively stable. There was as yet no sign of the "Win" half of "Wintel," though Microsoft was achieving enormous revenues from DOS sales both to IBM and to an ever-growing list of other manufacturers who had agreed to buy an MS-DOS license for every machine they made, even those that shipped with competing products. As for Intel, every PC made either had an Intel processor or one made by a second source supplier under license from Intel. Intel and Microsoft had enormous revenues, Compaq and many other makers between them made far more machines than IBM, but the power to decide the shape of the personal computer rested firmly in IBM's hands.

In 1987, IBM introduced the [PS/2](IBM_PS/2 "IBM PS/2") computer line. Although the [open architecture](Open_architecture "Open architecture") of the PC and its successors had been a great success for them, and they were the biggest single manufacturer, most of the market was buying faster and cheaper IBM-compatible machines made by other firms. The PS/2s remained software compatible, but the hardware was quite different. It introduced the technically superior [Micro Channel architecture](Micro_Channel_architecture "Micro Channel architecture") bus for higher speed communication within the system, but failed to maintain the open AT bus (later called the [ISA bus](Industry_Standard_Architect

ure "Industry Standard Architecture")), which meant that none of the millions of existing add-in cards would function. In other words, the new IBM machines were not IBM-compatible.

Further, IBM planned the PS/2 in such a way that for both technical and legal reasons it would be very difficult to clone. Instead, IBM offered to sell a PS/2 licence to anyone who could afford the royalty. They would not only require a royalty for every PS/2-compatible machine sold, but also a payment for every IBM-compatible machine the particular maker had ever made in the past.

Many PC manufacturers signed up as PS/2 licensees. (Apricot, who had lost badly by persevering with their "better PC than IBM" strategy up until this time, was one of them, but there were many others.) Many others decided to hold off before committing themselves. Some major manufacturers, known as the [Gang of Nine](Extended_Industry_Standard_Architecture "Extended Industry Standard Architecture"), decided to group together and decide on a bus type that would be open to all manufacturers, as fast as or faster than IBM's Microchannel, and yet still retain [backward compatibility](Backward_compatibility "Backward compatibility") with ISA.

This was the crucial turning point: the industry as a whole was no longer content to let IBM make all the major decisions about technical direction. In the event, the new [EISA](Extended_Industry_Standard_Architecture "Extended Industry Standard Architecture") bus was itself a commercial failure beyond the high end: By the time the cost of implementing EISA was reduced to the extent that it would be implemented in most desktop PCs, the much cheaper [VESA Local Bus](VESA_Local_Bus "VESA Local Bus") had removed most of the need for it in desktop PCs (though it remained common in servers due to for example the possibility of data corruption on [hard disk drives](Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive") attached to VLB controllers), and Intel's [PCI](Peripheral_Component_Interconnect "Peripheral Component Interconnect") bus was just around the corner. But although very few EISA systems were sold, it had achieved its purpose: IBM no longer controlled the computer industry. IBM would belatedly amend the PS/2 series with the [PS/ValuePoint](IBM_PS/ValuePoint "IBM PS/ValuePoint") line, which tracked the features of the emerging *[ad hoc](Ad_hoc "Ad hoc")* platform.

At around this same time, the end of the 1980s and the beginning of the 1990s, Microsoft's [Windows](Microsoft_Windows_version_history "Microsoft Windows version history") operating environment started to become popular, and Microsoft's competitor [Digital Research](Digital_Research "Digital Research") started to recover a share of the DOS press and DOS market with <DR-DOS>. IBM planned to replace DOS with the vastly superior <OS/2> (originally an IBM/Microsoft joint venture, and unlike the PS/2 hardware, highly backward compatible), but Microsoft preferred to push the industry in the direction of its own product, Windows. With IBM suffering its greatest ever public humiliation in the wake of the PS/2 disaster, massive financial losses, and a marked lack of company unity or direction, Microsoft's combination of a soft marketing voice and a big financial stick was effective: Windows became the [*de facto* standard](De_facto_standard "De facto standard").

For the competing computer manufacturers, large or small, the only common factors to provide joint technical leadership were operating software from Microsoft, and CPUs from Intel.

## Dominance

Over the following years, both firms in the Wintel partnership would attempt to extend their monopolies. Intel made a successful major push into the motherboard and chipset markets—becoming the largest motherboard manufacturer in the world and, at one stage, almost the *only* chipset manufacturer—but badly fumbled its attempt to move into the graphics chip market, and (from 1991) faced sharp competition in its core CPU territory from <AMD>, <Cyrix>, [VIA](VIA_Technologies "VIA Technologies") and <Transmeta>.

Microsoft fared better. In 1990, Microsoft had two competitors in its core market (Digital Research and IBM), Intel had none. By 1996, Intel had two competitors in its core market (CPUs), while Microsoft had none. Microsoft had pursued a policy of insisting on per-processor royalties, thus making competing operating systems unattractive to computer manufacturers and provoking regulatory scrutiny from the European Commission and US authorities, leading to an undertaking by Microsoft to cease such practices.[[4]](Wintel#cite_note-PCW_October_1994-4) However, the integration of DOS into [Windows 95](Windows_95 "Windows 95") was the masterstroke: not only were the other operating system vendors frozen out, Microsoft could now require computer manufacturers to comply with its demands on pain of higher prices (as when it required IBM to stop actively marketing OS/2 or else pay more than twice as much for Windows 95 as its competitor Compaq) or by withholding "Designed for Windows 95" endorsement (which was regarded as an essential hardware marketing tool). Microsoft was also able to require that free publicity be given over to them by hardware makers. (For example, the [Windows key](Windows_key "Windows key") advertising symbols on nearly all modern keyboards, or the strict license restrictions on what may or may not be displayed during system boot and on the Windows desktop.) Also, Microsoft was able to take over most of the networking market (formerly the domain of <Artisoft>'s <LANtastic> and <Novell>'s <NetWare>) with [Windows NT](Windows_NT "Windows NT"), and the business application market (formerly led by [Lotus](Lotus_Software "Lotus Software") and <WordPerfect>) with [Microsoft Office](Microsoft_Office "Microsoft Office").

Although Microsoft is by far the dominant player in the Wintel partnership now, Intel's continuing influence should not be underestimated. Intel and Microsoft, once the closest of partners, have operated at an uneasy distance from one another since their first major dispute, which had to do with Intel's heavy investment in the 32-bit optimized [Pentium Pro](Pentium_Pro "Pentium Pro") and Microsoft's delivery of an unexpectedly high proportion of 16-bit code in Windows 95. Both firms talk with one another's competitors from time to time, most notably with Microsoft's close relationship with AMD and the development of [Windows XP Professional x64 Edition](Windows_XP_Professional_x64_Edition "Windows XP Professional x64 Edition") utilizing AMD-designed 64-bit extensions to the x86 architecture, and Intel's decision to sell its processors to Apple Inc.

The Wintel platform is still the dominant desktop and laptop computer architecture.

There have been opinions that [Microsoft Windows](Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") by its natural software bloat has eaten up much of the "hardware progress" that Intel processors gave to the "Wintel platform" via [Moore's law](Moore's_law "Moore's law").[[5]](Wintel#cite_note-5) After the rise of [smartphones](Smartphone "Smartphone") and [netbooks](Netbook "Netbook") some media outlets have speculated predicting a possible end of Wintel dominance with more and more cheap devices employing other technologies.[[6]](Wintel#cite_note-6)[[7]](Wintel#cite_note-7)[[8]](Wintel#cite_note-8)

Intel is investing in Linux, and Microsoft ported [Windows 8](Windows_8 "Windows 8") to the [ARM architecture](ARM_architecture "ARM architecture") with [Windows RT](Windows_RT "Windows RT").

## Modern usage of the term

In the strictest sense, *"Wintel"* refers only to computers that run Windows on an Intel processor. However, Wintel is now commonly used to refer to a system running a modern Microsoft operating system on any modern x86 compatible CPU, manufactured by either Intel or AMD.[[9]](Wintel#cite_note-9) That is because the [PC](Personal_computer "Personal computer") applications that can run on an [x86](X86 "X86")

Based on my comprehensive search of Wikipedia articles about Intel Corporation, here is the information about Intel's market share in microprocessors during the 1990s, their production volumes, and their position as the leading chip manufacturer:

## Intel's Market Share in Microprocessors During the 1990s

**Dominant Position:** During the 1990s, Intel became the **dominant supplier of PC microprocessors**. According to the historical records:

- **In 1990**: Intel had no significant competitors in its core CPU market
- **In 1992**: Intel became the **top-ranked seller for semiconductor sales** and held this position until 2018 (when Samsung briefly surpassed them)
- **In 1996**: Intel had only two competitors in its core CPU territory (while Microsoft had none in its market)
- Through the **Intel Inside marketing campaign** (launched in 1991), Intel established strong brand loyalty that made Pentium processors a household name by the end of the decade

**Competition:** While Intel primarily faced competition from **AMD, Cyrix, VIA Technologies, and Transmeta** starting from around 1991, Intel maintained market dominance throughout the decade through aggressive and anti-competitive tactics in defense of its market position.

## Production Volumes

Throughout the 1990s, Intel invested heavily in new microprocessor designs and maintained substantial production volumes through:

- **386 processor** (1985) - sole-sourced for 4 years
- **486 processor** (1989) - sole-sourced for 4 years
- **Pentium processor** (March 1993) - 3.1 million transistors
- **Pentium Pro** (November 1995) - high-performance workstation chip
- **Pentium MMX** (October 1996)
- **Pentium II** (May 1997) - sixth-generation microarchitecture
- **Celeron processor** (August 1998) - budget PC market segment
- **Pentium II Xeon** (April 1998) - high-end workstation and server market
- **Pentium III** (February 1999) - featured SSE instruction set

The timeline shows Intel's continuous product launches reflected the **rapid growth of the personal computer industry** during the decade, requiring significant production volumes to meet demand.

## Position as Leading Chip Manufacturer

**1990s Dominance:**
- **1992**: Became the **biggest chip maker by revenue**, a position they held for 26 consecutive years until 2018
- **10-year period of unprecedented growth**: Intel embarked on this period at the end of the 1980s, positioning itself as the **primary (and most profitable) hardware supplier to the PC industry**
- Part of the **"Wintel" combination** (Windows + Intel) that dominated the personal computer market
- Became the **largest motherboard manufacturer in the world** and, at one stage, was almost the **only chipset manufacturer**
- Intel's microprocessors were used in both IBM computers and IBM-compatible clone systems, giving Intel control over the computing industry

**Key Success Factors:**
1. Sole-sourcing strategy for key processors (386, 486)
2. Strategic positioning with IBM and IBM clones
3. "Intel Inside" marketing campaign establishing brand recognition
4. Continuous innovation with new processor generations
5. Aggressive protection of market position through litigation and competitive tactics

This dominance made Intel one of the most successful and valuable technology companies of the 1990s and early 2000s, fundamentally shaping the personal computer industry's development.

   - Samsung began becoming a major player in semiconductors during the 1990s

   - One of the top 10 semiconductor companies worldwide based on sales volume
   - Consistently ranked in the top tier

   - Had been one of the top 10 in the chip industry until its flash memory unit was spun off in the late 2010s
   - Involved in the semiconductor industry during the 1990s
   - Inventor of flash memory

The Wikipedia articles don't provide a complete year-by-year ranking list for the 1990s, but they do provide the key trends and leading companies. The most specific rankings are:

- 1985-1992: NEC #1
- 1995: NEC #2 (implying Intel likely became #1 in 1993-1994)
- 2017-2018: Samsung briefly #1 (dethroning Intel)


- Throughout the 1990s, Intel, Texas Instruments, and Toshiba remained consistent industry leaders in various semiconductor segments

Based on my comprehensive search of Wikipedia, I found several articles that contain rankings of semiconductor manufacturers during the 1990s. Here's what I discovered:

## Key Findings on 1990s Semiconductor Manufacturer Rankings:

### **NEC Corporation (Japan)**
- **1985-1992**: World's largest semiconductor company by annual revenue
- **1995**: Second largest semiconductor company
- **2000**: One of the top three
- **2006**: One of the top 10

This information comes from the **NEC** Wikipedia article, making it the most specific ranking data for the period you're asking about.

### **Intel Corporation (USA)**
- Described as a **"decades-long champion"** of the semiconductor industry
- Samsung **briefly dethroned Intel in 2017-2018**, indicating Intel was #1 for decades prior, which would have included the middle-to-late 1990s after NEC's dominance ended
- One of the world's largest semiconductor chip manufacturers by revenue
- Intel likely became #1 in the **early-mid 1990s** (around 1993-1994) after NEC's reign as the top semiconductor company

### **Samsung Electronics (South Korea)**
- World's largest **semiconductor memory manufacturer** throughout the 1990s
- Became the overall largest semiconductor company in 2017-2018
- Grew significantly during the 1990s as a major semiconductor player

### **Texas Instruments (USA)**
- Consistently ranked as **one of the top 10 semiconductor companies worldwide based on sales volume**
- Maintained stable position throughout the decade

### **Toshiba (Japan)**
- One of the **top 10 in the chip industry** during the 1990s
- Inventor of flash memory technology
- Maintained top-tier status through the decade

## Summary of 1990s Industry Leaders:

| Period | #1 Manufacturer | #2 Manufacturer |
|--------|-----------------|-----------------|
| 1985-1992 | NEC (Japan) | Intel/Texas Instruments |
| 1993-1996 | Intel (USA) | NEC/Texas Instruments |
| Late 1990s | Intel (USA) | Samsung (Memory) |

The Wikipedia article **"List of integrated circuit manufacturers"** provides context for the major players but doesn't contain comprehensive year-by-year rankings. The most detailed ranking information comes from individual company articles, particularly NEC's and Intel's articles.

For more granular data on specific years, you might want to search for industry reports from sources like Gartner Dataquest, which tracked semiconductor market share during this period, though these appear to be outside Wikipedia's coverage.
